title: DevOps Mastery
subtitle: Linux, CI/CD, Docker, Kubernetes, cloud, observability

modules.title: DevOps Fundamentals
modules.summary: What DevOps is and the loop from commit to customer.

lessons.title: What DevOps is, and the path from commit to customer

blocks.text: DevOps means the team that writes the software is also responsible for running it, and uses automation so that shipping a change is routine instead of an event. The work forms a loop: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor, and feed what you learn back into the plan.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: You already live a slice of this: Xcode Cloud or fastlane builds your app, runs tests and uploads to TestFlight. DevOps is the same idea for the backend, extended past "upload" to cover the servers, the rollout, the monitoring and the 3 a.m. alert.
Why it matters

When developers "threw code over the wall" to a separate operations team, releases were rare, large and risky, and each side blamed the other. Small, frequent, automated releases fail less and are fixed faster.
Where you meet it
Any company that ships software more than a few times a year.
Scenario

A developer fixes a rounding bug in checkout totals. Twenty minutes after the merge the fix is serving customers, having been tested, packaged, scanned and rolled out gradually, with nobody logging in to a server.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR DEV["Developers"] --> GIT["Git repository
code, pipeline, manifests"] GIT --> CI["CI/CD system
build, test, scan"] CI --> REG["Artifact registry
container images"] REG --> STG["Staging"] STG --> PRD["Production
cluster"] PRD --> OBS["Monitoring
metrics, logs, alerts"] OBS -->|"feedback, incidents"| DEV IAC["Infrastructure as code"] --> STG IAC --> PRD

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  P["Plan"] --> C["Code"] --> B["Build"] --> T["Test"] --> R["Release"] --> D["Deploy"] --> O["Operate"] --> M["Monitor"]
  M -->|"feedback"| P

blocks.text: Commands
Shows the last five commits. Every production change should trace back to one of these.
Shows the revisions that have been deployed, so you can answer "what changed?" during an incident.
Exercise
Map your current mobile release process onto the DevOps loop.

items: Write down each step from "PR merged" to "users have the build"
Mark each step manual or automated
For each manual step, note what could go wrong and who would notice
Open the flagship walkthrough and find the backend equivalent of each step

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can name the backend equivalent of TestFlight (staging), App Store review (approval gate) and phased release (canary or rolling update).
Troubleshooting

rows: Deploys are scary and happen monthly
Large batches: many changes ship together, so any failure is hard to attribute.
Ship smaller changes more often behind feature flags.
"It works on my machine"
Environments differ in versions and configuration.
Build one artifact (a container image) and promote that same artifact through every environment.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Everything in version control: code, pipeline, infrastructure, dashboards.
Build once, deploy the same artifact everywhere.
Make rollback a routine, tested operation.
Measure the four DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore service.

blocks.text: Security

items: Automation concentrates power: the pipeline can deploy to production, so protect it like production.
Security checks belong inside the pipeline, not in a review at the end.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is DevOps?
blocks.text: A way of working where development and operations share ownership of delivery and reliability, supported by automation (CI/CD, infrastructure as code, monitoring) so changes are small, frequent and reversible. It is a practice, not a job title or a tool.

blocks.title: What are the DORA metrics?
blocks.text: Deployment frequency and lead time for changes measure speed. Change failure rate and time to restore service measure stability. Strong teams improve both together.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which practice most directly removes "works on my machine"?
options: Promoting one immutable artifact through all environments
quiz.why: If staging and production run the identical image, the environment is no longer a variable.

modules.title: Linux Mastery
modules.summary: Filesystem, text tools, permissions, processes, resources, systemd, kernel isolation.

lessons.title: The filesystem and moving around

blocks.text: Linux organises everything as one tree of directories that starts at "/" (called root). There are no drive letters. Config lives in /etc, logs in /var/log, your files in /home/you. The shell is a program that reads the commands you type and runs them.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: On iOS your app sees only its own sandbox. On a server you can walk the whole building: /etc is the control room with every switch, /var/log is the CCTV archive, /home is the staff lockers, and /tmp is the whiteboard that gets wiped.
Why it matters
Servers have no screen. Every deployment, config change and investigation happens through a text shell, usually over SSH. Fluency here is the base everything else stands on.
Where you meet it
Every cloud VM, every container image, every CI runner, and inside every Kubernetes pod when you run kubectl exec.
Scenario

The checkout service is deployed to /srv/checkout, its systemd unit sits in /etc/systemd/system, nginx config in /etc/nginx, and its failures land in /var/log. Knowing where to look is half of every incident.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD R["/ (root)"] --> ETC["/etc
configuration"] R --> VAR["/var
changing data"] R --> HOME["/home
user files"] R --> SRV["/srv
service data"] R --> TMP["/tmp
temporary"] VAR --> LOG["/var/log
logs"] ETC --> NGX["/etc/nginx"] SRV --> CO["/srv/checkout
the app"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart LR A["You type: ls -la"] --> B["Shell splits it into
program + arguments"] B --> C["Shell finds 'ls'
by searching PATH"] C --> D["Kernel starts a
new process"] D --> E["ls asks the kernel
to read the directory"] E --> F["Output printed,
exit code returned"]

blocks.text: Commands
Exercise
Take a dated backup of a file before changing it, the habit that saves you in production.

items: Go to your home directory with cd
Create backups/2026 with one mkdir command
Copy deploy.sh into it
Rename the copy to deploy.sh.bak with mv
List the directory in long format to confirm

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: ls -l backups/2026 shows deploy.sh.bak owned by dev.
Troubleshooting

rows: bash: cd: /srv/chekout: No such file or directory
A typo, or a relative path used from the wrong directory.
Run pwd, then ls the parent directory to see the real name.
Permission denied when listing a directory
Your user lacks read (r) or enter (x) permission on it.
Check with ls -ld DIR. Use sudo only if you understand why access is restricted.
A config file "disappeared" after an edit
mv or cp overwrote it silently.
Restore from your backup copy. Use cp -i and mv -i to be asked before overwriting.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Copy a config to NAME.bak before editing it.
Use absolute paths in scripts; relative paths depend on where the script was started.
Run ls on a path before you run rm on it.
Keep application code, config and data in separate directories so deploys never touch data.

blocks.text: Security

items: rm has no undo and no trash.
Files in /tmp are readable by other users unless you restrict them.
Hidden files such as .env often hold secrets; ls -la shows them, so does a careless screenshot.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between an absolute and a relative path?
blocks.text: An absolute path starts at / and means the same thing from anywhere. A relative path is resolved from the current directory, so its meaning changes with pwd.

blocks.title: What lives in /etc, /var and /tmp?
blocks.text: /etc holds system-wide configuration, /var holds data that grows while the system runs (logs, databases, caches), /tmp holds scratch files that may be cleared on reboot.

blocks.title: How does the shell find the program when you type "ls"?
blocks.text: It searches each directory listed in the PATH environment variable, in order, and runs the first executable named ls.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: You are in /var/log/nginx and run "cd ../..". Where are you?
quiz.why: Each .. goes up one level: nginx -> log -> var.

quiz.q: Which command is safest to run first before "rm -r build/"?
quiz.why: Listing the exact path shows what you are about to delete and costs nothing.

lessons.title: Reading and searching text: logs are your evidence

blocks.text: Almost everything on a server is plain text: config files, logs, command output. Small tools each do one job (show, filter, count) and the pipe symbol | connects them, sending the output of one into the next.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A pipe is like chaining Swift collection operators: lines.filter { $0.contains("502") }.map { $0.ip }.count. Each tool is one operator and | is the dot between them.
Why it matters
A busy service writes millions of log lines a day. You cannot read them; you have to ask them questions.
Where you meet it
Incident response, checking a deploy, finding which client is hammering an API, extracting numbers for a report.
Scenario

Customers report failed checkouts. The nginx access log records every request with its status code. In four commands you can count the failures, see when they started and see which endpoint is affected.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  subgraph P1["Process: grep"]
    I1["stdin (0)"]
    O1["stdout (1)"]
    E1["stderr (2)"]
  end
  subgraph P2["Process: wc -l"]
    I2["stdin (0)"]
    O2["stdout (1)"]
  end
  F["access.log"] --> I1
  O1 -->|"pipe: a kernel buffer"| I2
  O2 --> T["Your terminal"]
  E1 -->|"errors skip the pipe"| T

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart LR A["cat access.log
all lines"] -->|pipe| B["grep ' 502 '
keep failures"] B -->|pipe| C["awk '{print $7}'
keep the URL column"] C -->|pipe| D["sort"] D -->|pipe| E["uniq -c
count each URL"]

blocks.text: Commands
Exercise
Produce a one-line incident summary from the access log: how many 502s, the first one, and the affected URLs.

items: Count the lines containing " 502 "
Print the first matching line with its line number
Print column 7 (the URL) of only the 502 lines
Count each distinct URL with sort | uniq -c

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You get 4 failures, starting 09:14:03, on /api/checkout (3) and /api/health (1).
Troubleshooting

rows: grep prints nothing
No line matched. This is a result, not an error (exit code 1).
Loosen the pattern, add -i, and confirm you are reading the right file.
Permission denied reading /var/log/nginx/access.log
Logs are readable only by root and the adm group because they contain IP addresses and URLs.
Use sudo, or ask to be added to the adm group.
uniq -c shows the same value several times
uniq only merges adjacent lines.
Put sort before uniq.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Use less or tail on logs, never cat on a multi-gigabyte file.
Start broad, then narrow by adding one pipe stage at a time.
Search with a timestamp prefix to scope an incident window.
Prefer structured (JSON) logs in your own services so tools can parse them reliably.

blocks.text: Security

items: Logs often contain personal data and tokens. Do not paste raw log lines into public channels.
sed -i rewrites the file in place; preview without -i first.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you find the top 5 client IPs in an nginx access log?
blocks.text: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5. Extract the IP column, group identical values, count, sort by count descending, take five.

blocks.title: What is the difference between tail -f and less +F?
blocks.text: Both follow a growing file. less +F lets you press Ctrl+C to stop following and scroll or search backwards, then F to resume.

blocks.title: What does a pipe actually connect?
blocks.text: The standard output (file descriptor 1) of the left process to the standard input (file descriptor 0) of the right one, through a kernel buffer. Both processes run at the same time.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: What does "grep -v healthz access.log" print?
options: Lines that do not contain healthz
quiz.why: -v inverts the match. It is the usual way to drop noisy health-check lines.

quiz.q: Why "sort | uniq -c" and not just "uniq -c"?
quiz.why: Identical lines must be next to each other for uniq to merge them.

lessons.title: Users, groups and permissions

blocks.text: Every file has an owner, a group and three sets of permissions: for the owner, for the group, for everyone else. Each set is read (r), write (w), execute (x). Every process runs as some user, and the kernel checks these bits on every access. root (user 0) bypasses the checks.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Like iOS entitlements, but per file. rw- r-- --- reads as: the owner may read and edit, teammates in the group may read, strangers get nothing.
Why it matters
A server runs many programs. If the web server is compromised, permissions decide whether the attacker can also read the database password.
Where you meet it
Secrets files, SSH keys (ssh refuses keys that are readable by others), service accounts, shared deploy directories, container images that should not run as root.
Scenario
checkout-api runs as the unprivileged user "app". Its .env file holding DATABASE_URL is mode 600 owned by app, so the nginx user www-data cannot read it even if nginx is exploited.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR P["Process
runs as user 'app'"] --> K{"Kernel checks
file mode"} K -->|"owner match: rw-"| A["allowed"] K -->|"group match: r--"| G["read only"] K -->|"other: ---"| D["Permission denied"]

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Reading "ls -l" output

blocks.code:
-rw-------  1 app   app    74 Nov 10 09:12 .env
│└┬┘└┬┘└┬┘     │     │
│ │  │  │      │     └─ group
│ │  │  │      └─ owner
│ │  │  └─ others:  ---  = 0
│ │  └─ group:      ---  = 0
│ └─ owner:         rw-  = 4+2 = 6      => mode 600
└─ type: - file, d directory, l link

r = 4   w = 2   x = 1
644 = rw-r--r--   normal file
600 = rw-------   secret
755 = rwxr-xr-x   program or directory
On a directory, x means "may enter".

blocks.text: Exercise
Make deploy.sh runnable by you only, and prove a secret is protected.

items: Show the current mode of deploy.sh
Set it to 700
Try to read /srv/checkout/.env as dev and note the error
Read it with sudo and note that the simulator masks the password

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: ls -l deploy.sh starts with -rwx------ and the plain cat of .env fails with Permission denied.
Troubleshooting

rows: bash: ./deploy.sh: Permission denied
The file lacks the execute bit.
chmod u+x deploy.sh
The service cannot read its own config after a deploy
Files were copied as root, so the service user no longer owns them.
sudo chown -R app:app /srv/checkout, and deploy as the service user in future.
ssh: "UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE"
The key is readable by group or others.
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

blocks.text: Best practices

items: One dedicated non-login user per service.
Secrets: mode 600, owned by the service user.
Grant access through groups, not by loosening "others".
Give sudo for specific commands, not blanket root.

blocks.text: Security

items: chmod 777 fixes the symptom by removing the protection. It is never the answer.
A setuid root binary runs as root for whoever starts it; audit them.
Root inside a container is root on the host unless user namespaces are used: run containers as a non-root user.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What does chmod 750 mean?
blocks.text: Owner 7 = rwx, group 5 = r-x, others 0 = nothing. Typical for a directory the service owns and an ops group may browse.

blocks.title: A file is mode 644 but a user still cannot read it. Why?
blocks.text: Reading a file also needs execute (x) permission on every directory in its path. Another cause is an ACL, SELinux or AppArmor policy.

blocks.title: Why should services not run as root?
blocks.text: A bug or exploit in the service then has full control of the machine. As an unprivileged user the damage is limited to what that user can touch.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which mode suits a file holding a database password?
quiz.why: 600 lets only the owner read and write it.

quiz.q: What does x mean on a directory?
options: You can enter it and reach files inside
quiz.why: Execute on a directory is the right to traverse it.

lessons.title: Processes, signals and what "kill" really does

blocks.text: A process is a running program. The kernel gives each one an ID (PID), its own memory and a parent. A signal is a short message sent to a process. kill does not kill: it sends a signal. SIGTERM (15) asks the process to shut down; SIGKILL (9) makes the kernel remove it with no chance to clean up.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: SIGTERM is applicationWillTerminate: the app gets a moment to save state. SIGKILL is the iOS watchdog killing the app: no callback runs, whatever was in flight is lost.
Why it matters
Every deploy stops old processes and starts new ones. Whether customers see errors during a deploy depends on whether the old process got to finish its requests.
Where you meet it
systemd stop, docker stop and Kubernetes pod termination all do the same thing: send SIGTERM, wait a grace period, then send SIGKILL.
Scenario

When Kubernetes replaces a checkout pod it sends SIGTERM and waits 30 seconds by default. A server that handles SIGTERM finishes in-flight payments first. One that ignores it is killed mid-request, and a customer is charged with no order created.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  K["Kernel"] --> S["systemd (PID 1)"]
  S --> N["nginx master (812)"]
  N --> W1["nginx worker (813)"]
  S --> C["checkout-api (uvicorn)"]
  S --> PG["postgres (940)"]
  S --> SSH["sshd (701)"]
  SSH --> B["your bash shell"]
  B --> CMD["the command you just ran"]
  CMD -. "exit code returns to the parent" .-> B

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["kill PID
(SIGTERM)"] --> B{"Process has a
handler?"} B -->|yes| C["Stop accepting work,
finish requests, exit 0"] B -->|no| D["Default action:
terminate immediately"] A2["kill -9 PID
(SIGKILL)"] --> E["Kernel removes the
process. Cannot be
caught or ignored"] C --> F["Exit code reported
to the parent"] D --> F E --> F

blocks.text: Commands
Exercise
Find what is burning CPU and stop it the polite way.

items: Run top and note the process near 100% CPU
Send it SIGTERM with plain kill
Run top again and compare the load average
Try to kill nginx (PID 812) without sudo and read the error
Run sudo kill -9 on nginx, then check its status: systemd restarted it with a new PID

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: gzip is gone from top, and nginx is active again with a different Main PID.
Troubleshooting

rows: Load average is far above the number of CPU cores
More work is runnable than there are cores, or processes are stuck waiting on disk.
top: check %us (CPU-bound) versus %wa (waiting on I/O), then find the process.
kill PID does nothing
The process ignores SIGTERM or is stuck in a system call.
Wait the grace period, then kill -9 as a last resort and expect lost in-flight work.
A process shows state Z (zombie)
It has exited but its parent never collected the exit code.
Zombies use no CPU or memory. Fix or restart the parent; you cannot kill a zombie.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Always SIGTERM first; reserve -9 for processes that are truly stuck.
Make your services handle SIGTERM: stop accepting, drain, exit.
Run long-lived programs under a supervisor (systemd, Kubernetes) so they are restarted.
Check the exit code: 0 success, 137 = killed by SIGKILL (128+9), 143 = SIGTERM (128+15).

blocks.text: Security

items: You can only signal your own processes unless you are root.
Command-line arguments are visible to every user through ps: never pass passwords as arguments.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL?
blocks.text: SIGTERM is a request the process can catch to shut down cleanly. SIGKILL is enforced by the kernel and cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, so no cleanup runs.

blocks.title: A container exits with code 137. What happened?
blocks.text: 137 = 128 + 9, so it received SIGKILL. Usually the kernel OOM killer (memory limit exceeded) or a stop whose grace period expired. Check for OOMKilled in kubectl describe pod or the kernel log.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
blocks.text: A process has its own address space and file descriptors. Threads are execution paths inside one process sharing that memory. Linux schedules both as tasks.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Exit code 143 means the process…
Which signal can a process NOT handle?
quiz.why: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are acted on by the kernel and never delivered to a handler.

lessons.title: Disk, memory and ports: the three things that run out

blocks.text: A server has finite disk, memory and network ports. df shows how full each disk is, du shows which directory is using the space, free shows memory, and ss shows which program is listening on which port. Only one process may listen on a given address and port.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: df is the iPhone Storage screen, du is tapping into one app to see its size, free is the memory gauge in Xcode, and a port is like a URL scheme: only one app can claim it.
Why it matters
Full disk, exhausted memory and port conflicts are among the most common causes of outages, and each takes one command to confirm.
Where you meet it
First five minutes of almost any "the server is acting strange" investigation.
Scenario

checkout-api fails to start with "address already in use". ss -tlnp shows another process already listening on port 8000. Separately, the database volume is at 96%: when it reaches 100% PostgreSQL stops accepting writes and checkout fails for everyone.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph Server N["nginx
0.0.0.0:80"] --> A["checkout-api
127.0.0.1:8000"] A --> P["postgres
127.0.0.1:5432"] end I["Internet"] --> N I -. "blocked: bound to
localhost only" .-> P

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Alert: disk almost full"] --> B["df -h
which filesystem?"] B --> C["du -sh on its top directories"] C --> D["Drill into the largest"] D --> E{"What is it?"} E -->|"old logs"| F["Rotate and compress,
fix retention"] E -->|"df full but du small"| G["Deleted file still open:
lsof +L1, restart the process"] E -->|"millions of tiny files"| H["Inodes exhausted:
df -i"] E -->|"real data growth"| I["Add capacity"] F --> J["Verify with df -h,
add an alert at 80%"] G --> J H --> J I --> J

blocks.text: Commands
Exercise
Answer three questions an on-call engineer asks first.

items: Which filesystem is closest to full, and what is mounted there?
How much memory is actually available for new programs?
Which process is listening on port 8000, and on which address?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: /var/lib/postgresql at 96%, about 2.3Gi available, and nc (PID 2217) on 127.0.0.1:8000.
Troubleshooting

rows: "No space left on device" but df -h shows free space
The filesystem ran out of inodes (too many small files).
df -i to confirm, then find and remove the directory with millions of tiny files.
Disk still full after deleting a huge log
A running process still holds the deleted file open, so the space is not released.
lsof +L1 to find it, then restart or signal that process to reopen its logs.
A process vanished; logs show nothing
The kernel OOM killer ended it to free memory.
journalctl -k | grep -i "out of memory", then add memory or set limits.
Service works on the server but not from outside
It is bound to 127.0.0.1, or a firewall blocks the port.
ss -tlnp to see the bind address; bind to 0.0.0.0 only if it is meant to be public.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Alert on disk at 80%, not 100%.
Rotate logs (logrotate) and set retention.
Put databases on their own volume so logs cannot fill it.
Bind internal services to localhost or a private interface.

blocks.text: Security

items: Every listening port is attack surface: review ss -tlnp output on every new server.
A database listening on 0.0.0.0 with a public IP will be found by scanners within minutes.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: free shows only 400MB "free" on an 8GB server. Is it out of memory?
blocks.text: Not necessarily. Linux uses spare RAM as page cache and counts it under buff/cache. The "available" column estimates what programs can still get. Low available plus swap activity or OOM kills is the real warning.

blocks.title: What is the difference between binding to 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0?
blocks.text: 127.0.0.1 accepts connections only from the same machine. 0.0.0.0 accepts on every network interface, including public ones.

blocks.title: How do you find what is filling a disk?
blocks.text: df -h to find the filesystem, then du -sh on its top-level directories and drill into the largest, or du -ah DIR | sort -rh | head.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which column of "free -h" tells you how much memory new programs can use?
quiz.why: available includes reclaimable cache; free does not.

quiz.q: Two programs try to listen on 0.0.0.0:8000. What happens?
options: The second fails with "address already in use"
quiz.why: A listening address and port pair belongs to one socket (unless SO_REUSEPORT is used deliberately).

lessons.title: systemd services and logs

blocks.text: systemd is the first process the kernel starts (PID 1). It starts every other service, restarts them when they crash and collects their output. You describe a service in a small "unit" file, control it with systemctl and read its logs with journalctl.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: systemd is launchd for Linux, and a unit file is a launchd plist: what to run, as whom, with which environment, and what to do when it exits.
Why it matters
A program started by hand in a terminal dies when you log out and does not come back after a reboot or crash. A service does.
Where you meet it
Every app deployed straight onto a VM. Also the kubelet and container runtime on every Kubernetes node.
Scenario

This is the incident in the simulator: checkout-api.service is in state "failed". The fix path is the one you will use for years: status, logs, find the cause, fix it, start, verify from the customer side.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR U["Unit file
/etc/systemd/system/
checkout-api.service"] -->|"read by"| SD["systemd (PID 1)"] SD -->|"starts as User=app"| P["uvicorn process
127.0.0.1:8000"] P -->|"stdout and stderr"| J["journald"] J -->|"journalctl -u"| YOU["You"] SD -->|"Restart=on-failure"| P NG["nginx :80"] -->|"proxy_pass"| P CL["Customer"] --> NG

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["systemctl status checkout-api"] --> B{"Active?"} B -->|"failed"| C["journalctl -u checkout-api -n 50"] C --> D["Read the LAST error line"] D --> E["Fix the cause
(port, config, permission)"] E --> F["sudo systemctl start checkout-api"] F --> G["curl the health endpoint"] G --> H["curl through nginx
as the customer would"] B -->|"active"| G

blocks.text: Commands
/etc/systemd/system/checkout-api.service

blocks.code:
[Unit]
Description=Checkout API (FastAPI)
After=network.target            # start only after networking is up

[Service]
User=app                        # never root
WorkingDirectory=/srv/checkout
EnvironmentFile=/srv/checkout/.env   # secrets stay out of this file
ExecStart=/srv/checkout/venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
Restart=on-failure              # restart after a crash, not after a clean stop
RestartSec=2

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target      # "enable" makes it start at boot

blocks.text: After editing a unit file: sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then restart the service.
Exercise
Resolve ticket OPS-412 in the simulator and write the three-line incident note.

items: Reproduce the customer symptom with curl through nginx
Read the service status and its logs
Identify the process holding port 8000
Stop it, start the service, verify
Write: what broke, why, how it was fixed

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: All mission checkpoints beside the terminal turn green and curl returns HTTP 200.
Troubleshooting

rows: Failed to start: Interactive authentication required
Changing service state needs root.
Prefix with sudo.
Service is "active" but the site returns 502
The process is running but not listening where the proxy expects, or still starting.
ss -tlnp to compare the port and address with proxy_pass in the nginx config.
Unit changes have no effect
systemd caches unit files.
sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then restart.
start-limit-hit / "Start request repeated too quickly"
The service crashed repeatedly and systemd gave up.
Fix the cause from the logs, then systemctl reset-failed NAME and start it.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Read logs before restarting: a restart destroys the evidence and often the bug returns.
Use reload instead of restart when the service supports it.
Set Restart=on-failure so a crash heals itself, and alert on restart count.
Verify from the outside, not just "active (running)".

blocks.text: Security

items: Use User= and never run application services as root.
Keep secrets in an EnvironmentFile with mode 600, not inline in the unit.
Hardening options such as NoNewPrivileges=true and ProtectSystem=strict shrink the blast radius.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Walk me through debugging a service that will not start.
blocks.text: systemctl status for state and exit code, journalctl -u for the last error, then check the usual causes in order: config syntax, missing environment, permissions on files, port already in use, dependency not reachable. Fix, start, verify with a real request.

blocks.title: restart versus reload?
blocks.text: restart stops the process and starts a new one, dropping open connections. reload asks the running process to re-read its configuration without exiting, if it supports that (nginx does).

blocks.title: What does "systemctl enable" do?
blocks.text: It makes the unit start at boot by linking it into a target. It does not start it now; that is "start", or "enable --now" for both.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A service is in state "failed". What do you run first?
quiz.why: The logs say why it failed. Restarting first hides the evidence and usually fails again.

quiz.q: nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway. Where is the problem?
options: nginx could not get a valid response from the backend
quiz.why: 502 means the proxy itself is up, but its upstream refused the connection or answered badly.

lessons.title: Namespaces, cgroups and the OOM killer: what a container really is

blocks.text: A container is not a small virtual machine. It is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel has been told to isolate and limit. Namespaces control what the process can see (its own process list, network, filesystem, hostname). cgroups control how much it can use (CPU, memory, I/O). When a memory limit is exceeded, the kernel OOM killer ends a process.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A namespace is the iOS app sandbox: the app believes it has the device to itself. A cgroup is the jetsam memory limit: cross it and the system terminates you without asking.
Why it matters

Virtual machines isolate by running a whole second operating system, which costs gigabytes and takes seconds to boot. Namespaces and cgroups give most of that isolation to a normal process that starts in milliseconds.
Where you meet it
Docker, containerd, Kubernetes pods, systemd services (each gets its own cgroup), CI job isolation.
Scenario

The checkout pod has a memory limit of 512Mi. A memory leak pushes it past that, the kernel kills the container, Kubernetes marks it OOMKilled with exit code 137 and restarts it. From the outside you see restarts climbing and brief error spikes.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD K["One Linux kernel"] --> NS["Namespaces: what you SEE"] K --> CG["cgroups: what you may USE"] NS --> N1["pid: own process tree,
your app is PID 1"] NS --> N2["net: own interfaces,
ports and routes"] NS --> N3["mnt: own filesystem
(the image layers)"] NS --> N4["uts, ipc, user"] CG --> C1["memory.max = 512M"] CG --> C2["cpu.max = half a core"] CG --> C3["pids.max, io.max"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart LR A["Container memory
reaches memory.max"] --> B["Kernel tries to
reclaim page cache"] B --> C{"Enough freed?"} C -->|yes| D["Continue"] C -->|no| E["OOM killer picks a
process in the cgroup"] E --> F["SIGKILL, exit 137"] F --> G["Runtime reports
OOMKilled"] G --> H["Kubernetes restarts
the container"]

blocks.text: Commands
Lists the namespaces on the machine and the process that owns each.
Inside a container, prints the memory limit in bytes ("max" means unlimited). This is cgroup v2.
Shows which cgroup a process belongs to.
Starts a shell in a new PID namespace. Inside it, ps shows only that shell as PID 1. This is the core trick of every container runtime.

rows: `--pid`
new process-ID namespace
`--fork`
run the command as a child so it becomes PID 1
`--mount-proc`
mount a fresh /proc so ps reflects the new namespace

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: ps aux inside shows two processes. Type exit to leave.
Searches kernel messages for OOM kills.

blocks.code: Out of memory: Killed process 1877 (node) total-vm:2911044kB
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: Exercise
On a Linux VM or inside any container, see the walls for yourself. (The built-in terminal simulates one machine and does not model namespaces.)

items: Run a container: docker run --rm -it --memory 64m alpine sh
Inside, run ps aux: your shell is PID 1 and nothing else is visible
Run cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max and convert the bytes to MiB
From the host, run ps aux | grep "sh" and find the same process with a different PID

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: memory.max prints 67108864, and the process is visible from the host but the host is not visible from the container.
Troubleshooting

rows: Pod restarts with reason OOMKilled, exit code 137
The container exceeded its memory limit.
Compare real usage with the limit; fix the leak or raise the limit. Set the runtime heap (JVM, Node) below the container limit.
Latency spikes with CPU well under 100%
CPU throttling: the container used its cgroup CPU quota for this period and was paused.
Check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total; raise or remove the CPU limit while keeping the request.
Application sees all host cores and memory
Old runtimes read /proc, which is not namespaced for these values.
Use a runtime version that is container-aware, or set worker counts explicitly.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Always set a memory request and limit; treat the limit as a hard wall.
Set CPU requests for scheduling; be careful with CPU limits on latency-sensitive services.
Make PID 1 in your container handle signals, or use an init such as tini.
One main process per container.

blocks.text: Security

items: Containers share the host kernel: a kernel exploit crosses the boundary. VMs give stronger isolation.
Run as non-root, drop capabilities, and never use --privileged for an application.
Mounting the Docker socket into a container gives it root on the host.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is a container, at the kernel level?
blocks.text: A normal process started in its own set of namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) so it sees an isolated system, attached to cgroups that cap its resources, with a root filesystem assembled from image layers by an overlay filesystem.

blocks.title: Container versus VM?
blocks.text: A VM virtualises hardware and runs its own kernel: strong isolation, heavier, slower to start. A container shares the host kernel and isolates at the process level: light and fast, but the kernel is a shared attack surface.

blocks.title: Why might a container be OOM-killed while the node has free memory?
blocks.text: The limit is enforced per cgroup. The container hit its own memory.max regardless of what the node has free.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which kernel feature limits how much memory a container may use?
quiz.why: Namespaces isolate what is visible; cgroups account for and limit resources.

quiz.q: Inside a container, your app is PID 1. On the host it is…
options: an ordinary process with a different PID
quiz.why: The PID namespace only changes the view from inside.

modules.title: Networking Mastery
modules.summary: IP and CIDR, DNS, TCP, HTTP, TLS and a troubleshooting method.

lessons.title: IP addresses, subnets and CIDR

blocks.text: An IP address identifies a network interface. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits written as four numbers (10.0.1.15). A subnet is a block of neighbouring addresses. CIDR notation such as 10.0.1.0/24 says "the first 24 bits name the network, the remaining 8 bits name hosts inside it", which gives 256 addresses. Private ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) are not routable on the internet; NAT translates them to a public address on the way out.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A CIDR block is a street: 10.0.1.0/24 is "MG Road, houses 0 to 255". The prefix length says how long the street name is; a shorter prefix (/16) is a whole district.
Why it matters
Networks are split into subnets to control which machines can talk to each other and which are reachable from the internet.
Where you meet it
Designing a cloud VPC, writing firewall and security-group rules, Kubernetes pod and service ranges, reading any network diagram.
Scenario

The shop VPC is 10.0.0.0/16. Load balancers sit in public subnets 10.0.1.0/24 and 10.0.2.0/24. checkout-api pods and the database sit in private subnets with no public IPs. The database security group allows port 5432 only from the application subnet CIDR.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  I["Internet"] --> IGW["Internet gateway"]
  subgraph VPC["VPC 10.0.0.0/16 (65,536 addresses)"]
    subgraph PUB["Public subnet 10.0.1.0/24"]
      LB["Load balancer"]
      NAT["NAT gateway"]
    end
    subgraph APP["Private subnet 10.0.10.0/24"]
      API["checkout-api"]
    end
    subgraph DB["Private subnet 10.0.20.0/24"]
      PG["PostgreSQL"]
    end
  end
  IGW --> LB --> API --> PG
  API -. "outbound only" .-> NAT --> IGW

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Host 10.0.10.5 sends to an IP"] --> B{"Destination inside
my subnet 10.0.10.0/24?"} B -->|yes| C["Deliver directly
on the local network"] B -->|no| D["Send to the default gateway"] D --> E{"Destination private
and routable in the VPC?"} E -->|yes| F["Route table forwards it
to the other subnet"] E -->|"no: internet"| G["NAT gateway rewrites the
source to a public IP"] G --> H["Internet gateway"] H --> I["Reply returns, NAT maps it
back to 10.0.10.5"]

blocks.text: Commands
Lists network interfaces and their addresses.

rows: `ip -br addr`
brief one-line-per-interface form

blocks.text: Shows the routing table: which interface or gateway each destination uses.

blocks.code:
default via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0
10.0.1.0/24 dev eth0 scope link
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: No "default" line means the machine cannot reach anything outside its own subnet.
Exercise
Plan subnets for a small production VPC using the calculator below.

items: Enter 10.0.0.0/16 and note how many addresses it holds
Find the usable host range of 10.0.10.0/24
How many /24 subnets fit inside a /16?
Is 10.0.20.7 inside 10.0.20.0/28? Check the range

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: 65,536 addresses; 10.0.10.1 to 10.0.10.254; 256 subnets; yes (range .0 to .15).
Troubleshooting

rows: Two VPCs cannot be peered
Their CIDR ranges overlap, so routing is ambiguous.
Plan non-overlapping ranges up front; renumbering later is painful.
A private instance cannot download packages
No NAT gateway route for outbound traffic.
Add a default route from the private subnet to a NAT gateway.
Cloud subnet has fewer usable IPs than expected
Providers reserve addresses (AWS reserves 5 per subnet).
Size subnets with headroom; Kubernetes pods consume IPs quickly.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Keep databases and application servers in private subnets.
Leave room to grow: a /16 VPC with /20 or /24 subnets.
Spread subnets over at least two availability zones.
Document the IP plan before building.

blocks.text: Security

items: A public IP plus an open port equals exposed to the whole internet.
Allow by source CIDR or security group, never 0.0.0.0/0 for admin ports such as 22 and 5432.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How many usable hosts are in a /26?
blocks.text: 32 - 26 = 6 host bits, 2^6 = 64 addresses, minus network and broadcast = 62 usable (59 on AWS, which reserves 5).

blocks.title: What does NAT do?
blocks.text: It rewrites the private source address of outgoing packets to a public one and remembers the mapping so replies return to the right machine. Private hosts can reach out but cannot be reached from outside.

blocks.title: Public versus private subnet in a cloud VPC?
blocks.text: A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway. A private subnet does not; its outbound traffic, if any, goes through a NAT gateway.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: How many addresses does 10.0.1.0/24 contain?
quiz.why: 32 - 24 = 8 host bits, 2^8 = 256 (254 usable).

quiz.q: Which is a private (non-internet-routable) address?

lessons.title: DNS: turning names into addresses

blocks.text: Computers connect to IP addresses, people remember names. DNS is the worldwide directory that maps one to the other. Your device asks a resolver, which asks the root servers, then the .com servers, then the domain's own authoritative servers, and caches the answer for the record's TTL (time to live).

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Like asking reception for someone's desk: reception does not know everyone, but knows which floor manager to ask, who knows which team lead to ask. Then reception remembers the answer for a while.
Why it matters
Servers change IP addresses constantly (deploys, scaling, failover). Names stay stable while the addresses behind them change.
Where you meet it
Every request your app makes starts with a lookup. Also service discovery inside Kubernetes (CoreDNS), failover between regions, and domain ownership checks for TLS certificates.
Scenario

The mobile app calls api.shop.example.com. That is a CNAME to the CDN, which resolves to an edge IP. Inside the cluster, checkout-api reaches inventory by the name inventory.production.svc.cluster.local, answered by CoreDNS.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD APP["App"] --> OS["OS resolver cache
and /etc/hosts"] OS --> REC["Recursive resolver
(ISP, 1.1.1.1, VPC resolver)"] REC --> ROOT["Root servers
know where .com is"] REC --> TLD[".com servers
know example.com's name servers"] REC --> AUTH["Authoritative servers
hold the actual records"] AUTH --> ZONE["Zone: A, AAAA, CNAME,
MX, TXT, NS + TTL"] REC -. "caches every answer for its TTL" .-> REC

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App as Mobile app
  participant R as Resolver (ISP or 8.8.8.8)
  participant Root as Root servers
  participant TLD as .com servers
  participant Auth as example.com name servers
  App->>R: api.shop.example.com ?
  R->>Root: who handles .com ?
  Root-->>R: ask the .com servers
  R->>TLD: who handles example.com ?
  TLD-->>R: ask ns1.example.com
  R->>Auth: api.shop.example.com ?
  Auth-->>R: A 203.0.113.10, TTL 300
  R-->>App: 203.0.113.10 (cached for 300s)

blocks.text: Commands
Performs the lookup step by step from the root servers, showing each delegation. Use it to find which level gives a wrong answer.
Shows which DNS resolver this machine uses.
Common record types

blocks.code:
A      name -> IPv4 address          api.shop.example.com.  300 IN A     203.0.113.10
AAAA   name -> IPv6 address
CNAME  name -> another name          www   300 IN CNAME shop.example.com.
MX     mail servers for the domain
TXT    free text: domain verification, SPF, DKIM
NS     which servers are authoritative for this zone

TTL (the number) = seconds a resolver may cache the answer.

blocks.text: Exercise
Tell a DNS failure apart from a server failure.

items: Look up a name that exists and read the ANSWER section and TTL
Look up one that does not and find the status field
curl the missing name and note the curl error number
Compare with curl http://localhost:9999 (name resolves, nothing listening)

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: NXDOMAIN and curl (6) for a DNS failure; curl (7) when the name resolves but the port is closed.
Troubleshooting

rows: curl: (6) Could not resolve host
The name does not exist, or the resolver is unreachable.
dig NAME, then dig @1.1.1.1 NAME. If the second works, your resolver is the problem.
Some users still reach the old server after a DNS change
Resolvers cache the old record until its TTL expires.
Lower the TTL to 60 seconds a day before a planned migration, then raise it again afterwards.
Works on your laptop, fails in a pod
The pod uses the cluster DNS, with different search domains.
kubectl exec into the pod and run nslookup there; check CoreDNS pods and /etc/resolv.conf.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Lower TTLs before migrations, not during.
Use at least two authoritative name servers in different networks.
Monitor resolution of your own domain from outside your network.
Set an auto-renew on the domain registration itself.

blocks.text: Security

items: Whoever controls your DNS can redirect all your traffic: protect the registrar account with MFA.
Remove DNS records that point at cloud resources you have deleted, or someone else can claim the resource and serve content on your name (subdomain takeover).

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter? Start with DNS.
blocks.text: The browser checks its cache, the OS cache and /etc/hosts, then asks the configured resolver. The resolver walks root, TLD and authoritative servers, returns the address and caches it for the TTL. Then TCP, TLS and HTTP follow.

blocks.title: A record versus CNAME?
blocks.text: An A record maps a name directly to an IPv4 address. A CNAME maps a name to another name, which is then resolved. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records on the same name, which is why the zone apex needs A or ALIAS records.

blocks.title: What is TTL and how does it affect failover?
blocks.text: How long resolvers may cache the answer. A long TTL reduces lookups but means a change or failover takes up to that long to reach everyone.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: dig reports "status: NXDOMAIN". What does it mean?
quiz.why: NXDOMAIN is the authoritative "no such name".

quiz.q: You changed an A record with TTL 3600. How long until all users see it?
quiz.why: Resolvers may serve the cached answer until the TTL (3600 s) expires.

lessons.title: TCP, HTTP and TLS: what one API call is made of

blocks.text: TCP provides a reliable, ordered connection between two IP:port pairs, opened with a three-step handshake. TLS runs on top of TCP: the server proves its identity with a certificate and both sides agree on encryption keys. HTTP runs on top of that: a request (method, path, headers, body) and a response (status code, headers, body). UDP is the alternative to TCP: no connection and no delivery guarantee, used where speed matters more (DNS, video, HTTP/3).

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: TCP is a phone call: you both confirm you can hear each other before talking. TLS is checking the other person's ID and then switching to a language only you two understand. HTTP is the actual conversation, in a fixed question-and-answer format.
Why it matters

Each layer solves one problem: IP delivers packets, TCP makes delivery reliable, TLS makes it private and authenticated, HTTP gives it meaning. When a request fails, the layer it failed at tells you where to look.
Where you meet it
Every URLSession or Dio call from your apps, every service-to-service call, every health check.
Scenario

A checkout POST: DNS lookup, TCP handshake to port 443, TLS handshake with the certificate for api.shop.example.com, then "POST /checkout". The status code that comes back tells you which component objected.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD H["HTTP
method, path, headers, status"] --> T["TLS
identity and encryption"] T --> C["TCP
reliable, ordered bytes between two ports"] C --> I["IP
packets routed between addresses"] I --> L["Link
Wi-Fi, Ethernet, cellular"] H -. "fails as 4xx / 5xx" .-> X1["look at the application or proxy"] T -. "fails as certificate error" .-> X2["look at the certificate and hostname"] C -. "fails as refused / timeout" .-> X3["look at the port, firewall, service"] I -. "fails as unreachable" .-> X4["look at routing and DNS"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Server :443
  Note over C,S: TCP three-way handshake
  C->>S: SYN
  S-->>C: SYN-ACK
  C->>S: ACK
  Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 handshake
  C->>S: ClientHello (supported ciphers, server name)
  S-->>C: ServerHello + certificate
  C->>S: Finished (keys agreed)
  Note over C,S: HTTP, encrypted
  C->>S: POST /checkout
  S-->>C: 201 Created

blocks.text: Commands
Shows every stage of a request: name resolution, TCP connect, TLS handshake and certificate, request and response headers.

rows: no progress meter
verbose
`-o /dev/null`
discard the body

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: The last line printed before the failure names the stage that broke.

blocks.code: curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'dns %{time_namelookup}s  connect %{time_connect}s  tls %{time_appconnect}s  first-byte %{time_starttransfer}s  total %{time_total}s\n' https://example.com
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Prints how long each stage took. The gap between tls and first-byte is the server thinking time.
Status codes and who is usually responsible

blocks.code:
2xx  success            200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xx  redirect           301 permanent, 302 temporary, 304 not modified
4xx  the CLIENT erred   400 bad request, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed,
                        404 not found, 429 too many requests
5xx  the SERVER erred   500 application bug or unhandled exception
                        502 proxy could not get a valid answer from the backend
                        503 no healthy backend, or overloaded
                        504 the backend did not answer before the proxy timeout

blocks.text: Exercise
Map four failures to the layer that failed.

items: curl a host that does not exist
curl localhost on a port nothing listens on
curl the API through nginx while the backend is down
For each, write down: DNS, TCP, TLS or HTTP?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: (6) = DNS. (7) connection refused = TCP. 502 = HTTP reached the proxy but the backend failed.
Troubleshooting

rows: Connection refused
The host answered, but nothing is listening on that port.
On the server: ss -tlnp. Check the service is running and bound to the right address.
Connection timed out
Packets are being dropped silently: firewall, security group or wrong IP.
Check firewall and security-group rules and routing. Refused is fast; timeout is slow.
SSL certificate problem: certificate has expired
The certificate passed its notAfter date and renewal did not happen.
Renew and reload the server; then automate renewal and alert 21 days before expiry.
504 Gateway Timeout
The backend is alive but slower than the proxy timeout: slow query, lock, or exhausted worker pool.
Check backend latency and database metrics before raising any timeout.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: TLS everywhere, including service-to-service.
Set explicit timeouts on every client; the default is often "wait forever".
Retry only idempotent requests, with backoff and jitter.
Reuse connections (keep-alive, HTTP/2) to avoid repeated handshakes.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never disable certificate verification (curl -k, or trusting all certificates in an app) outside a throwaway local test.
Redirect HTTP to HTTPS and send HSTS.
Keep TLS 1.2 as the minimum; prefer 1.3.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Difference between 502, 503 and 504?
blocks.text: 502: the proxy got an invalid or no response from the upstream (crashed, refused). 503: no capacity or no healthy upstream. 504: the upstream accepted the request but did not answer within the proxy timeout.

blocks.title: TCP versus UDP?
blocks.text: TCP is connection-oriented with ordering, retransmission and congestion control. UDP sends independent datagrams with no guarantees and less overhead. DNS queries, streaming and QUIC (HTTP/3) use UDP.

blocks.title: What does the TLS handshake establish?
blocks.text: Server identity (a certificate chained to a trusted CA and matching the hostname), an agreed cipher, and shared session keys derived by key exchange, so later traffic is encrypted and tamper-evident.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: "Connection refused" most likely means…
options: The host is up but nothing listens on that port
quiz.why: The server actively rejected the connection with a TCP reset. Dropped packets produce a timeout instead.

quiz.q: Which status says the client sent too many requests?
quiz.why: 429 Too Many Requests is the rate-limit response.

lessons.title: Network troubleshooting: a method, not guessing

blocks.text: Work up the layers in order and stop at the first one that fails: does the name resolve, can you open a TCP connection, does TLS complete, does HTTP return what you expect? Then test from more than one place to learn where the break is.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Debugging a failed network call in an app: first is the device online, then does the host resolve, then is it an SSL error, then what status came back. Same ladder, more rungs.
Why it matters
Under pressure people jump to their favourite theory. A fixed order finds the fault faster and gives you evidence to hand to another team.
Where you meet it
Any "it cannot connect" or "it is slow" report, between any two components.
Scenario

Order placement times out. From a checkout pod: DNS for the payment service resolves, the TCP connection opens, and the request hangs. That rules out DNS and the network and points at the payment service or its dependencies.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  C["Client"] --> D["DNS"] --> E["Edge / CDN"] --> LB["Load balancer"] --> P["Proxy"] --> S["Service"] --> DB["Database"]
  D -. "dig, nslookup" .- T1["name resolution"]
  E -. "openssl s_client" .- T2["certificate"]
  LB -. "curl -v, target health" .- T3["HTTP status"]
  P -. "error log, nginx -t" .- T4["routing"]
  S -. "ss -tlnp, logs" .- T5["listening?"]
  DB -. "nc -vz host 5432" .- T6["port reachable?"]

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Tests whether a TCP port accepts connections, without speaking any protocol.

rows: verbose
just connect and close, send nothing

blocks.text: Starts a temporary pod full of network tools inside the cluster, so you test from where the application runs. It is deleted when you exit.

rows: delete the pod on exit
`-it`
interactive terminal

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: On a production cluster this creates a pod: use a namespace you are allowed to use and follow your team policy.
Exercise
In the request journey simulator, break one component at a time and predict the symptom before you run it.

items: Break DNS: what does the app see?
Break the load balancer targets: which status code?
Break the backend service: 502 or 504?
For each, name the first command you would run

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Your predictions match the simulator for at least five of the hops.
Troubleshooting

rows: Works from your laptop, fails from the server
Different network path: private DNS, security groups, egress rules.
Always reproduce from the failing source.
Intermittent failures, roughly one request in three
One of three backends is unhealthy but still in rotation.
Check load-balancer target health and readiness probes; hit each backend directly.
ping fails but the site works
ICMP is blocked, which is common.
Test the real port with curl or nc instead.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Reproduce from the source that fails.
Change one thing at a time and re-test.
Write down each command and result as you go; that becomes the postmortem timeline.
Capture evidence before restarting anything.

blocks.text: Security

items: Packet captures contain real user data: store and share them accordingly.
Do not open a firewall to 0.0.0.0/0 "just to test".

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: A service cannot reach its database. How do you debug it?
blocks.text: From the service host or pod: resolve the name, test the port with nc, check credentials and TLS with the real client, then check the database side (listening address, max connections, firewall or security group, pg_hba). State what each result rules out.

blocks.title: Refused versus timed out?
blocks.text: Refused is an immediate TCP reset: the host is reachable and nothing listens. A timeout means packets vanish: firewall, routing or a dead host.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: DNS resolves and TCP connects, then TLS fails. Which is a plausible cause?
quiz.why: DNS and TCP already succeeded, so the fault is in the TLS layer.

quiz.q: Why test from inside a pod instead of your laptop?
options: The pod uses the cluster network, DNS and policies
quiz.why: The failure belongs to a specific network path; reproduce on that path.

modules.title: Git and Version Control
modules.summary: Commits, branches, merging, conflicts, rebasing, undoing, tags and team workflows.

lessons.title: Commits and the three areas

blocks.text: Git records the history of a project as a chain of commits. A commit is a full snapshot of every tracked file plus a message, an author and a pointer to the commit before it. Your work moves through three areas: the working tree (the files you edit), the staging area (the draft of the next commit) and the repository (committed history). git add moves changes into the draft; git commit turns the draft into history.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: You already use Git from Xcode or Android Studio. Think of staging as choosing which changed files go into this particular pull request: you may have edited five files, but only three belong to the fix you are about to record.
Why it matters
Without version control nobody can answer "what changed, when, and why did it break?". With it, any earlier state can be inspected or restored, and many people can work at once.
Where you meet it
Every codebase, and in DevOps also every pipeline definition, Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifest and Terraform file. If it is not in Git, it is not reproducible.
Scenario

The checkout-api repository holds the application, its Dockerfile, its Jenkinsfile and its Kubernetes manifests. A commit to main is the single event that the whole delivery pipeline reacts to, and the commit ID becomes the image tag running in production.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR WT["Working tree
files you edit"] -->|"git add"| IX["Staging area
draft of next commit"] IX -->|"git commit"| REPO["Local repository
history"] REPO -->|"git push"| REMOTE["Remote
(origin)"] REMOTE -->|"git fetch / pull"| REPO REPO -->|"git switch / restore"| WT

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart LR A["Edit files"] --> B["git status
what changed?"] B --> C["git diff
review it"] C --> D["git add FILE
stage it"] D --> E["git diff --staged
last check"] E --> F["git commit -m"] F --> G["git log --oneline"]

blocks.text: Commands
.gitignore and first-time setup

blocks.code:
# .gitignore: files Git must never track
.env                # secrets
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
node_modules/
dist/
.DS_Store

# One-time identity, stored in ~/.gitconfig
git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global pull.rebase true     # optional: rebase instead of merge on pull

blocks.text: A .gitignore entry only prevents new files being tracked. A file that is already committed stays tracked until you remove it with git rm --cached.
Exercise
Make two separate commits from one editing session, to feel what the staging area is for.

items: Create NOTES.md with echo and append a line to README.md with >>
Run git status: one untracked file, one modified file
Stage and commit only NOTES.md
Run git status again: README.md is still modified and unstaged
Stage and commit README.md with its own message
Read the result with git log --oneline

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Two new commits appear in the graph, each containing one file.
Troubleshooting

rows: A secret was committed
git add . swept in .env, or the file was not ignored.
Rotate the secret first: assume it is compromised. Then remove it from history and add it to .gitignore. Deleting it in a later commit does not remove it from earlier ones.
Committed to the wrong branch
You forgot to switch first.
If not pushed: create the right branch at this commit (git branch NAME), then move the wrong branch back with git reset --hard HEAD~1.
git commit says "nothing to commit" but files changed
The changes are not staged.
git add the files, or use git commit -a for tracked files.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Commit small, complete changes: one reason per commit.
Write the subject as an instruction: "fix: round checkout total", then explain why in the body.
Review git diff --staged before every commit.
Never commit secrets, build output or dependencies.

blocks.text: Security

items: History is permanent and widely copied. A leaked credential must be rotated, not just deleted.
Use a pre-commit secret scanner such as gitleaks.
Sign commits or enforce verified commits on protected branches where provenance matters.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the staging area for?
blocks.text: It lets you compose a commit deliberately from part of your working changes, so each commit is one coherent change even when your working tree holds several.

blocks.title: What does a commit contain?
blocks.text: A snapshot of the whole tracked tree, a message, author and committer details, and the ID of its parent commit or commits. Its ID is a hash of all of that, so changing anything creates a different commit.

blocks.title: How do you undo a change that is staged, and one that is not?
blocks.text: git restore --staged FILE unstages and keeps the edit. git restore FILE discards an unstaged edit permanently.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: You edit a file, run git add, then edit it again. What does git commit record?
quiz.why: git add copies the content at that moment into the staging area. The later edit is unstaged.

quiz.q: Which command sends commits to teammates?
quiz.why: commit is local. push uploads to the remote.

lessons.title: Branches, merging and conflicts

blocks.text: A branch is a movable name that points at a commit. Creating one is instant and copies nothing. HEAD is the branch you are on. When you commit, that branch moves forward. Merging brings another branch's work into yours: if your branch has not moved since they split, its pointer simply slides forward (fast-forward); if both moved, Git combines them with a three-way merge using their common ancestor, and records a merge commit with two parents. A conflict happens only when both sides changed the same lines.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A branch is a bookmark, not a copy of the book. Two people add chapters after the same page; merging binds both sets in. If you each rewrote the same paragraph, Git cannot choose and asks you.
Why it matters
Branches let work in progress stay separate from the code that is deployed, and let several people change the same project without waiting for each other.
Where you meet it
Every pull request is a branch. Release branches, hotfix branches and preview environments all rely on them.
Scenario

Two teammates each branched from the same commit of checkout-api. One added a /metrics endpoint, the other changed how the total is calculated, which main also changed. The first merges cleanly; the second conflicts on one line and a person has to decide what the correct calculation is.
Architecture

blocks.code:
gitGraph
  commit id: "checkout"
  commit id: "health"
  branch feature/metrics
  commit id: "metrics"
  checkout main
  branch feature/discounts
  commit id: "discounts"
  checkout main
  commit id: "rounding" tag: "v1.4.0"
  merge feature/metrics
  merge feature/discounts tag: "v1.5.0"

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["git merge feature"] --> B{"Has main moved
since the branch split?"} B -->|no| C["Fast-forward:
move the pointer"] B -->|yes| D["Three-way merge using
the common ancestor"] D --> E{"Same lines changed
on both sides?"} E -->|no| F["Merge commit created"] E -->|yes| G["CONFLICT: markers
written into the file"] G --> H["Edit file, keep the right code"] H --> I["git add FILE"] I --> J["git commit"]

blocks.text: Commands
What a conflict looks like in the file

blocks.code:
def checkout(order: dict) -> dict:
<<<<<<< HEAD
    total = round(sum(i["price"] * i["qty"] for i in order["items"]), 2)
=======
    subtotal = sum(i["price"] * i["qty"] for i in order["items"])
    total = subtotal * (1 - order.get("discount", 0))
>>>>>>> feature/discounts
    return {"total": total, "status": "placed"}

# Above the ======= is your branch (HEAD). Below it is the branch being merged.
# A correct resolution keeps BOTH intentions: apply the discount AND round.

    subtotal = sum(i["price"] * i["qty"] for i in order["items"])
    total = round(subtotal * (1 - order.get("discount", 0)), 2)

blocks.text: Resolving a conflict is a code decision, not a Git chore. Run the tests after resolving.
Exercise
Complete both merges in the Git visualizer, resolving the conflict so that the discount is applied and the total is still rounded.

items: Merge feature/metrics and note it needed no help although both branches edited app/main.py
Merge feature/discounts and read the CONFLICT message
Open app/main.py in the editor under the graph and find the three marker lines
Replace the conflict block with code that keeps both intentions, then save
git add app/main.py and git commit
Look at the merge commit in the graph: it has two parents

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: The "resolve the conflict" checkpoint turns green and cat app/main.py shows no <<<<<<< markers.
Troubleshooting

rows: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in FILE
Both branches changed the same lines since their common ancestor.
Edit the file, remove the markers, keep the correct code, git add, git commit. Or git merge --abort to back out.
error: Your local changes would be overwritten by checkout
You have uncommitted edits to a file that differs on the target branch.
Commit them, or stash them, then switch.
The merge "worked" but the app is broken
A semantic conflict: the texts did not overlap but the changes are incompatible, for example one side renamed a function the other side calls.
Git only merges text. CI running tests on the merge result is what catches this.
error: The branch is not fully merged
git branch -d refuses to delete a branch whose commits exist nowhere else.
Merge it, or use -D if you really mean to discard that work.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Keep branches short-lived: the longer a branch lives, the larger and riskier the merge.
Pull main into your branch (or rebase onto it) often.
Delete branches after they merge.
Protect main: require a pull request, a review and green CI.

blocks.text: Security

items: Branch protection is an access control: without it anyone with write access can put unreviewed code into production.
Require CI checks to pass on the merge result, not only on the branch tip.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Fast-forward merge versus three-way merge?
blocks.text: Fast-forward is possible when the current branch is an ancestor of the other: Git just moves the pointer and creates no commit. Otherwise Git merges the two tips against their common ancestor and creates a merge commit with two parents.

blocks.title: When does Git report a conflict?
blocks.text: When both sides changed the same region of the same file differently relative to the merge base, or one side deleted a file the other modified. Changes to different regions of one file merge automatically.

blocks.title: What is HEAD?
blocks.text: A pointer to the current branch, and through it to the commit your working tree is based on. In a detached HEAD state it points straight at a commit instead of a branch.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Two branches edit different functions in the same file. What happens on merge?
options: Git asks which file to keep
quiz.why: Git merges line regions, not whole files. Non-overlapping changes combine automatically.

quiz.q: How many parents does a merge commit have?
quiz.why: One parent for each branch tip that was joined.

lessons.title: Rewriting and undoing: rebase, cherry-pick, revert, reset, tags

blocks.text: Rebase re-creates your commits on top of another branch so history becomes a straight line; each replayed commit gets a new ID. Cherry-pick copies one commit's change onto the current branch. Revert adds a new commit that undoes an old one. Reset moves a branch pointer backwards, dropping commits from it. A tag is a permanent name for a commit, used for releases. The one rule that governs all of them: rewriting commits that other people already have breaks their copies, so on shared branches you add commits (revert), you do not remove or replace them (reset, rebase, amend).

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Revert is publishing a correction notice: the original stays in the record. Reset is tearing pages out of the logbook: fine in your private notebook, unacceptable in the shared ledger. Rebase is rewriting your draft so it reads as if written after the latest edition.
Why it matters
A clean, linear history is easier to read and bisect. And when a bad change reaches production you need a way to undo it that is fast and does not surprise your teammates.
Where you meet it
Tidying a feature branch before review, carrying a hotfix to a release branch, undoing a bad deploy, tagging releases that CI turns into versioned images.
Scenario

A commit to checkout-api causes errors in production. The on-call engineer rolls the Deployment back first (seconds), then runs git revert on main and lets the pipeline ship the fix forward. Nobody force-pushes main.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  subgraph "Before"
    A1["A"] --> B1["B"] --> C1["C (main)"]
    B1 --> X1["X"] --> Y1["Y (feature)"]
  end
  subgraph "After: git rebase main (on feature)"
    A2["A"] --> B2["B"] --> C2["C (main)"] --> X2["X' (new ID)"] --> Y2["Y' (feature)"]
  end

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["I need to undo something"] --> B{"Has it been pushed
to a shared branch?"} B -->|yes| C["git revert COMMIT
adds an undoing commit"] B -->|no| D{"Keep the changes
in my files?"} D -->|"yes"| E["git reset --soft / --mixed"] D -->|"no, discard"| F["git reset --hard
DESTRUCTIVE"] C --> G["Push normally.
No force needed"]

blocks.text: Commands
Semantic versioning and conventional commits

blocks.code:
Version:  MAJOR . MINOR . PATCH          e.g. v1.5.0
  MAJOR  incompatible API change            v1.5.0 -> v2.0.0
  MINOR  new, backward-compatible feature   v1.5.0 -> v1.6.0
  PATCH  backward-compatible bug fix        v1.5.0 -> v1.5.1

Commit subject:  type(scope): description
  feat(checkout): apply discount codes      -> next MINOR
  fix(checkout): round total to 2 decimals  -> next PATCH
  feat!: remove /v1/checkout                -> next MAJOR (the ! marks a breaking change)
  docs, test, refactor, chore, ci           -> no release

Release tools read these subjects to pick the next version and write the changelog.

blocks.text: Exercise
See with your own eyes that rebase creates new commits and that revert preserves history.

items: Note the short ID of the commit on feature/metrics in the graph
Switch to feature/metrics and rebase it onto main: the ID changes and the branch now sits after main
Switch to main and merge it: the result is a fast-forward with no merge commit
Revert that commit: a new commit appears and the endpoint is gone from the file, but the original commit is still in history
Now try git reset --hard v1.4.0 and read the simulator note about what dropped off

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain why you would use revert, not reset, if those commits had already been pushed.
Troubleshooting

rows: Push rejected after a rebase or amend
You rewrote commits that were already on the remote, so your branch and the remote have diverged.
On your own feature branch: git push --force-with-lease. On a shared branch: do not; undo the rewrite and use revert.
Lost commits after git reset --hard
The branch pointer moved and the commits are no longer referenced.
git reflog shows where HEAD was; git reset --hard to that ID restores them. Unreferenced commits are garbage-collected after a few weeks.
The same conflict appears at every step of a long rebase
Each replayed commit touches the conflicting lines.
Squash the branch first, or merge instead. git rerere can remember resolutions.
You are in "detached HEAD" state
You checked out a tag or commit ID rather than a branch.
Fine for looking around. To keep work done there: git switch -c NEW-BRANCH.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Rebase and amend only what you have not shared.
Undo on shared branches with revert.
Prefer --force-with-lease to --force, and forbid force pushes to main entirely.
Tag every release with an annotated, immutable tag that matches the deployed image version.

blocks.text: Security

items: A force push to a protected branch can silently remove reviewed code or a security fix: block it in branch protection.
Tags can be moved unless protected. Deploy by commit ID or image digest, not by a mutable tag.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Merge versus rebase: when do you use each?
blocks.text: Rebase to update a private feature branch onto the latest main and keep history linear. Merge to integrate finished work into a shared branch, preserving what actually happened. Never rebase shared history.

blocks.title: A bad commit reached production. What do you do?
blocks.text: Restore service first by rolling back the deployment. Then git revert the commit on main so the pipeline ships the corrected state, and follow up with a proper fix and a test. Do not rewrite main.

blocks.title: reset --soft, --mixed and --hard?
blocks.text: All move the branch pointer. Soft keeps the staging area and files, so the changes are ready to recommit. Mixed (default) unstages them but keeps files. Hard overwrites files too, discarding uncommitted work.

blocks.title: What does cherry-pick do and when is it risky?
blocks.text: It applies the diff of one commit as a new commit elsewhere. Useful for backporting a fix. It duplicates the change under a different ID, which can cause confusing conflicts if the branches later merge.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: After "git rebase main" on your feature branch, the commit IDs on it…
quiz.why: A commit ID includes its parent. A new parent means a new commit.

quiz.q: Which is safe on a branch your team has already pulled?
quiz.why: revert only adds a commit. The others replace or remove existing commits.

lessons.title: Team workflows and how Git drives CI/CD

blocks.text: A workflow is the team's agreement on how branches are used. In trunk-based development everyone merges small changes into main at least daily and unfinished features hide behind feature flags. GitFlow uses long-lived develop and release branches with explicit hand-offs. Release branches let you patch an old version while main moves on. Whichever you choose, Git events are what trigger automation: a pull request runs CI, a merge to main builds and deploys, a tag publishes a versioned release.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Trunk-based is your App Store "phased release with remote config": ship continuously, switch features on separately. GitFlow is the old model of a release train with a code freeze and a release branch for each store submission.
Why it matters
Long-lived branches hide integration problems until the end, when they are most expensive. The workflow decides how often you integrate, and therefore how risky each release is.
Where you meet it
Trunk-based suits services deployed continuously. Release branches remain common for mobile apps, libraries and anything where several versions are supported at once.
Scenario

checkout-api is trunk-based: a pull request runs tests, merging to main builds the image tagged with the commit ID and deploys to staging, and approval promotes the same image to production. Your mobile apps, by contrast, cut release/8.38.0 so fixes can ship to the version in review while main continues.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR PR["Pull request
opened / updated"] -->|"webhook"| CI["CI: lint, test,
build (no deploy)"] M["Merge to main"] -->|"webhook"| CD["Build image :SHA
deploy to staging"] T["Tag v1.5.0"] -->|"webhook"| REL["Release: retag image :1.5.0,
changelog, promote"] CI -->|"status check"| PR

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
gitGraph
  commit id: "feat A"
  branch feature/b
  commit id: "wip B"
  checkout main
  commit id: "fix C"
  merge feature/b id: "merge B"
  commit id: "feat D" tag: "v1.5.0"
  branch release/1.5
  commit id: "hotfix" tag: "v1.5.1"
  checkout main
  commit id: "feat E"

blocks.text: Commands
Publishes a tag. On repositories where tags trigger release pipelines, this starts a release.
Lists the commits in one release that were not in the previous one: the raw material of a changelog and the first thing to read when a release misbehaves.
.git/hooks/pre-commit (a local guard)

blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs before every commit. A non-zero exit cancels the commit.
set -euo pipefail

if git diff --cached --name-only | grep -qE '(^|/)\.env$'; then
  echo "refusing to commit a .env file" >&2
