  exit 1
fi

if git diff --cached | grep -qE 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'; then
  echo "this looks like an AWS access key" >&2
  exit 1
fi

blocks.text: Hooks live in .git/hooks and are not shared by cloning, and anyone can skip them with --no-verify. Treat them as a convenience; enforce the same checks in CI.
Exercise
Experience the most common team event: someone pushed before you.

items: Read git status: your branch is behind origin/main
Make and commit a small change on main
Try to push and read the rejection
Pull, then look at the graph: either a merge commit or, with --rebase, a straight line
Push again and read the note about what it triggers
Tag the release and push the tag

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: origin/main and main point at the same commit in the graph, and you can say which webhook each push would send.
Troubleshooting

rows: Releases need a week of "stabilisation" before every launch
Long-lived branches: integration happens late and all at once.
Merge smaller changes more often and hide unfinished work behind flags.
A hotfix shipped, then the bug came back in the next release
The fix was made on the release branch and never carried to main.
Fix on main first, then cherry-pick to the release branch, and automate a check that release branches contain no unique fixes.
Pipeline did not run after a push
Webhook not delivered, or the branch or path filter excluded the change.
Check webhook deliveries in the repository settings and the trigger rules in the pipeline file.
CI is green on the branch but main breaks after merging
The branch was tested against an old main.
Require branches to be up to date before merging, or use a merge queue that tests the merge result.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Integrate at least daily.
One pipeline definition in the repository, triggered by Git events, never by hand.
Build once per commit and promote that artifact; do not rebuild per environment.
In a monorepo, trigger only the pipelines whose paths changed.

blocks.text: Security

items: Protected branches plus required reviews are your change-control record.
Restrict who may push tags that trigger releases.
Pipelines for pull requests from forks must not receive deployment secrets.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Trunk-based development versus GitFlow?
blocks.text: Trunk-based: one long-lived branch, short-lived feature branches merged at least daily, features gated by flags, releases cut from main. GitFlow: develop, feature, release and hotfix branches with scheduled releases. Trunk-based gives faster feedback and suits continuous delivery; GitFlow suits versioned products with slow release cycles, at the cost of late integration.

blocks.title: How does a Git commit become a running container?
blocks.text: The push sends a webhook to CI, which checks out that commit, tests it, builds an image tagged with the commit ID, pushes it to a registry and updates the deployment to that tag. The ID links production back to exact source.

blocks.title: Monorepo versus many repositories?
blocks.text: A monorepo makes cross-service changes atomic and tooling uniform, but needs path-based builds and scales poorly without investment. Many repos give teams independence and simple pipelines, but coordinated changes and shared-library upgrades become multi-step.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Your push is rejected as non-fast-forward. The right next step is…
quiz.why: The remote has commits you do not. Integrate them first; forcing would erase a teammate's work.

quiz.q: Why are Git hooks not enough to enforce a rule?
options: They are local and can be skipped
quiz.why: Hooks are not cloned and --no-verify bypasses them. CI is the enforcement point.

modules.title: Bash and Python Automation
modules.summary: Scripts, exit codes, conditions, loops, strict mode, cron, health checks and Python.

lessons.title: Your first scripts: variables, quoting and exit codes

blocks.text: A shell script is a text file of the same commands you type, run top to bottom. The first line (#!/usr/bin/env bash, the "shebang") says which program interprets it. Variables hold text: name="value" with no spaces around the equals sign, read back as "$name". Every command finishes with an exit code: 0 means success, anything from 1 to 255 means failure. That number, not the printed output, is how scripts, pipelines and schedulers decide what happens next.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: An exit code is a function that returns Bool and nothing else. A CI stage is simply "run this command; if it returns non-zero, stop the pipeline". Your fastlane lane fails the same way.
Why it matters
Anything you do twice by hand you will eventually do wrong. A script does it the same way every time and can be reviewed, versioned and run by a machine at 3 a.m.
Where you meet it
CI pipeline steps, container entrypoints, deploy and rollback scripts, cron jobs, server bootstrap, and the glue between tools.
Scenario

Every "sh" step in the checkout-api Jenkinsfile is a shell command whose exit code decides whether the pipeline continues. "pytest" returning 1 is the only reason a broken commit never reaches production.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD CALLER["Caller: you, cron, or a CI stage"] -->|"./script.sh arg1"| SH["bash process
has its own variables"] ENV["Environment variables
inherited from the caller"] --> SH SH -->|"starts a child process per command"| C1["curl"] SH --> C2["grep"] C1 -->|"exit code"| SH C2 -->|"exit code"| SH SH -->|"exit code 0 to 255"| CALLER SH -->|"stdout, stderr"| OUT["terminal or log file"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["./script.sh arg1 arg2"] --> B["Kernel reads the shebang,
starts bash"] B --> C["bash reads line 1"] C --> D["Expand variables
and substitutions"] D --> E["Run the command"] E --> F["Store its exit code in $?"] F --> G{"More lines?"} G -->|yes| C G -->|no| H["Script exits with the code
of the last command"]

blocks.text: Commands
Parses the script and reports syntax errors without running anything. Do this before the first real run.

blocks.code: (no output means the syntax is valid)
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: Runs a script. It needs the execute permission, and what it does to the machine depends entirely on its contents: read a script before you run it.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: "Permission denied": chmod u+x deploy.sh. "bad interpreter": wrong shebang, or Windows line endings.
Prints the exit code of the command that just finished.
A linter for shell scripts. It finds unquoted variables, unreachable code and dozens of classic mistakes. Run it in CI.
Quoting rules

blocks.code:
name="checkout api"

echo "$name"      # double quotes: variables expand, spaces preserved  -> checkout api
echo '$name'      # single quotes: completely literal                 -> $name
echo $name        # unquoted: split into two words on the space

file="my report.txt"
rm $file          # WRONG: tries to delete "my" and "report.txt"
rm "$file"        # right: one argument

today=$(date +%F)            # command substitution: capture output
count=$((count + 1))         # arithmetic
echo "${name}_backup"        # braces mark where the variable name ends

# Rule: quote every variable, "$like_this", unless you have a specific reason not to.

blocks.text: Exercise
Edit the basics script in the lab and predict each result before running it.

items: Run it unchanged and match each output line to the line of script that produced it
Change replicas to 1: which branch of the if runs?
Add a fourth environment to the for loop
Tick "Trace" and run again to see each command as bash executes it
Replace "ls /does/not/exist" with "ls /etc" and note how $? changes

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state what $? is after a successful command and after a failed one, without running it.
Troubleshooting

rows: name = "value" gives "command not found"
Spaces around = make bash treat name as a command.
Write name="value".
A path with spaces breaks the script
An unquoted variable was split into several words.
Quote it: "$path".
The script works by hand but fails in CI or cron
It depends on your interactive environment: PATH, current directory, variables from your profile.
Use absolute paths, set what you need at the top, and cd to a known directory.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Start scripts with a shebang and a one-line comment saying what it does.
Quote every variable.
Return meaningful exit codes and document them.
Run shellcheck and bash -n in CI.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never run a script piped straight from the internet (curl URL | bash) without reading it.
Do not pass secrets as command-line arguments: they are visible in ps. Use environment variables or files with mode 600.
A script run with sudo does everything as root. Keep privileged scripts short and reviewed.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is an exit code and why does it matter?
blocks.text: An integer from 0 to 255 returned by every process. 0 is success. Shells, CI systems, systemd and Kubernetes probes all decide what to do next from it, so a script that prints "error" but exits 0 is treated as a success.

blocks.title: Single quotes versus double quotes?
blocks.text: Single quotes keep everything literal. Double quotes allow variable and command substitution but still stop word splitting and globbing.

blocks.title: What does the shebang do?
blocks.text: When a file is executed, the kernel reads the first line and runs the named interpreter with the file as its argument. #!/usr/bin/env bash finds bash through PATH, which is more portable than a fixed path.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: What does echo '$HOME' print?
quiz.why: Single quotes prevent all expansion.

quiz.q: A script prints "FAILED" and then finishes normally. What does CI conclude?
options: Success, because the exit code is 0
quiz.why: CI reads the exit code, not the text. The script must exit non-zero.

lessons.title: Conditions, loops, functions and pipes

blocks.text: if runs a command and branches on its exit code; [ ... ] is itself just a command that tests files, strings and numbers. for repeats over a list of words; while repeats as long as a command succeeds. A function groups commands under a name and reads its arguments as $1, $2. A pipe feeds one command's output to the next; > writes output to a file (replacing it) and >> appends. && runs the next command only on success, || only on failure.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: if in bash is "if this call did not throw". [ -f file ] is a tiny function that returns true or false. Pipes are chained transforms on a stream, like map and filter on a Sequence.
Why it matters
Real automation has to decide (is the service already healthy?), repeat (try five times) and reuse (the same check before and after a deploy).
Where you meet it
Health checks that retry, scripts that loop over servers or environments, validation of arguments, log summaries.
Scenario

After deploying checkout-api, the pipeline runs a health check that polls /health in a loop, sleeping between attempts, and exits 1 if it never sees HTTP 200. That exit code is what triggers the automatic rollback.

blocks.text: The four structures

blocks.code:
# if: branch on the exit code of ANY command
if systemctl is-active --quiet nginx; then
  echo "nginx is running"
elif [ -f /etc/nginx/nginx.conf ]; then
  echo "installed but stopped"
else
  echo "not installed"
fi

# for: once per word
for env in dev staging production; do
  echo "checking $env"
done

# while: as long as the command succeeds
attempt=0
while [ "$attempt" -lt 5 ]; do
  attempt=$((attempt + 1))
done

# function: arguments are $1 $2 ..., "return" sets its exit code
is_healthy() {
  [ "$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "$1")" = "200" ]
}
is_healthy http://localhost:8000/health && echo "up" || echo "down"

items: Validate arguments at the top and exit with a usage message.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never build a command by pasting untrusted input into a string and running it (eval, or unquoted variables): that is command injection.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between [ and [[ in bash?
blocks.text: [ is the portable test command: its arguments are ordinary words, so unquoted variables can break it. [[ is bash syntax: no word splitting inside, pattern and regex matching with == and =~, and && / || work inside. Use [[ in bash scripts and [ when the script must run under plain sh.

blocks.title: What does 2>&1 mean?
blocks.text: Redirect file descriptor 2 (stderr) to wherever descriptor 1 (stdout) currently points. Order matters: "> file 2>&1" sends both to the file; "2>&1 > file" sends only stdout to the file.

blocks.title: Write a retry loop for a flaky command.
blocks.text: for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do cmd && break; sleep $((i * 2)); done, then check whether it ultimately succeeded and exit non-zero if not. Mention backoff, a maximum and that only idempotent actions should be retried.

options: Runs cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeded
Runs cmd2 only if cmd1 failed

quiz.q: Which test checks that a directory exists?
quiz.why: -d is directory, -f is regular file, -z is empty string.

lessons.title: Scripts you can trust in production: strict mode, idempotency, cron

blocks.text: A production script must stop when something goes wrong, be safe to run twice, and tell someone when it fails. "set -euo pipefail" is strict mode: -e exits on the first failing command, -u treats an unset variable as an error, pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails. Idempotent means running it again leaves the system in the same state instead of doing the work twice. cron runs commands on a schedule written as five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Strict mode is the difference between try! and ignoring errors. Idempotency is a PUT rather than a POST: retrying it is harmless. A non-idempotent deploy script is like a "place order" button with no idempotency key.
Why it matters
Without strict mode a script carries on after a failed step and does damage with half-built state: the classic example is cd failing and the following rm -rf running in the wrong directory.
Where you meet it
Deploy and rollback scripts, backups, log rotation, certificate renewal, health checks, runbooks turned into code.
Scenario

The incident you fixed by hand in the Linux module (checkout-api cannot start because its port is held) is written here as a script. It checks health first, refuses to act if the situation is not the one it understands, fixes the cause, verifies from the customer side, and exits non-zero if the fix did not work.

blocks.text: Strict mode, cleanup and log rotation

blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail          # stop on error, on unset variables, on failed pipe stages

workdir=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() { rm -rf "$workdir"; }
trap cleanup EXIT          # runs on success, failure or Ctrl+C

: "${DEPLOY_ENV:?DEPLOY_ENV must be set}"     # fail fast with a clear message

# ---------- /etc/cron.d/checkout-backup ----------
# m  h  dom mon dow  user  command
30 2  *   *   *    app   /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1

# ---------- /etc/logrotate.d/checkout ----------
/var/log/checkout/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 14          # keep 14 old files
    compress
    missingok
    notifempty
    copytruncate       # for apps that keep the file open
}

blocks.text: trap ... EXIT and mktemp are real bash but are not implemented by the lab interpreter. The cron explainer in the script lab turns any five-field schedule into words.

cron has a minimal PATH and environment, and no terminal.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: set -euo pipefail at the top of every script.
Make scripts idempotent: check the current state before changing it.
Verify the outcome the user cares about, not that the commands ran.
A backup you have never restored is not a backup: test restores on a schedule.
Keep cron entries, scripts and logrotate config in version control.

blocks.text: Security

items: Scheduled jobs often run with elevated rights: restrict who can edit them and the scripts they call.
A script writable by a less privileged user but run by root is a privilege-escalation path. Check file ownership.
Backups contain everything: encrypt them and control access as tightly as the original data.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What does set -euo pipefail do, and what are its gotchas?
blocks.text: -e exits on a failing command, -u errors on unset variables, pipefail makes a pipeline fail when any stage fails. Gotchas: -e does not apply inside conditions or before && and ||, grep returning 1 for "no match" will stop the script unless handled, and behaviour inside functions called from conditions surprises people.

blocks.title: What makes a script idempotent, and why does it matter?
blocks.text: Running it any number of times produces the same end state. It checks before acting: create the directory only if missing, skip if already healthy. It matters because automation retries, and a retry of a non-idempotent step does the work twice.

blocks.title: How would you make sure a nightly backup is actually working?
blocks.text: Exit non-zero on failure, log to a known file, send a heartbeat on success and alert when it is missing, monitor backup age and size, and run automated test restores.

lessons.title: Python for automation: when a script outgrows Bash

blocks.text: Bash is ideal for gluing commands together. Once a script needs real data structures, JSON, HTTP calls with error handling, or more than about fifty lines of logic, Python is clearer and safer. The same rules still apply: return a meaningful exit code, be idempotent, time out every network call.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Bash is a Shortcuts automation: perfect for chaining existing actions. Python is writing the small command-line tool properly, with types, functions and tests.
Why it matters
Parsing JSON with grep and sed breaks the first time the format shifts. Python has a real parser, real exceptions and a standard library that covers HTTP, files, dates and subprocesses.
Where you meet it
Calling cloud and Kubernetes APIs, release tooling, data migration helpers, custom health checks, anything that reads or writes JSON or YAML.
Scenario

The health check that gates a checkout-api deploy exists in both languages in this repository. The Python version distinguishes "the server answered with an error" from "the server could not be reached", which the pipeline can report differently.

blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Poll a health endpoint until it answers 200, or give up.

The same job as examples/bash/healthcheck.sh, using only the standard library.
Usage: python3 healthcheck.py http://localhost:8000/health [attempts]
"""
import sys
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request


def check(url: str, timeout: float = 3.0) -> int:
    """Return the HTTP status, or 0 when the server cannot be reached."""
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout) as response:
            return response.status
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
        return error.code  # the server answered, with an error status
    except (urllib.error.URLError, TimeoutError, OSError):
        return 0  # DNS failure, connection refused or timeout


def main() -> int:
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        print("usage: healthcheck.py <url> [attempts]", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    url = sys.argv[1]
    attempts = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 10

    for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
        status = check(url)
        if status == 200:
            print(f"healthy after {attempt} attempt(s)")
            return 0
        print(f"attempt {attempt}/{attempts}: got {status}, retrying in 2s")
        time.sleep(2)

    print(f"unhealthy: {url} never returned 200", file=sys.stderr)
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

blocks.text: Standard library only, so it runs anywhere Python 3 is installed. This file was executed for real against a local test server while building the academy: exit 0 when healthy, exit 1 when unreachable.

lessons.title: Apache HTTP Server: virtual hosts and reverse proxying

blocks.text: Apache is a web server, like Nginx. It serves files, terminates HTTPS and passes requests on to an application. You configure it with virtual hosts, one per site, and switch features on by enabling modules. You will meet it in older systems and shared hosting, so you need to be able to read and fix its configuration.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Two makes of car. The pedals do the same job in both, but the switches are in different places. If you can drive one, you can drive the other after ten minutes of finding the indicators.
Why it matters

A large share of existing websites still run on Apache, and many companies have it somewhere. Knowing only Nginx leaves you stuck the day an incident lands on an Apache box. The concepts are the ones you already know; the file names and commands differ.
Where you meet it
Legacy applications, PHP sites, shared hosting, and enterprise software that ships with it. On Debian and Ubuntu the package and service are called apache2; on Red Hat systems, httpd.
Scenario

checkout-api is moved onto an older server that already runs Apache for another site. Instead of installing Nginx beside it, you add a virtual host that terminates HTTPS and proxies to the application on port 8000, exactly as the Nginx lesson did.

blocks.caption: Changes the local environment

blocks.text: Debian and Ubuntu: enables the modules needed for HTTPS and reverse proxying. Takes effect after a restart.

A reverse-proxy virtual host (illustrative)

blocks.code:
# /etc/apache2/sites-available/shop.conf
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName api.shop.example
    Redirect permanent / https://api.shop.example/
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName api.shop.example

    SSLEngine on
    SSLCertificateFile    /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.shop.example/fullchain.pem
    SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.shop.example/privkey.pem

    # Reverse proxy to checkout-api on this machine.
    ProxyPreserveHost On
    ProxyPass        /health !
    ProxyPass        / http://127.0.0.1:8000/
    ProxyPassReverse / http://127.0.0.1:8000/
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"

    ErrorLog  ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/shop-error.log
    CustomLog ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/shop-access.log combined
</VirtualHost>

Check the application is running and listening on the address in ProxyPass. On Red Hat systems SELinux may block the connection.
403 Forbidden for static files
File permissions, or no Require directive granting access to the directory.
Check ownership and the Directory block.
Changes have no effect
The site is in sites-available but not enabled, or Apache was not reloaded.
a2ensite, configtest, reload.
Slow under many connections
The prefork model uses one process per connection.
Use the event MPM, and put long-lived connections behind a proxy designed for them.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: configtest before every reload.
Reload, not restart, for configuration changes.
One file per site, with its own logs.
Define an explicit default virtual host that returns nothing useful.
Use the event MPM unless a module requires prefork.
Avoid .htaccess where you control the main configuration: it is read on every request.
Keep the configuration in Git and deploy it like code.

blocks.text: Security

items: Hide version details: ServerTokens Prod and ServerSignature Off.
Disable modules you do not use.
Never leave ProxyRequests On: it turns the server into an open proxy.
Redirect HTTP to HTTPS and use current TLS settings.
Restrict directories explicitly with Require; do not rely on files being hard to guess.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Apache versus Nginx?
blocks.text: Both serve files, terminate TLS and reverse proxy. Nginx uses an event-driven design that handles many connections with little memory. Apache uses processes or threads per connection (with an event mode for keep-alive), has per-directory .htaccess files and a very large module ecosystem. New systems usually choose Nginx; Apache is common in existing ones.

blocks.title: How does Apache choose a virtual host?
blocks.text: By the address and port the request arrived on, then by matching the Host header against ServerName and ServerAlias. If none match, the first virtual host defined for that port is used.

blocks.title: What is an MPM?
blocks.text: A multi-processing module: how Apache handles connections. Prefork uses one process per connection, worker uses threads, event uses threads and hands idle keep-alive connections to a listener so they do not hold a worker.

blocks.title: What is .htaccess and why avoid it?
blocks.text: A per-directory configuration file read at request time, which lets users without access to the main configuration change settings. It costs a file lookup on every request and scatters configuration, so prefer the main configuration when you control it.

blocks.title: How do you apply an Apache change with no downtime?
blocks.text: apachectl configtest, then a graceful reload, which lets workers finish current requests before picking up the new configuration.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: No ServerName matches the request. Apache…
options: uses the first virtual host for that port
quiz.why: The first one defined is the default.

quiz.q: Before reloading you should run…
quiz.why: It catches syntax errors before they matter.

quiz.q: "Invalid command ProxyPass" means…
options: a typing mistake in the URL
the proxy module is not enabled
quiz.why: Directives come from modules.

lessons.title: Servers and SSH: getting onto a machine you cannot touch

blocks.text: A server is a computer that runs your software for other people. It can be a physical machine you rent whole (bare metal), a virtual machine (a slice of a physical one, which is what a cloud "instance" is), or a container on someone else's machine. Each has a private IP address inside its network and may also have a public one reachable from the internet. You operate it through SSH: an encrypted remote shell. SSH logs you in with a key pair: the server holds your public key, and you prove you hold the matching private key without ever sending it.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A key pair is like App Store code signing. The public half is the certificate anyone may see; the private half stays in your Keychain and signs proof that you are you. Losing the private key means being locked out; leaking it means someone else is you.
Why it matters

Servers sit in data centres with no screen or keyboard. Everything from the first install to the 3 a.m. fix happens over a network connection, so that connection has to be both convenient and hard to forge.
Where you meet it
Cloud VMs (EC2, Compute Engine, Azure VMs, Hetzner, DigitalOcean), bastion hosts in front of private networks, CI agents, and Kubernetes nodes when something is wrong below the cluster.
Scenario

Before checkout-api ran on Kubernetes it ran on one Ubuntu VM. The deploy user logs in with a key, the database server has no public IP at all and is reached by jumping through the web server, and nobody knows the root password because root cannot log in.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR L["Your laptop
private key"] -->|"SSH, port 22"| B["shop-web
public IP 203.0.113.10
private IP 10.0.1.15"] B -->|"ProxyJump"| D["shop-db
private IP 10.0.20.15
no public IP"] I["Internet"] -->|"80 / 443"| B I -. "no route" .-> D subgraph VPC["Private network 10.0.0.0/16"] B D end

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram participant C as Your laptop participant S as Server (sshd) C->>S: TCP connect to port 22 S-->>C: Host key (the server's identity) Note over C: First time: "trust this fingerprint?"
saved in ~/.ssh/known_hosts C->>S: Encrypted channel agreed C->>S: I am "deploy", and I hold this public key S-->>C: Prove it: sign this challenge C->>S: Signature made with the private key Note over S: Public key is in
~deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys? S-->>C: Logged in: a shell as deploy

blocks.text: Commands
Connects with debug output showing each step: which keys are offered, which is accepted, where it stops. The first tool for any SSH problem.
Lists the keys your SSH agent is holding. The agent keeps unlocked keys in memory so you type the passphrase once.
~/.ssh/config on your machine

blocks.code:
# ~/.ssh/config on YOUR machine: short names for servers.
# Then:  ssh shop-web      instead of      ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 deploy@203.0.113.10

Host shop-web
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User deploy
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    IdentitiesOnly yes

# A private server reached THROUGH the bastion host (no public IP of its own).
Host shop-db
    HostName 10.0.20.15
    User deploy
    ProxyJump shop-web

blocks.text: ProxyJump reaches a private server through a public one without copying your private key onto the bastion.
Exercise
Create a key pair and read what protects it.

items: Generate an ed25519 key in the simulated terminal
List ~/.ssh in long format: what are the modes of the two files, and of the directory?
Print the public key. This is the only part you ever give to a server
Run ss -tlnp and find which address sshd listens on
On your own Mac: run ssh-add -l and cat ~/.ssh/config to see what you already have

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: The private key is mode 600, the directory is 700, and you can say which file is safe to paste into a ticket.
Troubleshooting

rows: Permission denied (publickey)
The server does not have your public key for that user, you are offering a different key, or permissions on ~/.ssh on the server are too open.
ssh -v shows which keys were offered. Check ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server and that ~/.ssh is 700 and the file 600.
Connection timed out
A firewall or security group drops port 22, or the IP is wrong.
Check the cloud security group and the server firewall. A timeout means packets vanish; it is never a key problem.
Connection refused
The host is reachable but sshd is not running or listens on another port.
Use the cloud provider's console access to check systemctl status ssh.
WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED
The server's host key differs from the one you saved: the server was rebuilt, the IP was reused, or someone is intercepting.
Confirm the rebuild with whoever owns the server, then ssh-keygen -R HOST. Do not blindly delete the entry.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: One key pair per person per device, protected by a passphrase.
Give servers names in ~/.ssh/config.
Reach private servers through a bastion with ProxyJump, never by copying keys onto servers.
Prefer short-lived access (SSH certificates, cloud session managers) over long-lived keys as the team grows.

blocks.text: Security

items: The private key never leaves your machine and is never committed, emailed or pasted.
Remove a person's public key from every server the day they leave.
Agent forwarding (-A) lets root on the remote server use your keys. Use ProxyJump instead.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does SSH key authentication work?
blocks.text: The server holds the user's public key in authorized_keys. During login the client signs a session-specific challenge with the private key and the server verifies the signature with the public key. The private key is never transmitted, so nothing reusable can be captured.

blocks.title: Difference between a virtual machine and a bare-metal server?
blocks.text: Bare metal is the whole physical machine: full performance and isolation, slow to provision. A VM is a slice presented by a hypervisor: created in seconds, resizable, shares hardware with others. Cloud instances are VMs.

blocks.title: What is a bastion host?
blocks.text: The single hardened server with a public IP through which administrators reach machines in private subnets. It shrinks the attack surface to one audited entry point.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which file do you copy to a server so you can log in?
quiz.why: The .pub file is the public key. The private key never leaves your machine.

quiz.q: "Connection timed out" on SSH most likely means…
quiz.why: Authentication errors come back immediately. A timeout means no reply at all.

lessons.title: The first hour on a new server: users, SSH hardening, firewall, updates

blocks.text: A new server with a public IP is scanned by automated attackers within minutes. Four changes close most of the doors: use a personal account with sudo instead of root, allow SSH logins by key only, run a firewall that drops everything except the ports you serve, and keep packages patched. The order matters, because two of these can lock you out of your own server.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: It is the server version of App Transport Security plus Keychain rules: deny by default, open exactly what is needed, and never ship with the debug door open.
Why it matters
Almost every real compromise of a small server is one of: a guessed password, an unpatched package, or a service that was never meant to be public but was listening on 0.0.0.0.
Where you meet it
Any VM you run yourself. On managed platforms the provider does part of this, but security groups and patching remain yours.
Scenario

The shop's web server allows 22 from the office, 80 and 443 from anywhere, and nothing else. PostgreSQL listens on localhost only, so even a firewall mistake does not expose it. Two independent layers have to fail before the database is reachable.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR NET["Internet"] --> SG["Cloud security group
(outside the server)"] SG --> UFW["ufw firewall
(on the server)"] UFW -->|"22 from office only"| SSHD["sshd
keys only, no root"] UFW -->|"80, 443"| NGX["nginx"] UFW -. "everything else dropped" .-> X["denied"] NGX --> APP["checkout-api
127.0.0.1:8000"] APP --> PG["postgres
127.0.0.1:5432"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Log in as the default user"] --> B["Create your own user, add to sudo"] B --> C["Install your public key for that user"] C --> D["Open a SECOND terminal and
confirm the new login works"] D --> E["Disable root login and passwords
sshd -t, then reload"] E --> F["ufw allow OpenSSH"] F --> G["ufw allow 80, 443"] G --> H["ufw enable"] H --> I["apt update and upgrade,
enable unattended upgrades"] I --> J["Verify from OUTSIDE:
only 22, 80, 443 answer"]

blocks.text: Commands
Checks the SSH server configuration for errors. Silence means it is valid. Always run before reloading sshd.
Applies new SSH settings. Existing sessions stay open, which is your safety net: test a new login before you close the old one.
Installs security updates automatically every day. Decide deliberately whether it may reboot the server.
examples/ssh/sshd_hardening.conf

blocks.code:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf
# Test with:  sudo sshd -t      Apply with:  sudo systemctl reload ssh
# Keep your current session open and confirm a NEW login works before closing it.

PermitRootLogin no                 # nobody logs in as root; use sudo
PasswordAuthentication no          # keys only: ends password guessing
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AllowUsers deploy                  # only these accounts may log in
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 30
X11Forwarding no

blocks.text: Dropping this file into /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ overrides the defaults without editing the main file.
Exercise
Complete the hardening checkpoints beside the terminal, including the mistake everyone makes once.

items: Try to enable the firewall straight away and read what would have happened
Allow SSH, then web traffic, then enable
Read the rule table
Run ss -tlnp: which services listen on 0.0.0.0 and which on 127.0.0.1?
Explain why port 5432 is safe twice over
Add a rule allowing 5432 from a single IP, then delete it by number

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: All checkpoints are green and you can name the two layers protecting the database.
Troubleshooting

rows: Locked out after enabling the firewall
No rule allowed SSH before the default-deny policy took effect.
Use the cloud provider's serial or web console to log in and run ufw allow OpenSSH. Prevention: allow SSH first, and test from a second terminal.
Locked out after editing sshd_config
Password login was disabled before the key was installed, or a syntax error stopped sshd.
Console access again. Always sshd -t, reload not restart, and keep one session open while testing a new one.
The port is allowed in ufw but still unreachable
The cloud security group is a separate firewall in front of the server.
Open the port in both. Then check the service listens on 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1.
Thousands of failed SSH logins in the logs
Internet-wide bots guessing passwords. Normal for any public IP.
With password authentication off they cannot succeed. Add fail2ban or restrict port 22 to known addresses to cut the noise.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Deny by default; open ports one at a time with a reason.
Restrict SSH to known source addresses or a VPN where you can.
Bind internal services to 127.0.0.1 or a private interface.
Patch automatically and reboot on a schedule.
Put all of this in a script or image so the next server is identical.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never leave PasswordAuthentication on for an internet-facing server.
sudo for named users leaves an audit trail; a shared root password does not.
Check what is actually exposed from outside (nmap from another network), not what you believe is configured.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: You get a fresh Ubuntu server with a public IP. What do you do first?
blocks.text: Create a personal sudo user with my key, verify I can log in, disable root and password logins, enable a default-deny firewall allowing only SSH and the service ports, apply updates and enable automatic security updates, and confirm from outside what is reachable. Then capture those steps as code.

blocks.title: Security group versus host firewall?
blocks.text: A security group is enforced by the cloud network before traffic reaches the instance and is managed through the provider API. A host firewall runs inside the OS. Using both gives defence in depth: one misconfiguration alone does not expose a service.

blocks.title: Why bind a database to 127.0.0.1?
blocks.text: It then accepts connections only from the same host, whatever the firewall says. It turns an exposure that would need one mistake into one that needs two.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which must you do BEFORE "ufw enable" on a remote server?
quiz.why: The default policy denies incoming connections, including your own SSH session.

quiz.q: A service listens on 127.0.0.1:5432. Who can connect?
options: Only processes on the same server
quiz.why: The loopback address is reachable only from the machine itself.

lessons.title: Running several applications on one server

blocks.text: One server has one IP address but 65,535 ports. Each application listens on its own port: the API on 8000, the admin dashboard on 3000, Redis on 6379, PostgreSQL on 5432. Only one of them, the reverse proxy, faces the internet on 80 and 443. It reads each request's Host header and path and forwards it to the right local port. systemd keeps every process running and restarts it if it dies.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The server is an office building with one street address. nginx is reception: visitors arrive at the front door and are sent to the right floor by who they ask for. The floors do not have their own street doors.
Why it matters
A small product does not need a machine per component, and one public entry point means one place for TLS, logging and access rules.
Where you meet it
Side projects, internal tools, staging environments, and most products in their first years. It is also exactly the problem containers and Kubernetes later solve at larger scale.
Scenario

The shop runs on one Ubuntu VM: nginx serves the storefront files and proxies /api/ to checkout-api, admin.shop.example.com goes to the dashboard process, and a background worker reads jobs from Redis. Five systemd units, two open ports.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR U["Internet"] -->|"80 / 443"| N["nginx
the only public listener"] subgraph S["One Ubuntu server"] N -->|"Host: shop.example.com, path /"| ST["static files
/var/www/shop"] N -->|"path /api/"| API["checkout-api
127.0.0.1:8000"] N -->|"Host: admin.shop.example.com"| ADM["admin dashboard
127.0.0.1:3000"] API --> PG["PostgreSQL
127.0.0.1:5432"] API --> R["Redis
127.0.0.1:6379"] W["background worker
(no port)"] --> R W --> PG end

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A["Request arrives on port 443"] --> B["nginx reads the Host header"]
  B --> C{"Which server block?"}
  C -->|"shop.example.com"| D{"Which location?"}
  C -->|"admin.shop.example.com"| E["proxy to 127.0.0.1:3000"]
  D -->|"/api/..."| F["proxy to 127.0.0.1:8000"]
  D -->|"anything else"| G["serve a file from disk"]
  F --> H["checkout-api answers"]
  H --> I["nginx relays the response"]

blocks.text: Commands
Lists every running service: the quickest inventory of what a server is doing.
Asks nginx for a specific virtual host without needing DNS. Useful for testing a new site before its DNS record exists.

rows: send a header

blocks.text: examples/systemd/checkout-api.service

blocks.code:
[Unit]
Description=Checkout API (FastAPI)
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=app
Group=app
WorkingDirectory=/srv/checkout
EnvironmentFile=/srv/checkout/.env
ExecStart=/srv/checkout/venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2

# Hardening: the service cannot gain privileges or write outside its own directory.
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true
ReadWritePaths=/srv/checkout

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

blocks.text: One unit file per application. The nginx side of this setup is examples/nginx/many-apps.conf, loaded in the sandbox below.
Exercise
Trace three requests to three different applications through one nginx.

items: Send each preset request and read which server block and location handled it
Send http://unknown.example.org/ : which site answers, and why?
Mark checkout-api #1 as down and request /api/health: what does the customer see, and what does the storefront do?
Add a fourth app: a location /worker-status/ proxied to 127.0.0.1:8001, and test it
On paper, list the five systemd units this server needs

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain why a crashed API returns 502 for /api/ while the storefront keeps working.
Troubleshooting

rows: bind: address already in use
Two applications were configured for the same port.
ss -tlnp to see who holds it. Keep a written port map.
The wrong site appears for a hostname
No server_name matched, so nginx used the default server block.
Check server_name spelling and DNS. Add an explicit default_server that returns 444 so mistakes are obvious.
One app's memory leak takes down all of them
They share one machine with no limits; the kernel OOM killer picks a victim.
Set MemoryMax= in each systemd unit, and move the database to its own machine first.
After a reboot half the apps are down
They were started by hand and never enabled.
systemctl enable each unit, then test with a real reboot.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Only the proxy listens publicly; everything else binds to 127.0.0.1.
One systemd unit and one system user per application.
Keep a port map in the repository.
The database is the first thing to move to its own server or a managed service.
Rebuild the server from scripts regularly to prove you can.

blocks.text: Security

items: Separate system users mean one compromised app cannot read another's secrets.
The admin dashboard needs more than an obscure hostname: restrict it by source IP or put authentication in front.
One server is one failure domain and one blast radius. Know when you have outgrown it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How can many websites share one IP address and port?
blocks.text: The client sends the hostname in the HTTP Host header (and in the TLS SNI field). The web server picks the matching virtual host. That is name-based virtual hosting.

blocks.title: When would you stop running everything on one server?
blocks.text: When you need availability through a machine failure, independent scaling of components, isolation between workloads, or zero-downtime deploys. The first step is usually moving the database out, then adding a second app server behind a load balancer.

blocks.title: What does a reverse proxy do that the app could not do itself?
blocks.text: It terminates TLS, serves static files efficiently, routes by host and path, buffers slow clients, applies limits and logs every request in one consistent place, so each application stays simple and private.

blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Two processes on one server both want port 8000. What happens?
quiz.why: A listening address and port belongs to one socket.

quiz.q: How does nginx tell shop.example.com from admin.shop.example.com on the same IP?
quiz.why: Both names resolve to one IP; the requested name travels inside the request.

modules.title: DNS, HTTP, HTTPS and TLS
modules.summary: Certificates, the chain of trust, Let's Encrypt, renewal, and pointing or moving a domain.

lessons.title: TLS certificates, Let's Encrypt and automatic renewal

blocks.text: A TLS certificate is a signed statement: "this public key belongs to shop.example.com, valid from this date to that date". It is signed by a certificate authority (CA), whose own certificate is signed by a root that browsers and operating systems already trust. That is the chain of trust. Let's Encrypt is a free CA that issues certificates automatically: a client such as Certbot proves you control the domain by answering a challenge, receives the certificate, configures the web server, and renews it before it expires. Certificates are deliberately short-lived, so renewal must be automatic.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: It is the same model as Apple code signing: Apple's root signs an intermediate, which signs your distribution certificate, which signs the app. A device trusts the app because it can follow that chain to a root it already holds. And like provisioning profiles, certificates expire and take the product down with them if nobody is watching.
Why it matters
Without TLS anyone on the network path can read and alter traffic. Without certificates, encryption alone would not tell you who you are encrypting to.
Where you meet it
Every public website and API, service-to-service traffic inside clusters, database connections, and the Kubernetes API itself.
Scenario

shop.example.com and api.shop.example.com share one Let's Encrypt certificate. Certbot's timer checks twice a day and renews when about a third of the lifetime remains. An external monitor alerts at 14 days left, because the renewal job failing silently is the usual way certificates expire.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD R["Root CA certificate
pre-installed in every client"] -->|signs| I["Intermediate CA
(for example Let's Encrypt R13)"] I -->|signs| L["Leaf certificate
CN / SAN: shop.example.com
valid 90 days"] L --- K["Private key
stays on your server, mode 600"] S["Your server sends:
leaf + intermediate (fullchain.pem)"] --> C["Client verifies: chain to a trusted root,
dates, hostname, signature"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram participant B as Certbot (on your server) participant CA as Let's Encrypt participant D as DNS / your web server B->>CA: I want a certificate for shop.example.com CA-->>B: Prove control: serve this token at
/.well-known/acme-challenge/TOKEN B->>D: Place the token (HTTP-01 challenge) CA->>D: GET http://shop.example.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/TOKEN D-->>CA: The token CA-->>B: Verified. Here is your certificate B->>B: Install fullchain.pem and privkey.pem,
reload nginx, schedule renewal

blocks.text: Commands
Rehearses renewal of every certificate against the staging service. Nothing is changed. Run it after any change to nginx, the firewall or DNS.
Decodes a certificate file: who it is for, who signed it, when it is valid and which hostnames it covers.

blocks.code:
subject=CN=shop.example.com
issuer=C=US, O=Let's Encrypt, CN=R13
notAfter=Jan 12 08:14:02 2027 GMT
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: Shows when the renewal timer last ran and when it runs next.
examples/nginx/https.conf
ssl_certificate must point at fullchain.pem, not cert.pem. Certbot writes this file for you when run with --nginx.
Exercise
Recognise each certificate failure from the client side, and see why fixed renewal schedules are being retired.

items: Open each scenario in the lab and read the curl error number and message
For "missing intermediate": why does it work in a desktop browser and fail in your mobile app?
On the timeline, switch off automatic renewal and drag forward: on which day does the first customer notice?
Change the lifetime to 45 days: would a cron job that renews every 60 days work?
On your Mac, inspect a real site: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can map curl (60) messages to expired, wrong hostname, missing intermediate and self-signed without the lab.
Troubleshooting

rows: certificate has expired
Renewal stopped working and nobody was alerted.
Renew, reload, verify from outside; then fix the renewal path and add expiry monitoring.
Certbot: "Timeout during connect (likely firewall problem)"
Let's Encrypt could not reach port 80 on the address the domain resolves to.
Check the DNS A record, the security group and ufw for port 80. The HTTP challenge needs port 80 even if the site is HTTPS-only.
Works in the browser, fails in curl and in the app
The server sends only the leaf certificate.
Use fullchain.pem. Test with openssl s_client, which shows the chain the server actually sends.
The certificate was renewed but clients still see the old one
nginx was not reloaded, so it still holds the old file in memory.
Add a deploy hook: certbot renew --deploy-hook "systemctl reload nginx".
too many certificates already issued
A rate limit, usually hit by a script requesting new certificates in a loop.
Wait for the limit window, and use --dry-run or the staging environment while testing.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Automate issuance and renewal; never renew by hand on a calendar reminder.
Renew at about two thirds of the lifetime, not on a fixed number of days.
Monitor days-to-expiry from outside and alert at 14 days.
Redirect HTTP to HTTPS and send HSTS once you are sure HTTPS works everywhere.
TLS 1.2 minimum, 1.3 preferred.

blocks.text: Security

items: The private key is the secret. Mode 600, never in Git, never in a container image, never in a ticket.
If a key leaks, revoke the certificate and issue a new key pair: renewing with the same key does not help.
Disabling certificate verification in a client removes the protection entirely. Do not ship it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What does a client verify about a server certificate?
blocks.text: That the chain of signatures leads to a root it trusts, that the current time is within the validity period, that the requested hostname appears in the subject alternative names, and that the server proves possession of the private key during the handshake. Revocation may also be checked.

blocks.title: How does Let's Encrypt verify domain ownership?
blocks.text: Through an ACME challenge. HTTP-01: the CA fetches a token from http://domain/.well-known/acme-challenge/. DNS-01: you publish a TXT record, which also allows wildcard certificates and works for servers not reachable on port 80.

blocks.title: Why are certificate lifetimes getting shorter?
blocks.text: Short lifetimes limit the damage of a leaked key and of mis-issuance, since revocation is unreliable in practice. Let's Encrypt issues 90-day certificates today and has published a schedule down to 64 days in February 2027 and 45 days in February 2028; industry rules cap all public certificates at 47 days from 2029. This only works with automation.

blocks.title: A certificate expired in production. What do you do, in order?
blocks.text: Renew and reload to restore service, verify from outside, then find why renewal failed (logs, challenge reachability, hook), add expiry alerting, and write it up. The lasting fix is monitoring the outcome, not the job.
