blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which file should ssl_certificate point at?
quiz.why: fullchain.pem holds the leaf and the intermediate, so clients can build the chain.

quiz.q: curl says "unable to get local issuer certificate" but Chrome works. The likely cause is…
options: Missing intermediate in what the server sends
quiz.why: Browsers can fetch or cache intermediates; strict clients cannot.

lessons.title: Pointing a domain at your server, and moving it without downtime

blocks.text: You rent a domain name from a registrar. The registrar records which name servers are authoritative for it. On those name servers you create records: an A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, a CNAME maps a name to another name. To put a site live you create an A record for the server's public IP, wait for it to resolve, then request a certificate. To move a site you lower the record's TTL in advance, run old and new servers side by side, switch the record, and only then retire the old one.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The registrar is the phone company that owns your number; the name servers are the directory that says which desk the number rings; the TTL is how long callers keep the old desk number in their contacts before asking again.
Why it matters
DNS is the first step of every request and the slowest to correct, because answers are cached all over the world. Most "the site is down for some users" incidents during a migration are DNS caching.
Where you meet it
Launching a site, adding a subdomain, migrating between servers or providers, failing over between regions, and proving domain ownership for certificates and email.
Scenario

The shop moves from one VM to a load balancer. A day before, the A record's TTL goes from an hour to 60 seconds. On the day the record is switched, both old and new keep serving for a while, traffic on the old server is watched until it reaches zero, then the TTL is raised again and the old server is removed.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD REG["Registrar
you own shop.example.com
NS -> ns1.dnshost.net"] --> NS["Authoritative name servers
(your DNS provider)"] NS --> Z["Zone records"] Z --> A1["shop.example.com A 203.0.113.10 TTL 300"] Z --> A2["api.shop.example.com A 203.0.113.10"] Z --> C1["www CNAME shop.example.com"] Z --> T1["_acme-challenge TXT (certificate proof)"] A1 --> SRV["Your server / load balancer"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Day -1: lower TTL to 60s"] --> B["Wait at least the OLD TTL"] B --> C["Build the new server; test it by IP
with curl --resolve"] C --> D["Switch the A record to the new IP"] D --> E["Both servers keep serving"] E --> F{"Traffic on the old
server reached zero?"} F -->|no| E F -->|yes| G["Raise TTL back to 300-3600s"] G --> H["Retire the old server"] D -. "something wrong?" .-> R["Switch the record back:
takes 60s, not an hour"]

blocks.text: Commands
Shows which name servers are authoritative for a domain: where its records really live.
Asks an authoritative server directly, bypassing every cache. Use it to check a change took effect at the source.
Sends a request to a specific IP while using the real hostname for TLS and the Host header. This tests a new server before DNS points at it.

rows: `--resolve HOST:PORT:IP`
override DNS for this one request

blocks.text: A small zone

blocks.code:
; name                     TTL    type   value
shop.example.com.          300    A      203.0.113.10
api.shop.example.com.      300    A      203.0.113.10
www.shop.example.com.      3600   CNAME  shop.example.com.
shop.example.com.          3600   MX     10 mail.provider.example.
shop.example.com.          3600   TXT    "v=spf1 include:provider.example ~all"

; The zone apex (shop.example.com itself) cannot be a CNAME.
; Use A / AAAA records, or the provider's ALIAS / ANAME feature for load balancers.

blocks.text: Exercise
Plan a zero-downtime move of the shop to a new IP, with the exact commands.

items: In the terminal, look up shop.example.com and read the TTL in the answer
Write the five steps of the migration in order, with a rollback for each
Write the curl --resolve command you would use to test the new server before the switch
Which record would you need for a wildcard certificate, and why can it not be validated over HTTP?
On your Mac, find the name servers and TTL of a domain you use with dig

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Your plan never has a moment where a cached answer points at a server that is switched off.
Troubleshooting

rows: Some users reach the new server, others the old
Resolvers are still serving the old record until its TTL expires.
Expected during a switch. Keep the old server running; next time lower the TTL a day ahead.
The record is correct at the provider but does not resolve
The registrar points at different name servers than the ones you edited.
dig +short NS domain and compare with where you made the change.
Certificate issuance fails right after creating a record
The CA's resolvers do not see the new record yet, or a negative answer is cached.
Query the authoritative server directly, wait, retry.
A deleted cloud resource's hostname now serves someone else's content
A dangling CNAME pointed at a resource that was released and re-registered by a stranger.
Remove the record. Delete DNS records before deleting the resources they point to.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Lower TTLs a day before a planned change and raise them afterwards.
Test the new target by IP before switching.
Keep DNS records in code (Terraform) with review.
Turn on registrar lock and auto-renew for the domain itself.

blocks.text: Security

items: The registrar account controls everything: protect it with strong MFA and few users.
Dangling records lead to subdomain takeover.
CAA records restrict which certificate authorities may issue for your domain.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you migrate a live site to a new IP without downtime?
blocks.text: Lower the TTL in advance and wait out the old one, bring up and test the new target by IP, switch the record, keep both serving until the old one is idle, then raise the TTL and decommission. Keep a rollback at each step.

blocks.title: Why can the apex of a domain not be a CNAME?
blocks.text: A CNAME must be the only record at its name, but the apex must also hold SOA and NS records. Providers offer ALIAS or ANAME records that behave like a CNAME but answer with addresses.

blocks.title: Registrar versus DNS provider?
blocks.text: The registrar sells the name and tells the registry which name servers are authoritative. The DNS provider runs those name servers and holds the records. They can be the same company or different ones.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: When should you lower a record's TTL for a migration?
options: At the moment of the switch
At least one old-TTL period before the switch
quiz.why: Resolvers that cached the record with the old TTL keep it until that time passes.

quiz.q: Which command queries the authoritative server and bypasses caches?
quiz.why: Naming the server with @ asks it directly.

modules.title: Nginx and Reverse Proxies
modules.summary: Server blocks, location matching, reverse proxying, load balancing and failover.

lessons.title: Nginx configuration: server blocks and location matching

blocks.text: An nginx configuration is a tree of directives. A directive is a name, arguments and a semicolon; a block is a directive with braces containing more directives. A server block describes one website: the port it listens on and the hostnames it answers to. Inside it, location blocks decide what to do with each URL path. nginx picks exactly one location per request using fixed rules: an exact match (=) wins outright; otherwise it finds the longest matching prefix, and if any regular-expression location (~) also matches, the regex wins unless the prefix was marked ^~.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Server blocks are like routes keyed on host in a router; locations are the path patterns. The surprising part, as with any router, is precedence: the most specific rule wins, not the first one written.
Why it matters
nginx is the most widely deployed web server and proxy. Its ingress controller is also what routes traffic in many Kubernetes clusters, using the same configuration language.
Where you meet it
In front of almost every web application: serving static files, terminating TLS, proxying to app servers, and load balancing.
Scenario

The storefront's HTML, CSS and images are files on disk served directly by nginx, with long cache lifetimes on assets. A tiny /healthz location lets the load balancer check nginx itself without touching any application.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD M["nginx.conf
main context"] --> E["events { }"] M --> H["http { }"] H --> INC["include conf.d/*.conf
and sites-enabled/*"] INC --> S1["server { }
listen 80
server_name shop.example.com"] INC --> S2["server { }
another site"] INC --> UP["upstream { }
a named group of backends"] S1 --> L1["location = /healthz"] S1 --> L2["location ~* \.(css|js|png)$"] S1 --> L3["location /"]

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Prints the complete configuration nginx is actually using, with every include expanded. Use it when you cannot find where a setting comes from.
Follows the error log. It names the file, the upstream and the reason for every failure: read it before changing anything.
Applies new configuration by starting new workers; existing connections finish on the old ones. Prefer this to restart.
examples/nginx/static-site.conf
Exercise
Predict the winning location for five requests, then check.

items: Before sending anything, write down which location you expect for /, /healthz, /css/site.css, /img/logo.png and /missing
Send each and compare with the trace
Change "location ~* ..." to a prefix "location /css/" and resend /css/site.css and /img/logo.png: what changed?
Delete a semicolon and read the validator message and its line number
Add "location ^~ /img/ { return 403; }" and explain why the regex no longer applies to images

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can recite the matching order without looking and explain why order in the file matters only among regex locations.
Troubleshooting

rows: nginx: [emerg] directive "listen" is not terminated by ";"
A missing semicolon. nginx reports the line where it noticed, which is often the next line.
Look at the line above the one reported.
404 for a file that exists
root plus the URI does not point where you think, or the nginx user cannot read the directory.
The error log prints the exact path nginx tried. Check permissions on every directory in that path.
A location you wrote is never used
A regex location matches the same URI and takes precedence over your prefix.
Use ^~ on the prefix, or make the regex narrower.
403 Forbidden on a directory
No index file exists and directory listing is off.
Add the index file or point root at the right directory.
Changes have no effect
The file is not included, or nginx was not reloaded.
nginx -T to confirm it is loaded; nginx -t then reload.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: nginx -t before every reload, without exception.
One file per site in sites-available, enabled by a symlink.
Prefer prefix locations; use regex only when you must.
Keep configuration in Git and deploy it like code.

blocks.text: Security

items: Set server_tokens off so the version is not advertised.
Do not serve a directory that contains .git, .env or backups: deny dotfiles explicitly.
An explicit default server that returns 444 stops your site answering to hostnames you do not own.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does nginx choose a location block?
blocks.text: Exact match first. Otherwise it remembers the longest matching prefix; if that prefix has ^~ it is used. If not, regex locations are tested in the order they appear and the first match wins. If no regex matches, the remembered prefix is used.

blocks.title: root versus alias?
blocks.text: root appends the full request URI to the path. alias replaces the matched location part with the path. For location /img/ with root /data, /img/a.png maps to /data/img/a.png; with alias /data/, it maps to /data/a.png.

blocks.title: reload versus restart?
blocks.text: reload re-reads the configuration and gracefully replaces worker processes with no dropped connections, and is refused if the config is invalid. restart stops nginx and starts it again, dropping connections, and fails to come back if the config is broken.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Locations "/", "/img/" and "~ \.png$" exist. Which handles /img/logo.png?
options: whichever is first in the file
quiz.why: A matching regex beats a prefix unless the prefix is marked ^~.

quiz.q: What should you run before "systemctl reload nginx"?
quiz.why: It validates the configuration without applying it.

lessons.title: Reverse proxy and load balancing

blocks.text: A reverse proxy accepts requests on behalf of applications and forwards them. proxy_pass names the destination. Because the application now sees nginx as its client, nginx must pass on the original hostname, client address and scheme in headers. An upstream block names a group of identical backends; nginx spreads requests across them (round-robin by default) and, if one fails, retries on the next. Timeouts decide how long nginx waits before giving up, which is the difference between a 502 (could not get an answer) and a 504 (the answer took too long).

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A forward proxy is a personal assistant who makes calls for you; the other side does not know who is really calling. A reverse proxy is a company switchboard: callers dial one number and never learn which desk answered.
Why it matters
It lets you run several copies of an application behind one address, replace them without downtime, and keep TLS, limits and logging out of application code.
Where you meet it
In front of any application server (uvicorn, gunicorn, Node.js, Puma), as a cloud load balancer's target, and as the ingress controller in Kubernetes.
Scenario

checkout-api runs as two processes on ports 8000 and 8001. nginx balances between them. During a deploy one is restarted while the other serves; if one crashes, customers see nothing because the failed attempt is retried on the healthy one.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR C["Client"] -->|"HTTPS"| N["nginx
reverse proxy"] N -->|"round-robin, weight 2"| A1["checkout-api #1
127.0.0.1:8000"] N -->|"weight 1"| A2["checkout-api #2
127.0.0.1:8001"] A1 --> DB["PostgreSQL"] A2 --> DB N -. "adds X-Forwarded-For,
X-Forwarded-Proto, Host" .-> A1

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Prints only the status and total time: a quick probe to repeat while you change things.
For every 502 or 504 the error log states the upstream address and the cause: "Connection refused", "upstream timed out", "no live upstreams".
examples/nginx/load-balancer.conf
The many-apps example shows the other key rule: a URI on proxy_pass (even just a trailing slash) replaces the matched location prefix.
Exercise
Produce a 200, a 502 and a 504 on purpose and explain each from the trace.

items: Send 12 requests: confirm the 2:1 split from weight=2
Take #1 down and send 12: all succeed. Find "trying the next server" in the trace
Take both down: which status, and which phrase in the trace?
Make both slow: which status now? Change proxy_read_timeout to 60s and resend
Switch to the "Several apps" preset, remove the trailing slash from proxy_pass and compare what the backend receives

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state, without the sandbox, which of 502 and 504 means "nothing answered" and which means "too slow".
Troubleshooting

rows: 502 Bad Gateway
The backend is down, crashed mid-request, or listening somewhere else.
Error log first. Then ss -tlnp on the backend port and the application's own logs.
504 Gateway Time-out
The backend accepted the request but did not answer within proxy_read_timeout: a slow query, a lock, an exhausted worker pool.
Find why the backend is slow. Raising the timeout hides the problem and ties up connections.
The app builds http:// links or redirect loops behind HTTPS
The app sees plain HTTP from nginx and does not know the client used HTTPS.
Send X-Forwarded-Proto and configure the framework to trust proxy headers.
Every request in the app log comes from 127.0.0.1
The app logs the TCP peer, which is nginx.
Send X-Forwarded-For and have the app read it, trusting it only from your proxy.
404 from the backend for a path that exists
The trailing-slash rule on proxy_pass changed the URI the backend received.
With a URI on proxy_pass the location prefix is replaced; without one the path is passed unchanged. Decide which you want and test it.
WebSocket connections fail through the proxy
Upgrade headers are hop-by-hop and are not forwarded by default.
proxy_http_version 1.1, plus proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade and Connection "upgrade".

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Always set Host, X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto.
Set explicit, short connect timeouts and realistic read timeouts.
Run at least two backends so one can restart.
Retry only what is safe to repeat: by default nginx does not retry non-idempotent requests such as POST after they were sent.
Expose a cheap health endpoint on every backend.

blocks.text: Security

items: Backends must not be reachable directly, or clients can forge X-Forwarded-For and bypass the proxy's rules.
Limit request body size (client_max_body_size) and rate-limit expensive endpoints at the proxy.
Do not proxy to a hostname taken from user input.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What happens to the URI with "proxy_pass http://backend/" versus "proxy_pass http://backend"?
blocks.text: With a URI part (the trailing slash counts) nginx replaces the part of the request URI that matched the location with that URI. Without one, the original URI is passed unchanged. For location /api/, /api/health becomes /health in the first case and stays /api/health in the second.

blocks.title: How does nginx load balance, and what happens when a backend dies?
blocks.text: Round-robin by default, optionally weighted, or least_conn or ip_hash. Open-source nginx uses passive health checks: after failed attempts (max_fails within fail_timeout) a server is skipped for a while, and the failed request is retried on the next server per proxy_next_upstream.

blocks.title: Forward proxy versus reverse proxy?
blocks.text: A forward proxy acts for clients reaching out to the internet and hides the clients. A reverse proxy acts for servers, receiving requests from the internet and hiding the backends.

blocks.title: Why might retrying a failed request at the proxy be dangerous?
blocks.text: If the backend processed the request but the response was lost, a retry runs it twice: two orders, two charges. Retries are safe only for idempotent requests or when the application uses idempotency keys.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: location /api/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000/; } receives /api/orders. The backend sees…
quiz.why: The URI part "/" replaces the matched prefix "/api/".

quiz.q: Both backends are up but answer after 45s; proxy_read_timeout is 30s. The client gets…
quiz.why: The backend accepted the connection but did not respond in time: Gateway Time-out.

modules.title: CI/CD Fundamentals
modules.summary: Integration, delivery and deployment; artifacts, environments, approvals, strategies and rollback.

lessons.title: CI/CD: from commit to a running release

blocks.text: Continuous Integration: every push is automatically built and tested, so a broken change is caught in minutes. Continuous Delivery: every change that passes is packaged and ready to release with one approval. Continuous Deployment: there is no approval; passing changes go to production automatically. A pipeline is the ordered list of stages that does this, defined in a file in the repository.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: CI is the PR check that builds your app and runs unit tests. Delivery is the automatic TestFlight upload. Deployment would be releasing to the App Store with no human pressing the button.
Why it matters
Manual builds and deploys are slow, are done differently each time, and depend on whoever remembers the steps.
Where you meet it
Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI and others. The concepts are the same; only the file syntax differs.
Scenario

A push to main of the checkout repository triggers: tests, image build tagged with the commit SHA, vulnerability scan, push to the registry, deploy to staging, an approval, then a rolling deploy to production with automatic rollback if the new pods never become healthy.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR GH["Git host"] -->|"webhook"| CTL["CI controller
schedules jobs"] CTL --> AG1["Agent 1
runs the stages"] CTL --> AG2["Agent 2"] CRED["Credential store"] -. "injected at run time" .-> AG1 AG1 -->|"docker push"| REG["Registry"] AG1 -->|"kubectl"| STG["Staging cluster"] AG1 -->|"kubectl, after approval"| PRD["Production cluster"] REG --> STG REG --> PRD AG1 -->|"status"| GH

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart LR A["git push"] --> B["Webhook
triggers CI"] B --> C["Test"] C --> D["Build image
tag = commit SHA"] D --> E["Scan"] E --> F["Push to
registry"] F --> G["Deploy
staging"] G --> H{"Approve?"} H --> I["Deploy
production"] I --> J{"Healthy?"} J -->|no| K["Roll back"] J -->|yes| L["Done"]

blocks.text: Commands
Builds the image and tags it with the commit SHA so the running version always maps to exact source.

rows: `-t NAME:TAG`
name and tag the image
build context: the directory sent to the builder

blocks.text: Scans the image for known vulnerabilities and fails the stage if serious ones are found.

rows: `--exit-code 1`
return failure when findings exist, so the pipeline stops
`--severity`
which levels count

blocks.text: Waits until the rollout finishes or the timeout passes. The exit code tells the pipeline whether the deploy succeeded.
Returns the Deployment to its previous revision. This changes production: it is the standard rollback.
examples/jenkins/Jenkinsfile
Declarative pipeline. Credentials are referenced by ID and injected at run time; nothing secret is in the file.
Exercise
Predict where each kind of mistake is caught.

items: Open the pipeline visualizer and run it clean
Inject "failing unit test" and note which later stages never run
Inject "critical vulnerability" and "bad release": at which stage is each caught?
Decline the approval gate and see what stays unchanged

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain why a failed health check triggers a rollback while a failed test never touches any environment.
Troubleshooting

rows: Pipeline fails at docker push: unauthorized
Registry credentials are missing, expired or lack push permission.
Check the credential ID in the pipeline and its expiry; test docker login on the agent.
Tests pass locally and fail in CI
Different dependency versions, missing environment variables, or tests depending on order or time.
Run tests in the same container image CI uses; pin dependency versions.
Pipeline takes 40 minutes
No caching, serial stages, an oversized test suite on every push.
Cache dependencies and image layers, run independent stages in parallel, split fast and slow tests.
Rollout status times out
New pods never become Ready: crash, failing readiness probe, missing secret.
kubectl describe pod and kubectl logs on a new pod; roll back first if customers are affected.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Fail fast: cheapest checks first.
Tag images with the commit SHA, never deploy "latest".
The pipeline definition lives in the repository and is reviewed like code.
Every deploy has an automated health check and a tested rollback.

blocks.text: Security

items: Secrets come from a credential store and are masked in logs; never echo them.
CI agents hold deploy credentials: restrict who can change the pipeline on protected branches.
Pin third-party actions and plugins to exact versions.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Continuous delivery versus continuous deployment?
blocks.text: Delivery: every passing change is releasable and a human decides when. Deployment: every passing change is released automatically. The difference is the manual gate.

blocks.title: Why tag images with the commit SHA instead of "latest"?
blocks.text: A SHA tag is immutable and traceable: you know exactly which code is running and can roll back to an exact prior image. "latest" moves, so two nodes can run different code under the same tag.

blocks.title: How do you make a deployment safe?
blocks.text: Small change, automated tests, a staging run of the same artifact, gradual rollout (rolling or canary), readiness-gated traffic, automated health verification, and an automatic rollback path.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A unit test fails in CI. What happens to production?
options: Nothing: the pipeline stops before any deploy
quiz.why: Later stages do not run after a failed stage, so no image is built or deployed.

quiz.q: What should an image tag in production be?
options: the commit SHA or a version
quiz.why: It must identify one exact build.

lessons.title: Artifacts, environments and deployment strategies

blocks.text: A pipeline turns a commit into an artifact: one immutable, versioned package (for a backend, a container image) stored in a registry. That same artifact is promoted through environments, usually staging then production, with configuration supplied by each environment rather than baked in. How the new version replaces the old one in production is the deployment strategy. A rolling update swaps instances a few at a time. Blue-green runs the new version in full beside the old and flips traffic at once. A canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version and widens it only while the numbers stay good.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The artifact is the exact .ipa that passed TestFlight: you promote that build to the App Store, you do not rebuild it. A canary is App Store phased release: 1% of users, then 2%, 5%, and you can pause when crash rates rise.
Why it matters

Rebuilding per environment means production runs something that was never tested. And replacing every instance at once means any defect reaches every customer at the same moment with no quick way back.
Where you meet it
Every delivery system: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Argo Rollouts, Spinnaker, and the managed deploy services of each cloud.
Scenario

checkout-api is built once per commit and tagged with the commit ID. Staging and production pull that same tag; only environment variables and secrets differ. Production uses a rolling update guarded by a readiness probe, and the pipeline rolls back automatically if the rollout does not complete. Payment changes go out as a 5% canary first.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR C["Commit 9f3c2ab"] --> B["Build ONCE"] B --> R["Registry
checkout-api:9f3c2ab"] R --> S["Staging
same image + staging config"] S -->|"tests pass"| G{"Approval gate"} G --> P["Production
same image + production config"] CFG1["staging secrets and settings"] -.-> S CFG2["production secrets and settings"] -.-> P P -->|"unhealthy"| RB["Roll back to
checkout-api:previous"]

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Shows the digest of an image tag. The digest (sha256:…) identifies the exact bytes; deploy by digest when you need certainty that nothing moved.
Waits for a rolling update to finish and exits non-zero if it does not. This exit code is what lets a pipeline decide to roll back.
Returns to the previous revision. It is itself a rolling update, in reverse.
Lists revisions, so you can see what was running before and roll back to a specific one with --to-revision.
The same three strategies, compared

blocks.code:
Rolling update         Blue-green              Canary
Extra capacity   one surge instance     100% (a full second     small (the canary
                                         copy during release)    instances)
Bad version      limited by readiness   everyone, briefly       a small percentage
reaches          probe, else grows      (if it passes tests)
Rollback         gradual (a rollout     instant (flip back)     instant (weight 0)
                 in reverse)
Needs            readiness probes       two environments and    traffic splitting and
                                        a switchable router     metrics you trust
Both versions    yes, during rollout    no (one or the other)   yes, during analysis
serve at once
Good default     most services          releases that must be   high-risk changes,
for                                     all-or-nothing          high-traffic services

Whichever you use: database changes must work with BOTH the old and new code
(expand, deploy, then contract), because a rollback puts the old code back.

blocks.text: Exercise
For each strategy, find out how many customers a bad release reaches and how fast you can undo it.

items: Run all three strategies with a healthy version and compare peak capacity
Set version 2 to "crashes at startup": in which strategies do customers notice?
Set it to "starts fine, returns wrong results": compare the exposure numbers
Explain why the readiness probe protected you in one case and not the other
Decide which strategy you would use for a checkout pricing change, and why

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state, for each strategy, the capacity cost, the exposure to a silent bug and the rollback speed.
Troubleshooting

rows: Staging passed but production broke
The artifact was rebuilt for production, or configuration differs in a way nobody tested.
Promote the identical image by tag or digest. Keep per-environment differences to configuration and make those differences small and visible.
Rollback made things worse
A database migration removed or renamed something the old code needs.
Expand-and-contract: add the new column, deploy code that works with both, backfill, and remove the old column only in a later release.
The rollout succeeded but customers see errors
Health checks only prove the process answers; they say nothing about correct behaviour.
Verify with real metrics after deploy (error rate, latency, a synthetic checkout) and use a canary for risky changes.
Errors appear only while a deploy is in progress
Old pods are killed before they finish requests, or old and new versions are incompatible.
Handle SIGTERM gracefully, add a preStop delay, and keep API changes backward compatible.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Build once, promote the same artifact, deploy by immutable tag or digest.
Separate deploy (the code is running) from release (customers see it) with feature flags.
Every deploy has an automated verification and an automated way back.
Practise rollback until it is boring.
Keep environments as similar as you can afford.

blocks.text: Security

items: The registry is part of your supply chain: restrict who can push and scan what is pushed.
Production credentials belong to the production stage only, behind the approval gate.
An approval gate is a control only if the approver can see what they are approving: link the diff and the test results.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments.
blocks.text: Rolling replaces instances gradually with little extra capacity; rollback is gradual. Blue-green stands up a full copy and switches traffic at once; rollback is instant but capacity doubles. Canary shifts a small share of traffic, compares metrics and widens; it limits exposure best but needs traffic splitting and trustworthy metrics.

blocks.title: Why "build once, deploy many"?
blocks.text: It guarantees that what was tested is what runs in production. Rebuilding can pull different dependency versions or base images, so the tested artifact and the deployed one are no longer the same thing.

blocks.title: How do you deploy a database schema change with zero downtime?
blocks.text: Expand and contract. First add the new structure in a backward-compatible way. Deploy code that writes both and reads the new. Backfill. Only when no running version needs the old structure, remove it. Each step is independently reversible.

blocks.title: What is the difference between deploying and releasing?
blocks.text: Deploying puts code on servers. Releasing exposes behaviour to users. Feature flags separate them, so code can ship dark, be enabled for a few users, and be turned off without a deploy.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which strategy gives the fastest rollback?
quiz.why: The old environment is still running, so switching back is one routing change.

quiz.q: A bug passes all health checks but returns wrong prices. Which strategy limits the damage most?
quiz.why: A canary exposes only a small share of traffic and compares its metrics before going further.

modules.title: Jenkins Mastery
modules.summary: Controller and agents, writing a Jenkinsfile, credentials, parallel stages, and a method for red builds.

lessons.title: Jenkins architecture: controller, agents, jobs and credentials

blocks.text: Jenkins is an automation server. The controller is its brain: it stores configuration, receives webhooks, schedules work and shows the web interface. It should not run builds itself. Agents are the machines (or containers) that do the work; each has a number of executors, which is how many builds it runs at once, and labels describing what it can do, such as "macos" or "docker". A job describes what to build; a pipeline job reads its steps from a Jenkinsfile in the repository. Credentials are stored encrypted on the controller and injected into a build only where a pipeline asks for them. Plugins add nearly every integration.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The controller is Xcode Cloud's scheduler; agents are the Macs that actually compile. A label is like requiring "a machine with Xcode 16": the build waits until one with that capability is free.
Why it matters
Builds need different operating systems and tools, run many at a time, and must not be able to break the system that schedules them. Splitting scheduling from execution solves all three.
Where you meet it

Jenkins remains common in companies that host their own CI, need macOS agents for mobile builds, or have years of existing pipelines. The same controller-and-runner split exists in GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and Buildkite.
Scenario

A merge to checkout-api sends a webhook to the controller. It queues a build, finds a Linux agent with Docker, and runs the Jenkinsfile there. The mobile app's build queues for the single macOS agent instead; when that Mac is offline, mobile builds wait in the queue while backend builds carry on.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR GIT["Git host"] -->|"webhook: push"| CTL["Jenkins controller
schedules, stores config,
serves the UI"] CTL --> Q["Build queue"] Q -->|"label: docker"| A1["linux-1
2 executors"] Q -->|"label: docker"| A2["linux-2
2 executors"] Q -->|"label: macos"| A3["mac-1
1 executor"] CTL --- CR["Credential store
(encrypted)"] CR -. "injected per step" .-> A1 A1 --> REG["Registry"] A1 --> K8S["Cluster"] CTL --- PL["Plugins"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram participant G as Git host participant C as Controller participant A as Agent G->>C: Webhook: push to main C->>C: Find the job, read the Jenkinsfile C->>C: Queue the build Note over C: Wait for an agent with
the required label and a free executor C->>A: Start the build in a workspace A->>G: Check out the commit A->>A: Run stages A-->>C: Stream the console log A-->>C: Result, test reports, artifacts C->>G: Report commit status

Starts a local Jenkins controller for learning. The named volume keeps its configuration between restarts.

`-v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home`
persist jobs, plugins and credentials

Prints the one-time password for the first login on a fresh install.
Reads the build queue through the API: the quickest check for "why has my build not started?". Needs an API token on a secured server.
Vocabulary, mapped to other CI systems

blocks.code:
Jenkins               GitHub Actions          GitLab CI           What it is
controller            (hosted service)        GitLab instance     schedules and stores
agent / node          runner                  runner              machine that runs builds
executor              (one job per runner)    concurrent setting  parallel slots on an agent
label                 runs-on                 tags                capability a job requires
job / pipeline        workflow                pipeline            what to run
stage                 job                     stage               a named phase
step                  step                    script line         one action
Jenkinsfile           .github/workflows/*.yml .gitlab-ci.yml      pipeline as code
credentials           secrets                 CI/CD variables     injected secrets
plugin                action                  include / component reusable integration
shared library        reusable workflow       include / template  shared pipeline code

blocks.text: Exercise
See why a build can be stuck without having failed.

items: Run the Flutter pipeline as it is and note which agent every stage used
Take mac-1 offline and build again: read the message and the result
Bring it back, then change the first line to "agent any": which stage fails, and with what error?
Mark the appstore-api-key credential as missing: which stages still pass?
Explain what you would monitor so that a stuck queue is noticed

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can tell apart "no agent available" (queued), "wrong agent" (tool not found) and "credential missing" (one stage fails).
Troubleshooting

rows: Build sits at "Waiting for next available executor"
No online agent has the required label, or all executors are busy.
Check the agent list and the queue. Add capacity or fix the label; alert on queue time.
Agent shows offline
The agent process stopped, the machine is down, or it cannot reach the controller.
Check the agent log on the node and the network path. Ephemeral agents that are recreated per build avoid most of this.
The controller is slow or runs out of memory
Builds running on the controller, too many plugins, or years of build history.
Set the controller's executors to 0, prune plugins, and discard old builds.
A plugin update broke pipelines
Plugins change behaviour and depend on each other.
Pin plugin versions, test upgrades on a staging controller, and keep configuration as code so you can rebuild.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Zero executors on the controller: it schedules, agents build.
Use ephemeral agents (containers or cloud VMs) so every build starts clean.
Keep jobs and configuration as code: Jenkinsfile in each repository, Configuration as Code for the controller.
Install few plugins and update them deliberately.
Back up the Jenkins home directory and practise restoring it.

blocks.text: Security

items: The controller holds every credential: patch it promptly and never expose it to the internet without authentication.
Anyone who can edit a Jenkinsfile that runs with deploy credentials can use them: protect branches and review pipeline changes.
Scope credentials to folders or jobs, not globally.
Builds run arbitrary code: isolate agents from each other and from production networks.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain the Jenkins controller and agent model.
blocks.text: The controller schedules builds, stores configuration and credentials and serves the UI. Agents connect to it and execute builds in workspaces. Labels route builds to agents with the right tools; executors set how many builds an agent runs concurrently.

blocks.title: Why should builds not run on the controller?
blocks.text: Builds execute arbitrary code. On the controller that code sits beside all credentials and configuration and competes for the resources that scheduling needs, so one bad build can compromise or stall everything.

blocks.title: How do you scale Jenkins?
blocks.text: Add agents, preferably ephemeral ones provisioned on demand (Kubernetes pods, cloud VMs). Keep the controller small and stateless in configuration, and split very large installations into several controllers by team.

quiz.q: A build needs macOS and the only Mac agent is offline. The build…
quiz.why: Jenkins queues it until an agent with the label is available.

quiz.q: Where should the pipeline definition live?
options: In a Jenkinsfile in the repository
quiz.why: In the repository it is versioned, reviewed and changes with the code it builds.

lessons.title: Writing a Jenkinsfile: stages, parallelism, credentials and post actions

blocks.text: A declarative Jenkinsfile is one pipeline block. agent says where it runs. stages lists the phases in order; each stage has steps, and a failing step stops the pipeline. parallel runs several stages at once. when makes a stage conditional, for example only on the main branch. environment sets variables. withCredentials makes a secret available to the steps inside it and nowhere else, masked in the log. post runs after a stage or the whole pipeline depending on the outcome: always, success, failure. input pauses for a person to approve.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: It is a fastlane Fastfile with structure imposed on it: lanes become stages, before_all and error blocks become post, and match or the App Store key become withCredentials.
Why it matters
A pipeline in the repository changes with the code, is reviewed like code and can be rebuilt on a new Jenkins from nothing. Pipelines configured by clicking in the UI can do none of that.
Where you meet it
Every repository built by Jenkins. The shapes carry over directly to other CI systems.
Scenario

The checkout-api Jenkinsfile runs tests inside a Python container, builds and scans an image, publishes it using registry credentials that exist only for those two commands, deploys to staging, waits for an approval on main, deploys to production, and rolls back in a post block if the rollout fails.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD P["pipeline"] --> AG["agent
where it runs"] P --> OP["options
timeout, concurrency"] P --> EN["environment
variables"] P --> ST["stages"] P --> PO["post
always / success / failure"] ST --> S1["stage('Test')"] ST --> S2["stage('Checks')
parallel"] ST --> S3["stage('Deploy')"] S1 --> ST1["steps: sh, junit"] S2 --> PA["stage A"] S2 --> PB["stage B"] S3 --> W["when { branch 'main' }"] S3 --> CR["withCredentials { sh ... }"] S3 --> SP["post { failure { rollback } }"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A["Stage starts"] --> B{"when condition true?"}
  B -->|no| SK["Skipped"]
  B -->|yes| C["Acquire agent"]
  C --> D["Run steps in order"]
  D --> E{"A step failed?"}
  E -->|no| F["post: always, success"]
  E -->|yes| G["post: always, failure"]
  F --> H["Next stage"]
  G --> I["Remaining stages skipped"]
  I --> J["Pipeline post: always, failure"]
  H --> K["... last stage"] --> L["Pipeline post: always, success"]

blocks.text: Commands
A step: run a shell command on the agent. A non-zero exit code fails the stage. Single quotes pass the text to the shell untouched, so $VARIABLES are expanded by the shell, not by Groovy.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: With double quotes Groovy interpolates first, which prints secrets into the process list and the log. Use single quotes for anything involving credentials.
Publishes test results so Jenkins shows which tests failed and tracks them over time. Put it in post { always } so it runs when tests fail.
Stores build outputs with the build so they can be downloaded later. Fails if the pattern matches nothing, unless allowEmptyArchive is true.

blocks.code: input message: 'Deploy this build to production?'
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Pauses the pipeline until a person clicks Proceed or Abort. This is the manual approval gate.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: A paused build holds its agent unless the input runs with "agent none". Add a timeout so forgotten approvals expire.
Re-runs the enclosed steps if they fail. Use it for operations that fail transiently and are safe to repeat, such as an upload.
examples/jenkins/Jenkinsfile
The mobile equivalents are examples/jenkins/Jenkinsfile.flutter and Jenkinsfile.ios; a Node.js one with per-stage containers is Jenkinsfile.node. All four are loaded in the simulator.
Exercise
Change a real Jenkinsfile and predict the effect before each run.

items: Run it clean and read the stage view
Select "a test fails": which stages run, and does junit still record results? Why is it in post { always }?
Move the docker login line out of the withCredentials block and run: read the error
Switch the branch to feature/discounts: which stages are skipped, and by what?
Add a new stage that runs "ruff check ." in parallel with Test, and make it work
Remove the timeout option, choose "the test command hangs" and read what the simulator says

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain what each of these would cost in a real team: no timeout, credentials in the wrong scope, junit outside post.
Troubleshooting

rows: ERROR: Could not find credentials entry with ID 'x'
The ID is misspelled, the credential was deleted, or it is stored in a folder this job cannot see.
Compare the ID with Manage Jenkins → Credentials, including its scope.
unauthorized: authentication required at docker login
The credential exists but the token expired or was rotated.
Update the stored secret. Prefer short-lived tokens issued per build to stored long-lived ones.
ERROR: No test report files were found
The test command failed before writing its report, or the path is wrong.
Read upwards for the first error. This message is usually a consequence, not the cause.
The build hangs for hours
A command is waiting for input or a network call that never returns, and no timeout is set.
Set options { timeout(...) } on every pipeline and a shorter one around risky steps.
sh: flutter: not found
The stage ran on an agent, or in a container image, that does not have the tool.
Fix the agent label or the image. Print versions at the start of the build to make this obvious.
A secret appears in the console log
It was interpolated by Groovy in a double-quoted string, or echoed.
Single-quote sh commands that use secrets. Then rotate the leaked secret.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Declarative syntax unless you truly need scripted.
A timeout on every pipeline.
Test reports and cleanup in post { always }.
Credentials bound for the smallest possible block.
Run independent checks in parallel; fail fast on the cheap ones.
Move logic repeated across repositories into a shared library, versioned and tested.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never print or interpolate secrets; bind them with withCredentials and use single quotes.
Pull requests from forks must not run with deploy credentials.
Treat the Jenkinsfile as privileged code: require review for changes to it.
Pin the versions of container images used as build agents.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Declarative versus scripted pipelines?
blocks.text: Declarative has a fixed structure (pipeline, agent, stages, steps, post) that Jenkins validates before running; it is easier to read and covers most needs. Scripted is plain Groovy with full control flow and no enforced structure. A script block lets declarative pipelines drop into Groovy where needed.

blocks.title: How do you handle secrets in a Jenkins pipeline?
blocks.text: Store them in the credential store, bind them with withCredentials around only the steps that need them, reference them from single-quoted shell commands so they are not interpolated, rely on masking in logs but never print them, scope them to the folder or job, and rotate them.

blocks.title: What is a shared library and when would you write one?
blocks.text: A Git repository of Groovy code that pipelines import with @Library, exposing custom steps such as deployToKubernetes(...). Write one when several repositories repeat the same pipeline logic, so a fix is made once. Version it, because every pipeline depends on it.

blocks.title: How would you speed up a 40-minute pipeline?
blocks.text: Measure per stage first. Then run independent stages in parallel, cache dependencies and image layers, run only the tests affected by the change on pull requests, use bigger or more agents, and move slow suites to a later or nightly stage.

quiz.q: Where should the junit step go so results are recorded when tests fail?
options: Right after the test command in steps
quiz.why: A failing test command stops the steps block; post { always } still runs.

quiz.q: Why use single quotes in sh 'docker login -p $PASS'?
options: So the shell, not Groovy, expands the secret
quiz.why: Groovy interpolation would put the secret value into the command line and the log.

lessons.title: When the pipeline is red: a method for build failures

blocks.text: Pipeline failures fall into a small number of kinds. The code is wrong (a test or compile error). A dependency could not be fetched. A credential is missing or expired. The agent is wrong, offline or died. Something outside failed (registry, cluster, network). A step hung. Or the deploy succeeded mechanically and the new version is unhealthy. Finding which kind takes a fixed routine: go to the first failed stage, find the first error in its log, read the command above it, and ask what changed since the last green build.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Like reading a crash report: skip the hundred frames of noise at the bottom, find the first frame in your code. In a build log the last error is usually a consequence of the first.
Why it matters
A red pipeline blocks everyone. The instinct to press "rebuild" wastes twenty minutes each time and teaches nothing; a method finds the cause in two.
Where you meet it
Any CI system. The categories and the routine are the same in GitHub Actions and GitLab CI.
Scenario

The checkout-api build goes red at 16:05. The last stage in the log complains about a missing test report, but the first error, forty lines up, is pip failing to reach the package index. Nothing is wrong with the code; an egress rule changed that afternoon.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph Yours["Usually your change"] T["Test or compile failure"] C["Pipeline syntax"] end subgraph Platform["Usually the platform"] A["Agent offline, wrong label,
disk full, disconnected"] Q["Stuck in queue"] end subgraph Outside["Usually something outside"] D["Dependency download"] R["Registry upload"] K["Credential expired"] H["Cluster rejects or
rollout unhealthy"] end Yours --> F["Fix the code"] Platform --> G["Fix or replace the agent"] Outside --> I["Retry may help.
Then fix the dependency on it"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Build is red"] --> B["Open the FIRST failed stage"] B --> C["Find the FIRST 'ERROR' in its log"] C --> D["Read the command just above it"] D --> E{"What kind?"} E -->|"assertion, compile"| F["Code: reproduce locally"] E -->|"not found / exit 127"| G["Wrong agent or image"] E -->|"unauthorized, credentials"| H["Credential: check store and expiry"] E -->|"resolve, 503, timeout"| I["Outside: is it failing for everyone?"] E -->|"timed out, no output"| J["Hang: find the step, add a timeout"] E -->|"rollout timed out"| K["Deploy: describe and logs on a new pod"] F --> L{"Passed last time
with the same commit?"} L -->|yes| M["Flaky: quarantine and fix"] L -->|no| N["Real regression"]

blocks.text: Commands
Lists every commit since the last successful build: the complete list of suspects when the failure is in code.
Opens a shell in the same container image the pipeline uses, with your code mounted. Reproducing in the CI image removes "works on my machine" in one step.

rows: delete the container on exit
`-v "$PWD":/app`
mount the current directory
`-w /app`
start in it

blocks.text: For a failed rollout: the Events section says why the new pod is not Ready (image pull, crash, failing probe).
The output of the crashed container: the application's own explanation.
Error text → cause

blocks.code:
"exit code 1" after test output           a test failed: read the assertion
"exit code 127" / "not found"             tool missing on this agent or image
"Could not resolve host" / "ETIMEDOUT"    network or DNS from the agent
"Could not find a version that satisfies" dependency or index problem
"Could not find credentials entry"        credential ID wrong, deleted or out of scope
"unauthorized" / "denied"                 credential expired, rotated or lacks permission
"503" / "connection reset" on upload      registry trouble: retry, then check its status
"No space left on device"                 agent disk full: clean workspaces and images
"ChannelClosedException"                  the agent went away mid-build
"Cancelling nested steps due to timeout"  a step hung
"No test report files were found"         consequence: the tests never produced a report
"timed out waiting for the condition"     the rollout did not become healthy
"Still waiting to schedule task"          not a failure: no agent with that label

blocks.text: Exercise
Diagnose six failures from their logs alone, the way you would on call.

items: For each fault in the list, run the build and write down: first failed stage, first error line, category
For "dependency download fails": which later error in the log is only a consequence?
For "agent disconnects": what work is lost, and would a retry of the whole build be safe?
For "new release never becomes healthy": what state is production in at the end, and how do you know?
Set the registry credential to expired and compare the message with "missing"
For each, say whether pressing rebuild would have helped

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Your category for each matches the table above, and you can say which failures a blind rebuild would fix (one: the transient registry error).
Troubleshooting

rows: Fails in CI, passes locally
Different tool versions, missing environment variables, tests depending on order, time zone or leftover files.
Run the tests in the CI container image locally. Pin versions.
Passes on rebuild without any change
A flaky test or a transient external failure.
Do not normalise it. Track flaky tests, quarantine them, and add targeted retries only around external calls.
No space left on device on the agent
Old workspaces, Docker images and layers accumulate.
Clean workspaces after builds, prune images on a schedule, or use ephemeral agents.
The deploy stage is green but the service is down
The pipeline did not verify the outcome, only that commands ran.
End deploy stages with rollout status and a real health request; fail the stage on either.
Everything fails at once across all repositories
A shared dependency: the registry, the package index, DNS, a shared library, or expired shared credentials.
Check what the failing builds have in common before reading any single log.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Read the first error, not the last.
Make pipelines print tool versions and the commit at the start.
Keep the build green: a red main branch is the team's first priority.
Measure and publish flaky-test and queue-time numbers.
Every deploy stage ends by verifying the service, and rolls back if it cannot.

blocks.text: Security

items: Debugging by printing environment variables leaks secrets into logs that many people can read.
Do not disable a failing security scan to get a release out; record a time-boxed exception with an owner.
Rerunning a deploy stage by hand skips the gates before it: rerun the pipeline instead.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: A pipeline that was green yesterday is red today with no code change. How do you approach it?
blocks.text: No code change points outside the code: a dependency version that floated, an expired credential, a changed base image, an agent problem or an external service. I find the first error, classify it, check whether other pipelines fail the same way, and compare with the last green run's log.

blocks.title: How do you deal with flaky tests?
blocks.text: Treat flakiness as a defect with an owner. Detect it by rerunning failures and recording pass-on-retry, quarantine the test so it stops blocking, fix the cause (timing, shared state, order dependence, real race conditions), and track the count over time.

blocks.title: The deploy stage timed out waiting for the rollout. What now?
blocks.text: Check whether the automatic rollback ran and production is serving the old version. Then describe a new pod for events, read its previous logs, and compare configuration and secrets with the last good revision. Fix forward only after service is confirmed healthy.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A log ends with "No test report files were found". Where is the real problem most likely?
options: Earlier: the test command never ran to completion
quiz.why: The report is missing because something before it failed.

quiz.q: Which failure is a reasonable candidate for an automatic retry?
options: A 503 from the registry during upload
quiz.why: It is transient and repeating an upload is safe.

lessons.title: Jenkins shared libraries and secrets in pipelines

blocks.text: When fifty repositories each have their own Jenkinsfile, the same stages are copied fifty times and drift apart. A shared library is a Git repository of pipeline code that every Jenkinsfile can call, so "how we build a service" is defined once. The same lesson covers the other thing every pipeline gets wrong sooner or later: handling secrets.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A restaurant chain. Each branch does not invent its own recipe for the house sauce. Head office writes it once, branches follow it, and when the recipe improves every branch gets the improvement.
Why it matters

Copied pipelines mean a security fix must be made fifty times, and some copies are always missed. A library gives one place to add a scan, change a registry or fix a bug. And pipelines hold powerful credentials, so careless handling in one Jenkinsfile can leak a key that reaches production.
Where you meet it
Any Jenkins installation with more than a handful of pipelines. The library lives in its own repository with a vars directory of steps, is registered in Jenkins, and is versioned with tags.
Scenario

The security team wants every image scanned before it is pushed. With copied Jenkinsfiles that is fifty pull requests. With a shared library it is one change to standardPipeline, tagged v3, and each team moves to it by changing one line. The checkout-api Jenkinsfile shrinks to two lines.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph LIB["Repository: shop-pipelines (tagged v1, v2, v3)"] V["vars/standardPipeline.groovy
vars/deployTo.groovy"] SRC["src/... helper classes"] RES["resources/... templates"] end J["Jenkins controller
library registered: shop-pipelines"] -->|"fetches at build start"| LIB R1["checkout-api/Jenkinsfile
@Library('shop-pipelines@v3')"] --> J R2["cart-api/Jenkinsfile"] --> J R3["catalogue-api/Jenkinsfile"] --> J J --> AG["Agent runs the stages"] CRED["Credentials store"] -->|"bound only inside the step"| AG AG -->|"masked in the log"| LOG["Build log"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["A stage needs a secret"] --> B{"Can a short-lived identity
be used instead (OIDC, a role)?"} B -->|"yes"| C["Use it. Nothing to store or leak"] B -->|"no"| D["Store it in the Jenkins credentials store"] D --> E["Bind it with withCredentials,
around the one step that needs it"] E --> F{"Is it interpolated by Groovy
in a double-quoted string?"} F -->|"yes"| G["Risk: the value is put into the command line,
visible in process lists. Use single quotes
so the shell reads the variable"] F -->|"no"| H["The shell reads it from the environment"] G --> H H --> I{"Could output contain it?
(set -x, env, error dumps)"} I -->|"yes"| J["Masking is a backstop, not a guarantee.
Remove the debug output"] I -->|"no"| K["Done. Scope ends with the block"]

blocks.text: Commands

blocks.code: git tag v3 && git push origin v3
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: In the library repository: publishes a version that Jenkinsfiles can pin with @v3. Pipelines pinned to a branch pick up changes at once, which is how one bad commit breaks every build.
Asks the Jenkins server to validate a declarative Jenkinsfile without running it. Needs credentials for your server.
A quick search for secrets or suspicious names written into pipeline code.
Scans the repository history for committed secrets.
A shared library step and the Jenkinsfile that uses it (illustrative)
The library is pinned to a tag. Teams upgrade deliberately, and a mistake in the library reaches one team at a time instead of all of them at once.
Exercise
Design a shared library from the four pipelines in the Jenkins simulator.

items: Open the FastAPI and Node.js pipelines side by side. List the stages that are the same
List what differs: these become the parameters of the shared step
Write the two-line Jenkinsfile each service would have afterwards
In the simulator, find where a credential is used. Is it scoped to one step or the whole pipeline?
A new scan must be added to every service. Describe the rollout with tags
What goes wrong if every Jenkinsfile uses @Library('shop-pipelines@main')?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain what a shared library is, why it is pinned to a version, and how a secret should enter a pipeline step.
Troubleshooting

rows: No such DSL method standardPipeline
The library is not loaded: a missing @Library line, a wrong name, or the file is not in vars.
Check the library name registered in Jenkins and that the file is vars/standardPipeline.groovy.
Every pipeline broke at the same time
They all track the library's main branch, and a bad change was merged.
Revert the library change. Then pin to tags.
Scripts not permitted to use method…
The Groovy sandbox blocked a call the library makes.
Trusted global libraries run outside the sandbox; otherwise an administrator approves the signature. Prefer simpler code over approvals.
A secret shows as plain text in the log
It was transformed (base64, a substring) so masking no longer matches, or printed by a debug option.
Rotate it, then remove the output.
A change to the library has no effect
The pipeline is pinned to an older tag.
That is the design. Move the pin.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: One standard pipeline per kind of service, with a small set of parameters.
Pin libraries to tags and upgrade deliberately.
Check the library itself: lint, unit checks, and a sample pipeline run before tagging.
Keep Jenkinsfiles tiny; logic belongs in the library.
Bind credentials around the single step that needs them.
Use single-quoted shell strings so secrets are read by the shell, not interpolated by Groovy.
Prefer short-lived cloud identities over stored keys.

blocks.text: Security

items: Whoever can change the shared library can change every pipeline, and so reach production. Protect it with reviews and branch protection.
Trusted libraries run outside the sandbox with full access to Jenkins.
Pull requests from forks must not get credentials.
Never pass secrets as build parameters: they are stored and shown in the UI.
Masking hides exact matches only. Treat any printed secret as leaked and rotate it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is a Jenkins shared library?
blocks.text: A versioned Git repository of reusable pipeline code. Files in vars become steps callable from any Jenkinsfile, src holds helper classes and resources holds templates. It removes duplication and gives one place to change how everything is built.

blocks.title: How do you roll out a change to a shared library safely?
blocks.text: Check it in the library's own pipeline, tag a new version, move a few pipelines to it, then the rest. Never have every pipeline follow the main branch.

blocks.title: How should secrets be used in a Jenkins pipeline?
blocks.text: From the credentials store, bound with withCredentials around the smallest block, read by the shell from the environment. Better still, replace stored secrets with short-lived identities.

blocks.title: Why is "${SECRET}" in a double-quoted sh step a problem?
blocks.text: Groovy substitutes the value before the shell runs, so it appears in the command line and can leak through process listings and logs. With single quotes the shell reads the environment variable itself.

blocks.title: What is the risk of a shared library?
blocks.text: It concentrates power: a bad or malicious change affects every pipeline. It needs the same protection as production, and versioning so failures are contained.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A library step lives in…
quiz.why: Files in vars become callable steps.

quiz.q: Pipelines should reference the library by…
quiz.why: So a bad change cannot break everyone at once.

quiz.q: A secret was printed in a build log. First you…
quiz.why: It must be assumed leaked.

modules.title: GitHub Actions
modules.summary: Workflows, runners and secrets, then reusable workflows, matrix builds, caching, environments and OIDC to the cloud. Two lessons; workflows are not simulated.

lessons.title: GitHub Actions: the same pipeline in workflow form

blocks.text: GitHub Actions is CI/CD built into GitHub. A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows. It declares the events that trigger it (on), and a set of jobs. Each job runs on a fresh runner (a virtual machine GitHub starts for you, or one you host) and consists of steps: either a shell command (run) or a reusable action (uses). Jobs run in parallel unless one needs another. Secrets come from the repository or an environment; an environment can require reviewers, which gives you an approval gate.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: If Jenkins is running your own build Macs, Actions is Xcode Cloud: the machines appear when a workflow starts and vanish when it ends, and you describe what to do in a file in the repository.
Why it matters

There is no CI server to operate, every job starts on a clean machine, and thousands of maintained actions cover common tasks. The trade is less control over the machines and a bill per minute on private repositories.
Where you meet it
Most open-source projects and a large share of companies whose code is on GitHub. GitLab CI and Bitbucket Pipelines follow the same model with different syntax.
Scenario

The checkout-api workflow runs tests on two Python versions for every pull request. On main it builds and pushes the image to the GitHub container registry using a token GitHub issues for that run, then waits for a reviewer on the production environment before deploying.
Architecture

push, pull_request,
schedule, manual"] --> WF["Workflow file
.github/workflows/ci.yml"] WF --> J1["job: test
matrix: 2 Python versions"] WF --> J2["job: image
needs: test"] WF --> J3["job: deploy-production

environment: production"] J1 --> R1["fresh runner VM"] J2 --> R2["fresh runner VM"] J3 --> R3["fresh runner VM"] SEC["Secrets and
environment protection"] -.-> J3 J2 --> REG["ghcr.io registry"]

blocks.text: Commands
Lists recent workflow runs with their status, using the GitHub CLI.
Prints only the log of the failed steps of the latest run: the quickest way to the first error.
Re-runs only the failed jobs. On a workflow that deploys, this can start a deployment.
Triggers a workflow manually (it must declare workflow_dispatch). It runs whatever the workflow does, including deploys.
examples/github-actions/ci.yml

blocks.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
# The same pipeline as examples/jenkins/Jenkinsfile, expressed for GitHub Actions.
name: checkout-api

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python: ["3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
          cache: pip
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-dev.txt
      - run: pytest -q --junitxml=reports/junit.xml
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: test-report-${{ matrix.python }}
          path: reports/junit.xml

  image:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  deploy-production:
    needs: image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production   # required reviewers on this environment are the approval gate
    steps:
      - run: echo "kubectl set image deployment/checkout-api checkout-api=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}"

blocks.text: matrix fans one job out into several. needs orders jobs. permissions limits what the run's automatic token may do. concurrency cancels superseded runs.
Exercise
Translate between the two systems until the concepts are the same thing to you.

items: Read the workflow and the FastAPI Jenkinsfile side by side
Find the Actions equivalent of: agent, stage, withCredentials, input, when { branch }, parallel
Which file would you change to add a third Python version? How many jobs would then run?
What plays the role of the Jenkins credential store, and where is the approval gate?
If you have a GitHub repository of your own, add a workflow that only runs "echo hello" on push and watch it run

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can map each of those six Jenkins concepts to its Actions counterpart without looking.
Troubleshooting

rows: The workflow did not trigger
The file is not on the default branch, the on: filter does not match, or the YAML is invalid.
Check the Actions tab for a parse error and compare the branch and path filters with the push.
Resource not accessible by integration
The automatic token lacks a permission the step needs.
Add the specific permission under permissions: (for example packages: write). Do not grant everything.
A secret is empty in a pull request from a fork
By design: secrets are not given to workflows triggered by forks.
Keep it that way. Split the workflow so untrusted code is only built and tested, never deployed.
Jobs are slow because dependencies download every time
Runners are fresh machines with no cache.
Use the cache built into setup actions or actions/cache, keyed on the lock file.
A job waits forever on "Waiting for a runner"
runs-on names a self-hosted label with no online runner.
Check the runner list. Same failure as a missing Jenkins agent label.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Set permissions: at the top and grant the minimum.
Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA, not a moving tag.
Use environments with required reviewers for production.
Use OpenID Connect to obtain short-lived cloud credentials instead of storing long-lived keys.
Factor repeated jobs into reusable workflows.

blocks.text: Security

items: A third-party action runs with your token and secrets: pin it and read it.
pull_request_target and workflow_run can expose secrets to untrusted code if misused.
Never interpolate untrusted text such as a pull request title directly into a run: script; pass it through an environment variable.
Self-hosted runners on public repositories let strangers run code on your machine.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do GitHub Actions and Jenkins differ?
blocks.text: Actions is a hosted service integrated with GitHub: runners are ephemeral, configuration is YAML in the repository, and reuse is through actions. Jenkins is self-hosted software you operate: long-lived or ephemeral agents, Groovy pipelines, plugins. Actions removes operations work; Jenkins gives more control over machines, networks and unusual build environments.

blocks.title: How do you deploy to a cloud from Actions without storing cloud keys?
blocks.text: Use OpenID Connect. The workflow requests a signed identity token from GitHub; the cloud provider is configured to trust tokens from a specific repository and branch and exchanges it for short-lived credentials. Nothing long-lived is stored.

blocks.title: What is a matrix build?
blocks.text: One job definition expanded into several jobs over combinations of variables, for example operating systems and language versions, run in parallel.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: In Actions, what is the closest equivalent of a Jenkins agent label?
quiz.why: runs-on selects the kind of runner the job requires.

quiz.q: How do you require a human approval before a production job?
quiz.why: Environment protection rules pause the job until a reviewer approves.

lessons.title: GitHub Actions in depth: reuse, matrix, caching, environments and OIDC

blocks.text: Past the first workflow, five features do most of the work. Reusable workflows let one file define how every repository builds. A matrix runs the same job across several versions at once. Caching stops each run downloading the same dependencies. Environments put an approval and their own secrets in front of a deployment. OIDC lets a job get short-lived cloud credentials without any stored key.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A restaurant chain. The head office writes one recipe card (the reusable workflow) that every branch follows. The kitchen tests the dish on three ovens at once (the matrix). Ingredients are prepared in advance (the cache). Nothing leaves for a banquet until the manager signs (the environment). And the delivery driver shows a badge issued for that one trip rather than carrying a master key (OIDC).
Why it matters

Copy-pasted workflows drift: thirty repositories, thirty slightly different pipelines, and a security fix that has to be made thirty times. Long-lived cloud keys stored as secrets are the most common way a CI system leaks access. These features remove both problems.
Where you meet it
Any organisation on GitHub with more than a few repositories. A platform team usually owns a "pipelines" repository of reusable workflows, and service repositories call them by version tag.
Scenario

checkout-api, payments and catalog each had a 120-line workflow. The platform team moves the build into shop/pipelines as build-service.yml. Each service now has a 20-line caller. The deploy job targets the production environment, which requires one reviewer, and assumes an AWS role through OIDC whose trust policy only accepts tokens from that repository and that environment.
Architecture

flowchart LR subgraph SVC["Service repository"] CI["ci.yml (caller)"] end subgraph PIPE["shop/pipelines repository"] RW["build-service.yml
on: workflow_call"] end CI -->|"uses: ...@v3
with inputs + secrets"| RW RW --> MX["Matrix: test on 3.11 and 3.12"] MX <--> CA["Dependency cache
keyed on lock file"] RW --> BLD["Build and push image"] CI --> DEP["deploy job
environment: production"] DEP --> APP{"Required reviewer
approves?"} APP -->|"yes"| OIDC["Request OIDC token
(id-token: write)"] OIDC --> STS["AWS STS checks the trust policy:
repository + environment"] STS --> ROLE["Short-lived role credentials"] ROLE --> PROD["Deploy"]

(called with uses: at job level)"] B -->|"no, a few steps"| C["Composite action

blocks.text: Commands
Lists the workflows in the current repository and whether each is active.
The last five runs of one workflow with their status and branch.
Prints only the log of the steps that failed. The fastest way to read a red build from a terminal.
Re-runs only the failed jobs of a run. If a deploy job is among them, it deploys again.
Starts a workflow that has a workflow_dispatch trigger. What it does depends on the workflow.
Shows the caches stored for the repository, with size and last use.
Removes every cache. The next runs are slower while caches rebuild; nothing else is lost.
Stores a secret on the production environment. It prompts for the value so that it stays out of shell history.
A reusable workflow and its caller

blocks.code:
# .github/workflows/build-service.yml  (the reusable workflow)
name: build-service
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      image:
        required: true
        type: string
    secrets:
      registry_token:
        required: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python: ["3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4          # pin to a commit SHA in real use
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
          cache: pip                        # restores ~/.cache/pip keyed on the lock file
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: make check

  build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker build -t ${{ inputs.image }}:${{ github.sha }} .
      - run: echo "${{ secrets.registry_token }}" | docker login registry.example.com -u ci --password-stdin
      - run: docker push ${{ inputs.image }}:${{ github.sha }}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# .github/workflows/ci.yml in each service repository (the caller)
#
# on:
#   push: { branches: [main] }
#   pull_request:
# concurrency:
#   group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
#   cancel-in-progress: true
# jobs:

#       image: registry.example.com/shop/checkout-api

#       registry_token: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}
#
#   deploy:

#     permissions:
#       id-token: write              # lets the job request an OIDC token
#       contents: read
#     steps:
#       - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4

#           role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/deploy-checkout
#           aws-region: ap-south-1
