blocks.text: Checked against the GitHub documentation for reusable workflows and for OIDC with AWS on 11 November 2026. Not run. The role ARN, account number and registry are placeholders. The documentation limits a chain to ten levels of workflows, and secrets pass only one level unless each level forwards them.
Exercise
Turn a single-repository workflow into a reusable one and call it, in a repository you own.

items: In a test repository, create .github/workflows/build-service.yml with on: workflow_call and one string input.
Create ci.yml with a job that has uses: ./.github/workflows/build-service.yml and passes the input.
Add a matrix with two language versions to the test job and set fail-fast: false.
Add cache: pip (or the equivalent for your language) to the setup step and run the workflow twice.
Create an environment called staging with yourself as required reviewer, and add a job that targets it.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: The second run shows a cache hit in the setup step, the matrix shows two test jobs, and the staging job waits for your approval before starting.
Troubleshooting

rows: The caller fails at once with "workflow is not reusable" or cannot find the file.
The called file has no on: workflow_call trigger, sits in a subdirectory of .github/workflows, or the caller cannot access that repository.
Add the trigger, keep the file directly in .github/workflows, and allow access to the pipelines repository under its Actions settings.
A secret is empty inside the reusable workflow.
Secrets are not passed automatically. The caller did not pass it, or an intermediate workflow in the chain did not forward it.
Pass it by name under secrets:, or use secrets: inherit when both are in the same organisation.
AWS replies "Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity".
The job lacks permissions: id-token: write, or the sub claim in the token does not match the trust policy. A job that uses an environment sends an environment subject, not a branch subject.
Add the permission, then compare the trust policy condition with the subject format your repository actually sends.
The cache never hits.
The key changes on every run, for example because it hashes a file that the build rewrites.
Key on the lock file only, and add restore-keys for a partial match.
Pull requests from forks fail where branches pass.
Workflows triggered by a fork do not receive secrets and get a read-only token.
Keep the fork path to tests that need no secrets. Do not switch to pull_request_target to get secrets while still checking out the fork's code.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Keep reusable workflows in one repository and have callers pin a tag or commit SHA, not a branch.
Set permissions at the top of every workflow, starting from contents: read, and add only what a job needs.
Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA. A tag can be moved to different code.
Use concurrency groups so that a new push cancels the outdated run, and so that two deployments never overlap.
Use OIDC for cloud access and remove stored cloud keys.
Put deployment secrets on environments, not on the repository, so that only approved jobs can read them.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never interpolate untrusted text such as a pull request title straight into a run: script. Pass it through an environment variable, or it can inject shell commands.
pull_request_target runs with secrets and a write token. Combining it with a checkout of the pull request's code hands those to anyone who opens a pull request.
Scope the cloud trust policy to one repository and one branch or environment. A wildcard over the organisation lets any repository assume the role.
Self-hosted runners on public repositories can be taken over by a pull request. Use them only with private repositories, and prefer runners that are destroyed after one job.
Printing a secret through base64 or character by character defeats log masking. Treat any secret that reached a log as leaked and rotate it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between a reusable workflow and a composite action?
blocks.text: A reusable workflow is a whole workflow called at the job level with uses:. It can contain several jobs, choose its own runners and use environments. A composite action is a bundle of steps called as one step inside a job, so it runs on the caller's runner. Share a complete pipeline with a reusable workflow; share a few repeated steps with a composite action.

blocks.title: How does OIDC replace stored cloud credentials in GitHub Actions?
blocks.text: The job asks GitHub for a signed token that states which repository, branch or environment it is running for. It presents that token to the cloud provider, which has been told to trust GitHub as an identity provider. The provider checks the claims against the role's trust policy and returns credentials that expire in about an hour. Nothing long-lived is stored, so there is nothing to leak or rotate.

blocks.title: Why pin an action to a commit SHA rather than a version tag?
blocks.text: A tag is a movable pointer. If the action's repository is compromised, the attacker can move v4 to malicious code and every workflow using that tag runs it on the next build, with access to your secrets. A commit SHA is immutable. Tools such as Dependabot can still propose updates to the pinned SHA.

blocks.title: A matrix job fails on one version and the others are cancelled. Why, and how do you change it?
blocks.text: fail-fast defaults to true, so the first failure cancels the rest of the matrix to save minutes. Setting strategy.fail-fast: false lets every combination finish, which is what you want when you need to know whether the failure is specific to one version.

quiz.q: A reusable workflow is called…
options: at the job level with uses:
quiz.why: It replaces a whole job; steps cannot call it.

quiz.q: Which permission lets a job request an OIDC token?
quiz.why: Without it the token request is refused.

quiz.q: Where should a production deploy key or secret live?
options: On an environment with required reviewers
quiz.why: Only jobs approved for that environment can then read it.

quiz.q: A good cache key for Python dependencies hashes…
quiz.why: The cache should change exactly when the dependencies do.

modules.title: Docker Mastery
modules.summary: Images, layers, Dockerfile, volumes, networking, and small, secure production images.

lessons.title: Volumes and container networking

blocks.text: A container's filesystem is disposable: anything written inside disappears when the container is removed. A volume is storage managed by Docker that lives outside any container and is attached at a path; a bind mount attaches a directory from the host instead. For networking, containers on the same user-defined network can reach each other by container or service name, because Docker runs a small DNS server for that network. Nothing is reachable from the host or the outside world unless you publish a port. And inside a container, "localhost" is the container itself, not the host and not its neighbours.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A container without a volume is an app whose data lives only in memory: relaunch and it is gone. A volume is the app's Documents directory, which survives reinstalling. Service names are like Bonjour names on a private network: only devices on that network can resolve them.
Why it matters
Containers are meant to be replaced constantly, so data and addresses must not be tied to any one of them.
Where you meet it
Databases in development, uploaded files, sharing configuration into a container, and every multi-container application.
Scenario

Locally, checkout-api talks to PostgreSQL at the hostname "db" and Redis at "redis". Only nginx publishes a port. The database keeps its files in a named volume, so recreating the containers after an image update loses nothing.
Architecture

flowchart LR H["Your machine
localhost:8080"] -->|"published 8080 → 80"| N["nginx"] subgraph NET["Docker network 'default' (private)"] N -->|"http://api:8000"| A["api"] A -->|"db:5432"| D["db (PostgreSQL)"] A -->|"redis:6379"| R["redis"] DNS["Docker DNS
resolves service names"] end D --- V["Named volume 'dbdata'
survives container removal"] N --- B["Bind mount ./nginx.conf
a file on your machine"] H -. "5432 is NOT published" .-> D

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["api connects to db:5432"] --> B["Ask Docker's DNS (127.0.0.11)
for 'db'"] B --> C{"A container named 'db'

blocks.text: Commands
Lists volumes. Each named volume is data that outlives containers.

blocks.code: docker run -d --name db -v dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=localdev postgres:16
blocks.caption: Changes the local environment

blocks.text: Starts PostgreSQL with its data directory on a named volume.

rows: `-v NAME:/path`
named volume: Docker manages where it lives
`-v /host/dir:/path`
bind mount: a host directory you choose
`:ro`
append to mount read-only

blocks.code: docker network create shop && docker run -d --network shop --name api checkout-api:dev
blocks.caption: Changes the local environment

blocks.text: Creates a user-defined network and attaches a container. Containers on it resolve each other by name.

blocks.code: docker exec api getent hosts db
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Asks, from inside one container, what the name of another resolves to.
Shows which container ports are published and to which host ports. No output means nothing is published.
Deletes a volume and all data in it. There is no undo.
Deletes every volume not used by a container, including the data of stopped projects.
Storage and port options at a glance

blocks.code:
Storage                      Lives where              Survives "docker rm"?   Use for
container writable layer     inside the container     no                      nothing you want to keep
named volume  -v data:/p     managed by Docker        yes                     databases, uploads
bind mount    -v ./dir:/p    a directory you choose   yes (it is your file)   source code in dev, config
tmpfs         --tmpfs /p     memory only              no                      scratch, secrets at runtime

Ports
-p 8080:80        host 8080 → container 80, on ALL host interfaces
-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80   only reachable from the host itself
EXPOSE 8000       documentation only: publishes nothing
(nothing)         still reachable by other containers on the same network

Names
on the default "bridge" network       containers reach each other by IP only
on a user-defined network             by container / service name (Docker DNS)
"localhost" inside a container        that container, never the host
"host.docker.internal" (Desktop)      the host machine

blocks.text: Exercise
Predict which connections work, then test each one.

items: Start the stack in the simulator
From your machine, try localhost:8080, localhost:5432 and db:5432. Explain each result
From the api container, try db:5432 and localhost:5432. Why does the second fail?
From api, try nginx:8080 and nginx:80. Which port do containers use to talk to each other?
Insert three rows, run "down", then "up" again: how many rows? Now run "down -v"
Publish the database by adding a ports entry and decide when that would be acceptable

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state the three rules: names resolve only inside the network; containers use container ports; only published ports reach the host.
Troubleshooting

rows: Connection refused to localhost:5432 from inside a container
localhost is the container itself.
Use the other container's service name: db:5432.
Could not resolve host: db
The containers are on the default bridge network or on different networks.
Put them on the same user-defined network. Compose does this for you.
The database is empty after recreating the container
Its data was in the container's writable layer.
Mount a named volume at the image's data directory.
Permission denied writing to a mounted directory
The container's user ID does not own the host directory.
Match the user ID, or use a named volume, which Docker initialises with the right ownership.
A published database port is being scanned from the internet
-p publishes on all interfaces and bypasses host firewall rules such as ufw.
Do not publish it, or bind to 127.0.0.1:5432:5432.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Named volumes for data, bind mounts for development source and configuration.
One user-defined network per application.
Publish only the entry point.
Treat containers as replaceable and volumes as precious: back volumes up.
Keep configuration in environment variables or mounted files, not in the image.

blocks.text: Security

items: Docker's port publishing writes its own firewall rules and can expose a port that ufw appears to block.
A bind mount of / or the Docker socket gives the container control of the host.
Mount read-only whenever the container does not need to write.
Volumes hold real data: they need the same access control and encryption as the database they back.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Volume versus bind mount?
blocks.text: A volume is storage created and managed by Docker, independent of the host's directory layout and portable across hosts. A bind mount maps a specific host path into the container, so it depends on the host and is ideal for development. Both outlive the container.

blocks.title: How do containers find each other?
blocks.text: On a user-defined network Docker runs an embedded DNS server that resolves container and service names to their current addresses. Containers on the same network connect by name and container port, with no published ports needed.

blocks.title: What does EXPOSE do?
blocks.text: It documents which port the image listens on and is used by tools as a hint. It does not publish the port; only -p or a Compose ports entry does.

quiz.q: Inside the api container, what does localhost:5432 refer to?

lessons.title: Production images: small, secure, reproducible, debuggable

blocks.text: A production image should contain your application and what it needs to run, and nothing else. A multi-stage build compiles in one stage with all its tools and copies only the result into a small final stage. A .dockerignore keeps junk and secrets out of the build. The process runs as a non-root user. The base image is pinned to a known version and rebuilt regularly to pick up security patches. Every image is identified by a digest, a hash of its exact contents, which is what you deploy when you need certainty.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: It is the difference between shipping a Release build with symbols stripped and shipping your whole DerivedData folder. Same app; one is small, the other leaks your tooling and takes ten times as long to download.
Why it matters

Every node downloads the image before it can start your service, so size is start-up time and recovery time. Every extra package is one more thing that can have a vulnerability and one more tool for an attacker who gets in.
Where you meet it
Every Dockerfile that reaches a registry.
Scenario

The checkout-api image went from about 1.4 GB to about 190 MB by switching to a slim base and a multi-stage build. Scale-up during a sale dropped from over a minute per new pod to a few seconds, and the weekly scan report shrank from hundreds of findings to a handful.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph S1["Stage 1: builder (discarded)"] B1["python:3.12-slim"] --> B2["compilers, headers"] --> B3["pip install → /install"] end subgraph S2["Stage 2: runtime (shipped)"] R1["python:3.12-slim"] --> R2["COPY --from=builder /install"] --> R3["COPY app"] --> R4["USER 10001"] end B3 -->|"only the installed packages"| R2 R4 --> IMG["Image
tag :9f3c2ab
digest sha256:4be1…"] IMG --> SCAN["Scan"] --> REG["Registry"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["docker build"] --> B["Send build context
(minus .dockerignore)"] B --> C["For each instruction"] C --> D{"Same instruction and inputs
as a cached layer?"} D -->|yes| E["Reuse layer"] D -->|no| F["Execute; this and ALL later
layers are rebuilt"] E --> G{"More instructions?"} F --> G G -->|yes| C G -->|no| H["Final stage becomes the image"] H --> I["Scan for known vulnerabilities"] I -->|"critical found"| J["Fail the build"] I -->|"clean"| K["Push with an immutable tag"]

blocks.text: Commands
Lists layers with their sizes and the instruction that made each: where the megabytes come from.
Shows the digest of each image: the hash that identifies its exact content.
Lists known vulnerabilities in an image's packages. trivy image NAME does the same job.
Starts a shell in the image instead of its normal command, to look around when a container will not start.

rows: `--entrypoint sh`
override the image's start command
remove on exit

blocks.text: Runs with a read-only filesystem, no Linux capabilities and a non-root user: the hardened way an orchestrator should run it.

rows: `--read-only`
the container cannot modify its own filesystem
`--cap-drop ALL`
remove all kernel capabilities
`--user`
run as this UID

blocks.text: Attaches a toolbox shell to a running container even when its image has no shell. It is a Docker Desktop feature that may need a paid plan; kubectl debug does the same job in Kubernetes.
examples/docker/Dockerfile

blocks.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- Stage 1: install dependencies (build tools stay in this stage) ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
# Copy only the dependency list first so this layer is cached
# until requirements.txt itself changes.
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

# ---- Stage 2: small runtime image ----
FROM python:3.12-slim
# Never run as root inside the container.
RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local
COPY app ./app
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

blocks.text: Pair it with a .dockerignore listing .git, .venv, .env, node_modules and local data.
Exercise
Get the image as small and clean as you can, and know what each change bought.

items: Note the starting size and the number of findings
Switch to the slim base: how much was the base image alone?
Turn on multi-stage: which layer disappears, and why is it safe to remove?
Add the .dockerignore: what was being copied in?
Clear the remaining findings one at a time and read each
Try the Alpine base and read the caveat it adds
If you did Lab 4: run docker history on your own image and compare

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Under 200 MB with no findings, and you can explain what multi-stage removes that a smaller base does not.
Troubleshooting

rows: The image is far larger than the application
A full base image, build tools left in, caches, or a huge build context.
docker history shows the layer responsible. Slim base, multi-stage, --no-cache-dir, .dockerignore.
A secret is found in a published image
It was copied or passed as a build argument and remains in a layer.
Rotate it. Use build secrets (--mount=type=secret) and .dockerignore; deleting it in a later layer does not remove it.
The same tag behaves differently on two nodes
A mutable tag such as latest was pushed again; nodes pulled at different times.
Use immutable tags (commit ID) or deploy by digest.
Cannot exec into the container to debug: no shell
Minimal or distroless images contain no shell by design.
Use an ephemeral debug container (docker debug, kubectl debug) rather than adding tools to the image.
Permission denied at startup after adding USER
The app writes to a directory owned by root, or binds a port below 1024.
chown what it must write during the build, write to a mounted volume, and listen on a high port.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Multi-stage builds; ship only runtime contents.
Slim or distroless bases, pinned, rebuilt on a schedule.
Non-root user, read-only filesystem, no extra capabilities.
Immutable tags; deploy by digest where it matters.
Scan in CI and fail on fixable critical findings.
One process per container, logging to stdout.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never bake secrets into images or pass them as build arguments.
Generate an SBOM and sign images so you can prove what is running and where it came from.
A scan lists known vulnerabilities only; it does not make an image safe.
Pull base images from sources you trust and pin them by digest for critical systems.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is a multi-stage build and why use it?
blocks.text: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where later stages copy selected files from earlier ones. Build tools, source and intermediate files stay in the discarded stages, so the final image holds only what is needed at run time: smaller, faster to pull and with less attack surface.

blocks.title: Tag versus digest?
blocks.text: A tag is a movable name that can be pointed at a different image later. A digest is the hash of the image content and never changes. Deploying by digest guarantees every node runs identical bytes.

blocks.title: How do you debug a container that has no shell?
blocks.text: Attach an ephemeral debug container that shares its process and network namespaces (kubectl debug, docker debug), read its logs and exit code, and reproduce locally with the entrypoint overridden on a debug variant of the image.

blocks.title: How would you reduce vulnerabilities in your images?
blocks.text: Fewer packages first: minimal base and multi-stage. Then pin and regularly rebuild to pick up patches, scan in CI with a policy on fixable criticals, and remove what the scan keeps finding rather than accepting it.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which change removes compilers from the final image?
quiz.why: The build stage is discarded; only what you COPY --from it is kept.

quiz.q: Why is deploying the tag "latest" risky?
options: It can point at different images at different times
quiz.why: A mutable tag gives no guarantee that two pulls return the same image.

lessons.title: Images, containers and the Dockerfile

blocks.text: An image is a read-only package holding your application, its dependencies and a minimal operating-system filesystem. A container is a running instance of an image: an isolated process. A Dockerfile is the recipe that builds the image, one instruction per layer. A registry stores images so other machines can pull them.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The image is the .ipa: built once, identical everywhere. The container is the app running on a device. The registry is TestFlight or the App Store. The Dockerfile is the build script that produced the .ipa.
Why it matters
Before containers, "deploy" meant installing the right language version and libraries on each server and hoping they matched your laptop. An image carries its environment with it.
Where you meet it
Local development, CI builds, and as the unit that Kubernetes, ECS and every modern platform deploys.
Scenario

CI builds checkout-api into an image tagged with the commit SHA and pushes it to the registry. Each Kubernetes node pulls that exact image and starts it as a container. Staging and production run the same bytes.
Architecture

flowchart LR DF["Dockerfile"] -->|"docker build"| IMG["Image
(stack of layers)"] IMG -->|"docker push"| REG["Registry"] REG -->|"docker pull"| H["Any host"] H -->|"docker run"| C1["Container 1"] H -->|"docker run"| C2["Container 2"]

(slow layer, cached)"] C --> D["COPY app/"] D --> E["CMD uvicorn ..."] X["You edit app code"] -.->|"only layers from here
are rebuilt"| D

Exercise
Understand layer caching well enough to make builds fast.

items: Open the Docker visualizer and build once
Change "application code" and rebuild: which layers are reused?
Change "requirements.txt" and rebuild: why is it slower?
Explain why COPY requirements.txt comes before COPY app

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state the rule: a changed layer invalidates every layer after it, so put what changes least first.
Troubleshooting

rows: Container exits immediately
The main process ended or crashed. A container lives exactly as long as its PID 1.
docker ps -a for the exit code, docker logs NAME for the reason.
App runs but localhost:8000 refuses connections
Port not published, or the app listens on 127.0.0.1 inside the container.
Publish with -p and make the app listen on 0.0.0.0.
Image is 1.5 GB
Full base image, build tools left in, caches not cleaned.
Use a slim base, multi-stage builds and --no-cache-dir.
Data vanished after recreating the container
It was written to the container writable layer.
Store data in a named volume or outside the container.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: One process per container; logs go to stdout.
Pin base image versions; rebuild regularly for security patches.
Order instructions from least to most frequently changed.
Keep images small: less to pull, less to patch, less to attack.

blocks.text: Security

items: Run as a non-root USER.
Never bake secrets into an image: every layer is readable by anyone who can pull it, even if a later layer deletes the file.
Scan images in CI and use minimal base images.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Image versus container?
blocks.text: An image is an immutable template made of layers. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of it: the image layers plus a thin writable layer and an isolated process.

blocks.title: How does Docker layer caching work?
blocks.text: Each instruction produces a layer keyed by the instruction and its inputs. If nothing changed, the cached layer is reused. Once one layer changes, every later layer is rebuilt, so stable steps such as dependency installation go before frequently changing ones such as copying source.

blocks.title: CMD versus ENTRYPOINT?
blocks.text: ENTRYPOINT is the executable that always runs; CMD supplies default arguments that docker run can override. With only CMD, the whole command is replaceable.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: You delete a secret file in a later Dockerfile layer. Is it gone from the image?
options: No, it remains in the earlier layer
quiz.why: Layers are additive. The earlier layer still contains the file and can be extracted.

quiz.q: Why copy requirements.txt before the application code?
options: So the slow dependency layer stays cached when only code changes
quiz.why: Code changes then invalidate only the cheap final layers.

modules.title: Docker Compose
modules.summary: A whole stack in one file: start order, health checks, networking and volumes.

lessons.title: Docker Compose: a whole stack in one file

blocks.text: Compose describes a multi-container application in one YAML file: each service, its image or build, ports, environment, volumes and what it depends on. "docker compose up" creates a private network, starts everything in dependency order and gives each service a hostname equal to its name. "docker compose down" removes it all again, keeping named volumes unless you add -v. depends_on controls start order; on its own it only waits for the other container to start, not for the software inside to be ready. To wait for readiness, the dependency needs a healthcheck and the dependent needs condition: service_healthy.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: It is a Podfile for running infrastructure: instead of a list of libraries to link, a list of services to run together, checked into the repository so every developer gets the same environment with one command.
Why it matters
A realistic application is several processes. Starting five containers by hand with the right flags, in the right order, on the right network is slow and nobody does it the same way twice.
Where you meet it
Local development, integration tests in CI, demos, and small single-server deployments. It is not a production orchestrator: it does not reschedule across machines or scale itself.
Scenario

A new engineer clones checkout-api and runs one command. Ninety seconds later nginx, the API, a worker, PostgreSQL and Redis are running and talking to each other, with the same service names the code uses everywhere else.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  F["compose.yaml"] -->|"docker compose up"| P["Project 'checkout'"]
  subgraph P2["Created for the project"]
    NW["network: checkout_default"]
    VOL["volume: checkout_dbdata"]
    C1["nginx"] --> C2["api"]
    C4["worker"]
    C2 --> C3["db"]
    C2 --> C5["redis"]
    C4 --> C3
    C4 --> C5
  end
  P --> P2
  H["localhost:8080"] --> C1
  C3 --- VOL

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["docker compose up -d"] --> B["Read and validate the file"] B --> C["Create network and volumes"] C --> D["Start services with no dependencies:
db, redis"] D --> E["db healthcheck: pg_isready"] E --> F{"Healthy?"} F -->|"not yet"| E F -->|yes| G["Start api and worker
(condition: service_healthy)"] G --> H["Start nginx
(depends_on: api)"] H --> I["Stack is up"]

blocks.text: Commands
Creates and starts everything in the file, in the background. Run again after editing the file: only changed services are recreated.

rows: detached
`--build`
rebuild images first
`--wait`
return only when services are healthy

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: docker compose ps
Lists the project's containers with state, health and published ports.
Follows one service's logs. Without a name, all services interleaved.

blocks.code: docker compose exec db psql -U shop
blocks.caption: Changes the local environment

blocks.text: Runs a command inside a running service container: here, a database shell.
Validates the file and prints the fully resolved configuration, with variables substituted. The equivalent of nginx -t.
Stops and removes the containers and network. Named volumes, and the data in them, are kept.
Also deletes the named volumes: the database contents are gone.
examples/docker/compose.yaml

blocks.code:
# Local development stack for checkout-api. Start with: docker compose up -d
services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    ports:
      - "8080:80"            # the ONLY port published to your machine
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - api

  api:
    build: .
    expose:
      - "8000"               # reachable by other services, not from your machine
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://shop:localdev@db:5432/shop
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
      APP_VERSION: compose
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    restart: unless-stopped

  worker:
    build: .
    command: python -m app.worker
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://shop:localdev@db:5432/shop
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started
    restart: unless-stopped

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: shop
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: localdev   # local only; never reuse in production
      POSTGRES_DB: shop
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U shop"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

volumes:
  dbdata:

blocks.text: Only nginx has a ports entry. The api uses expose, which documents the port without publishing it.
Exercise
See with your own eyes why depends_on alone is not enough.

items: Bring the stack up and read the timeline: when does api start relative to db?
Replace the api's depends_on block with a plain list (- db and - redis) and bring it up again
Read the "connection refused" line and the restart count
Now also delete "restart: unless-stopped" from api: what state does it end in?
Restore the file, then delete the db healthcheck: what does Compose say?
Add a ports entry on redis that reuses host port 8080 and read the error

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain the difference between "started" and "ready", and name the two settings that together make start-up reliable.
Troubleshooting

rows: The api exits at startup with "connection refused" to the database
depends_on waited only for the database container to start, not for PostgreSQL to accept connections.
Add a healthcheck to the database and condition: service_healthy to the dependent. Also make the app retry.
port is already allocated
Another container or a program on your machine uses that host port.
Change the left-hand number of the ports mapping, or stop the other process.
Changes to the code have no effect
The image was not rebuilt.
docker compose up -d --build, or bind-mount the source in development.
Old data keeps coming back after "down"
The named volume persists by design.
docker compose down -v when you really want a clean database.
A variable shows up empty in the container
It is set in your shell but not passed in, or the .env file is not where Compose looks.
docker compose config shows the resolved values.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Commit the compose file; keep secrets in an untracked .env.
Healthchecks on stateful services and service_healthy on what depends on them.
Publish only what you need on your machine.
Pin image versions.
Use the same service names the application uses in other environments.

blocks.text: Security

items: Compose files often contain development passwords: never reuse them elsewhere, and keep real ones out of the file.
A published port is open on every interface of your machine, including on public Wi-Fi.
Compose on a production server has no self-healing across machines and no secret store: know what you are giving up.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What does depends_on guarantee?
blocks.text: Start order. By default only that the dependency's container has been started. With condition: service_healthy it waits until the dependency's healthcheck passes. It never replaces retry logic in the application, because dependencies can restart later.

blocks.title: How do services in a Compose project reach each other?
blocks.text: Compose creates a network for the project and attaches every service. Docker's DNS resolves each service name to its container, so the api connects to db:5432 using the container port. Published ports are only for access from the host.

blocks.title: Compose versus Kubernetes?
blocks.text: Compose runs a set of containers on one machine from one file: ideal for development and tests. Kubernetes schedules across many machines, replaces failed instances, scales, rolls out updates gradually and manages configuration and secrets. The concepts map closely: service to Deployment plus Service, volume to PersistentVolumeClaim, healthcheck to probes.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: "docker compose down" does what to named volumes?
quiz.why: Volumes are removed only with -v.

quiz.q: api has "depends_on: [db]". When does api start?
options: When the db container has started
At the same time as db
quiz.why: Without a health condition, Compose waits only for the container to start.

modules.title: Kubernetes Mastery
modules.summary: Core objects, config, probes, resources, networking, storage and workload types, RBAC, autoscaling, scheduling and troubleshooting. Also internals (network plugin, DNS, admission, operators) and service mesh. Also running several clusters.

lessons.title: Kubernetes internals: networking, DNS, admission and operators

blocks.text: Under the objects you use every day, four mechanisms do the work. A network plugin gives every pod an address and connects them. A DNS service turns Service names into addresses. Admission control checks or changes every object before it is stored. And the control loop pattern, which can be extended with your own resource types and controllers, called operators.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A city. The network plugin is the road system and house numbering. DNS is the phone book. Admission control is the planning office that approves or amends every building application. Operators are specialised contractors: you file a one-page request for "a bakery" and they handle the hundred steps to build and maintain one.
Why it matters

Most hard cluster incidents are in these layers: pods that cannot reach each other, name lookups that fail under load, a deployment rejected by a policy, a resource that "does nothing" because its controller is down. You cannot debug what you cannot picture.
Where you meet it
Every cluster. Managed services choose the network plugin and run DNS for you, but you still size it, write policies, install operators and debug all four.
Scenario

checkout-api calls the payments Service. The name payments.production.svc.cluster.local is resolved by CoreDNS to a virtual address. kube-proxy rules on the node rewrite that to one payment pod's address. The network plugin routes the packet to that pod, on another node, where a NetworkPolicy allows it. Earlier, when the pod was created, an admission webhook checked its image signature and another injected a sidecar.
Architecture

flowchart TB K["kubectl apply"] --> API["API server"] subgraph ADM["Admission"] MUT["Mutating webhooks
add defaults, inject sidecars"] VAL["Validating webhooks and policies
Pod Security, signed images"] end API --> MUT --> VAL --> ETCD[("etcd")] ETCD --> CTRL["Built-in controllers
Deployment, ReplicaSet, endpoints"] ETCD --> OP["Operators: your controllers
watching custom resources"] CTRL --> SCHED["Scheduler"] --> KUBELET["kubelet on a node"] KUBELET --> CRI["Container runtime (CRI)"] KUBELET --> CNI["Network plugin (CNI)
pod IP, routes, NetworkPolicy"] KUBELET --> CSI["Storage plugin (CSI)
attach and mount volumes"] POD["Pod"] -->|"name lookup"| DNS["CoreDNS"] POD -->|"Service virtual IP"| KP["kube-proxy rules
pick a backend pod"] KP --> POD2["Destination pod"]

Commands
The system pods: CoreDNS, the network plugin's agents, kube-proxy. Restarts or pods all on one node here explain many strange failures.
Starts a temporary pod and resolves a Service name from inside the cluster. The first check when "the service is unreachable".
The pod addresses behind a Service. Empty means the selector matches nothing or no pod is ready.

blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: CoreDNS configuration: which domains it serves and where it forwards other lookups.
Every admission webhook. A webhook whose service is down, with failurePolicy Fail, blocks all matching creates and updates.
Custom resource types installed in the cluster. Each belongs to an operator.
Every kind of object the API server knows, built-in and custom.
Sends the object through admission without storing it. Shows exactly what a policy or webhook would reject or change.
Deletes a custom resource type and every object of that type with it. With an operator, that can mean deleting the real databases they represent.
A custom resource definition and an object of that kind (illustrative)

blocks.code:
# A custom resource: a new kind of object the cluster learns about.
# The definition (CRD) teaches the API server the shape; a controller acts on it.
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databases.shop.example
spec:
  group: shop.example
  scope: Namespaced
  names: { kind: Database, plural: databases, singular: database }
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                engine: { type: string }
                sizeGb: { type: integer }
---
# Once that exists, teams can ask for a database like any other object.
# An operator (a controller you install) sees this and creates the real thing.
apiVersion: shop.example/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: production
spec:
  engine: postgres
  sizeGb: 100

blocks.text: A CRD by itself only stores objects. Nothing happens until a controller watching that kind acts on them. Argo CD's Application, from the GitOps lesson, is exactly this pattern.
Exercise
Use the Service debugging lab and the flowchart to locate failures at each layer.

items: In the lab, work through the four reasons a Service does not answer. Map each to a box in the flowchart
Which failures show as "connection refused" and which as a timeout?
A name resolves from one pod and fails from another. Name two layers to suspect and the command for each
A Deployment is rejected with "admission webhook denied the request". Where do you look, and how do you see the reason without creating anything?
You create a Database object and nothing happens. What is missing?
In incident 8 of the simulator, which internal component failed and why did it affect every service?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can trace a request from one pod to another through DNS, the Service, policy and the network plugin, and say what an operator is.
Troubleshooting

rows: Intermittent "name resolution failed" across many services
CoreDNS is overloaded, being killed for memory, or has too few replicas.
Scale and spread CoreDNS, raise its memory, consider a node-local DNS cache.
External lookups are slow from pods
The search path makes each lookup try several cluster suffixes first.
Use fully qualified names ending in a dot, or lower ndots for that pod.
Pods cannot be created: no IP addresses available
The network plugin's address pool or the subnet is exhausted.
Larger pod ranges; on cloud plugins, more subnets or prefix delegation.
Nothing can be deployed anywhere
An admission webhook's backend is down and its failure policy is Fail.
Restore the webhook service. Scope webhooks narrowly and exclude system namespaces.
A custom resource is stuck and cannot be deleted
A finalizer is waiting for a controller that is not running.
Get the operator running. Removing the finalizer by hand skips its clean-up.
NetworkPolicy is ignored
The installed network plugin does not enforce it.
Use a plugin that does, such as Calico or Cilium.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Treat CoreDNS as a critical service: several replicas, spread out, monitored.
Size pod address space generously at cluster creation.
Use a network plugin that enforces NetworkPolicy.
Keep admission webhooks few, fast, highly available and narrowly scoped.
Check manifests against policies in pull requests, not only at admission.
Install operators deliberately: each is software you now run and upgrade.
Back up etcd, or use a managed control plane that does.

blocks.text: Security

items: Admission is where cluster-wide rules are enforced. Anyone who can change webhook configuration can bypass or break them.
A mutating webhook can alter every pod. Treat it as highly privileged code.
Operators often hold broad permissions. Review their RBAC before installing.
Without NetworkPolicy any pod can query DNS for every Service name and connect to it.
etcd holds every Secret. Restrict access and encrypt it at rest.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does a pod reach a Service by name?
blocks.text: The pod's resolver asks CoreDNS, using search domains to expand the short name. CoreDNS returns the Service's virtual IP. Rules installed on each node by kube-proxy (or an eBPF data plane) rewrite that address to one of the ready pod IPs from the Service's endpoints, and the network plugin routes the packet there.

blocks.title: What does a CNI plugin do?
blocks.text: It is called when a pod starts to give it a network interface and an IP address and to set up routes so every pod can reach every other pod without NAT. Many also enforce NetworkPolicy and provide encryption or observability.

blocks.title: What are admission controllers?
blocks.text: Steps that run after authentication and authorisation and before an object is stored. Mutating ones can change the object, such as adding defaults or sidecars; validating ones can reject it, such as Pod Security or image policy. They can be built in or external webhooks.

blocks.title: What is an operator?
blocks.text: A controller that manages an application through custom resources. You declare the desired state in an object of a new kind, and the operator creates and maintains the underlying resources, encoding the operational knowledge a person would otherwise apply.

blocks.title: What is etcd and what happens if it is lost?
blocks.text: The consistent key-value store holding all cluster state. Running pods keep running without it, but nothing can change: no scheduling, scaling or healing. Without a backup, the cluster's definition is gone.

quiz.why: The name resolved, so DNS worked.

quiz.q: A CRD without a controller…
quiz.why: Something must watch the objects and act.

quiz.q: An admission webhook's backend is down and its failure policy is Fail. Result?
quiz.why: Which is why webhooks must be scoped and highly available.

lessons.title: Service mesh: what it adds and what it costs

blocks.text: A service mesh puts a small proxy next to every service and sends all traffic between services through those proxies. Because the proxies see every call, they can encrypt it, check who is calling, retry or time out, shift traffic gradually to a new version, and report metrics, all without changing application code. The price is another layer to run and to debug.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Giving every employee a personal assistant who handles all their calls. The assistants verify who is on the line, keep a log, redial when a line drops, and follow company-wide rules. Staff just talk. But you now employ twice as many people, and when a call fails you must work out whether it was the person or the assistant.
Why it matters

With many services in many languages, every team re-implements timeouts, retries, encryption and metrics, slightly differently. A mesh moves that into the platform, where it is uniform and can be changed by configuration. It is also the usual way to get encrypted, authenticated service-to-service traffic.
Where you meet it

Larger microservice platforms with real needs for mutual TLS, fine-grained traffic control or uniform telemetry. Common implementations are Istio and Linkerd; Cilium offers a sidecar-free approach. Small systems rarely need one.
Scenario

The shop must encrypt all internal traffic for an audit and wants canary releases for checkout-api. Instead of changing thirty services, the platform team enables a mesh: every pod gets a proxy, mutual TLS is switched on for the namespace, and a routing rule sends 10% of checkout traffic to the new version. The dashboards gain per-route success rates for every service for free.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph CP["Control plane (istiod)"] CFG["Distributes routing rules,
policies and certificates"] end subgraph PA["Pod: checkout-api"] A["App container"] <--> SA["Sidecar proxy (Envoy)"] end subgraph PB["Pod: payments"] SB["Sidecar proxy"] <--> B["App container"] end SA <-->|"mutual TLS, retries,
timeouts, load balancing"| SB CFG -. "config + short-lived certificates" .-> SA CFG -.-> SB GW["Ingress gateway"] --> SA SA -. "metrics, traces, access logs" .-> OBS["Observability"] SB -.-> OBS

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Istio: new pods in the namespace get a sidecar proxy injected by a mutating admission webhook. Existing pods are unchanged until restarted.
With injection working, each pod shows 2/2 containers: the application and the proxy.
Checks mesh configuration for mistakes, such as a routing rule that refers to a missing destination.
Whether each sidecar has received the latest configuration from the control plane. STALE means it is behind.
The sidecar's access log. Response flags here say whether the proxy or the application caused a failure.
Restarts pods so they pick up a newly enabled or upgraded sidecar.
Removes the label. After the next restart pods run without sidecars, and with strict mutual TLS elsewhere they can no longer talk to meshed services.
A canary route and strict mutual TLS in Istio (illustrative)

blocks.code:
# Istio: send 10% of traffic to the new version of checkout-api (illustrative).
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: production
spec:
  hosts: [checkout-api]
  http:
    - route:
        - destination: { host: checkout-api, subset: stable }
          weight: 90
        - destination: { host: checkout-api, subset: canary }
          weight: 10
      timeout: 2s
      retries: { attempts: 2, perTryTimeout: 1s, retryOn: 5xx }
---
# Require encrypted, authenticated connections between all pods in the namespace.
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: production
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

blocks.text: Retries here multiply with any retries in the application. Decide which layer retries, and switch the other off.

Troubleshooting

rows: Pods show 1/1 after enabling injection
They were created before the label was set, or the injection webhook is not matching.
Restart the workload; check the namespace label.
503 errors after switching to strict mutual TLS
A caller without a sidecar sends plain text, which is now refused.
Use permissive mode during migration and move to strict when every caller is in the mesh.
A routing rule has no effect
The host does not match the Service, or the subset is not defined in a DestinationRule.
istioctl analyze.
Latency increased
Each call now crosses two proxies, or proxy resources are too small.
Measure the overhead, size the proxies, and check for doubled retries.
The application starts before its proxy and fails its first calls
Container start order.
Use native sidecar support or the option that holds the application until the proxy is ready; make the application retry at start-up.
Jobs never complete
The sidecar keeps running after the job's container exits.
Native sidecars, or exclude Jobs from injection.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Adopt a mesh for a stated need, not because others have one.
Start with one namespace and permissive mutual TLS.
Retries and timeouts live in one layer only.
Budget proxy CPU and memory per pod; it adds up.
Upgrade the mesh regularly, control plane first, with a canary.
Keep routing rules in Git with the rest of the deployment configuration.
Consider simpler options first: NetworkPolicy, the ingress controller, OpenTelemetry.

blocks.text: Security

items: Mutual TLS gives each workload a cryptographic identity and encrypts traffic between pods.
Authorisation policies can then allow calls by identity, not by network address.
The control plane issues certificates for everything. It is a high-value target.
A sidecar is not a hard boundary: a compromised application container can often bypass it. Keep NetworkPolicy as well.
Permissive mode accepts plain text. Do not leave it on after migration.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is a service mesh?
blocks.text: An infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication. A data plane of proxies, usually one sidecar per pod, carries all traffic; a control plane configures them. It provides mutual TLS, traffic management such as retries, timeouts and weighted routing, and uniform telemetry, without application changes.

blocks.title: When would you not use one?
blocks.text: With few services, a small team, or needs that NetworkPolicy, an ingress controller and OpenTelemetry already meet. A mesh adds latency, resource cost, upgrade work and a new failure layer.

blocks.title: How does mutual TLS work in a mesh?
blocks.text: The control plane issues each workload a short-lived certificate tied to its service account. Proxies on both sides present and verify certificates, so traffic is encrypted and each side knows the other's identity. Rotation is automatic.

blocks.title: Sidecar versus sidecar-less meshes?
blocks.text: Sidecars put a proxy in every pod: strong isolation per workload, but cost per pod and lifecycle problems. Newer designs use a per-node component or eBPF for the basics and shared proxies only where needed, reducing overhead.

blocks.title: How does a mesh enable canary releases?
blocks.text: Routing rules split traffic by weight or by request attributes between versions, independent of how many pods each has. A controller can raise the weight step by step while watching error rate and latency, and roll back automatically.

quiz.q: The data plane of a mesh is…
options: the proxies next to each service
quiz.why: They carry the traffic; the control plane configures them.

quiz.q: App retries 2 times, mesh retries 2 times. Worst case calls per request?
quiz.why: Three attempts at each layer multiply: 3 x 3.

quiz.q: A good reason to adopt a mesh is…
options: a requirement for encrypted, authenticated internal traffic
quiz.why: Adopt for a need you can state.

lessons.title: Running more than one cluster

blocks.text: Sooner or later one Kubernetes cluster is not enough: you want production apart from staging, a second region, or a limit on how much one failure can break. Multi-cluster work comes down to four problems. How the same configuration reaches every cluster. How users are routed to the right one. How services find each other across clusters. And where the data lives, which is the hard one.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A restaurant opening a second branch. The menu and recipes must stay the same in both (configuration). Customers need to be sent to the nearest open branch (routing). The branches sometimes borrow from each other (cross-cluster calls). And there is one set of accounts that both must agree on (data). Opening the second kitchen is easy. Keeping the books consistent is not.
Why it matters

A single cluster is a single blast radius: a bad upgrade, a broken admission webhook or a regional outage takes everything. More clusters reduce that risk, but each one adds upgrade work, cost and drift. Knowing the patterns lets you add clusters for a reason and keep them identical.
Where you meet it
Any organisation past its first production cluster: separate clusters per environment, per region for latency or disaster recovery, per team or tenant for isolation, and sometimes per cloud.
Scenario

The shop runs production in Mumbai. After a regional incident it adds a cluster in Hyderabad. Argo CD on a small management cluster deploys every app to both from one Git repository, with a per-region overlay. Route 53 sends users to the nearest healthy region. checkout-api is stateless and runs in both. The orders database stays primary in Mumbai with a replica in Hyderabad, so a regional failover is a deliberate database promotion, not an automatic event.
Architecture

flowchart TD GIT["Git: deploy repository
base + overlays per region"] --> ARGO["Argo CD on a management cluster
ApplicationSet with a cluster generator"] ARGO -->|"sync"| C1["Cluster: Mumbai (production)"] ARGO -->|"sync"| C2["Cluster: Hyderabad (production)"] ARGO -->|"sync"| C3["Cluster: staging"] U["Users"] --> GLB["Global DNS or load balancer
latency routing + health checks"] GLB --> I1["Ingress, Mumbai"] GLB --> I2["Ingress, Hyderabad"] I1 --> A1["checkout-api (stateless)"] I2 --> A2["checkout-api (stateless)"] A1 --> DB1[("PostgreSQL primary")] A2 -->|"writes cross region,
or fail over"| DB1 DB1 -. "asynchronous replication" .-> DB2[("PostgreSQL replica")] A2 -. "reads" .-> DB2 OBS["Central metrics, logs and traces
labelled by cluster"] -.- C1 OBS -.- C2

# Argo CD on a management cluster deploys the same app to every cluster

kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:

  namespace: argocd
spec:

        targetRevision: main
        path: "apps/checkout-api/overlays/{{metadata.labels.region}}"

Troubleshooting

rows: A change meant for staging was applied to production.
The default kubectl context pointed at production.
Pass --context in every command and script, show the context in the shell prompt, and keep production write access behind a separate, short-lived login.
The same app behaves differently in two clusters.
Drift: a manual change in one, a different add-on version, or a different Kubernetes version.
Deploy everything, add-ons included, from Git with automatic sync and self-heal, and compare versions as a routine check.
After failing over to the second region, some recent orders are missing.
Replication is asynchronous, so the replica was behind the primary when it was promoted.
State the acceptable data loss up front, monitor replication lag, and reconcile from the old primary when it returns.
Traffic keeps going to a region whose cluster is unhealthy.
The global health check tests the load balancer, which is up, rather than the application behind it.
Health-check an endpoint served by the application that reflects its dependencies.
Dashboards mix up metrics from two clusters.
Series from both clusters have the same labels.
Add a cluster label at the collector in each cluster and include it in every dashboard and alert.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Treat clusters as replaceable. You should be able to build a new one from Git and move workloads to it.
Use one source of truth and one delivery tool for all clusters. Differences belong in small overlays.
Keep clusters on the same Kubernetes and add-on versions, and upgrade the least critical one first.
Keep cross-cluster calls rare. Prefer each region being self-sufficient, with only data replicated.
Rehearse regional failover on a schedule, including the database promotion.
Label every metric, log and trace with its cluster.

blocks.text: Security

items: A management cluster that can deploy everywhere holds credentials for every cluster. Protect it as the most sensitive system you run.
Give each cluster its own credentials and identities. A compromise of staging must not reach production.
Do not copy long-lived kubeconfig files with admin rights between machines. Use short-lived tokens from single sign-on.
Encrypt and authenticate traffic between clusters, and allow only the specific services that need it.
Apply the same admission policies everywhere. One cluster with weaker rules becomes the way in.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Why would you run several Kubernetes clusters instead of one large one?
blocks.text: To limit blast radius, so that a bad upgrade or a control-plane fault affects only part of the system. To separate environments, so that experiments in staging cannot harm production. To be present in more than one region for latency or disaster recovery. For hard isolation between tenants or for compliance. And sometimes because of scale limits. The cost is more upgrades, more spend on control planes and idle capacity, and the constant risk of drift, so each additional cluster should have a stated reason.

blocks.title: How do you keep many clusters consistent?
blocks.text: With GitOps. A single repository describes every application and add-on, with a shared base and small per-cluster overlays. A controller such as Argo CD or Flux, driven by something like an ApplicationSet with a cluster generator, applies it to every registered cluster and reverts manual changes. Cluster creation is itself code, policies are enforced by an admission controller everywhere, and version differences are reported as a matter of routine.

blocks.title: Compare active-active and active-passive across two regions.
blocks.text: In active-passive, one region serves all traffic and the other stands ready; failover means redirecting traffic and promoting the database. It is simpler and data stays consistent, but the standby is unproven until used and failover takes minutes. In active-active both regions serve users, which gives lower latency and no idle capacity, and failover is just removing one region. The difficulty is data: either writes go to one primary across regions, or you adopt a database built for multi-region writes and accept its trade-offs.

blocks.title: How can a service in one cluster call a service in another?
blocks.text: The simplest way is through the other cluster's public or internal ingress, treating it like any external dependency with its own name, TLS and authentication. For closer integration, the Multi-Cluster Services API exports a Service so that it gets a shared name across a set of clusters, and service meshes such as Istio, Linkerd and Cilium can join clusters so that calls are encrypted and load-balanced across them. Each step adds coupling, so it is worth asking first whether the regions can be independent.

is simpler for data but has idle capacity

lessons.title: Pods, Deployments and Services: how checkout stays up

blocks.text: Kubernetes runs containers across a group of machines (a cluster) and keeps them running. You do not start containers yourself; you declare what you want ("3 copies of checkout-api, version 1.4.0") and controllers keep changing reality until it matches. A Pod is the smallest unit: one or more containers sharing a network address. A Deployment keeps N identical pods alive and rolls out new versions. A Service gives those ever-changing pods one stable name and address.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: SwiftUI and Flutter are declarative: you describe the UI for a state and the framework reconciles the screen to match. Kubernetes does the same for servers. The YAML is your build() method; the controllers are the framework diffing desired against actual, forever.
Why it matters
With one server you can restart things by hand. With fifty services on a hundred machines that fail at random, you need a system that notices and repairs without you.
Where you meet it
Managed offerings such as EKS, GKE and AKS, and self-managed clusters. It is the default platform for running microservices.
Scenario

checkout-api runs as 3 pods. One crashes at 2 a.m. Its container exits, the kubelet restarts it; if the node itself dies, the Deployment controller sees 2 pods where 3 are wanted and creates a replacement, the scheduler places it on a healthy node, and once its readiness probe passes the Service starts sending it traffic. Nobody is paged.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD U["Client"] --> ING["Ingress / Load balancer"] ING --> SVC["Service: checkout-api
stable name and virtual IP"] SVC --> P1["Pod 1"] SVC --> P2["Pod 2"] SVC --> P3["Pod 3"] DEP["Deployment
replicas: 3"] -.->|"owns"| RS["ReplicaSet"] RS -.->|"creates and replaces"| P1 RS -.-> P2 RS -.-> P3

blocks.code:
flowchart LR A["Pod crashes"] --> B["ReplicaSet sees
2 of 3"] B --> C["Creates a new
Pod object"] C --> D["Scheduler picks
a node"] D --> E["Kubelet pulls image,
starts container"] E --> F["Readiness probe
passes"] F --> G["Service adds it
to endpoints"]

blocks.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: production
  labels:
    app: checkout-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-api
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1        # one extra pod may exist during a rollout
      maxUnavailable: 0  # never drop below 3 ready pods
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout-api
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
      containers:
        - name: checkout-api
          image: registry.example.com/shop/checkout-api:1.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          env:
            - name: APP_VERSION
              value: "1.4.0"
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: checkout-db
                  key: url
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8000
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8000
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: production
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: checkout-api   # traffic goes to every READY pod with this label
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80          # port other services call
      targetPort: 8000  # port the container listens on

Troubleshooting

rows: CrashLoopBackOff
The container starts and exits repeatedly: bad config, missing environment variable or secret, failing dependency, or a bug at startup.
kubectl logs POD --previous, then kubectl describe pod POD for the exit code and events.
ImagePullBackOff
Wrong image name or tag, or the node lacks registry credentials.
kubectl describe pod: the event states which. Check the tag exists and the imagePullSecret.
Pending
No node satisfies the pod: insufficient CPU or memory for its requests, taints, or an unbound volume.
kubectl describe pod and read the FailedScheduling message.
Service returns no response although pods are Running
Selector does not match pod labels, or pods are not Ready, or targetPort is wrong.
kubectl get endpointslices for the service; compare selector with pod labels.
OOMKilled, exit code 137
The container exceeded its memory limit.
Check actual usage, fix the leak or raise the limit.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Always set resource requests; the scheduler depends on them.
Readiness probe on every service that receives traffic.
At least 2 replicas, spread across nodes and zones.
Change the cluster through version-controlled YAML, not ad-hoc kubectl edit.

blocks.text: Security

items: Run as non-root with a read-only root filesystem.
Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded: enable encryption at rest and restrict access with RBAC.
Give each workload its own ServiceAccount with the least permissions.
Default-deny NetworkPolicies so a compromised pod cannot reach everything.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What happens when you run kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml?
blocks.text: kubectl sends the object to the API server, which authenticates, authorises, runs admission, validates and stores it in etcd. The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pod objects. The scheduler assigns each pod to a node. The kubelet on that node tells the container runtime to pull the image and start the containers, runs probes and reports status back.

blocks.title: Liveness versus readiness probe?
blocks.text: Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic; failing it removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it. Liveness decides whether the container is restarted. Pointing liveness at a dependency can cause restart storms.

blocks.title: How does a rolling update avoid downtime?
blocks.text: New pods are added gradually (maxSurge) and old ones removed only as new ones become Ready (maxUnavailable). Traffic goes only to Ready pods, and old pods get SIGTERM with a grace period to finish requests.

blocks.title: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through it.
blocks.text: describe the pod for events and last state (exit code, reason). logs --previous for the crash output. Check recent changes: image, config, secrets. Reproduce the container command locally if needed. Roll back if it started with a deploy.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A pod is Running but READY shows 0/1. Does it receive traffic from the Service?
quiz.why: Only pods that pass readiness are listed in the Service endpoints.

quiz.q: You delete one pod of a 3-replica Deployment. What happens?
quiz.why: The ReplicaSet reconciles actual (2) to desired (3).

quiz.q: Which component decides which node a new pod runs on?
quiz.why: The scheduler filters and scores nodes, then binds the pod to one.

lessons.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets: configuration outside the image

blocks.text: The same image must run in every environment, so anything that differs between them (URLs, feature flags, log levels, passwords) is supplied from outside. A ConfigMap holds non-secret settings as key-value pairs. A Secret holds sensitive ones. A pod consumes either as environment variables or as files mounted into the container. Two facts trip everyone up: environment variables are read once at start, so changing a ConfigMap does not change running pods; and a Secret is only base64-encoded, which is encoding, not encryption.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A ConfigMap is your xcconfig or --dart-define values, kept apart from the binary. A Secret is the Keychain entry: same idea, but access to it is controlled separately and it must never sit in the repository.
Why it matters
Baking configuration into the image means a rebuild per environment, which breaks "build once, deploy everywhere". Baking in secrets means anyone who can pull the image has them.
Where you meet it
Every workload. Also how TLS certificates reach an Ingress, how registry credentials reach the kubelet, and how applications get cloud credentials.
Scenario

checkout-api reads LOG_LEVEL and PAYMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS from a ConfigMap and DATABASE_URL from a Secret that a secrets manager keeps in sync. Staging and production run the identical image with different ConfigMaps. Changing the timeout is a config change that triggers a normal rolling update.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR CM["ConfigMap checkout-config
LOG_LEVEL, timeouts, flags"] -->|"envFrom / env"| POD["Pod: checkout-api"] SEC["Secret checkout-db
url"] -->|"env valueFrom secretKeyRef"| POD SEC2["Secret api-shop-tls"] -->|"mounted as files"| ING["Ingress controller"] SM["Secrets manager
(Vault, cloud KMS)"] -->|"External Secrets Operator
keeps it in sync"| SEC GIT["Git"] -->|"ConfigMap YAML is safe to commit"| CM GIT -. "never the Secret values" .-> SEC

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Edit the ConfigMap"] --> B{"How does the pod consume it?"} B -->|"environment variable"| C["Running pods keep the OLD value"] C --> D["A rollout is needed"] D --> E["kubectl rollout restart, or
a hash in the name / annotation
changes the pod template"] B -->|"mounted file"| F["File updates in the pod
within about a minute"] F --> G{"Does the app re-read the file?"} G -->|yes| H["New value in use, no restart"] G -->|no| D E --> I["New pods start with the new value"]

blocks.text: Commands

blocks.code: kubectl create configmap checkout-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info -n production --dry-run=client -o yaml
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Prints the ConfigMap YAML without creating anything. The usual way to generate a manifest to commit.

rows: `--from-literal KEY=VALUE`
one entry
`--from-file PATH`
a file becomes one entry
`--dry-run=client -o yaml`
print instead of create

blocks.code: kubectl create secret generic checkout-db --from-literal=url="$DATABASE_URL" -n production
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Creates a Secret from a value held in your shell, so it never touches a file or your shell history as a literal.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Typing the value directly on the command line stores it in shell history.

blocks.code: kubectl get secret checkout-db -n production -o jsonpath="{.data.url}" | base64 -d
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Reads and decodes a Secret. It demonstrates the point: anyone allowed to "get" Secrets can read them in plain text. On a real cluster the output is a credential: do not paste it anywhere.
Replaces every pod gradually so they start again and pick up changed environment variables.

blocks.code: kubectl exec deploy/checkout-api -n production -- env | grep LOG_LEVEL
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Shows what a running container actually has. On a real cluster avoid dumping the whole environment: it contains secrets.
examples/kubernetes/configmap.yaml + secret.example.yaml

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: checkout-config
  namespace: production
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  PAYMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: "8"
  FEATURE_DISCOUNT_CODES: "true"
---
# EXAMPLE ONLY. Never commit a real Secret manifest: base64 is encoding, not encryption.
# Create real ones with:  kubectl create secret generic checkout-db --from-literal=url=...
# or sync them from a secrets manager (External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets, Vault).
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: checkout-db
  namespace: production
type: Opaque
stringData:
  url: postgresql://shop:REPLACE_ME@db.internal:5432/shop

blocks.text: The Deployment in examples/kubernetes/deployment.yaml consumes the Secret with env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef.
Exercise
See how a config change is turned into a safe rollout.

items: In the Kustomize lab, build the production overlay and find the ConfigMap name with its hash suffix
Find the same name inside the Deployment under envFrom
Change LOG_LEVEL in the production overlay and rebuild: both names change
Explain why a changed name in the pod template makes Kubernetes roll the pods
Explain what would have happened with a fixed ConfigMap name

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can say why pods did not pick up an edited ConfigMap, and name two ways to make them.
Troubleshooting

rows: CreateContainerConfigError
The pod references a ConfigMap, Secret or key that does not exist in its namespace.
kubectl describe pod names the missing object or key. Create it, or fix the name.
Config was changed but the app still uses the old value
Environment variables are fixed when the container starts.
Roll the Deployment, and automate it with a hashed name or a checksum annotation.
A Secret manifest with base64 values was committed to Git
base64 was mistaken for protection.
Rotate the credential. Use Sealed Secrets, External Secrets or SOPS so only encrypted data or references live in Git.
The app cannot read its mounted secret file
The container runs as a non-root user without read permission on the volume.
Set defaultMode on the volume or fsGroup in the pod securityContext.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Identical image everywhere; all differences in ConfigMaps and Secrets.
Make config changes trigger rollouts through hashed names or checksum annotations.
Keep secret values in a secrets manager and sync them in.
Mount secrets as files when the app can re-read them; this allows rotation without restarts.
Mark ConfigMaps and Secrets immutable when they are versioned by name.

blocks.text: Security

items: Enable encryption at rest for Secrets in etcd; it is not on by default everywhere.
RBAC "get" on Secrets is the ability to read every credential in the namespace: grant it narrowly.
Environment variables leak through crash dumps, debug endpoints and child processes; files are easier to protect.
Anyone who can create a pod in a namespace can mount any Secret in it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: ConfigMap versus Secret?
blocks.text: Both hold key-value data consumed as environment variables or files. Secrets are meant for sensitive data: they are base64-encoded, can be encrypted at rest, are kept in memory-backed volumes on nodes and can be access-controlled separately. Neither is encrypted by default in a way that protects against someone with API access.

blocks.title: You updated a ConfigMap and the application did not change. Why?
blocks.text: If it is consumed as environment variables, those are set at container start. Mounted files do update, after a delay, but only help if the application re-reads them. The normal fix is to roll the pods, ideally triggered automatically by a content hash in the name or a pod-template annotation.

blocks.title: How should secrets be managed with GitOps?
blocks.text: Never commit plain or base64 values. Either commit encrypted secrets that only the cluster can decrypt (Sealed Secrets, SOPS) or commit references and let an operator fetch the values from a secrets manager (External Secrets Operator, CSI driver).
