blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A Kubernetes Secret value is, by default…
quiz.why: base64 is reversible encoding. Encryption at rest must be configured.

quiz.q: You change a ConfigMap used via envFrom. Running pods…
options: get the new value at once
keep the old value until they are restarted
quiz.why: Environment variables are read when the container starts.

lessons.title: Health probes and graceful shutdown

blocks.text: Kubernetes only knows a container is healthy if you tell it how to check. A readiness probe decides whether the pod receives traffic: fail it and the pod is taken out of the Service, not restarted. A liveness probe decides whether the container is restarted: fail it and the kubelet kills it. A startup probe holds the other two back until a slow application has finished starting. Shutdown is the mirror image: the pod gets SIGTERM, a grace period (30 seconds by default) to finish its requests, then SIGKILL.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Readiness is "the till is open". Liveness is "the cashier is breathing". A cashier waiting for the card network is alive and should not be replaced, but should stop taking customers. Mixing the two up means firing every cashier whenever the card network blips.
Why it matters

A process can be running and useless: still starting, deadlocked, or cut off from its database. Without probes Kubernetes sends customers to it anyway, and rolling updates cannot tell a good new version from a broken one.
Where you meet it
Every container that serves traffic. Readiness is also what makes rolling updates, load balancing and autoscaling safe.
Scenario

checkout-api exposes /ready (can I serve now, including my dependencies?) and /health (is this process itself working?). During a deploy, a new pod joins the Service only after /ready passes. When the database has a brief outage, pods go unready and come back by themselves; none is restarted, because /health does not check the database.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  K["kubelet on the node"] -->|"startupProbe"| C["Container"]
  K -->|"livenessProbe: /health"| C
  K -->|"readinessProbe: /ready"| C
  C -->|"liveness fails"| R["Container restarted"]
  C -->|"readiness fails"| E["Removed from EndpointSlice"]
  E --> S["Service stops routing to it"]
  C -->|"readiness passes"| A["Added to EndpointSlice"]
  A --> S2["Service routes to it"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram participant API as API server participant EP as Endpoints / Service participant K as kubelet participant P as Pod (checkout-api) API->>P: Pod marked Terminating par at the same time API->>EP: Remove pod from endpoints and K->>P: preStop hook (e.g. sleep 5) K->>P: SIGTERM end Note over P: Stop accepting new requests,
finish the ones in flight P-->>K: Process exits 0 Note over K: If still running after
terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30s) K->>P: SIGKILL

blocks.text: Commands
Events show probe failures with the reason: "Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503" or "Liveness probe failed ... container will be restarted".
Watches pods live. READY 0/1 with status Running means readiness is failing; a climbing RESTARTS count means liveness is failing or the process crashes.

rows: keep watching for changes

blocks.text: Logs of the container instance that was just restarted, which is where the reason usually is.
Lets you call the probe endpoints yourself on localhost:8000 to see exactly what the kubelet sees.
examples/kubernetes/deployment.yaml (probes are near the end)

blocks.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: production
  labels:
    app: checkout-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-api
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1        # one extra pod may exist during a rollout
      maxUnavailable: 0  # never drop below 3 ready pods
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout-api
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
      containers:
        - name: checkout-api
          image: registry.example.com/shop/checkout-api:1.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          env:
            - name: APP_VERSION
              value: "1.4.0"
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: checkout-db
                  key: url
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8000
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8000
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

blocks.text: For a slow starter add: startupProbe with httpGet /health, periodSeconds 5, failureThreshold 30, which allows up to 150 seconds to start.
Exercise
Produce each probe failure on purpose and fix it with the right setting.

items: Run the healthy scenario and read the timeline
Choose the slow-starting app: count the restarts, then enable the startup probe
Choose the deadlock: what restarts it? Disable liveness and look at the timeline colour
Choose "liveness checks the database": how many restarts for an outage the app did not cause? Untick it
Choose "no probes at all": how many seconds of traffic went to a pod that could not answer?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state what each probe does on failure, and why a liveness probe must not depend on anything outside the container.
Troubleshooting

rows: Pod restarts in a loop right after starting
Liveness begins before the application has started.
Add a startup probe sized for the slowest start, rather than a large initialDelaySeconds on liveness.
All pods restart together when the database is slow
The liveness endpoint checks the database.
Liveness checks only the process. Dependencies belong in readiness.
A burst of 502s on every deploy
Pods exit before the load balancer has stopped sending them requests, or they ignore SIGTERM and are killed mid-request.
Handle SIGTERM by draining, add a short preStop sleep, and make the grace period longer than the longest request.
Rollout is stuck with new pods at 0/1
The readiness probe never passes: wrong path or port, or the app really is not ready.
describe the pod for the probe error, then call the endpoint through a port-forward.
Pods flap between ready and not ready under load
The probe timeout is shorter than the response time when busy.
Raise timeoutSeconds and failureThreshold, keep the probe endpoint cheap, and treat it as a sign of saturation.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Every serving container has a readiness probe.
Liveness is simple, local and cheap; never a dependency check.
Use a startup probe for anything that can take more than a few seconds to start.
Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting, drain, exit 0.
terminationGracePeriodSeconds is longer than preStop plus your slowest request.

blocks.text: Security

items: Probe endpoints are reachable by anything that can reach the pod: return status, not internals.
exec probes run a command inside the container on every period; keep them minimal.
A deep health endpoint that touches many dependencies is an easy way to amplify load during an incident.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain liveness, readiness and startup probes.
blocks.text: Readiness controls membership of Service endpoints: failing means no traffic, no restart. Liveness controls restarts: failing means the kubelet kills and restarts the container. Startup disables both until it succeeds, to protect slow-starting applications from being killed during startup.

blocks.title: What goes wrong if liveness checks the database?
blocks.text: A database problem makes every pod fail liveness at once. They are all restarted, which cannot fix the database, removes all capacity, and adds a thundering herd of reconnecting pods when it recovers. Dependency state belongs in readiness.

blocks.title: How do you achieve zero-downtime shutdown of a pod?
blocks.text: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, so for a short time traffic still arrives. Add a preStop delay so routing catches up, then on SIGTERM stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests and exit, all within the termination grace period.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A readiness probe fails. Kubernetes…
quiz.why: The pod is removed from Service endpoints and left running.

quiz.q: Which probe protects a slow-starting app from being killed?
quiz.why: Liveness and readiness do not run until the startup probe has succeeded.

lessons.title: Requests, limits and quality of service

blocks.text: Each container declares two numbers per resource. The request is what it is guaranteed: the scheduler adds up requests to decide which node has room. The limit is the most it may use. CPU and memory behave differently when the limit is hit: CPU is throttled (the container is paused for part of each time slice and gets slower), memory cannot be throttled, so the container is killed (OOMKilled) and restarted. From these numbers Kubernetes derives a quality-of-service class that decides who is evicted first when a node runs short.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The request is the table you booked; the restaurant will not overbook it. The limit is how much of the buffet you may take. Go over your CPU allowance and you are made to wait; go over your memory allowance and you are shown the door.
Why it matters
Without requests the scheduler packs nodes blindly and they overload. Without memory limits one leaking pod can take down every neighbour on its node.
Where you meet it
Every container in every pod, plus namespace-level ResourceQuota and LimitRange that enforce defaults and ceilings per team.
Scenario

checkout-api requests 250m CPU and 256Mi, with a 512Mi memory limit and no CPU limit. The scheduler reserves a quarter of a core per pod. A memory leak in one release hits 512Mi and is OOM-killed with exit code 137: visible as a restart count and a short error spike, and contained to that pod.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD SPEC["Container spec
requests: cpu 250m, memory 256Mi
limits: memory 512Mi"] --> SCH["Scheduler
looks at REQUESTS only"] SCH --> NODE["Node: allocatable 4 CPU, 16Gi
sum of requests must fit"] SPEC --> KUB["kubelet + kernel cgroups
enforce LIMITS"] KUB -->|"CPU over limit"| TH["Throttled: slower, stays alive"] KUB -->|"memory over limit"| OOM["OOMKilled: exit 137, restarted"] SPEC --> QOS["QoS class"] QOS --> G["Guaranteed: evicted last"] QOS --> B["Burstable"] QOS --> BE["BestEffort: evicted first"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["New pod created"] --> B["Scheduler filters nodes:
free = allocatable - sum of requests"] B --> C{"Any node with enough
free CPU and memory?"} C -->|no| D["Pending: Insufficient cpu / memory"] D --> E["Cluster autoscaler may add a node"] C -->|yes| F["Pod bound to the node and started"] F --> G{"Usage versus limits"} G -->|"memory > limit"| H["OOMKilled, container restarts"] G -->|"cpu > limit"| I["CPU throttled, latency rises"] G -->|"within limits"| J["Runs normally"] J --> K{"Node itself short of memory?"} K -->|yes| L["kubelet evicts pods:
BestEffort, then Burstable"]

blocks.text: Commands
Current CPU and memory use per container (needs metrics-server). Compare with requests and limits.
The "Allocated resources" section shows the sum of requests and limits on the node as a percentage of its capacity: how full the scheduler considers it.

blocks.code: kubectl get pod POD -n production -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Prints the pod's QoS class: Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort.
Why the container last died. "OOMKilled" settles the question.
Shows the namespace's total allowance and how much is used. A full quota rejects new pods with a "forbidden: exceeded quota" error.
Choosing the numbers

blocks.code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m        # what the pod needs in normal operation (p50 to p90 of real usage)
    memory: 256Mi    # set close to real steady-state usage
  limits:
    memory: 512Mi    # a hard wall; set with headroom above the request
    # cpu: (often omitted for latency-sensitive services, to avoid throttling)

# Units: 1000m = 1 CPU core.  Mi = mebibytes (1024-based), M = megabytes (1000-based).
#
# Guaranteed   requests == limits for both cpu and memory, on every container
# Burstable    at least one request or limit set, but not the above
# BestEffort   nothing set
#
# A limit with no request makes the request equal to the limit.

blocks.text: Exercise
Cause each resource outcome and read why it happened.

items: Start from the defaults and note the QoS class
Use "Memory leak": what happens, and what exit code would you see?
Use "CPU spike with a CPU limit": is the pod killed? What does the user notice?
Remove the CPU limit and repeat: what changed?
Use "Nothing set at all" and read the eviction order
Make the request larger than the node and read the scheduling message

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain why exceeding a memory limit kills and exceeding a CPU limit only slows, and what the scheduler does and does not look at.
Troubleshooting

rows: Pod restarts with reason OOMKilled, exit code 137
The container exceeded its memory limit.
Compare usage with the limit over time. Fix the leak, or raise the limit. For JVM and Node, set the heap below the container limit.
High latency while CPU usage looks moderate
CPU throttling against the limit, visible only in throttling metrics.
Check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total. Raise or remove the CPU limit and keep the request.
Pending: 0/5 nodes are available: Insufficient cpu
No node has enough unreserved CPU for the request, even if actual usage is low.
Right-size requests, add nodes, or let the cluster autoscaler do it.
Pods evicted with "The node was low on resource: memory"
The node ran out because pods used more than they requested.
Set memory requests close to real usage so the scheduler does not overpack.
New pods rejected: exceeded quota
The namespace ResourceQuota is used up.
Free resources, lower requests or raise the quota deliberately.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Always set CPU and memory requests, from measured usage.
Always set a memory limit.
Be cautious with CPU limits on latency-sensitive services.
Use LimitRange defaults so nothing runs without requests.
Review requests against real usage regularly: over-requesting is the main source of wasted cloud spend.

blocks.text: Security

items: Limits are a containment control: without them one compromised or buggy pod can starve a node.
ResourceQuota stops one team or one runaway controller from consuming a shared cluster.
Do not rely on QoS for isolation between tenants who do not trust each other.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Requests versus limits?
blocks.text: Requests are reserved capacity used for scheduling and as the guaranteed share under contention. Limits are enforced ceilings at run time: CPU above the limit is throttled, memory above the limit gets the container OOM-killed.

blocks.title: Why do some teams not set CPU limits?
blocks.text: CPU is compressible: under contention each container still gets its requested share, so a limit mainly throttles workloads when spare CPU exists, which hurts tail latency. Memory is not compressible, so a memory limit is still needed.

blocks.title: What are the QoS classes and why do they matter?
blocks.text: Guaranteed, Burstable and BestEffort, derived from requests and limits. They set OOM scores and eviction order when a node is under pressure: BestEffort goes first, Guaranteed last.

blocks.title: A pod is Pending though nodes look idle in monitoring. Why?
blocks.text: The scheduler works from requests, not usage. Nodes can be fully reserved by requests while using little. Check Allocated resources on the nodes, and also taints, affinity and volume constraints.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: The scheduler places pods based on…
quiz.why: It reserves the requested amount; real usage is not considered.

quiz.q: A container exceeds its CPU limit. It is…
quiz.why: CPU is compressible, so the kernel slows the container down instead of killing it.

lessons.title: Services, DNS, Ingress and NetworkPolicy

blocks.text: Every pod gets its own IP, and those IPs change whenever pods are replaced. A Service is a stable name and virtual IP in front of a changing set of pods chosen by label. ClusterIP is reachable only inside the cluster; NodePort opens a port on every node; LoadBalancer asks the cloud for an external load balancer. Cluster DNS (CoreDNS) turns a Service name into its IP. An Ingress (or the newer Gateway API) routes HTTP from outside to Services by host and path, through one shared entry point. A NetworkPolicy is a firewall rule between pods; without any, every pod can reach every other.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A Service is a department phone number that always reaches whoever is on shift. DNS is the directory that gives you the number. Ingress is the reception desk for visitors from outside. A NetworkPolicy is the door-badge rule for which departments may walk into which.
Why it matters
Pods are replaced constantly, so nothing can depend on a pod address. And a flat network where a compromised pod can reach the database directly is one bug away from a breach.
Where you meet it
Every call between services, every request from the internet, and every security review of a cluster.
Scenario

A customer request hits the cloud load balancer, then the ingress controller, which matches api.shop.example.com/checkout and forwards to the Service checkout-api, which picks a Ready pod. checkout-api calls inventory by the name inventory.production.svc.cluster.local. A default-deny policy means only the ingress controller may call checkout-api on port 8000.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR U["Internet"] --> LB["Cloud load balancer"] LB --> IC["Ingress controller pods"] IC -->|"host + path rule"| SVC["Service checkout-api
ClusterIP 10.96.12.7:80"] SVC --> P1["Pod 10.244.1.10:8000"] SVC --> P2["Pod 10.244.2.11:8000"] P1 -->|"inventory.production.svc.cluster.local"| DNS["CoreDNS"] DNS --> SVC2["Service inventory"] SVC2 --> P3["inventory pods"] NP["NetworkPolicy: default deny,
allow ingress-nginx to checkout:8000"] -.-> P1

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["checkout calls http://inventory/stock"] --> B["Resolver adds search domains:
inventory.production.svc.cluster.local"] B --> C["CoreDNS returns the Service ClusterIP"] C --> D["Packet sent to the ClusterIP"] D --> E["Node rules (kube-proxy or eBPF)
pick one Ready endpoint"] E --> F{"NetworkPolicy allows
this source and port?"} F -->|no| G["Dropped: the caller times out"] F -->|yes| H["Delivered to the pod IP
on targetPort"] H --> I{"Container listening
on that port?"} I -->|no| J["Connection refused"] I -->|yes| K["Response returns"]

blocks.text: Commands
Services with their types and IPs, and the pod addresses behind each. An empty endpoint list is the commonest cause of "the Service does not answer".
Routing rules, hosts and the external address assigned to the ingress.

`--restart=Never`

Lists policies. If any policy selects a pod, traffic to it not explicitly allowed is dropped.
examples/kubernetes/ingress.yaml + networkpolicy.yaml

blocks.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: production
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [api.shop.example.com]
      secretName: api-shop-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /checkout
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: checkout-api
                port:
                  number: 80
---
# Default deny: no pod in the namespace accepts traffic unless another policy allows it.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
---
# Then allow exactly one path: the ingress controller may call checkout-api on 8000.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-to-checkout
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-api
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8000

blocks.text: The Gateway API (Gateway and HTTPRoute objects) is the successor to Ingress and separates the platform team's gateway from each application team's routes. The concepts are the same.
Exercise
Diagnose a silent Service four different ways.

items: Apply each of the four breakages in the lab, one at a time
For each, read the three command outputs and the ordered checks
Which breakage leaves endpoints listed but still fails? Why?
Which two leave the endpoint list empty although pods are Running?
Write the three commands you would run, in order, for this problem on a real cluster

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Your order is: are there endpoints, do labels match the selector, are the pods Ready, does targetPort match the container port.
Troubleshooting

rows: Service has no endpoints
The selector matches no pod labels, the pods are not Ready, or the Service is in another namespace.
Compare kubectl get pods --show-labels with the Service selector.
Connection refused although endpoints exist
targetPort is not the port the container listens on, or the app binds to 127.0.0.1.
Match targetPort to the container port and bind the app to 0.0.0.0.
Could not resolve host from inside a pod
Wrong name or namespace, or CoreDNS is unhealthy.
Use service.namespace for cross-namespace calls. Check the CoreDNS pods in kube-system.
Ingress returns 404
No rule matches that host and path, or the ingress class does not match the controller.
Check the host header, the path type and ingressClassName.
Ingress returns 503
The rule matches but the backing Service has no ready endpoints.
Debug the Service as above.
Calls between two services time out after a policy was added
A NetworkPolicy now selects the destination and does not allow that source.
Add an explicit allow for the source pods and port. Remember DNS: egress policies must allow port 53.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Call services by DNS name, never by IP.
ClusterIP for internal services; one shared Ingress or Gateway for HTTP from outside.
Start each namespace with a default-deny policy and add specific allows.
Name Service ports and reference them by name.
Terminate TLS at the ingress with automated certificates.

blocks.text: Security

items: NetworkPolicies are enforced only if the CNI plugin supports them; on some clusters they are silently ignored.
A Service of type LoadBalancer or NodePort exposes the workload publicly: review each one.
Default-deny egress as well as ingress limits what a compromised pod can reach, including cloud metadata endpoints.
The ingress controller sees all traffic and holds all TLS keys: treat it as critical.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What are the Service types?
blocks.text: ClusterIP: a virtual IP reachable inside the cluster. NodePort: also opens a fixed port on every node. LoadBalancer: also provisions an external load balancer through the cloud provider. ExternalName: a DNS alias to an outside name. Headless (clusterIP: None): no virtual IP, DNS returns pod IPs directly.

blocks.title: How does a pod find another service?
blocks.text: Through cluster DNS. The pod's resolv.conf points at CoreDNS and has search domains for its namespace, so "inventory" resolves to inventory.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local and returns the Service ClusterIP.

blocks.title: Service versus Ingress?
blocks.text: A Service load-balances TCP or UDP to a set of pods at layer 4. An Ingress routes HTTP at layer 7 by host and path to Services, sharing one entry point and one place for TLS.

blocks.title: What is the default network behaviour between pods, and how do you restrict it?
blocks.text: Every pod can reach every other pod in the cluster. NetworkPolicies select pods and list allowed sources or destinations; once a pod is selected by any policy, everything not allowed is denied. A default-deny policy per namespace is the usual baseline.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which Service type is reachable only from inside the cluster?
quiz.why: ClusterIP provides an internal virtual IP only.

quiz.q: With no NetworkPolicy in a namespace, pods there…
quiz.why: The default is allow-all until a policy selects the pod.

lessons.title: Storage and other workload types: StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob

blocks.text: A Deployment suits stateless services: any pod is interchangeable. Other work needs other controllers. Storage first: a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a request for a disk of some size; a StorageClass describes how to make one; the resulting PersistentVolume (PV) is the actual disk, which outlives pods. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable name (db-0, db-1), its own PVC, and ordered start-up, which databases need. A DaemonSet runs one pod on every node, for agents such as log collectors. A Job runs a pod to completion and retries on failure. A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Deployment pods are taxis: any one will do. StatefulSet pods are numbered lockers: locker 2 is always locker 2 and keeps its contents. A DaemonSet is the fire extinguisher on every floor. A Job is an errand; a CronJob is the errand on your calendar.
Why it matters
A database cannot have its disk swapped for an empty one on restart, a log agent must be on every node including new ones, and a batch task must finish and stop rather than be restarted forever.
Where you meet it
Databases, queues and caches run in the cluster; monitoring and logging agents; migrations, reports, clean-ups and backups.
Scenario

The shop's abandoned-basket clean-up is a CronJob every 15 minutes that must never overlap with itself. Logs from every node are shipped by a DaemonSet. The staging database is a single-replica StatefulSet with a 20Gi volume; in production the team uses a managed database instead, because running a database well needs more than a StatefulSet.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD SS["StatefulSet db
serviceName: db"] --> P0["Pod db-0"] SS --> P1["Pod db-1"] P0 --> C0["PVC data-db-0"] P1 --> C1["PVC data-db-1"] C0 --> V0["PV: 20Gi cloud disk"] C1 --> V1["PV: 20Gi cloud disk"] SC["StorageClass
provisioner, disk type"] -. "creates on demand" .-> V0 HS["Headless Service db"] --> D0["db-0.db.production.svc"] HS --> D1["db-1.db.production.svc"] DS["DaemonSet log-agent"] --> N1["one pod on every node"] CJ["CronJob"] -->|"each schedule"| J["Job"] --> JP["Pod runs to completion"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Pod with a PVC is created"] --> B{"PVC bound to a PV?"} B -->|no| C["StorageClass provisions a disk"] C --> D["PV created and bound to the PVC"] B -->|yes| E["Scheduler picks a node
in the disk's zone"] D --> E E --> F["Disk attached to the node,
mounted into the container"] F --> G["Pod runs and writes data"] G --> H["Pod deleted or node fails"] H --> I["StatefulSet recreates the pod
with the SAME name"] I --> J["Same PVC, same data, re-attached"]

blocks.text: Commands
Claims and the volumes bound to them, with size, access mode, storage class and status.
Available storage classes and which is the default. The reclaim policy column says what happens to the disk when the claim is deleted.
The non-Deployment controllers in a namespace.
Runs a CronJob's job once, now. Useful for testing, and it really runs the task.
Output of a Job's pod.
Deletes the claim. With the default reclaim policy (Delete) the underlying disk and all its data are destroyed.
examples/kubernetes/statefulset.yaml + cronjob.yaml

blocks.code:
# A single PostgreSQL instance with its own disk. For learning: production databases
# usually run on a managed service or under an operator that handles failover and backups.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: production
spec:
  clusterIP: None          # headless: gives each pod a stable DNS name (db-0.db)
  selector:
    app: db
  ports:
    - port: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: production
spec:
  serviceName: db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5432
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-admin
                  key: password
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"]
            periodSeconds: 5
  volumeClaimTemplates:      # one PersistentVolumeClaim per pod, kept when the pod is replaced
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 20Gi
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: expire-abandoned-baskets
  namespace: production
spec:
  schedule: "*/15 * * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid          # never run two at once
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 300
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2                # retry a failed pod twice, then mark the Job failed
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 600     # kill it if it runs longer than 10 minutes
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: expire
              image: registry.example.com/shop/checkout-api:1.4.0
              command: ["python", "-m", "app.jobs.expire_baskets"]
              resources:
                requests:
                  cpu: 100m
                  memory: 128Mi
                limits:
                  memory: 256Mi

blocks.text: Deleting a StatefulSet does not delete its PVCs: that is deliberate, and it means disks are left behind (and billed) until you remove them.
Exercise
Choose the right controller for each job, and predict what survives a pod deletion.

items: For each of these, name the controller: the checkout API, a PostgreSQL replica set, a node log shipper, a nightly sales report, a one-off database migration
In the StatefulSet example, find volumeClaimTemplates: what will the PVC for the first pod be called?
If pod db-0 is deleted, what name does its replacement get and which data does it see?
In the CronJob example, what does concurrencyPolicy: Forbid prevent? What do backoffLimit and activeDeadlineSeconds do?
After deleting the StatefulSet, what is still there and still costing money?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, CronJob, Job. The PVC is data-db-0, the replacement is db-0 with the same data, and the PVCs remain after the StatefulSet is deleted.
Troubleshooting

rows: Pod Pending: pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims
No StorageClass can satisfy the claim, or no default class exists.
kubectl describe pvc. Name a valid storageClassName or set a default.
Pod stuck ContainerCreating with a Multi-Attach error
A ReadWriteOnce volume is still attached to another node, often after a node failure.
Wait for the old attachment to be released or remove the stale pod. Deployments with ReadWriteOnce volumes need the Recreate strategy.
Pod cannot schedule: volume node affinity conflict
The disk is in one zone and no node with room exists there.
Add capacity in that zone. Use WaitForFirstConsumer binding so disks are created where the pod lands.
A CronJob has not run for hours
It was suspended, missed its startingDeadlineSeconds, or a previous run is still going with Forbid.
kubectl describe cronjob, and look at its Jobs.
Thousands of completed Job pods fill the namespace
No history limit or TTL.
Set successfulJobsHistoryLimit and ttlSecondsAfterFinished.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Prefer a managed database; if you run one in the cluster, use a mature operator.
Back up the data, not just the volume, and test restores.
Know your reclaim policy before deleting any claim.
Jobs must be idempotent: they can be retried or run twice.
Set concurrencyPolicy, deadlines and history limits on every CronJob.
Give DaemonSets tolerations so they run on every node that needs them.

blocks.text: Security

items: Volumes hold the real data: encrypt them and restrict who can create pods in the namespace, since any pod can mount a claim there.
DaemonSets often run privileged with host access; they are high-value targets.
A CronJob with broad credentials is an unattended privileged process: scope its ServiceAccount tightly.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Deployment versus StatefulSet?
blocks.text: Deployment pods are interchangeable, get random names and share nothing. StatefulSet pods have stable ordinal names and network identities, a dedicated PersistentVolumeClaim each from volumeClaimTemplates, and are created, updated and deleted in order.

blocks.title: Explain PV, PVC and StorageClass.
blocks.text: A PVC is a namespaced request for storage. A StorageClass defines how volumes are provisioned. A PV is the provisioned volume, cluster-scoped, bound to exactly one claim. Dynamic provisioning creates the PV when the claim appears.

blocks.title: When would you use a DaemonSet?
blocks.text: For something that must run on every node, or every node of a kind: log and metrics agents, CNI and CSI components, node security agents.

blocks.title: How do you run a database migration in Kubernetes?
blocks.text: As a Job (or a pre-upgrade hook that creates one) that runs to completion before the new application version rolls out, written to be idempotent and backward compatible so a rollback of the app still works.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which controller gives each pod its own persistent volume and a stable name?
quiz.why: volumeClaimTemplates plus ordinal naming.

quiz.q: You delete a StatefulSet. Its PersistentVolumeClaims are…
quiz.why: They are kept on purpose to protect data, and must be removed separately.

lessons.title: ServiceAccounts and RBAC: who may do what

blocks.text: Every call to the Kubernetes API is made by an identity: a person, or a ServiceAccount, which is the identity of a pod. Role-based access control answers one question per call: may this subject perform this verb (get, list, create, patch, delete…) on this resource in this namespace? A Role is a list of allowed verb-and-resource pairs inside one namespace; a ClusterRole is the same cluster-wide. A RoleBinding grants a role to subjects in one namespace; a ClusterRoleBinding grants it everywhere. There are no deny rules: anything not granted is refused.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: It is the same model as IAM policies or App Store Connect roles. A Role is a job description; a RoleBinding is the appointment letter that gives that job to a specific person in a specific office.
Why it matters
By default a pod can reach the API with its ServiceAccount token. If that account can read Secrets or create pods, one compromised container owns the namespace, or the cluster.
Where you meet it
Human access, CI pipelines that deploy, controllers and operators, and every pod that calls the Kubernetes API.
Scenario

checkout-api runs as its own ServiceAccount, allowed to read ConfigMaps and exactly one named Secret. The pipeline's ServiceAccount may patch Deployments in production and nothing else: it cannot read Secrets or delete anything. Developers may view pods and logs in every namespace and change nothing.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR SA["ServiceAccount
production/checkout-api"] --> RB["RoleBinding
(namespace: production)"] RB --> R["Role config-reader
get/list/watch configmaps
get secret 'checkout-db'"] CI["ServiceAccount ci/ci-deployer"] --> RB2["RoleBinding in production"] RB2 --> R2["Role deployer
patch/update deployments"] G["Group developers"] --> CRB["ClusterRoleBinding"] CRB --> CR["ClusterRole pod-reader
get/list/watch pods, pods/log
in ALL namespaces"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Request arrives at the API server"] --> B["Authentication:
who is this? (token, certificate, OIDC)"] B -->|"unknown"| X["401 Unauthorized"] B --> C["Authorization (RBAC)"] C --> D{"Any binding for this subject
whose role allows
verb + resource + namespace?"} D -->|no| Y["403 Forbidden"] D -->|yes| E["Admission controllers:
mutate, then validate"] E -->|"rejected by policy"| Z["Denied with the policy message"] E --> F["Stored in etcd, acted on"]

blocks.text: Commands

blocks.code: kubectl auth can-i patch deployments -n production --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:ci-deployer
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Asks the API server whether a subject may do something, without doing it. The fastest way to test a role.

rows: `--as=SUBJECT`
impersonate; needs impersonation rights
`--list`
list everything the subject may do in the namespace

blocks.text: Everything your current identity may do in a namespace.
Every binding with its subjects. Review this for cluster-admin grants.
The rules in a role, in readable form.
Grants a user the built-in admin role in one namespace. Granting access is a production change: prefer doing it through reviewed manifests.
examples/kubernetes/rbac.yaml

blocks.code:
# Identity for the checkout pods, and exactly what it may do.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: production
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: config-reader
  namespace: production
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["secrets"]
    resourceNames: ["checkout-db"]   # this one secret only
    verbs: ["get"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: checkout-api-config-reader
  namespace: production
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: checkout-api
    namespace: production
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: config-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
# The pipeline's identity may update Deployments in production, nothing else.
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: production
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "patch", "update"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: ci-deployer
  namespace: production
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: ci-deployer
    namespace: ci
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: deployer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
# Developers may look at pods and their logs in every namespace, and change nothing.
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: developers-pod-reader
subjects:
  - kind: Group
    name: developers
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

blocks.text: Attach the ServiceAccount to the pod with spec.serviceAccountName. If the pod never calls the Kubernetes API, also set automountServiceAccountToken: false.
Exercise
Read a set of roles and predict each access decision before checking it.

items: As checkout-api: predict get, list and delete on configmaps and secrets in production, then compare with the matrix
Why is "get secrets/checkout-db" allowed while "list secrets" is not?
As ci-deployer: what can it do in production, and in staging?
As developers: change namespace and confirm the access follows them everywhere
Edit the YAML: add "delete" to the deployer role, then remove it
Change the developers ClusterRoleBinding to a RoleBinding in staging and explain the result

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain the difference between RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding, and why resourceNames cannot restrict list.
Troubleshooting

rows: Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden: User "x" cannot list resource "pods" in API group "" in the namespace "production"
No binding grants that verb on that resource there.
The message names exactly what is missing. Add the narrowest rule that covers it.
A pod gets 403 from the API
It runs as the namespace's default ServiceAccount, which has no permissions.
Create a dedicated ServiceAccount, bind a role, set serviceAccountName.
The role looks right but access is still denied
Wrong apiGroup (deployments are in "apps"), a subresource such as pods/log is missing, or the binding is in another namespace.
kubectl auth can-i with --as, then check apiGroups and the binding namespace.
The pipeline can deploy but cannot read rollout status
It has patch but lacks get, list and watch on deployments or replicasets.
Add the read verbs it needs.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: One ServiceAccount per workload; never use default.
Grant in a namespace with Role and RoleBinding unless cluster scope is truly needed.
No wildcards in verbs or resources.
Bind groups from your identity provider, not individual users.
Keep RBAC in Git and review it like code.
Audit who holds cluster-admin regularly.

blocks.text: Security

items: list or watch on Secrets returns their contents: it is equivalent to reading every secret.
The ability to create pods in a namespace is the ability to use any ServiceAccount and mount any Secret there.
Rights to create or edit roles and bindings, or the escalate, bind and impersonate verbs, allow privilege escalation.
Short-lived, audience-bound tokens are the default for pods; do not create long-lived token Secrets without a reason.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Role versus ClusterRole, and RoleBinding versus ClusterRoleBinding?
blocks.text: A Role is namespaced; a ClusterRole is cluster-wide and can also cover non-namespaced resources. A RoleBinding grants a Role or a ClusterRole within one namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding grants a ClusterRole in all namespaces. Binding a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding is a common way to reuse one definition per namespace.

blocks.title: How does a pod authenticate to the Kubernetes API?
blocks.text: With its ServiceAccount token, projected into the pod as a short-lived, automatically rotated file. The API server validates it and RBAC authorises the call against bindings for that ServiceAccount.

blocks.title: How would you give a CI pipeline permission to deploy safely?
blocks.text: A dedicated ServiceAccount with a namespaced Role limited to get, list, watch, patch and update on the specific workload kinds, no access to Secrets, short-lived credentials obtained through OIDC federation, and separate identities per environment.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A RoleBinding in "production" references a ClusterRole. Where does it grant access?
quiz.why: A RoleBinding always grants within its own namespace.

quiz.q: RBAC rules can…
quiz.why: RBAC is additive. What is not granted is refused.

lessons.title: Autoscaling and scheduling: HPA, cluster autoscaler, affinity, taints, disruption budgets

blocks.text: Three autoscalers work at different levels. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of pods to hold a metric at a target, using desired = ceil(current replicas × current value ÷ target). The Vertical Pod Autoscaler changes requests. The cluster autoscaler adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled and removes nodes that are underused. Where pods land is steered by the scheduler: affinity and anti-affinity attract or repel pods, topology spread constraints balance them across zones, taints keep pods off a node unless they carry a matching toleration. A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many pods may be taken down at once by planned operations such as node drains.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The HPA is opening more checkout lanes when queues grow. The cluster autoscaler is renting more floor space when there is no room for another lane. Anti-affinity is "do not put both pharmacists on the same shift". A disruption budget is "maintenance may close one lane at a time, never all".
Why it matters
Traffic changes by the hour, nodes fail and are upgraded constantly, and three replicas on the same node are one failure, not three.
Where you meet it
Every production service with variable load, and every cluster that is ever upgraded.
Scenario

checkout-api runs 3 to 12 pods at a 60% CPU target, spread across three zones, with a budget that keeps at least 2 available. When a sale starts the HPA adds pods; some go Pending for lack of room; the cluster autoscaler adds a node about a minute later. During a cluster upgrade nodes are drained one at a time and the budget stops a drain from removing too many checkout pods.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD M["metrics-server / Prometheus"] --> HPA["HorizontalPodAutoscaler
target 60% CPU, 3 to 12"] HPA -->|"sets replicas"| D["Deployment checkout-api"] D --> PODS["Pods"] PODS -->|"some Pending:
no room"| CA["Cluster autoscaler"] CA -->|"adds / removes"| NODES["Node group"] SCHED["Scheduler"] -->|"spread across zones,
anti-affinity, taints"| NODES PDB["PodDisruptionBudget
minAvailable: 2"] -. "limits evictions" .-> PODS DRAIN["kubectl drain / upgrade"] -. "must respect" .-> PDB

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Traffic rises"] --> B["Average CPU 90% against a 60% target"] B --> C["HPA: desired = ceil(3 x 90 / 60) = 5"] C --> D["Deployment scaled to 5"] D --> E{"Room on existing nodes?"} E -->|yes| F["Pods start; Ready in seconds"] E -->|no| G["Pods Pending"] G --> H["Cluster autoscaler adds a node
(about 1 to 3 minutes)"] H --> F F --> I["CPU falls back toward 60%"] I --> J["Traffic drops"] J --> K["HPA waits out the stabilisation window
(5 minutes by default), then scales down"]

blocks.text: Commands
Current and target metric values, and current, minimum and maximum replicas.
Conditions and events explaining each scaling decision, or why it cannot scale (for example missing metrics or missing requests).
Which node each pod is on: the quick check that replicas are actually spread.
Disruption budgets with how many disruptions are currently allowed. Zero allowed means a drain will wait.
Marks a node unschedulable. Existing pods stay; new ones go elsewhere.
Cordons the node and evicts its pods, respecting disruption budgets, so it can be maintained or removed.

rows: `--ignore-daemonsets`
DaemonSet pods cannot be moved; skip them
`--delete-emptydir-data`
accept losing scratch data in emptyDir volumes

blocks.text: examples/kubernetes/hpa.yaml + pdb.yaml, and spreading

blocks.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: production
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: checkout-api
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60
---
# During voluntary disruptions (node drains, upgrades) keep at least 2 checkout pods running.
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: production
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-api
---
# In the Deployment's pod template: spread replicas across zones,
# and let only pods that tolerate the taint use the dedicated nodes.
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: checkout-api
  tolerations:
    - key: workload
      operator: Equal
      value: payments
      effect: NoSchedule

blocks.text: Exercise
Check the HPA formula against the simulator, then run out of room.

items: Enable the HPA and set traffic to 300 req/s. Work out the replica count by hand with the formula, then compare
Raise traffic to 600 req/s and watch replicas climb
Drain one node, then scale to 10: read the FailedScheduling event
Explain what the cluster autoscaler would do next on a real cluster, and how long it would take
Lower traffic and note that replicas do not drop at once

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Your hand calculation matches, and you can explain why the HPA cannot help when pods are Pending.
Troubleshooting

rows: HPA shows <unknown>/60%
No metrics: metrics-server is missing, or the pods have no CPU request for a percentage to be computed against.
Install metrics-server and set CPU requests.
Replicas oscillate up and down
The target is too tight, the metric is noisy, or start-up load triggers scaling.
Tune behavior.stabilizationWindowSeconds and scaling policies; make readiness accurate.
Scaled up but the service is still slow
New pods are Pending while a node is added, or the bottleneck is elsewhere (database, a downstream service).
Keep headroom or overprovision; find the real bottleneck before adding replicas.
kubectl drain hangs
A disruption budget allows zero disruptions: too few replicas, or pods are not Ready.
Fix the unready pods or add replicas. Do not delete the budget to get past it.
All replicas landed on one node
No spread constraint or anti-affinity.
Add topology spread constraints across zones and hosts.
HPA and the manifest fight over replicas
The Deployment manifest sets replicas, so each apply resets what the HPA chose.
Omit replicas from manifests managed by an HPA.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Scale on a metric that tracks load: CPU for CPU-bound services, requests per second or queue depth otherwise.
minReplicas of at least 2, spread across zones.
A disruption budget for every service with more than one replica.
Do not combine HPA and VPA on the same metric.
Leave headroom: new nodes take minutes.
Load-test scaling before the sale, not during it.

blocks.text: Security

items: Taints protect dedicated nodes only if admission control prevents arbitrary tolerations.
Autoscaling turns a traffic flood into a cloud bill: set sane maximums and rate-limit at the edge.
Node pools for sensitive workloads should be isolated with taints, labels and network policy together.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does the HPA decide how many replicas to run?
blocks.text: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetricValue ÷ targetValue), computed from the average across ready pods, clamped to min and max, with a tolerance band and a stabilisation window to avoid flapping. CPU percentage is relative to the pods' CPU requests.

blocks.title: HPA, VPA and cluster autoscaler: how do they fit together?
blocks.text: HPA changes pod count, VPA changes pod requests, the cluster autoscaler changes node count in response to unschedulable pods and underused nodes. HPA plus cluster autoscaler is the common pairing; VPA is used in recommendation mode or for workloads that cannot scale out.

blocks.title: What is a PodDisruptionBudget and what does it not protect against?
blocks.text: It limits voluntary disruptions, such as drains and autoscaler scale-down, to keep a minimum number of pods available. It does nothing for involuntary failures such as a node crashing.

blocks.title: Taints and tolerations versus node affinity?
blocks.text: A taint repels pods from a node unless they tolerate it: the node chooses. Node affinity attracts a pod to nodes with certain labels: the pod chooses. Dedicated node pools usually need both.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: 4 pods at 90% CPU, target 60%. The HPA wants…
A PodDisruptionBudget limits…
quiz.why: It applies to planned disruptions that go through the eviction API.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Kubernetes: a method for any broken workload

blocks.text: Almost every failure can be found by walking the chain in one direction and stopping at the first broken link. Outside-in for "it does not respond": DNS, load balancer, Ingress, Service, endpoints, pod, container, dependency. And for a pod that is not Running and Ready, its status names the stage that failed: Pending means it could not be scheduled, ImagePullBackOff means the image could not be fetched, CrashLoopBackOff means the process starts and dies, Running but not Ready means the readiness probe fails. Three commands produce nearly all the evidence: get for state, describe for events, logs for the application's own explanation.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: It is reading a crash from the outside in, like a failed network call in an app: is the device online, does the host resolve, did TLS succeed, what status came back, what did the server log. You never start by guessing.
Why it matters
A cluster has many moving parts and the symptom ("502", "timeout") is rarely where the fault is. A fixed order is faster than intuition, and leaves a trail you can hand to someone else.
Where you meet it
On call. Also every failed deploy.
Scenario

Checkout returns 503 after a deploy. The Ingress is fine and matches. The Service has zero endpoints. The new pods are Running but 0/1 Ready. describe shows the readiness probe getting 503 from /ready. The logs say DATABASE_URL is not set: the new chart version renamed the Secret key. Rollback first; fix the key; redeploy.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR U["Client"] --> DNS["DNS"] --> LB["Load balancer"] --> ING["Ingress"] --> SVC["Service"] --> EP["Endpoints"] --> POD["Pod"] --> C["Container"] --> DEP["Dependency:
database, other service"] DNS -. "dig" .- t1["does the name resolve?"] ING -. "kubectl get ingress" .- t2["does a rule match?"] SVC -. "kubectl get endpointslices" .- t3["any endpoints?"] POD -. "kubectl describe pod" .- t4["scheduled, pulled, Ready?"] C -. "kubectl logs --previous" .- t5["why did it exit?"] DEP -. "debug pod: nc, curl" .- t6["reachable from the pod?"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["kubectl get pods"] --> B{"Pod status?"} B -->|"Pending"| P["describe pod: FailedScheduling
resources, taints, affinity, unbound PVC"] B -->|"ImagePullBackOff"| I["describe pod: wrong tag,
or missing imagePullSecret"] B -->|"CreateContainerConfigError"| CC["Missing ConfigMap, Secret or key"] B -->|"CrashLoopBackOff"| CR["logs --previous + exit code:
1 app error, 137 OOM or killed,
126/127 bad command"] B -->|"Running, 0/1 Ready"| R["describe pod: readiness probe failure,
then call the endpoint"] B -->|"Running, Ready"| S{"Service has endpoints?"} S -->|no| SL["Selector, namespace, port"] S -->|yes| N["From a debug pod: curl the Service,
then check Ingress and NetworkPolicy"] CR --> F["Was there a recent deploy or config change?"] R --> F F -->|yes| RB["Roll back first, investigate second"]

blocks.text: Commands
State, restarts, age, IP and node for every pod. Always the first command.
Read from the bottom: Events. Then "Last State" for the exit code and reason of the previous container.
The crashed instance's last words.

rows: `--previous`
the container before the current restart
`-c NAME`
pick a container in a multi-container pod
`--since=10m`
limit by time

blocks.text: A namespace-wide timeline: scheduling, pulls, kills, probe failures. Events expire after about an hour.
What changed and when. Most incidents start with a change.
Returns to the previous revision. The usual first action when a deploy caused the problem.
Adds a temporary debugging container to a running pod, sharing its network and processes. For images with no shell.

rows: `--target`
share the process namespace of this container

blocks.text: A shell in a production container. Look, do not change: anything you alter is lost on restart and bypasses review.
Status and exit code reference

blocks.code:
STATUS                        MEANS                                   LOOK AT
Pending                       not scheduled                           describe: FailedScheduling
ContainerCreating (stuck)     volume, CNI or image pull in progress   describe: events
ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff cannot fetch the image                  tag, registry, imagePullSecrets
CreateContainerConfigError    referenced ConfigMap/Secret missing     describe: which object or key
CrashLoopBackOff              starts, exits, back-off between tries   logs --previous, exit code
Running 0/1                   readiness probe failing                 describe: probe error
Terminating (stuck)           finalizer or unresponsive node          finalizers, node status
Evicted                       node ran short of memory or disk        describe: reason; node pressure
OOMKilled (last state)        memory limit exceeded                   usage vs limit

EXIT CODE
0     finished normally (a server should not exit)
1     application error: read the logs
126   command found but not executable
127   command not found: wrong image or entrypoint
137   SIGKILL: OOM, or grace period expired
143   SIGTERM: asked to stop

blocks.text: Exercise
Diagnose five failures from status and events alone.

items: In the cluster simulator deploy the image that crashes: which status, and are customers affected?
Deploy the image that does not exist: which status and which event?
Drain a node and scale up until pods are Pending: read the event
In the Service debugging lab, apply each breakage and name the first command that reveals it
In the probe lab, find the configuration that produces Running but never Ready
For each, write: status, the one command that showed the cause, and the fix

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You map CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, Pending, 0/1 Ready and "no endpoints" to their causes without the flowchart.
Troubleshooting

rows: CrashLoopBackOff with empty logs
The process never started (exit 126 or 127), or was killed (137) before logging.
describe for the exit code. Check the image entrypoint and command; check for OOMKilled.
Works in staging, crashes in production
A difference in configuration, secrets, resources or network policy, not in the image.
Diff the rendered manifests for the two environments.
Intermittent 5xx with healthy-looking pods
One bad pod in rotation, pods killed without draining during deploys or scale-down, or a saturated dependency.
Look per pod, not at averages; correlate with rollouts and node events.
A namespace or pod is stuck Terminating
A finalizer is waiting for a controller that no longer exists, or the node is unreachable.
Find and fix the owner of the finalizer. Forcing deletion can orphan real resources.
Everything slow at once across the cluster
A shared layer: DNS, the CNI, the API server, or a noisy neighbour on shared nodes.
Check CoreDNS, node pressure and control-plane health before any single application.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Mitigate first: roll back, scale or shift traffic, then investigate.
Ask "what changed?" before anything else.
Collect evidence before restarting: describe output, previous logs, events.
Keep notes with timestamps: they become the incident timeline.
Turn every novel failure into an alert, a runbook entry or a guardrail.

blocks.text: Security

items: exec and debug in production are powerful: restrict them with RBAC and audit their use.
Do not copy secrets out of pods to "test something".
A debugging pod with broad tools and network access is a risk if left running: use --rm.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: A deployment was rolled out and the service returns 503. Walk me through it.
blocks.text: Confirm scope and check whether to roll back immediately. Then: does the Ingress route to the right Service, does the Service have endpoints, are the new pods Ready, what does describe say about probes, what do the logs say. Compare with the previous revision: image, config, secrets. Roll back, fix, add a check that would have caught it.

blocks.title: What is the difference between kubectl logs, describe and get events?
blocks.text: logs is the application's output. describe is Kubernetes' view of one object, including its recent events and last container state. get events is the namespace-wide stream of what controllers and kubelets did.

blocks.title: How do you debug a container that has no shell?
blocks.text: kubectl debug adds an ephemeral container with tools that shares the target's namespaces, or creates a copy of the pod with a different image or command. Combined with logs, exit codes and port-forwarding.

blocks.title: Pods are Pending. List the causes.
blocks.text: Insufficient CPU or memory for the requests, taints without tolerations, node selectors or affinity that match no node, unbound or zone-pinned volumes, a namespace quota, or too many pods per node. describe pod states which.
