blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which command shows why a pod is Pending?
quiz.why: The FailedScheduling event explains it; a Pending pod has no logs.

quiz.q: A deploy went out and errors started. First action?
quiz.why: Restore service first; the previous revision is known to work.

modules.title: Helm and Kustomize
modules.summary: Charts, values, releases and rollbacks; a base with overlays and patches.

lessons.title: Helm: charts, values, releases and rollbacks

blocks.text: An application on Kubernetes is several manifests that differ slightly per environment. Helm packages them as a chart: a folder of templates with placeholders, plus a values.yaml of defaults. Installing a chart with a set of values produces a release: a named, versioned instance in a namespace. Upgrading renders the templates again with new values and applies the difference. Helm records each revision, so a rollback re-applies an earlier one. helm template shows the exact YAML without touching a cluster.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A chart is a CocoaPod or pub package for infrastructure: versioned, reusable, with configuration options. values.yaml is its default configuration and your override file is your project's settings for it.
Why it matters
Copying manifests per environment drifts within weeks. Third-party software (ingress controllers, Prometheus, databases) would otherwise mean maintaining hundreds of lines of someone else's YAML.
Where you meet it
Installing third-party software into clusters, and packaging your own services when they need many options. Most infrastructure components ship as charts.
Scenario

checkout-api has one chart. Staging installs it with defaults and an image tag from CI. Production adds values-production.yaml: more replicas and an autoscaler. A bad upgrade is undone with one rollback command, which re-applies the previous revision's manifests.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph CHART["Chart: checkout-api/"] CY["Chart.yaml
name, version, appVersion"] V["values.yaml
defaults"] T["templates/
deployment, service, hpa"] end O["-f values-production.yaml"] --> R S["--set image.tag=9f3c2ab"] --> R V --> R["Helm renders templates"] T --> R R --> M["Plain Kubernetes manifests"] M -->|"apply"| K["Cluster"] R --> REL["Release 'checkout'
revision 3, stored as a Secret
in the namespace"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["helm upgrade --install checkout ./checkout-api -f values-production.yaml"] --> B["Merge values:
chart defaults, then -f files, then --set"] B --> C["Render every template"] C --> D{"Rendered output valid YAML
and valid Kubernetes objects?"} D -->|no| E["Error. Nothing is applied"] D -->|yes| F["Compare with the previous revision"] F --> G["Create, patch and delete resources"] G --> H["Record revision N+1"] H --> I{"--wait / --atomic:
did it become healthy?"} I -->|no, with --atomic| J["Automatic rollback to revision N"] I -->|yes| K["Release deployed"]

blocks.text: Commands
Renders the chart to YAML locally. Nothing is sent anywhere. Read this before any install or upgrade.

rows: `-f FILE`
a values file; repeat for several, later ones win
`--set key=value`
override one value; highest precedence
`--debug`
print the failing template on errors

blocks.text: Checks the chart for structural problems and obvious mistakes.

blocks.code: helm upgrade --install checkout ./checkout-api -n production -f values-production.yaml --set image.tag=9f3c2ab --atomic --timeout 5m
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Installs the release, or upgrades it if it exists. The command pipelines use.

rows: `--install`
install if the release does not exist yet
`--atomic`
roll back automatically if the upgrade does not become healthy
`--timeout`
how long to wait for readiness
`--dry-run`
render and validate against the cluster without changing it

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: helm status checkout -n production
Releases in a namespace with chart version, app version, revision and status.
Every revision of a release, with status and description.
The values supplied for the current revision. helm get manifest shows what was applied.
Re-applies revision 2 as a new revision. It restores Kubernetes objects only: it does not undo a database migration.
Deletes every resource the release created. PersistentVolumeClaims from StatefulSets are usually left behind.
values.yaml and templates/deployment.yaml

blocks.code:
# ---------- values.yaml ----------
# Defaults. Override per environment with -f values-production.yaml or --set key=value.
replicaCount: 2

image:
  repository: registry.example.com/shop/checkout-api
  tag: ""              # empty means: use the chart's appVersion

service:
  port: 80
  targetPort: 8000

env:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  PAYMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: "8"

existingSecret: checkout-db   # name of a Secret holding the key "url"

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    memory: 512Mi

autoscaling:
  enabled: false
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  targetCPU: 60

# ---------- templates/deployment.yaml ----------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
  namespace: {{ .Release.Namespace }}
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
    helm.sh/chart: {{ printf "%s-%s" .Chart.Name .Chart.Version }}
spec:
  {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }}
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  {{- end }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"
          ports:
            - containerPort: {{ .Values.service.targetPort }}
          env:
            {{- range $name, $value := .Values.env }}
            - name: {{ $name }}
              value: {{ $value | quote }}
            {{- end }}
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: {{ required "existingSecret must name the database Secret" .Values.existingSecret }}
                  key: url
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: {{ .Values.service.targetPort }}
            periodSeconds: 5

blocks.text: {{- trims the whitespace before an action. nindent N starts a new line and indents every line by N spaces: most "invalid YAML" errors in charts are a wrong nindent.
Exercise
Read a template, predict the output, then run a release through install, upgrade and rollback.

items: Read the deployment template and predict the image line before looking at the output
Install. Then set image.tag=9f3c2ab and read the diff before upgrading
Switch to production: which resource appears, and which field disappears from the Deployment? Find the template lines responsible
Change nindent 12 to nindent 3 and read the error
Rename autoscaling in values.yaml and read the nil pointer error
Roll back to revision 1 and look at the history: what revision number did the rollback get?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain value precedence, why replicas is omitted when the autoscaler is on, and why a rollback creates a new revision.
Troubleshooting

rows: Error: YAML parse error on templates/deployment.yaml
The template rendered text that is not valid YAML, nearly always indentation.
helm template --debug prints the rendered output. Check nindent values and where {{- removes line breaks.
nil pointer evaluating interface {}.enabled
The template reads .Values.a.b but a is missing from the values.
Add the key to values.yaml, or guard with default or with.
UPGRADE FAILED: another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress
An earlier operation was interrupted and left the release in a pending state.
helm history to find it, then helm rollback to the last good revision.
The upgrade "succeeded" but pods are crashing
Without --wait or --atomic Helm only confirms the API accepted the objects.
Use --atomic with a timeout in pipelines.
A value set with --set is ignored
The key path is wrong, or the type is not what the template expects (a string where a number is compared).
helm get values and helm template with the same flags; use --set-string for strings that look like numbers.
Someone edited the Deployment with kubectl and the next upgrade behaved oddly
Helm computes a three-way merge between the old manifest, the new manifest and the live object.
Do not hand-edit Helm-managed resources. Change values and upgrade.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Always read helm template or a diff before upgrading.
Pin chart versions; never install "latest".
Keep values files in Git, one per environment, small.
Use --atomic and --timeout in automation.
Do not put secrets in values files; reference existing Secrets.
Keep templates simple. If a chart needs heavy logic, the abstraction is wrong.

blocks.text: Security

items: Release records are stored as Secrets in the namespace and contain the full rendered manifests and values: anyone who can read Secrets there can read them.
A chart is code that creates cluster resources, including RBAC: review third-party charts and their default values before installing.
Verify chart provenance and pin versions; treat chart repositories as part of your supply chain.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is a Helm chart, a release and a revision?
blocks.text: A chart is a versioned package of templates and default values. A release is a named installation of a chart in a namespace. Each install, upgrade or rollback creates a new revision of the release, recorded so it can be inspected or re-applied.

blocks.title: How do values override each other?
blocks.text: The chart's values.yaml is the base. Files given with -f are merged over it in order, later ones winning. --set and --set-string are applied last. Maps merge key by key; lists are replaced whole.

blocks.title: What does helm rollback do, and what does it not do?
blocks.text: It applies the manifests of an earlier revision as a new revision. It does not restore data, undo database migrations or revert anything outside the release's Kubernetes objects.

blocks.title: Helm or Kustomize?
blocks.text: Helm is templating plus packaging and release management: best for distributing software with many options. Kustomize patches plain YAML with no templates: best for varying your own manifests per environment. Many teams use charts for third-party software and Kustomize for their own, or render charts and patch the result.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which has the highest precedence?
quiz.why: --set is applied after all values files.

quiz.q: helm template…
options: renders manifests locally without a cluster
quiz.why: It only renders. Nothing is applied.

lessons.title: Kustomize: a base and overlays, with no templates

blocks.text: Kustomize takes ordinary Kubernetes YAML and applies changes to it. A base directory holds the common manifests and a kustomization.yaml listing them. Each environment has an overlay: its own kustomization.yaml that points at the base and states only the differences, such as namespace, image tag, replica count, or a patch that changes a few fields. kustomize build (or kubectl apply -k) merges them and prints the final manifests. There are no placeholders in the files: the base is valid YAML you could apply as it is.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A base and overlays work like a Flutter flavour setup or Xcode build configurations: one shared definition, and per-environment files that override only what differs.
Why it matters

Templating turns YAML into a programming language that is hard to read and review. Patching keeps every file valid and makes "what is different in production?" a short file you can read in ten seconds.
Where you meet it
Varying your own manifests across environments; it is built into kubectl and is what Argo CD and Flux most often build from.
Scenario

The checkout base has a Deployment, a Service and a generated ConfigMap. The staging overlay sets namespace staging, one replica and the image tag CI just built. The production overlay sets three replicas, a pinned version, a different log level and a patch with larger resource requests.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD B["base/
deployment.yaml, service.yaml
kustomization.yaml"] --> S["overlays/staging/
kustomization.yaml"] B --> P["overlays/production/
kustomization.yaml
patch-resources.yaml"] S -->|"kustomize build"| SO["Staging manifests:
namespace staging, 1 replica,
image :9f3c2ab"] P -->|"kustomize build"| PO["Production manifests:
namespace production, 3 replicas,
bigger requests, LOG_LEVEL=warn"] SO --> K1["Staging cluster"] PO --> K2["Production cluster"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["kustomize build overlays/production"] --> B["Read kustomization.yaml"] B --> C["Load resources: follow ../../base
and build it first"] C --> D["Run generators:
configMapGenerator creates or merges"] D --> E["Apply patches to matching resources
(by kind and name)"] E --> F["Apply transformers:
replicas, images, labels, namespace"] F --> G["Append a content hash to generated
ConfigMap names and fix references"] G --> H["Print the final YAML"]

blocks.text: Commands
Builds and prints the final manifests. Nothing is applied. kustomize build does the same with the standalone binary.
Shows what applying the overlay would change in the cluster, compared with what is running.
Builds the overlay and applies it.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: kubectl rollout status deployment/checkout-api -n production
Rewrites the images entry in the kustomization.yaml of the current directory. This is how a pipeline records "deploy this build" as a Git change.
overlays/production/kustomization.yaml and its patch

blocks.code:
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

resources:
  - ../../base

namespace: production

images:
  - name: registry.example.com/shop/checkout-api
    newTag: 1.4.0

replicas:
  - name: checkout-api
    count: 3

configMapGenerator:
  - name: checkout-config
    behavior: merge
    literals:
      - LOG_LEVEL=warn

patches:
  - path: patch-resources.yaml

# ---------- patch-resources.yaml ----------
# Only the fields that differ in production. Everything else comes from the base.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: checkout-api
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi

blocks.text: A strategic-merge patch looks like a fragment of the resource. Lists of named items, such as containers, are merged by name, so the patch names the container and gives only the fields to change.
Exercise
Predict the built output of each overlay, then make three deliberate mistakes.

items: Build the base, then staging, and use "changes vs base" to list every difference
Build production: where did the memory limit come from? Which file would you edit to change it?
Change LOG_LEVEL in the production overlay: which two names change in the output, and why does that matter?
In staging, shorten the image name to checkout-api: the build succeeds. What did it silently not do?
Rename the patch target and read the error
Remove "behavior: merge" from the production generator and read the error

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can say which mistakes Kustomize reports and which it accepts silently, and why the config hash exists.
Troubleshooting

rows: no matches for Id Deployment…; failed to find unique target for patch
The patch names a resource that does not exist under that kind and name.
Use the name from the base, before any namePrefix, and the exact kind and apiVersion.
The image tag did not change
The images entry name does not match the image name in the manifest, so nothing was transformed. Kustomize does not warn.
The name must equal the image without its tag, including the registry path.
Pods did not restart after a config change
The ConfigMap was written by hand with a fixed name, so the pod template did not change.
Use configMapGenerator: the name gets a content hash and every reference is updated.
Old ConfigMaps pile up in the namespace
Each change creates a new hashed name and apply does not delete the old ones.
Apply with pruning, or let a GitOps tool with prune enabled remove them.
accumulating resources: … no such file or directory
A path in resources is wrong, usually the relative path to the base.
Paths are relative to the kustomization.yaml that lists them.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Keep the base deployable on its own.
Overlays contain only differences; if an overlay gets large, the base is wrong.
Review the built output in pull requests, not just the overlay.
Use generators for ConfigMaps so changes roll pods.
Let CI change image tags with kustomize edit set image and commit the result.

blocks.text: Security

items: Remote bases fetched from someone else's repository can change under you: pin them to a commit.
secretGenerator from literal values puts secrets in Git: use an external secrets mechanism instead.
The built output is what reaches the cluster; make policy checks run against that.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does Kustomize differ from Helm?
blocks.text: Kustomize has no templates or packaging: it layers patches and transformations over plain YAML. Helm templates YAML from values and manages versioned releases. Kustomize is simpler to read and review for your own manifests; Helm is better for distributing configurable software.

blocks.title: What is the hash suffix on generated ConfigMaps for?
blocks.text: The name changes whenever the content changes, and Kustomize rewrites references to it. The pod template therefore changes, which triggers a rolling update, and a rollback returns to the previous ConfigMap as well.

blocks.title: What is a strategic merge patch?
blocks.text: A partial resource merged into the target using knowledge of Kubernetes types: maps merge by key and certain lists, such as containers, merge by a key field (name) instead of being replaced. The alternative is a JSON 6902 patch, which lists explicit add, replace and remove operations by path.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: An overlay should contain…
options: a full copy of the base
only what differs from the base
quiz.why: The point is to state differences once and share the rest.

quiz.q: Why does configMapGenerator add a hash to the name?
options: So a content change rolls the pods
quiz.why: A new name changes the pod template, which triggers a rollout.

modules.title: GitOps and Argo CD
modules.summary: Git as the source of truth: sync, health, drift, prune, self-heal and rollback. Flux is mentioned, not covered.

lessons.title: GitOps with Argo CD: Git as the source of truth

blocks.text: In GitOps the desired state of a cluster lives in a Git repository, and a controller inside the cluster continuously makes reality match it. Nobody runs kubectl apply or pushes from a pipeline: you change Git, and the controller pulls. Argo CD is such a controller. An Application object says "this path in this repository belongs in this cluster and namespace". Argo CD reports two separate things: sync status (does the cluster match Git?) and health (are the resources working?). With automated sync it applies new commits by itself. Two further options are off by default: prune, which deletes resources removed from Git, and self-heal, which reverts changes made directly to the cluster.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: It is the reconciliation idea from Kubernetes, one level up. A Deployment keeps pods matching a spec; Argo CD keeps the specs matching Git. Like SwiftUI or Flutter, you edit the declaration and the framework brings the screen in line, and anything you poke in by hand is overwritten on the next pass.
Why it matters

When pipelines push to clusters, the cluster's real state is "whatever the last commands did", credentials for production live in CI, and manual fixes are invisible. With Git as the source of truth every change is reviewed, has an author and a history, and rollback is a revert.
Where you meet it
Teams running several clusters or environments, and anyone who needs an audit trail for production changes. Flux is the other common controller and follows the same principles.
Scenario

CI builds checkout-api, then commits the new image tag to the deployment repository. Argo CD notices the commit and syncs production. An engineer who "just scales it up" with kubectl during an incident finds the change reverted moments later, because self-heal is on: the fix has to go through Git, where the rest of the team can see it.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR DEV["Developer"] -->|"merge"| APP["App repository"] APP --> CI["CI: test, build image,
push to registry"] CI -->|"commit new image tag"| CFG["Deployment repository
(manifests, overlays, charts)"] subgraph CL["Cluster"] ARGO["Argo CD"] RES["Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps"] end ARGO -->|"pulls and compares"| CFG ARGO -->|"applies the difference"| RES RES -->|"live state"| ARGO CI -. "has NO cluster credentials" .-> CL

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Applications with their sync status and health.
One application in detail: the commit it is synced to, every resource with its status, and recent conditions.
The difference between Git and the cluster: exactly what a sync would change.
Applies Git to the cluster now.

rows: `--prune`
also delete resources no longer in Git
`--dry-run`
preview only

blocks.text: Past syncs with the commit each one deployed.

blocks.code: git revert HEAD && git push origin main
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: The GitOps rollback: a new commit that undoes the last one. Argo CD then syncs the cluster back. Reviewed and recorded like any other change.
Re-applies an earlier synced state to the cluster without changing Git. Argo CD refuses it while automated sync is enabled, and afterwards the app is OutOfSync until Git is reverted too.
examples/argocd/application.yaml

blocks.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/example/shop-deploy.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: kustomize/overlays/production
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: production
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true        # delete resources that were removed from Git (off by default)
      selfHeal: true     # undo manual changes made in the cluster (off by default)
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

blocks.text: Under automated sync, prune and selfHeal are both off unless you set them, and Argo CD does not retry a sync that failed for the same commit.
Exercise
Complete the six checkpoints in the GitOps simulator and explain each result.

items: Deploy 1.5.0 by committing, then reconcile
Scale by hand with kubectl and reconcile: what does Argo CD do with self-heal off?
Turn self-heal on and reconcile again
Commit the removal of the ConfigMap and reconcile: is it deleted? Turn on prune and press Sync
Commit the broken 1.5.1 image: read the two status badges. How can it be Synced and Degraded?
Press Rollback and read the refusal, then revert the commit instead
Commit the YAML typo and reconcile twice: what happens the second time?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state what Synced does and does not tell you, what prune and self-heal each add, and how to roll back.
Troubleshooting

rows: OutOfSync forever although nobody changed anything
A controller or webhook in the cluster keeps modifying a field that Git also sets: an HPA changing replicas, or defaults added by the API.
Remove the field from Git (replicas under an HPA), or add ignoreDifferences for it.
Synced, but the application is broken
Sync status only says the cluster matches Git. Git asked for something that does not work.
Look at health and the pods. Revert the commit.
A manual hotfix keeps disappearing
Self-heal is doing its job.
Commit the change. For a true emergency, disable automated sync on that application, and remember to restore it.
A sync failed and Argo CD does nothing more
Automated sync does not retry the same commit after a failure.
Push a fixing commit, trigger a manual sync, or configure a retry policy.
Resources deleted from Git still exist
Prune is off.
Sync with prune, or enable automated pruning once you trust the repository.
ComparisonError: failed to generate manifests
Helm or Kustomize could not build the path at that commit.
Build it locally at that commit; the error is the same one.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Keep deployment configuration in its own repository, separate from application code.
CI writes to Git; only the controller writes to the cluster.
Enable prune and self-heal deliberately, per application, once the repository is trustworthy.
One directory or overlay per environment; promotion is a pull request.
Protect the deployment repository like production: reviews, required checks, signed commits.
Alert on OutOfSync and Degraded applications.

blocks.text: Security

items: Write access to the deployment repository is write access to the cluster.
Pull-based delivery means no cluster credentials in CI, which removes a large attack surface.
Argo CD itself holds powerful credentials: restrict its projects, enable SSO and RBAC, keep it patched.
Never commit plain secrets: use Sealed Secrets, SOPS or External Secrets.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is GitOps?
blocks.text: An operating model with four properties: the desired state is declared, stored and versioned in Git, pulled automatically by an agent, and continuously reconciled so the running system converges on it and drift is corrected or reported.

blocks.title: Push-based versus pull-based deployment?
blocks.text: Push: a pipeline holding cluster credentials runs apply or helm upgrade. Simple, but the pipeline is highly privileged and the cluster can drift unnoticed. Pull: an in-cluster controller fetches from Git and applies. No external credentials, continuous drift detection, and Git is the record.

blocks.title: Sync status versus health in Argo CD?
blocks.text: Sync status compares live resources with what Git renders: Synced or OutOfSync. Health assesses whether the resources work: a Deployment with crashing pods is Degraded. They are independent: an application can be Synced and Degraded.

blocks.title: How do you roll back with GitOps?
blocks.text: Revert the commit in Git and let the controller sync. That keeps Git truthful and goes through review. A tool-level rollback changes the cluster only, is refused under automated sync in Argo CD, and leaves the application out of sync.

blocks.title: How does an HPA interact with GitOps?
blocks.text: The HPA changes replicas in the cluster, which differs from Git if Git sets replicas, so the controller reports drift or fights the HPA. Omit replicas from the manifest for autoscaled workloads, or tell the controller to ignore that field.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: With automated sync on and self-heal off, someone runs kubectl scale. Argo CD…
quiz.why: Changes made in the cluster do not trigger an automated sync unless self-heal is enabled.

quiz.q: An application is Synced and Degraded. That means…
options: the cluster matches Git, and what Git asks for is not working
quiz.why: Sync and health are separate questions.

modules.summary: The workflow, state and drift, variables and modules, reading a plan, and Terraform in CI. Not yet covered: writing providers, testing frameworks in depth, Terragrunt.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code and the Terraform workflow

blocks.text: Terraform lets you describe infrastructure in text files: networks, servers, databases, DNS records. You write what should exist. Terraform compares that with what does exist, shows you the difference as a plan, and makes the changes only after you approve them.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: An architect's drawing and a builder. You change the drawing, not the building. The builder walks the site with the drawing, lists what differs ("add a door here, remove that wall"), and waits for your signature before touching anything.
Why it matters

Infrastructure created by clicking in a console cannot be reviewed, repeated or rolled back, and nobody remembers why a setting is what it is. Text files in Git give you history, review, an identical staging environment, and a way to rebuild after a disaster.
Where you meet it

Anything with an API: cloud networks and servers, managed databases, Kubernetes clusters, DNS, monitoring dashboards, GitHub repositories. Terraform talks to each through a plugin called a provider. Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts usually stay with the tools from the earlier modules; Terraform creates the cluster they run on.
Scenario

checkout-api needs somewhere to run in AWS: a VPC, a subnet, firewall rules, a server and a bucket for invoices. Those eight resources are one Terraform configuration. Staging and production are the same files with different variable values, so "works in staging" means something.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph YOU["Your repository"] CFG["Configuration
*.tf files"] VARS["Values
terraform.tfvars"] end subgraph TF["terraform (CLI)"] CORE["Core
builds the graph,
computes the plan"] PROV["Provider plugin
hashicorp/aws"] end STATE[("State
what Terraform created")] API["AWS API"] REAL["Real resources
VPC, instance, bucket"] CFG --> CORE VARS --> CORE CORE <--> STATE CORE --> PROV PROV -->|"create, read,
update, delete"| API API --> REAL

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Edit the .tf files"] --> B["terraform init
download providers, connect to the state"] B --> C["terraform fmt and validate
syntax and references"] C --> D["terraform plan
read real resources, compare with the files"] D --> E{"Is the plan what
you intended?"} E -->|"no"| A E -->|"yes"| F["terraform apply
approve with yes"] F --> G["Provider calls the cloud API
in dependency order"] G --> H{"Every call succeeded?"} H -->|"yes"| I["State updated.
Commit the files"] H -->|"no"| J["Stops at the first error.
Completed resources stay and are recorded"] J --> A

blocks.text: Commands

Prepares the working directory: downloads the providers the configuration asks for, records their exact versions in .terraform.lock.hcl, and connects to the state backend. Run it once after cloning and again whenever providers, modules or the backend change.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Run any other command first and Terraform tells you to run init.
Rewrites the files into the standard layout. Changes whitespace only.

rows: `-check`
change nothing; exit non-zero if a file needs formatting (for CI)

blocks.text: Checks syntax, argument names and references without contacting the cloud. Catches typing mistakes in seconds.
Reads the current state of every managed resource, compares it with the configuration and prints what apply would do. It changes nothing.

rows: `-out=tfplan`
save the plan so apply runs exactly this and nothing newer
`-var-file=production.tfvars`
take variable values from this file

blocks.code: Plan: 8 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Read every resource marked with -/+ or -. Those are destroyed.
Computes a plan, shows it, and after you type yes makes the changes through the provider. Creates, changes and destroys real, billed infrastructure.

rows: `tfplan`
apply a saved plan without asking again
`-auto-approve`
skip the question. For pipelines applying a reviewed plan, not for people

blocks.text: Prints the output values recorded at the last apply: addresses, ids and names that people or other tools need.
Plans and, after approval, deletes every resource in the state. Data in databases and buckets is gone unless something else protects it.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Read the list before typing yes. Check which account and environment you are in first.
examples/terraform/aws/main.tf
Nothing here says in what order to create things. aws_subnet.public refers to aws_vpc.main.id, so Terraform knows the VPC comes first. References are the dependency graph.
Exercise
Create the eight resources in the Terraform lab and explain each step of the workflow.

items: Press plan before init and read the error
Run terraform init, then terraform plan. Find three values shown as (known after apply) and say why Terraform cannot know them yet
Open the Dependency graph tab and predict which resource is created first and which last
Run apply, read the plan, approve it, and compare the creation order with your prediction
Open the State tab and find the id of the VPC inside the subnet's attributes
Run plan again. What does it say, and why?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain what init, plan and apply each do, where the order of creation comes from, and why a second plan shows no changes.
Troubleshooting

rows: A command says to run terraform init
Providers are not installed in this directory, or the configuration changed which providers or backend it needs.
Run terraform init. It is safe to repeat.
Unsupported argument / Missing required argument
An argument name is misspelt, belongs to a different resource type, or was renamed in a newer provider version.
Check the resource page in the provider documentation for the version you have pinned.
Reference to undeclared resource
The reference names a resource block that does not exist, usually a typing mistake in the type or the name.
References have the form TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE and must match a resource block exactly.
apply failed half way
One API call was rejected: a wrong value, a missing permission or a quota. Terraform does not roll back.
Read the error, correct the configuration and apply again. The next plan contains only what is still missing.
Error: Cycle
Two resources refer to each other, so neither can be created first.
Break the loop. For two security groups that allow each other, define the rules as separate rule resources.
The plan wants to change things you did not touch
A provider upgrade changed defaults, or someone changed the resource by hand.
Read the plan line by line. See the lesson on state and drift.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Read the whole plan before every apply. The summary line is not enough.
Pin the Terraform version and provider versions, and commit .terraform.lock.hcl.
Keep everything in Git and change infrastructure through pull requests.
Run fmt and validate in CI so reviews are about the change, not the layout.
Tag every resource with project, environment and "managed by terraform".
Start small: one configuration per service and environment, not one for the whole company.

blocks.text: Security

items: Whoever can run apply can change or delete the infrastructure. Limit that to a pipeline and a few people.
Never put access keys or passwords in .tf or .tfvars files. Use short-lived credentials from your identity provider.
Add .terraform/ and any *.tfstate files to .gitignore.
A plan can show secret values. Treat plan output and CI logs as sensitive.
Review third-party modules before using them: they run with your credentials.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is infrastructure as code and why use it?
blocks.text: Describing infrastructure in versioned files that a tool applies, instead of creating it by hand. It gives review, history, repeatable environments, fast recovery and a single place that says what should exist.

blocks.title: What do init, plan and apply do?
blocks.text: init downloads providers and modules and connects to the state backend. plan refreshes the state from the real resources, compares it with the configuration and prints the changes without making them. apply performs a plan through the provider APIs and records the results in the state.

blocks.title: What does declarative mean here?
blocks.text: You state the end result, not the steps. Terraform works out which API calls are needed and in what order, and running it again when nothing has changed does nothing.

blocks.title: How does Terraform decide the order of operations?
blocks.text: From references. If one resource uses an attribute of another, it depends on it. Terraform builds a graph, creates along it, destroys in reverse, and runs independent resources in parallel. depends_on is for the rare dependency that no reference expresses.

blocks.title: Terraform or Ansible?
blocks.text: Terraform is for creating and changing infrastructure through APIs, with a state that tracks what it owns. Ansible is for configuring what runs inside machines. Many teams use both, and containers have reduced the need for the second.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: terraform plan…
options: shows what apply would change and changes nothing
quiz.why: A plan is a preview. Only apply changes real infrastructure.

quiz.q: How does Terraform know to create the VPC before the subnet?
options: The order of blocks in the file
The subnet refers to an attribute of the VPC
You list the order in a separate file
quiz.why: References between resources form the dependency graph.

quiz.q: apply fails on the sixth of eight resources. What is true afterwards?
options: The first five exist and are in the state
quiz.why: Terraform stops at the first error and keeps what completed. Fix the cause and apply again.

lessons.title: State, remote backends, locking and drift

blocks.text: The state is a file where Terraform records every real object it created and which block in your configuration it belongs to. Without it Terraform would not know that the server in AWS is "aws_instance.api". Teams keep the state in shared storage with a lock, so two people cannot change the same infrastructure at once.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A cloakroom. You hand over a coat and get a numbered ticket. The ticket book is the state: it links "ticket 14" to one particular coat. Lose the book and the coats are still there, but nobody knows whose they are. Two attendants writing in the book at the same moment make a mess, so there is one pen.
Why it matters

Cloud APIs have no idea which resources came from which Terraform configuration. The state holds that link, plus attributes that only exist after creation, such as ids and addresses. Because it is the one source of that knowledge, where it lives and who can write to it matter a great deal.
Where you meet it

Every Terraform project has a state. On a laptop it is terraform.tfstate in the working directory. In a team it lives in a remote backend: an S3 bucket, Azure Blob Storage, a Google Cloud Storage bucket, or HCP Terraform.
Scenario

During an incident someone resizes the checkout-api instance in the AWS console and adds a firewall rule for SSH. The state now disagrees with reality. This is drift. The next plan reads the real resources, reports what changed, and proposes to put them back to what the files say. Either you let it, or you decide the manual change was right and write it into the configuration.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR DEV["Engineer's laptop"] --> LOCK CI["CI pipeline"] --> LOCK subgraph S3["S3 bucket: shop-terraform-state (versioned, encrypted)"] LOCK["checkout/staging/terraform.tfstate.tflock
the lock: one writer at a time"] ST["checkout/staging/terraform.tfstate"] ST2["checkout/production/terraform.tfstate"] end LOCK --> ST ST -. "records ids of" .-> AWS["Real resources in AWS"] CONSOLE["Someone in the AWS console"] -. "changes by hand = drift" .-> AWS

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["terraform plan"] --> B{"Can it take the state lock?"} B -->|"no"| X["Error acquiring the state lock.
Someone else is running. Wait"] B -->|"yes"| C["Refresh: read every resource
in the state from the cloud API"] C --> D{"Does the real resource still exist?"} D -->|"no"| E["Dropped from the state.
Planned for creation again"] D -->|"yes"| F{"Real attributes equal the state?"} F -->|"no"| G["Reported as changed outside Terraform"] F -->|"yes"| H["Compare with the configuration"] G --> H E --> H H --> I{"Configuration equals reality?"} I -->|"yes"| J["No changes"] I -->|"no"| K["Plan to make reality match the files"] K --> L{"Was the manual change correct?"} L -->|"no"| M["Apply: Terraform reverts it"] L -->|"yes"| N["Put it in the configuration,
then plan shows no changes"]

blocks.text: Commands
Lists the address of every resource Terraform manages in this state.
Prints every recorded attribute of one resource, including ids and addresses assigned by the cloud.
Shows only what changed outside Terraform, without proposing to change any infrastructure. The way to look at drift on its own.
Accepts the drift into the state without changing real resources. The configuration still has to be updated to match, or the next plan will propose reverting it.
Renames a resource in the state so that renaming the block does not destroy and recreate it. A moved block in the configuration does the same and can be reviewed, so prefer that.
Makes Terraform forget a resource without deleting it. The real bucket stays; Terraform no longer manages it.
Brings an existing resource under management by writing it into the state. You still write the matching resource block. An import block in the configuration does this as part of a reviewed plan.
Removes a lock left behind by a run that crashed. If the other run is in fact still going, two writers now corrupt the state.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Confirm with the person or pipeline named in the lock that nothing is running.
examples/terraform/aws/backend.tf

use_lockfile makes Terraform create a lock object next to the state in the same bucket. Older configurations lock with a DynamoDB table instead; HashiCorp's documentation marks that as deprecated. Turn on bucket versioning so an earlier state can be restored.
Exercise
Cause drift three ways in the Terraform lab and decide what to do about each.

items: Apply the configuration so the state has eight resources
Press "Resize the instance to t3.large", then plan. Read the "changed outside of Terraform" note and the proposed action
Instead of applying, change instance_type to "t3.large" in terraform.tfvars and plan again. What does it say now?
Press "Open SSH (port 22) to the world", plan and apply. What happened to the rule?
Press "Terminate the instance" and plan. Why is the action a create and not a replace?
Tick "A colleague's apply is running" and try to plan. Read who holds the lock

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain what the state is for, what a refresh does, the two ways to resolve drift, and why the lock exists.
Troubleshooting

rows: Error acquiring the state lock
Another run holds the lock, or an earlier run crashed and left it behind.
Check who holds it from the lock info. Wait, or after confirming nothing is running, use force-unlock with the lock id.
Plan wants to create resources that already exist
Terraform is looking at an empty or different state: wrong backend key, wrong workspace or wrong directory.
Stop. Do not apply. Check the backend configuration and that init connected to the right state.
apply fails with "already exists"
The resource was created by hand or by another configuration, so it is not in this state.
Import it, or remove the duplicate definition.
The same change appears in every plan
Something else keeps changing the value: an autoscaler, another tool, or a default the API fills in.
Let one owner manage the field. Use lifecycle ignore_changes for fields that another system legitimately controls.
State file deleted or damaged
Local state lost with a laptop, or a bad manual edit.
Restore the previous version from the versioned bucket. Without a backup, every resource must be imported again.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Use a remote backend with locking from the first day, even when working alone.
Enable versioning and encryption on the state bucket.
One state per environment and per component, so a mistake has a small blast radius.
Never edit the state by hand. Use the state subcommands or moved, import and removed blocks.
Run a scheduled plan to detect drift before it surprises someone mid-change.
When a manual change was needed in an incident, write it into the configuration the same day.

blocks.text: Security

items: The state contains every attribute in plain text, including database passwords and private keys that resources generate. Treat the bucket like a secrets store.
Restrict the state bucket to the pipeline role and a few administrators; give most people read access to plans, not to state.
Block public access on the state bucket and require encryption in transit.
Marking a variable or output sensitive hides it from the screen, not from the state.
Write access to the state is effectively control of the infrastructure.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is Terraform state and why is it needed?
blocks.text: A record mapping each resource block to the real object it created, with that object's attributes. Terraform needs it to know what it owns, to find ids assigned by the cloud, to detect what was removed from the configuration, and to plan quickly.

blocks.title: How do teams share state safely?
blocks.text: A remote backend that stores one copy, encrypts it, keeps versions and locks during operations. With S3 that means a versioned, encrypted bucket with locking enabled, separate keys per environment, and tight access.

blocks.title: What is drift and how do you handle it?
blocks.text: A difference between real infrastructure and what Terraform last recorded, caused by a change made outside Terraform. Plan reports it. Either apply to revert it, or change the configuration to adopt it. Prevent it by removing console write access and detect it with scheduled plans.

blocks.title: How do you rename a resource without recreating it?
blocks.text: Add a moved block from the old address to the new one, or run terraform state mv. Without either, Terraform sees one resource removed and another added and plans a destroy and a create.

blocks.title: How do you bring an existing resource under Terraform?
blocks.text: Write the resource block, then import the real object into the state with an import block or the import command, and adjust the block until plan shows no changes.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Someone changes a managed resource in the console. The next terraform plan…
options: reports the change and proposes to revert it to the configuration
quiz.why: Terraform never edits your files. It makes reality match them.

quiz.q: Why is the state file sensitive?
options: It stores attributes, including secrets, in plain text
quiz.why: Sensitive values are hidden on screen but stored in full.

quiz.q: What is state locking for?
options: Stopping two runs writing the state at once
quiz.why: Concurrent writers would each overwrite the other's record of what exists.

lessons.title: Variables, outputs, modules and environments

blocks.text: Variables are the inputs of a configuration, outputs are its results, and a module is a folder of Terraform files used as one building block. Together they let you write the infrastructure once and create it several times with different values: staging and production, or one copy per service.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A function in code. Variables are the parameters, outputs are the return values, and the resources inside are the body. A module is that function put in a shared library. Staging and production are two calls with different arguments.
Why it matters

Copying a configuration for each environment means every fix must be made several times, and the copies slowly diverge until staging no longer predicts production. Parameters and modules keep one definition and make the differences explicit and small.
Where you meet it

Every real Terraform codebase. A common layout is a modules directory with reusable pieces (network, service, database) and an environments directory where each environment calls those modules with its own values and has its own state.
Scenario

checkout-api, the cart service and the catalogue service all need the same shape of infrastructure. One "service" module defines it. Each service calls the module with its name, size and scaling limits. Production passes three zones and larger instances; staging passes one zone and the smallest size.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TB subgraph REPO["infra repository"] subgraph MODS["modules/"] NET["network
VPC, subnets, routes"] SVC["service
instances, load balancer, firewall"] end subgraph ENVS["environments/"] STG["staging/main.tf
+ staging.tfvars"] PRD["production/main.tf
+ production.tfvars"] end end STG -->|"calls with small values"| NET STG --> SVC PRD -->|"calls with large values"| NET PRD --> SVC STG --> S1[("staging state")] PRD --> S2[("production state")] NET -. "outputs: vpc_id, subnet_ids" .-> SVC

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Plans with the values from one file. The usual way to choose an environment.
Overrides one variable for this run. Command-line values win over every file.
Supplies a variable through the environment, so a secret never sits in a file. The command in brackets stands for whatever your secret store provides.
Prints one output with no quotes, ready to use in a script.

rows: `-json`
all outputs as JSON for other tools

blocks.text: Re-resolves module and provider versions within the constraints you wrote and updates the lock file. Review the resulting plan carefully.
An interactive prompt for trying expressions and functions against the current configuration and state.
Lists workspaces: separate states for the same configuration and backend. Useful for short-lived copies; separate directories are clearer for long-lived environments.
examples/terraform/module-usage/main.tf

blocks.code:
# environments/production/main.tf
# The environment directory holds no resources of its own. It calls shared
# modules and passes the values that differ between environments.

module "network" {
  source = "../../modules/network"

  name     = "shop-production"
  vpc_cidr = "10.30.0.0/16"
  az_count = 3
}

module "checkout_api" {
  source = "../../modules/service"

  name          = "checkout-api"
  environment   = "production"
  instance_type = "t3.large"
  min_size      = 3
  max_size      = 12

  # Outputs of one module become inputs of another.
  vpc_id     = module.network.vpc_id
  subnet_ids = module.network.private_subnet_ids
}

# A module from the public registry, pinned to an exact version.
module "invoices_bucket" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/s3-bucket/aws"
  version = "5.2.0" # example pin: check the registry for the current release

  bucket = "shop-invoices-production"
}

output "checkout_api_url" {
  value = module.checkout_api.url
}

blocks.text: The environment file contains no resources. It reads as a description of production: which building blocks, with which values. The variables file of the simulator configuration (examples/terraform/aws/variables.tf) shows types, defaults and a validation rule.
Exercise
Use variables in the Terraform lab to change the configuration without touching main.tf.

items: Open variables.tf and list which variables have defaults and which must be given
In terraform.tfvars set environment = "dev" and plan. Which rule rejected it, and where is that rule written?
Set environment = "production" and plan from a fresh workspace. Find three places in the plan where the name changed
Delete the ami_id line from terraform.tfvars and plan. Read the error
Add a line colour = "blue" to terraform.tfvars and plan. Is it an error or a warning?
In main.tf replace var.instance_type with a conditional that gives t3.large in production and t3.micro otherwise, and plan for both environments

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state the order in which variable sources override each other, and explain how one configuration serves two environments.
Troubleshooting

rows: No value for required variable
The variable has no default and no source supplied a value.
Pass the right -var-file, or set it in terraform.tfvars. In CI, check the file path.
Production was planned with staging values
The wrong var file, or an auto-loaded terraform.tfvars overriding what you meant.
One directory and one state per environment, with that environment's values next to it, removes the choice.
Module not installed
A module block was added or its source changed since the last init.
Run terraform init.
Unsupported argument in a module block
The module has no variable of that name, often after a module upgrade renamed it.
Read the module's variables for the pinned version.
A module upgrade plans to destroy and recreate resources
Resource addresses inside the module changed.
Check the module's upgrade notes for moved blocks; do not apply a plan that destroys data stores without understanding it.
A value shows as (sensitive value) and you need to see it
The variable or output is marked sensitive.
terraform output -raw NAME prints it. Remember it is then in your terminal history and scrollback.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Give every variable a type and a description; add validation where a wrong value would be expensive.
Defaults for values that are safe everywhere; no default for what must be a deliberate choice, such as the environment.
Pin module versions exactly and upgrade them deliberately.
Keep modules small and single-purpose; pass ids between them through outputs.
One directory and one state per environment.
Write a module after the second or third copy, not before the first.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never commit real secrets in .tfvars. Read them from a secret store at run time.
Mark secret variables and outputs sensitive so they are not printed in plans and logs.
Sensitive values are still stored in the state.
Pin registry modules to an exact version and review what they create.
Give staging and production different credentials so a staging run cannot touch production.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you manage several environments with Terraform?
blocks.text: Shared modules hold the definitions. Each environment has its own directory that calls them with its own values, its own state and its own credentials. Promotion is applying the same module version to the next environment. Workspaces are an alternative for short-lived copies.

blocks.title: What is a module?
blocks.text: A directory of Terraform files used as a unit, with input variables and outputs. The directory you run Terraform in is the root module; it can call child modules from local paths, Git or a registry.

blocks.title: What is the order of precedence for variable values?
blocks.text: From lowest to highest: the default, environment variables named TF_VAR_name, terraform.tfvars, *.auto.tfvars files, then -var and -var-file options in the order given.

blocks.title: Variables, locals and outputs: what is the difference?
blocks.text: Variables are inputs set from outside. Locals are named expressions computed inside the module to avoid repetition. Outputs are values the module exposes to its caller or to people.

blocks.title: When would you not write a module?
blocks.text: When there is only one use and no clear boundary. A premature module adds parameters for cases that never arrive and makes simple changes harder to follow.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A variable is set in terraform.tfvars and also with -var on the command line. Which wins?
quiz.why: Command-line values have the highest precedence.

quiz.q: Marking an output sensitive…
options: hides it from plan and apply output
quiz.why: It controls display only. The state still holds the value.

quiz.q: The clearest way to keep staging and production apart is…
quiz.why: Separation that does not depend on remembering a flag.

lessons.title: Reading a plan, replacement, and Terraform in CI

blocks.text: A plan is a list of what Terraform will do to each resource: create it, change it where it stands, destroy it, or destroy it and create a new one. Reviewing infrastructure changes means reading that list, and above all finding the destroys. In a team the plan is produced by a pipeline on every pull request and applied only after someone has read it.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A removals quote. "Move the sofa to the other wall" and "throw the sofa away and buy a new one" may come from the same sentence in your email. The quote shows which one the company understood. You sign the quote, not your email.
Why it matters

Some settings can be changed on a live resource and others can only be set at creation. A one-line edit can therefore mean a brief restart or the deletion of a database. Only the plan tells you which, and the one summary line is not enough to tell.
Where you meet it

Every infrastructure pull request. Mature teams never run apply from a laptop against production: a pipeline plans on the pull request, attaches the plan for review, and applies exactly that plan after merge and approval.
Scenario

A developer wants checkout-api on a newer machine image and edits one line. The plan says the instance "must be replaced": destroyed, then created, with a new address and a gap in service. Changing the instance size instead is an in-place update with a short stop. Changing the VPC address range replaces the network and everything in it. Three one-line edits, three very different days.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR PR["Pull request
changes infra/*.tf"] --> PLAN["CI job: fmt, validate, plan
read-only role"] PLAN --> ART["Saved plan file
+ plan text on the pull request"] ART --> REV["Reviewer reads the plan,
looks for destroys"] REV -->|"approve and merge"| GATE["Environment approval"] GATE --> APPLY["CI job: apply the saved plan
write role"] APPLY --> CLOUD["AWS"] APPLY --> STATE[("Remote state + lock")] POL["Policy checks
no public buckets,
required tags"] --> PLAN

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Saves the plan to a file. Applying that file performs exactly what was reviewed, even if the code or the infrastructure changed afterwards (in which case Terraform refuses a stale plan).
Prints a saved plan in readable form.

rows: `-json`
machine-readable, for policy checks and summaries

blocks.text: Applies the saved plan without asking again. The approval happened in review.
Forces one resource to be destroyed and recreated although nothing in its configuration changed. For a machine that is misbehaving.
Plans for one resource and what it depends on. For getting out of a broken situation, not for routine work: it leaves the rest unchecked.
Shows what destroy would remove, without removing it.
Runs the module's test files. Depending on how they are written, tests check plans only or create real, billed resources and remove them afterwards.
examples/github-actions/terraform.yml

blocks.code:
# Plan on every pull request, apply only after merge to main.
# The plan is the review artifact: nobody approves infrastructure they have not read.
name: terraform

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["infra/**"]
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["infra/**"]

permissions:
  id-token: write # lets the job get short-lived AWS credentials through OIDC
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

concurrency:
  group: terraform-staging # one run at a time against this state
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra/environments/staging
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/terraform-plan
          aws-region: ap-south-1

      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3

      - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: infra/environments/staging/tfplan

  apply:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    needs: plan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging # add required reviewers here for production
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra/environments/staging
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/terraform-apply
          aws-region: ap-south-1

      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - run: terraform init -input=false

      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: infra/environments/staging

      # Applies exactly the plan that was produced above, nothing newer.
      - run: terraform apply -input=false tfplan

blocks.text: Two roles: the plan job can only read, the apply job can write and runs behind an environment approval. The apply job uses the plan file built on the same commit, and the concurrency group keeps runs against one state in a queue.
Exercise
Produce each kind of plan in the Terraform lab and say what would happen to checkout-api.

items: Apply the starting configuration
Change instance_type to "t3.small" and plan. Which symbol, and does the instance id change?
Change the last characters of ami_id and plan. Find the line marked "forces replacement". What happens to the public address?
Add vpc_cidr = "10.30.0.0/16" to terraform.tfvars and plan. Count the replacements, and find the one resource that is only updated
Run plan -destroy. Which resource stops it, and which line in main.tf is responsible?
In main.tf rename the bucket and plan. Explain why prevent_destroy also blocks this

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: For any plan you can list what is created, changed in place, replaced and destroyed, and name the argument behind each replacement.
Troubleshooting

rows: A small edit plans to replace a database
The argument you changed can only be set at creation.
Do not apply. Look for a way to make the change in place (many databases support modifying the setting through a different argument or a snapshot-and-restore migration).
Renaming a block plans a destroy and a create
To Terraform the address is the identity.
Add a moved block from the old address to the new one.
Instance cannot be destroyed
lifecycle prevent_destroy is set and the plan includes destroying that resource, possibly as part of a replacement.
This is the guard working. Change the plan so the resource survives, or remove the guard in a separate, reviewed change.
Saved plan is stale
The state changed after the plan was made: another apply ran in between.
Plan again and have the new plan reviewed.
apply in CI fails with AccessDenied
The pipeline role lacks a permission the change needs.
Add the specific permission to the apply role through its own reviewed change. Do not widen it to administrator access.
The plan in the pull request differs from what was applied
The apply job planned again instead of using the saved plan, and something changed in between.
Apply the saved plan file from the reviewed commit.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Search every plan for "must be replaced" and "will be destroyed" before anything else.
Put prevent_destroy on resources that hold data: databases, buckets, encryption keys.
Use create_before_destroy for resources that can exist twice during a swap.
Plan in CI on every pull request and apply only the reviewed plan.
Separate read-only and write credentials for plan and apply.
Add automated checks: tflint for mistakes, a scanner such as Trivy or Checkov for insecure settings, and policy rules for what your organisation forbids.
Make changes small. A plan of five resources gets read; a plan of five hundred gets approved unread.

blocks.text: Security

items: The apply role is among the most powerful identities in the company. Use short-lived credentials through OIDC, never stored access keys.
Require approval before apply in production, by someone other than the author.
Plans can contain secrets. Limit who can read pipeline logs and plan artifacts.
A pull request from a fork must not run plan with real credentials: a plan executes provider and module code.
Policy checks should block public buckets, open security groups and unencrypted storage before a person even reviews.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What does -/+ mean in a plan and why does it happen?
blocks.text: The resource will be destroyed and a new one created, because an argument that cannot be changed on an existing resource was modified. The plan marks that argument with "forces replacement". The new resource has a new id and usually new addresses.

blocks.title: How do you avoid downtime when a resource must be replaced?
blocks.text: create_before_destroy so the new one exists before the old one goes, when two can coexist. Otherwise put the resource behind a load balancer or DNS name and replace one of several at a time, or do a blue-green switch.

blocks.title: How would you run Terraform in CI/CD?
blocks.text: On pull requests: fmt check, validate, linting, security scan, then plan with a read-only role and publish the plan. After merge: an approval gate, then apply the saved plan with a write role, with a concurrency limit per state. Remote state with locking, short-lived credentials, and no applies from laptops.

blocks.title: What do prevent_destroy and ignore_changes do?
blocks.text: prevent_destroy makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail. ignore_changes tells Terraform not to act on differences in named arguments, for fields another system manages, such as a replica count set by an autoscaler.

blocks.title: A colleague removed a resource block and the plan shows a destroy of a production bucket. What do you check?
blocks.text: Whether removal was intended, whether the block was renamed or moved into a module (needs a moved block), and whether the right state is in use. If Terraform should stop managing it without deleting it, use a removed block or state rm.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A plan line ends with "# forces replacement". That resource will be…
quiz.why: The changed argument cannot be modified on an existing resource.

quiz.q: Why apply a saved plan file in CI rather than planning again?
options: So what runs is exactly what was reviewed
quiz.why: A fresh plan at apply time could contain changes nobody saw.

quiz.q: You rename a resource block. Without a moved block, Terraform plans to…
options: destroy the old and create a new one
quiz.why: The address is the identity; a new address is a new resource.

modules.title: AWS Cloud
modules.summary: IAM, VPC networking, EC2 with Auto Scaling and load balancers, S3, CloudFront, RDS, ElastiCache and EKS, plus Lambda, ECS and Fargate, and DNS in depth with Route 53. Not yet covered: organisations and landing zones.

lessons.title: AWS accounts and IAM: who may do what

blocks.text: Every call to AWS is made by an identity and is checked against policies: lists of allowed and denied actions on named resources. Nothing is allowed until a policy allows it. People and programs should work through roles, which hand out credentials that expire after a short time.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A hotel. Your key card opens your room and the gym, nothing else, and stops working at checkout. A cleaner's card opens rooms on one floor during one shift. Nobody is given the master key, and the door lock, not the receptionist's memory, enforces all of it.
Why it matters

An AWS account can create and delete anything, and spend any amount. Most serious cloud breaches start with a credential that was too powerful or lived too long. IAM is how you make each person and each program able to do its job and nothing more.
Where you meet it

Everywhere in AWS: an engineer listing instances, a pipeline pushing an image, checkout-api reading a secret, a load balancer writing logs to a bucket. Each is an identity making a signed API call that IAM allows or denies.
Scenario

checkout-api stores invoices in S3, reads its database password from Secrets Manager and publishes order events to a queue. It runs with a role whose policy allows exactly those three things on exactly those resources. If the service is compromised, the attacker cannot read another team's secrets, delete invoices or start servers.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph WHO["Identities"] H["Engineer
(signs in through
IAM Identity Center)"] CI["CI pipeline
(OIDC token)"] APP["checkout-api pod
(service account)"] end STS["AWS STS
issues temporary credentials"] subgraph ROLES["Roles = a trust policy + permission policies"] R1["role: developer-readonly"] R2["role: terraform-apply"] R3["role: checkout-api"] end H -->|"assume"| STS CI -->|"assume"| STS APP -->|"assume"| STS STS --> R1 STS --> R2 STS --> R3 R3 -->|"s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject"| S3["S3: shop-invoices"] R3 -->|"GetSecretValue"| SM["Secrets Manager: checkout/*"] R3 -->|"sqs:SendMessage"| Q["SQS: order-events"]

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Shows which account and identity your terminal is using right now. Run it before anything that changes resources.
Signs you in through your company identity provider and stores short-lived credentials for that profile. No access keys on disk.
Lists the managed policies attached to a role.
Prints the trust policy: who is allowed to assume this role.
Asks IAM whether an identity would be allowed an action on a resource, without performing it.
Creates a long-lived access key for a user. Almost always the wrong answer: use a role with temporary credentials instead.
Deletes a role. Anything running with it loses access at once.
examples/aws/checkout-api-policy.json

Listing a bucket is an action on the bucket (no /*); reading an object is an action on objects (with /*). Mixing those up is the most common reason an S3 policy "does not work". The last statement denies deletes outright, so no other policy can grant them by accident.
Exercise
Predict IAM decisions in the policy lab, then change the policy and predict again.

items: For each row in the table, say Allow, explicit deny or implicit deny before reading the answer
Click "Read an invoice from the staging bucket" and read why it is denied although s3:GetObject is allowed
Attach the broad second policy. Which rows change? Which row cannot change, and why?
Remove the Deny statement while the broad policy is attached. What can checkout-api do now?
Restore, then change the object ARN in ReadWriteInvoices to the bucket ARN (delete the /*). Which actions break?
Write a statement that lets the role read only objects under the prefix 2026/

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state the evaluation order from memory and explain the difference between an implicit and an explicit deny.
Troubleshooting

rows: AccessDenied although the policy "allows it"
The resource ARN in the policy does not match the one in the request: a missing /*, another region or account, or a different name.
Read the error: it names the action and the resource. Compare them character by character with the policy.
AccessDenied "with an explicit deny"
A Deny statement matches, in an identity policy, a resource policy, a permissions boundary or an organisation policy.
Find the Deny. Adding more Allow statements never helps.
ExpiredToken
Temporary credentials reached the end of their lifetime.
Sign in again or let the SDK refresh them. Long-running jobs should use a credential source that renews itself.
Commands hit the wrong account
A different profile or old environment variables are active in the terminal.
aws sts get-caller-identity, then set AWS_PROFILE or unset stale AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID variables.
Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRole
Either the caller has no permission to assume the role, or the role's trust policy does not list the caller.
Both sides must agree. Check the trust policy first.
It works in one account and not the other
Access across accounts needs an allow on both sides: the caller's identity policy and the resource or role in the other account.
Add the missing half.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Roles and temporary credentials for everything; no long-lived access keys.
People sign in through the company identity provider with multi-factor authentication.
One policy per job, scoped to named resources. Avoid "*" in Resource for anything that writes or deletes.
Separate AWS accounts for production and non-production: the strongest boundary AWS offers.
Lock away the root user: strong MFA, no access keys, used only for the few tasks that need it.
Review unused permissions regularly; IAM Access Analyzer reports them.
Manage IAM with Terraform so every permission change is reviewed.

blocks.text: Security

items: A leaked access key is used by attackers within minutes. Never commit one, and scan repositories for them.
iam:PassRole and iam:* let an identity grant itself more power. Treat them as administrator access.
Explicit Deny guardrails at the organisation level protect against mistakes in individual accounts.
CloudTrail records every API call with the identity that made it. Keep it on, in every region, with logs in a separate account.
Wildcards in a trust policy principal let anyone assume the role. Always name the principal and add conditions.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between an IAM user and a role?
blocks.text: A user is a permanent identity with long-lived credentials. A role has no credentials of its own: a trusted identity assumes it and receives temporary credentials. Roles are preferred for people (through federation) and for workloads.

blocks.title: How does IAM decide whether a request is allowed?
blocks.text: It gathers every policy that applies. A matching explicit Deny ends it. Otherwise the request needs an Allow, and must also pass any organisation policy and permissions boundary. With no matching Allow the result is an implicit deny.

blocks.title: How should an application on AWS get credentials?
blocks.text: From a role attached to where it runs: an instance profile on EC2, a task role on ECS, Pod Identity or IRSA on EKS. The SDK fetches and renews temporary credentials automatically. No keys in code, images or environment files.

blocks.title: How does a CI pipeline deploy to AWS without stored keys?
blocks.text: OIDC federation. The CI provider issues a signed token for the job; an IAM role trusts that provider with conditions on repository and branch; the job exchanges the token for temporary credentials.

blocks.title: What is least privilege in practice?
blocks.text: Start from nothing, grant the specific actions on the specific resources the job needs, measure what is used, and remove the rest. Guard dangerous actions with explicit denies and separate accounts.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: One policy allows s3:* on everything; another denies s3:DeleteObject. A delete request is…
options: allowed if the Allow was attached first
quiz.why: An explicit Deny always wins.

quiz.q: A role has no policy mentioning ec2. ec2:TerminateInstances is…
quiz.why: Everything not explicitly allowed is denied.

quiz.q: The preferred way for checkout-api to authenticate to AWS is…
options: an access key in an environment variable
quiz.why: Temporary, automatically rotated, scoped to the workload.

lessons.title: VPC networking: subnets, routes, gateways and firewalls

blocks.text: A VPC is your own private network inside AWS. You split it into subnets, one per Availability Zone. Route tables decide where traffic from each subnet can go, and security groups decide which connections each resource accepts. A subnet is "public" only if its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: An office building. The VPC is the building. Subnets are floors. The internet gateway is the front door to the street, and only the lobby floor has a corridor leading to it. Back-office floors have no way to the street; staff there send post through the mail room (the NAT gateway), which can send out and receive replies but accepts no visitors. Each room has its own door lock (a security group).
Why it matters

Servers and databases should not be reachable from the internet unless they have to be. A network design that exposes only the load balancer means a mistake in one firewall rule does not put the database online. The same design also decides how the system survives the loss of a data centre.
Where you meet it

Under every workload on AWS: EC2 instances, load balancers, RDS databases and EKS nodes and pods all get addresses in VPC subnets. The lessons from the networking module (CIDR, routing, TCP) apply unchanged.
Scenario

A customer's request reaches the load balancer in a public subnet, which forwards it to checkout-api in a private subnet, which queries PostgreSQL in a private data subnet. To take a payment, checkout-api calls the payment provider on the internet: outbound, through a NAT gateway. Each arrow is a route plus a security group rule, and each can be the reason checkout is down.
Architecture
