flowchart TB NET["Internet"] --> IGW["Internet gateway"] subgraph VPC["VPC 10.20.0.0/16 (region ap-south-1)"] IGW subgraph AZA["Availability Zone a"] PUBA["Public subnet 10.20.1.0/24
load balancer node, NAT gateway"] APPA["Private app subnet 10.20.11.0/24
checkout-api"] DBA["Private data subnet 10.20.21.0/24
PostgreSQL primary"] end subgraph AZB["Availability Zone b"] PUBB["Public subnet 10.20.2.0/24
load balancer node, NAT gateway"] APPB["Private app subnet 10.20.12.0/24
checkout-api"] DBB["Private data subnet 10.20.22.0/24
PostgreSQL standby"] end end IGW --> PUBA IGW --> PUBB PUBA --> APPA PUBB --> APPB APPA --> DBA APPB --> DBA APPA -. "outbound via NAT" .-> PUBA DBA -. "replication" .-> DBB

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Lists the VPCs in the current region with their address ranges.
Subnets of one VPC with their zone, range and how many addresses are left.
The routes that apply to one subnet. A 0.0.0.0/0 route to igw- means public; to nat- means private with outbound access; none means isolated.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: An empty result means the subnet uses the VPC's main route table: query that instead.
The inbound rules of one security group: ports, and the address ranges or other security groups allowed.
NAT gateways and the subnet each one sits in. That subnet must be a public one.

blocks.code: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0123456789abcdef0 --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group sg-0fedcba9876543210
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Adds an inbound rule allowing PostgreSQL from members of another security group. Takes effect immediately. In a Terraform-managed account this is drift: change the configuration instead.
Deletes a NAT gateway. Every private subnet routing through it loses outbound internet access at once.
examples/terraform/aws/main.tf (network part)

This small example has one public subnet. Look at what makes it public: aws_route_table.public has a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway, and aws_route_table_association.public attaches that table to the subnet. The three-tier design in the diagram adds private subnets, NAT gateways and a second zone.
Exercise
Break the network in the VPC lab one setting at a time and predict the symptom before reading it.

items: Start from "Working design" and read the hops of all five paths
Press "Public route missing". Which two paths fail, and which keeps working?
Press "NAT in a private subnet". What do customers notice? What does the payment team notice?
Press "Private route to the internet gateway". Why does outbound traffic still fail?
Press "Stateless ACL on the data subnet" and explain why a security group would not have had this problem
Set the database security group to "5432 from 0.0.0.0/0". Checkout still works. Why is it still a finding?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: For any broken connection you can name the checks in order: route out, gateway, security group, network ACL, and the route back.
Troubleshooting

rows: Connection times out
A security group or network ACL is dropping packets, or there is no route. Firewalls in AWS drop silently.
Check the route table of the source subnet, then the target's security group, then the ACLs. VPC Reachability Analyzer performs the same walk for you.
Connection refused
The network path works and the host answered: nothing is listening on that port.
Not a VPC problem. Check the process and the port on the target.
Private instances cannot reach the internet
No 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT gateway, the NAT is in a private subnet, or it was deleted and the route is now a blackhole.
Inspect the private route table and the NAT gateway's subnet.
An instance in a "public" subnet is unreachable
It has no public IP, or the subnet's route table has no route to the internet gateway.
A public subnet needs the route; the instance needs a public address; the security group needs the rule.
Works from one zone and not the other
The subnets in the second zone use a different route table or are missing from a subnet group.
Compare the route table associations zone by zone.
Cannot create more pods or instances: no free addresses
The subnet range is too small. AWS also reserves five addresses in every subnet.
Plan address space generously at the start; add a secondary range to the VPC and new subnets.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Three tiers: public subnets for load balancers only, private for applications, private for data.
At least two Availability Zones for anything that matters.
Security group rules that refer to other security groups, not to address ranges.
One NAT gateway per zone in production, so one zone failing does not cut outbound traffic for the others.
Use VPC endpoints for S3 and other AWS services: traffic stays private and avoids NAT charges.
Choose VPC ranges that do not overlap with other VPCs or the office network; you will want to connect them later.
Turn on VPC flow logs so refused connections can be investigated afterwards.

blocks.text: Security

items: Nothing in a private subnet should have a public address.
Never allow SSH or database ports from 0.0.0.0/0. Use Session Manager for shell access and no inbound SSH at all.
Security groups are stateful allow-lists; keep them narrow. Use network ACLs sparingly, for explicit subnet-wide blocks.
Restrict outbound traffic for sensitive tiers: a database has no reason to call the internet.
NAT gateways and data transfer are billed by the hour and by the gigabyte. An unused NAT gateway still costs money.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What makes a subnet public or private?
blocks.text: Only its route table. A public subnet has a default route to an internet gateway. A private one does not: it has a default route to a NAT gateway for outbound access, or no default route at all.

blocks.title: Security group versus network ACL?
blocks.text: A security group is attached to a resource, is stateful (replies are allowed automatically) and has allow rules only. A network ACL is attached to a subnet, is stateless (each direction needs its own rule) and has numbered allow and deny rules.

blocks.title: How does an instance in a private subnet reach the internet?
blocks.text: Its subnet's default route points to a NAT gateway in a public subnet. The NAT replaces the private source address with its own public one and tracks the connection so replies return. Nothing outside can start a connection to the instance.

blocks.title: A service in a private subnet cannot reach its database. How do you debug?
blocks.text: Timeout or refused? Timeout: confirm both are in the VPC and the right subnets, check the database security group allows the port from the service's security group, then network ACLs both ways. Refused: the database is not listening on that address or port. Reachability Analyzer and flow logs confirm.

blocks.title: How do you design a VPC for high availability?
blocks.text: Subnets of each tier in at least two zones, a load balancer spanning them, instances spread by an Auto Scaling group, a database with a standby in another zone, and a NAT gateway per zone so zones do not depend on each other.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A subnet is public when…
options: its route table has a default route to an internet gateway
quiz.why: The route decides. Names and addresses alone do nothing.

quiz.q: Where must a NAT gateway be created?
quiz.why: It needs its own route to the internet gateway.

quiz.q: A security group allows inbound 443. The reply traffic…
quiz.why: Security groups are stateful.

lessons.title: EC2, Auto Scaling and load balancers

blocks.text: EC2 gives you virtual servers by the second. An Auto Scaling group keeps a set number of identical servers running, replaces any that fail, and adds or removes servers as load changes. A load balancer gives customers one address and spreads their requests over whichever servers are healthy.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A supermarket. Tills are instances. The floor manager (the Auto Scaling group) opens more tills when queues grow, closes them when it is quiet, and replaces a broken till at once. The person at the front directing customers to an open till is the load balancer, who stops sending people to a till that has stopped responding.
Why it matters

One server is a single point of failure and a fixed capacity. Traffic to a shopping app varies many times over between a weekday night and a sale. Identical, disposable servers behind a load balancer survive failures and follow demand without anyone logging in to fix anything.
Where you meet it

Directly, for services that run on virtual machines. Indirectly, almost everywhere: EKS worker nodes are EC2 instances in Auto Scaling groups, and an Ingress on EKS becomes an Application Load Balancer.
Scenario

checkout-api runs on three instances in three zones behind an Application Load Balancer. During a sale, average CPU passes the target and the group adds instances. One instance hangs: its health check fails, the load balancer stops sending it traffic, and the group terminates it and starts a replacement. Deploying a new version is an instance refresh: new instances in, old ones out, a few at a time.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TB C["Customers"] --> DNS["Route 53
api.shop.example"] DNS --> ALB["Application Load Balancer
listener :443, TLS certificate"] ALB --> TG["Target group
health check: GET /health"] subgraph ASG["Auto Scaling group: min 3, max 12"] I1["Instance, zone a"] I2["Instance, zone b"] I3["Instance, zone c"] end TG --> I1 TG --> I2 TG --> I3 LT["Launch template
image, size, role, user data"] -. "how to build one" .-> ASG CW["CloudWatch metric
average CPU"] -. "scale out and in" .-> ASG I1 --> DB[("Database")] I2 --> DB I3 --> DB

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Instance stops answering /health"] --> B["Load balancer health check fails
several times in a row"] B --> C["Target marked unhealthy:
no new requests sent to it"] C --> D{"Auto Scaling group uses
load balancer health checks?"} D -->|"no"| E["Instance stays, serving nothing.
Capacity is quietly reduced"] D -->|"yes"| F["Group terminates the instance"] F --> G["Group launches a replacement
from the launch template"] G --> H["Instance boots, application starts"] H --> I{"Passes health checks?"} I -->|"no"| J["Terminated and tried again.
A bad image loops here: check the launch template"] I -->|"yes"| K["Registered with the target group.
Receives traffic"]

blocks.text: Commands
Running instances for one service, with size, zone and private address.
The group's limits, how many instances it wants, and the health of each.
The last few things the group did and why: launched for a scaling policy, terminated for a failed health check, or failed to launch.
Each target's state as the load balancer sees it, with a reason when unhealthy. The first command to run when the load balancer returns 5xx errors.
Opens a shell on an instance through Systems Manager: no SSH port, no keys, and the session is logged.
Changes how many instances the group runs, within its minimum and maximum. Useful before a known peak.
Replaces the group's instances in batches with ones built from the current launch template. This is a rolling deployment.
Permanently deletes an instance and, by default, its root disk. In an Auto Scaling group a replacement is launched.
Auto Scaling group for checkout-api (Terraform, illustrative)
Shown for reading; the Terraform lab does not model these resource types. health_check_type = "ELB" is the line that makes the group replace instances the load balancer has given up on.
Exercise
Trace what happens to checkout-api when an instance fails and when traffic doubles, using the diagrams and the rollout simulator.

items: On the architecture diagram, follow one request from the customer to the database
An instance hangs. Using the flowchart, list every step until capacity is back, and say who does each
Remove the line health_check_type = "ELB" in your head. What changes?
Average CPU rises from 40 to 80 percent with the target at 50. Roughly how many instances will the group want if it had three?
In the deployment strategies simulator, run a rolling release with a bad version and relate it to an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage
List what must be true of checkout-api for an instance to be safely terminated at any moment

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain the roles of the launch template, the Auto Scaling group, the target group and the health check, and why instances must be disposable.
Troubleshooting

rows: Load balancer returns 503
The target group has no registered or no healthy targets.
describe-target-health. Then find out why targets are failing the check or never registered.
Load balancer returns 502
A target accepted the connection and then closed it or sent an invalid reply: the application crashed, or its keep-alive timeout is shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout.
Check application logs on the target. Set the application's keep-alive timeout longer than the load balancer's idle timeout.
Load balancer returns 504
The target did not answer in time: overloaded, slow dependency, or a security group blocking the load balancer.
Check target response time and the security group between load balancer and target.
Instances launch and are terminated in a loop
New instances never pass the health check: the application fails to start, or the grace period is shorter than the start-up time.
Read the scaling activities, then the instance's boot log. Lengthen the health check grace period if the application is simply slow to start.
Scaling is too slow for a sudden peak
An instance takes minutes to boot and warm up, and the metric reacts after the load arrives.
Bake dependencies into the image, scale on a leading signal such as requests per target, and raise the minimum before known events.
Requests fail during deployments
Instances are terminated while still serving requests.
Connection draining (deregistration delay) on the target group, and graceful shutdown in the application on SIGTERM.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Treat instances as disposable: no manual changes, no data on the local disk.
Build an image with everything installed, so boot is fast and identical.
Spread across at least two zones, preferably three.
Use load balancer health checks for the group, with a meaningful /health endpoint.
Scale on a target (CPU or requests per target), and set sensible minimum and maximum limits.
Use Session Manager instead of SSH, and require IMDSv2.
Right-size from measurements; commit to Savings Plans only for the steady baseline.

blocks.text: Security

items: Instances in private subnets; only the load balancer is public.
An instance profile with a narrow role, never access keys on the disk.
Require IMDSv2 so a server-side request forgery bug cannot steal the instance's credentials easily.
Patch by replacing instances with a new image, on a schedule.
Terminate TLS on the load balancer with a managed certificate, and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Encrypt EBS volumes by default.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What does an Auto Scaling group do?
blocks.text: It keeps a desired number of instances running from a launch template across the subnets you give it, replaces unhealthy ones, and changes the desired number between a minimum and maximum according to scaling policies or schedules.

blocks.title: Application Load Balancer versus Network Load Balancer?
blocks.text: An ALB works at the HTTP layer: it routes by host and path, terminates TLS and understands requests. An NLB works at the TCP and UDP layer: very high throughput, static addresses, and it passes connections through without reading them.

blocks.title: The load balancer returns 502, 503 or 504. What does each suggest?
blocks.text: 503: no healthy targets to send to. 502: a target returned a broken response or closed the connection. 504: a target did not respond before the timeout. Each points to a different place to look.

blocks.title: How do you deploy a new version to instances with no downtime?
blocks.text: Build a new image, update the launch template, and run a rolling instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage, relying on health checks and connection draining. Or create a second group and switch the load balancer: blue-green.

blocks.title: How would you reduce EC2 cost?
blocks.text: Right-size from utilisation data, scale in when idle, use Savings Plans for the baseline and Spot for interruptible work, move to newer or ARM instance families, and delete unattached volumes and idle load balancers.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: An instance fails load balancer health checks. The load balancer…
options: stops routing new requests to it
quiz.why: The load balancer only routes. Replacing the instance is the Auto Scaling group's job.

quiz.q: Which piece defines the image, size and role of new instances?
quiz.why: The group builds instances from the launch template.

quiz.q: A 503 from an Application Load Balancer usually means…
quiz.why: Nothing is available to receive the request.

lessons.title: S3, CloudFront, RDS and ElastiCache

blocks.text: S3 stores files (called objects) in buckets, in practically unlimited amounts. CloudFront is a content delivery network that serves them from locations close to users. RDS runs a relational database such as PostgreSQL for you, taking care of backups, patching and failover. ElastiCache does the same for Redis-compatible caches.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: S3 is a warehouse with endless shelves where every box has a label and you fetch by label. CloudFront is a chain of corner shops stocking copies of the popular boxes. RDS is hiring a bank to hold your ledger: you write the entries, they handle the vault, the copies and the night guard.
Why it matters

Storing data durably and running a database well are hard and unforgiving. Managed services turn most of that work into settings. The choices that remain, such as who can read a bucket, how long backups are kept and whether there is a standby, are exactly the ones that decide whether an incident is an inconvenience or a disaster.
Where you meet it

S3 holds user uploads, invoices, static websites, logs, backups and Terraform state. CloudFront sits in front of websites, images and downloads. RDS holds orders, users and payments. ElastiCache holds sessions, carts and cached query results.
Scenario

When an order is paid, checkout-api writes the order to PostgreSQL on RDS, saves the invoice PDF in S3, and caches the customer's cart in ElastiCache. Product images reach the mobile app through CloudFront, never straight from S3. One night the database's zone fails: RDS promotes the standby in another zone and checkout-api reconnects to the same endpoint name within a minute or two.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR APP["Mobile app"] -->|"images"| CF["CloudFront"] CF -->|"origin access control"| IMG["S3: product images
(private bucket)"] APP -->|"API calls"| ALB["Load balancer"] ALB --> API["checkout-api"] API -->|"orders"| PRI[("RDS PostgreSQL
primary, zone a")] PRI -. "synchronous copy" .-> SBY[("Standby, zone b")] PRI -. "asynchronous copy" .-> RR[("Read replica
for reports")] PRI -->|"daily snapshot + logs"| BK["Automated backups
point-in-time recovery"] API -->|"cart, sessions"| EC["ElastiCache"] API -->|"invoice PDFs"| INV["S3: invoices
versioned, encrypted"] API -->|"database password"| SM["Secrets Manager"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["The primary database's zone fails"] --> B{"Multi-AZ enabled?"} B -->|"no"| C["Database is down until the zone returns,
or you restore a backup elsewhere"] C --> C1["Restore to a new instance:
new endpoint, data up to the last backed-up log"] B -->|"yes"| D["RDS detects the failure"] D --> E["Standby in another zone is promoted"] E --> F["The endpoint DNS name
now points to the new primary"] F --> G{"Does the application reconnect
and retry?"} G -->|"no"| H["Stuck on dead connections
until restarted"] G -->|"yes"| I["Service resumes, typically
in a minute or two"] I --> J["RDS builds a new standby
in the background"]

blocks.text: Commands
Lists objects under a prefix with sizes.
Uploads a file. Overwrites an existing object with the same key; with versioning on, the previous version is kept.
Creates a link that lets anyone holding it download this one object for five minutes, using your permissions. How an app shares a private file with a customer.
Shows the four settings that stop a bucket from being made public. All four should be true.
Databases with their size, whether they have a standby, and how many days of backups are kept.
Takes a manual snapshot, kept until you delete it. Do this before a risky schema change.
Creates a new database as it was at a chosen moment. It does not change the original; you then move the application or copy data across.
Deletes every object in the bucket and then the bucket itself.
Deletes a database without a last snapshot, and its automated backups with it by default. Deletion protection exists to make this command fail.
Invoices bucket and orders database (Terraform, illustrative)
Shown for reading; the Terraform lab models only the bucket. Notice how many lines are about not losing data: versioning, prevent_destroy, multi_az, backup retention, deletion protection.
Exercise
Decide the data-protection settings for checkout-api and check its S3 permissions in the IAM lab.

items: In the IAM lab, confirm checkout-api can read and write invoices but cannot delete them
Why does listing need the bucket ARN while reading needs the object ARN?
An engineer overwrites an invoice with an empty file. Which S3 setting lets you recover it, and how?
Someone runs a bad migration at 09:00 that corrupts the orders table. Using the commands above, describe the recovery and what data is lost
On the failover flowchart, find the step that depends on the application and not on AWS
Reports are slowing down checkout. Which component in the architecture diagram should they use instead of the primary?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain the difference between Multi-AZ and a read replica, between a backup and a standby, and name three settings that protect a bucket.
Troubleshooting

rows: AccessDenied reading from S3
The role lacks permission on that exact ARN, the bucket policy denies it, or the object is encrypted with a KMS key the role cannot use.
Check the identity policy, then the bucket policy, then the key policy.
S3 returns 403 for an object that does not exist
Without permission to list the bucket, S3 does not reveal whether a key exists.
Check the key name and prefix; grant s3:ListBucket if the application needs a proper 404.
CloudFront keeps serving an old file
The object is cached at the edge until its lifetime ends.
Use versioned file names for assets. An invalidation works for the occasional exception.
"too many connections" on the database
More application instances or pods than the database's connection limit can serve, usually after scaling out.
Use a connection pooler such as RDS Proxy or PgBouncer, and size pools per instance.
The application errors for minutes after a failover
It cached the old address or holds dead connections.
Connect by the endpoint name, respect DNS lifetimes, set connection timeouts and retry.
Database storage is full
Growth, bloat, or logs retained by a stuck replication slot.
Enable storage autoscaling and alert on free space well before it runs out.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Block public access on every bucket; serve public content through CloudFront.
Versioning on buckets that hold anything you cannot recreate.
Lifecycle rules to move old objects to cheaper storage classes and to expire old versions.
Multi-AZ for production databases; read replicas for read scaling, not for availability.
Backups with a retention period that matches the business need, and restore tests on a schedule.
Deletion protection and prevent_destroy on databases.
Cache what is expensive and can be stale; never treat the cache as the only copy.

blocks.text: Security

items: Buckets and databases in private networks, reachable only by the roles and security groups that need them.
Encryption at rest everywhere, and TLS required in transit.
Database passwords in Secrets Manager with rotation, not in environment files.
A presigned URL is a bearer token: keep lifetimes short.
Snapshots can be shared across accounts. Audit who can share or copy them.
Send S3 and database audit logs to an account the application team cannot modify.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Multi-AZ versus read replica in RDS?
blocks.text: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another zone for automatic failover; it is for availability and you do not read from it in the classic setup. A read replica is an asynchronous copy you can query; it is for scaling reads and may lag. Many production databases use both.

blocks.title: How do you recover from accidental data deletion in a database?
blocks.text: Point-in-time recovery: restore to a new instance at a moment just before the mistake, then either switch the application to it or copy the affected rows back. This works only within the backup retention period.

blocks.title: How do you serve private files from S3 to users?
blocks.text: Keep the bucket private. For shared content, CloudFront with origin access control so only the distribution can read the bucket. For per-user files, short-lived presigned URLs generated by the backend after it checks the user.

blocks.title: Is a standby a backup?
blocks.text: No. A standby copies every change, including a mistaken delete or corruption, within milliseconds. Backups let you go back in time. You need both.

blocks.title: How do you choose an S3 storage class?
blocks.text: By how often and how fast the data is read. Standard for frequent access, infrequent-access classes for data read rarely, Glacier classes for archives. Intelligent-Tiering when the pattern is unknown. Lifecycle rules move objects automatically.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A bad deploy deletes rows from the orders table. Which feature gets them back?
quiz.why: A standby replicates the delete. Backups let you go back to before it.

quiz.q: The safest way to make product images public is…
options: CloudFront in front of a private bucket
quiz.why: The bucket stays private; only the distribution may read it.

quiz.q: A read replica is mainly for…
quiz.why: It is an asynchronous copy you can query.

lessons.title: EKS: running checkout-api on Kubernetes in AWS

blocks.text: EKS is Kubernetes with AWS running the control plane for you. You bring worker nodes (or let AWS manage those too) and deploy with the same kubectl, Helm and Argo CD as on any cluster. What is specific to AWS is the wiring: pods get addresses from your VPC, an Ingress becomes an AWS load balancer, images come from ECR, and pods get AWS permissions through IAM roles.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Leasing a serviced factory instead of building one. The landlord runs the building's power, structure and security office (the control plane). You bring machines (nodes) and run your production line exactly as you would in your own factory, but the loading dock, mains water and keys are the landlord's systems and you must connect to them their way.
Why it matters

Running the Kubernetes control plane yourself means operating etcd, upgrades and certificates, with the whole platform at stake. A managed service removes that work. What remains is yours and is where the incidents happen: networking, permissions, node capacity and upgrades.
Where you meet it

This is the production destination for everything since the Docker module. The image from the pipeline, the Helm chart, the Argo CD application: on AWS they all land on EKS. AKS and GKE fill the same role in the other clouds.
Scenario

The pipeline builds checkout-api, pushes the image to ECR and commits the new tag to the deployment repository. Argo CD in the cluster syncs it. Pods start on nodes in private subnets, each with a VPC address. An Ingress makes the AWS Load Balancer Controller create an Application Load Balancer. The pods read invoices from S3 using the checkout-api role from the IAM lesson, given to them by EKS Pod Identity with no keys anywhere.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TB U["Customers"] --> ALB["Application Load Balancer
(created from the Ingress)"] subgraph AWSM["Managed by AWS"] CP["EKS control plane
API server, etcd, scheduler"] end subgraph VPC["Your VPC, private subnets in three zones"] subgraph N1["Node (EC2)"] P1["checkout-api pod
VPC address"] AG["Pod Identity agent"] end subgraph N2["Node (EC2)"] P2["checkout-api pod
VPC address"] ARGO["Argo CD"] end end ALB --> P1 ALB --> P2 CP <--> N1 CP <--> N2 CI["CI pipeline"] -->|"push image"| ECR["ECR registry"] CI -->|"commit new tag"| GIT["Deployment repository"] ARGO -->|"pull"| GIT N1 -->|"pull image"| ECR P1 -->|"temporary credentials
for role checkout-api"| S3["S3, Secrets Manager, SQS"] DEV["Engineer: kubectl"] -->|"IAM identity -> access entry"| CP

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Pod starts with
serviceAccountName: checkout-api"] --> B{"Is there a Pod Identity association for
this namespace and service account?"} B -->|"no"| C["No credentials injected.
The SDK falls back to the node's role
or finds none: AccessDenied"] B -->|"yes"| D["EKS adds credential settings
to the pod's environment"] D --> E["The AWS SDK in the app asks the
Pod Identity agent on its node"] E --> F{"Does the role's trust policy allow
pods.eks.amazonaws.com?"} F -->|"no"| G["Cannot assume the role: AccessDenied"] F -->|"yes"| H["Temporary credentials for the role,
renewed automatically"] H --> I["Pod calls S3"] I --> J{"Does the role's permission policy
allow this action on this resource?"} J -->|"no"| K["AccessDenied from S3"] J -->|"yes"| L["Success"]

blocks.text: Commands
Adds the cluster to your kubeconfig. kubectl will then get a token from your current AWS identity for each call.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: kubectl config current-context, then kubectl get nodes.
The cluster's Kubernetes version, status and API endpoint.
Nodes with their versions, addresses and zones.

blocks.code: aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 111122223333.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
blocks.caption: Changes the local environment

blocks.text: Logs Docker in to your ECR registry with a token valid for a few hours. Nodes do not need this: their role lets them pull.
Which service accounts in a namespace are linked to which IAM roles.

blocks.code: aws eks create-pod-identity-association --cluster-name shop-production --namespace production --service-account checkout-api --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/checkout-api
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Gives pods using that service account the permissions of the role. Pods already running must be restarted to pick it up.

blocks.code: kubectl exec deploy/checkout-api -n production -- env | grep AWS_CONTAINER
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Shows whether Pod Identity injected its settings into the pod. No output means no association matched when the pod started.
Upgrades the control plane by one minor version. It cannot be undone. Nodes and add-ons are upgraded separately afterwards. The version here is an example: check which versions EKS currently offers.
Deletes the cluster's control plane. Load balancers and volumes created by workloads can be left behind and keep costing money if the workloads were not removed first.
examples/aws/pod-identity-trust.json

The trust policy of the checkout-api role. It lets the EKS Pod Identity service assume the role on behalf of pods. Which pods is decided by the association (cluster, namespace, service account), not here, so the same role works unchanged in several clusters. AWS documents that Pod Identity is not available for pods on Fargate or Windows nodes; those use IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) instead.
Exercise
Follow checkout-api from a Git commit to a call to S3 on EKS, and find where each kind of failure would show.

items: On the architecture diagram, mark which parts AWS operates and which your team operates
List the four places an IAM identity is involved: the engineer, the pipeline, the node and the pod
A new pod logs AccessDenied calling S3. Use the flowchart to list the three different causes and the command that checks each
In the IAM lab, confirm what the checkout-api role may do once the pod has it
Pods are stuck Pending with "no free IP addresses". Which lesson explains this, and what is the fix?
Order these for an upgrade and say why: nodes, control plane, add-ons, checking for removed APIs

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can describe what EKS manages, how a pod gets AWS permissions without keys, and how traffic reaches a pod from the internet.
Troubleshooting

rows: kubectl: "You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)"
Your AWS identity is valid but has no access entry in the cluster, or you are using a different identity from the one you think.
aws sts get-caller-identity, then check the cluster's access entries.
Pod gets AccessDenied from an AWS service
No Pod Identity association, wrong service account name, a trust policy that does not allow the service, or a permission policy that does not allow the action.
Check in that order. Restart the pod after creating an association.
ImagePullBackOff from ECR
Wrong repository, tag or region; the node role lacks ECR read permission; or private nodes have no route to ECR.
kubectl describe pod for the exact message. Private subnets need a NAT gateway or ECR and S3 VPC endpoints.
Pods Pending: no free addresses
With the VPC CNI every pod takes an address from the subnet, and the subnets are full.
Larger subnets or a secondary range for pods; enable prefix delegation.
Ingress has no address
The AWS Load Balancer Controller is missing, lacks permissions, or cannot find subnets tagged for load balancers.
Read the controller's logs and the events on the Ingress.
Nodes NotReady after an upgrade
Version skew between control plane, kubelet and add-ons such as the CNI.
Upgrade add-ons to versions that match the cluster, then replace nodes.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Create the cluster, node groups and add-ons with Terraform; deploy workloads with GitOps.
Nodes in private subnets across three zones.
One IAM role per workload through Pod Identity; keep the node role minimal.
Plan pod address space before the first deployment.
Upgrade regularly, one minor version at a time: control plane, then add-ons, then nodes, after testing in staging.
Use a node autoscaler such as Karpenter with PodDisruptionBudgets on important workloads.
Separate clusters, and ideally accounts, for production and non-production.

blocks.text: Security

items: Restrict or make private the cluster API endpoint.
Map IAM identities to Kubernetes permissions with access entries and least privilege RBAC; avoid cluster-admin for people.
Block pods from the node's instance metadata, so they cannot borrow the node role.
Turn on control plane audit logs.
Scan images in ECR and admit only images from your own registry.
Encrypt Kubernetes Secrets with a KMS key, or keep secrets in Secrets Manager and sync them in.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What does EKS manage and what do you manage?
blocks.text: AWS runs the control plane: API server, etcd, scheduler, their availability and patching. You own nodes (unless using managed options), add-ons, networking, IAM integration, workloads, and deciding when to upgrade.

blocks.title: How do pods on EKS get AWS permissions?
blocks.text: A Kubernetes service account is linked to an IAM role. With EKS Pod Identity, an association maps cluster, namespace and service account to a role, and an agent on each node hands the pod temporary credentials. IRSA does the same through an OIDC provider and a web identity token. Neither uses stored keys.

blocks.title: How does traffic from the internet reach a pod on EKS?
blocks.text: DNS to an Application Load Balancer created by the AWS Load Balancer Controller from an Ingress. In IP mode the load balancer sends directly to pod addresses, which are real VPC addresses thanks to the VPC CNI; in instance mode it goes through a node port.

blocks.title: How do you upgrade an EKS cluster safely?
blocks.text: Read the release notes for removed APIs, upgrade staging first, then the control plane one minor version, then add-ons, then nodes by rolling replacement with PodDisruptionBudgets protecting capacity. Control plane upgrades cannot be rolled back.

blocks.title: What is specific about networking on EKS?
blocks.text: The VPC CNI gives each pod an address from the VPC subnets, so pods are directly routable and security groups and flow logs apply, but address space can run out. Subnet sizing matters more than on overlay networks.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: With EKS, AWS operates…
quiz.why: The API server and etcd are managed; workloads and their configuration are yours.

quiz.q: A pod should call S3. The right way to give it permission is…
options: an access key in a Secret
the node's role with broad access
an IAM role linked to its service account
quiz.why: Per-workload roles with temporary credentials, through Pod Identity or IRSA.

quiz.q: With the VPC CNI, each pod…
options: gets an address from the VPC subnet
quiz.why: Which is why subnets can run out of addresses.

lessons.title: Running code without servers: Lambda, ECS and Fargate

blocks.text: AWS offers several ways to run your code, and they differ in how much you manage. Lambda runs a function when an event arrives and bills per request; you manage no servers at all. ECS runs containers for you as long-lived services; with Fargate, AWS also supplies the machines. EKS is managed Kubernetes. Choosing between them is mostly a question of traffic shape and how much control you need.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Getting around a city. Lambda is a taxi: you pay per ride, there is nothing to park, but a taxi may take a moment to arrive and will not wait all day. ECS on Fargate is a leased car with a driver: always there, you say where to go, someone else maintains it. EKS is owning a fleet with your own garage: the most freedom, and the most upkeep.
Why it matters

Using Kubernetes for a small job that runs twice a day wastes money and attention. Using Lambda for a steady, high-traffic API can cost more and adds cold starts and connection problems. Knowing the options lets you pick the cheapest one that meets the need, and explain why.
Where you meet it

Lambda: event handlers, scheduled jobs, glue between services, spiky or low-volume APIs. ECS on Fargate: containerised services in teams that do not want to run Kubernetes. EKS: organisations that have standardised on Kubernetes or need its ecosystem.
Scenario

The shop keeps checkout-api on EKS, where the rest of the platform lives. A new job resizes product images when they are uploaded: it is short, bursty and triggered by S3, so it becomes a Lambda function. An internal reporting service owned by a small team, with steady light traffic, goes on ECS with Fargate behind the existing load balancer, so that team never has to learn Kubernetes.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph EV["Event driven"] S3["S3 upload"] --> L["Lambda: resize-image"] SQS["SQS queue"] --> L2["Lambda: send-receipt"] L2 -. "after repeated failures" .-> DLQ["Dead-letter queue"] end subgraph SVC["Long running"] ALB["Application Load Balancer"] --> TG["Target group (IP targets)"] TG --> T1["Fargate task"] TG --> T2["Fargate task"] ECSS["ECS service
desired count 2"] -. "keeps running, replaces failed" .-> T1 ECSS -.-> T2 end TD["Task definition
(image, CPU, memory, roles)"] --> ECSS ECR["ECR image"] --> T1 ER["Execution role:
pull image, write logs, read secrets"] -.-> T1 TR["Task role:
what the app itself may call"] -.-> T1 L --> CW["CloudWatch Logs"] T1 --> CW

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Lists functions with their runtime, memory and timeout.

blocks.code: aws lambda invoke --function-name resize-image --payload file://event.json --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out out.json
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Runs the function once with a test event. The function does whatever its code does, against real resources.
Streams the function's recent logs. The REPORT line of each invocation shows duration, memory used and whether it was a cold start (Init Duration).
Deploys a new version of the function. It takes effect for new invocations within seconds.
The services running in an ECS cluster.
Desired and running task counts and the latest events. The events explain a deployment that is stuck.
Starts a rolling replacement of every task, for example to pick up a new image behind the same tag.
Stops every task of the service. The service is down until the count is raised again.
An ECS task definition for Fargate (illustrative)

Not registered against a real account. The account number, role names and secret ARN are placeholders. Two roles do different jobs: the execution role is used by ECS to start the task, and the task role is used by your code.
Exercise
Decide where four workloads should run and justify each, on paper. No cloud account is needed.

items: Workload 1: a nightly job that exports yesterday's orders, runs about 4 minutes. Choose a compute option.
Workload 2: a public API with steady traffic of 800 requests per second, in a company with no Kubernetes.
Workload 3: a webhook receiver that gets a few hundred calls a day in bursts.
Workload 4: a machine-learning service that needs a GPU.
For each, write one sentence on why, and one on what would make you change your mind.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: A reasonable answer: 1 Lambda on a schedule, 2 ECS on Fargate (or EC2 for cost), 3 Lambda, 4 ECS on EC2 or EKS with GPU nodes. The lesson's decision flowchart should agree with you.
Troubleshooting

rows: A Lambda function is slow on the first request after a quiet period.
A cold start: AWS has to create an execution environment, load the code and run initialisation. Large packages and heavy start-up code make it worse.
Trim the package, move expensive set-up out of the import path, give it more memory (which also gives more CPU), or pay for provisioned concurrency on latency-sensitive paths.
Lambda invocations end with "Task timed out".
The function hit its configured timeout, often while waiting on a network call from inside a VPC with no route out.
Check that the subnet has a NAT gateway or the needed VPC endpoints, set timeouts on outbound calls, then raise the function timeout if the work is truly longer.
A database runs out of connections when traffic spikes.
Each concurrent Lambda execution opens its own connection, and concurrency can jump to hundreds.
Put RDS Proxy in front of the database, cap the function's reserved concurrency, and create the connection outside the handler so that it is reused.
An ECS task stops straight after starting with "CannotPullContainerError" or a secrets error.
The execution role cannot pull from ECR or read the secret, or the task has no network path to those services.
Read the stopped reason on the task, grant the execution role the missing permission, and check for a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints.
An ECS deployment never finishes; tasks start and are replaced in a loop.
New tasks fail the load balancer health check, so ECS keeps replacing them.
Compare the health check path and port with the container, lengthen the health check grace period for slow starters, and read the service events.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Give each function and each task its own narrow role. Do not share one role across workloads.
Make every event handler safe to run twice. Lambda and queues deliver at least once.
Configure a dead-letter queue or failure destination for asynchronous Lambda invocations, and alarm on it.
Set memory from measurement. More memory often finishes faster and can cost the same.
Enable the ECS deployment circuit breaker so that a failing release rolls back by itself.
Keep images in ECR with scanning on, and deploy by immutable tag or digest.

blocks.text: Security

items: Pass secrets through Secrets Manager or Parameter Store references, not as plain environment variables in the task definition or function configuration.
A Lambda function URL or API with no authoriser is public. Decide on purpose who may call it.
The task role is what an attacker gains if the container is compromised. Keep it to the exact resources the app needs.
Put Fargate tasks in private subnets with a security group that only admits the load balancer.
Resource policies decide who may invoke a function. A principal of "*" without a condition lets any account call it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is a Lambda cold start and how do you reduce it?
blocks.text: When no warm execution environment is free, AWS creates one: it sets up a small sandbox, loads the code and runs the initialisation outside the handler. That adds from tens of milliseconds to seconds to that request. To reduce it, keep the deployment package small, avoid heavy work at import time, choose a faster-starting runtime, raise memory, and for paths that must always be fast use provisioned concurrency, which keeps environments initialised.

blocks.title: What is the difference between the ECS task role and the task execution role?
blocks.text: The execution role is used by the ECS agent to get the task running: pulling the image from ECR, sending logs to CloudWatch and fetching secrets referenced in the task definition. The task role is assumed by the application inside the container when it calls AWS, for example to read an S3 bucket. Mixing them up gives either a task that cannot start or an application with far more access than it needs.

blocks.title: When would you choose ECS on Fargate over EKS?
blocks.text: When the team wants to run containers without operating Kubernetes. ECS has fewer concepts, no control plane to upgrade and tight integration with IAM and load balancers; Fargate also removes node management. EKS is the better choice when the organisation already has Kubernetes skills and tooling, needs the ecosystem of operators and controllers, or wants portability across clouds.

blocks.title: A Lambda function reads from an SQS queue and one message keeps failing. What happens and how do you handle it?
blocks.text: The message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and is retried, potentially blocking progress and wasting invocations. Configure a redrive policy on the queue so that after a set number of receives the message moves to a dead-letter queue, report partial batch failures so that good messages in the batch are not retried, alarm on the dead-letter queue depth, and make the handler idempotent.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: The maximum run time of one Lambda invocation is…
quiz.why: Longer work belongs in a container or a workflow service.

quiz.q: Which role lets ECS pull the image from ECR?
quiz.why: The execution role is used to start the task.

quiz.q: Fargate removes the need to manage…
options: the EC2 instances that run the containers
quiz.why: AWS supplies and patches the underlying machines.

quiz.q: Best fit for a steady 800 requests per second API in a company without Kubernetes?
quiz.why: Steady high traffic favours always-on containers.

lessons.title: DNS in depth with Route 53

blocks.text: Route 53 is the AWS service that answers DNS questions for your domain. Beyond plain name-to-address records, it can choose a different answer depending on health, weight, latency or the caller's location. That makes it the outermost traffic switch you have: it decides which region or which stack a user reaches before any load balancer is involved.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A receptionist with a directory. Ask for "the support desk" and they give you a room number. A good receptionist also knows which desks are staffed today (health checks), sends one visitor in ten to the new office to try it out (weighted), and directs you to the branch nearest your home (latency or geolocation). But visitors remember the room number for a while (the TTL), so a change is not instant.
Why it matters

DNS mistakes take the whole product offline while every server stays healthy, and they are slow to undo because answers are cached around the world. DNS is also how you fail over between regions and move traffic during migrations, so you need to understand caching, alias records and routing policies before you rely on them.
Where you meet it
Every public-facing system on AWS, plus private hosted zones for internal names inside VPCs. The same ideas apply to Cloud DNS, Azure DNS and Cloudflare.
Scenario

api.shop.example is an alias record pointing at the load balancer in Mumbai. For disaster recovery the team adds a second stack in Hyderabad and a failover pair: Route 53 health-checks the Mumbai origin and, after three failed checks, starts answering with Hyderabad. During a planned migration they use weighted records to send 5% of users to the new stack first.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD U["User's device"] --> RES["Recursive resolver
(ISP or public DNS, caches answers for the TTL)"] RES -->|"1. where is .example?"| ROOT["Root and TLD servers"] ROOT -->|"2. ask these name servers"| RES RES -->|"3. api.shop.example?"| R53["Route 53 public hosted zone
shop.example"] HC["Health checkers in several regions"] -. "probe /health" .-> ALB1 HC -. "status" .-> R53 R53 -->|"4. answer chosen by routing policy"| RES RES --> U U -->|"5. connect"| ALB1["Load balancer, Mumbai (primary)"] U -. "when primary is unhealthy" .-> ALB2["Load balancer, Hyderabad (secondary)"] subgraph VPC["Inside the VPC"] APP["App"] --> VR["VPC resolver"] VR --> PHZ["Private hosted zone
db.internal.shop.example"] end

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
The answer your resolver gives right now. An alias record shows as plain A records.
Follows delegation from the root down to the authoritative servers. Shows where a broken chain stops.
Asks one of the zone's own name servers directly, skipping every cache. This is the truth as Route 53 holds it.
Shows the answer with its remaining TTL in seconds, which tells you how long a cached value will live.
Every hosted zone and whether it is private. Two zones with the same name, one public and one private, are a common source of confusion.
The records for one name, including alias targets and routing policy, which dig cannot show.
What each health-checking region currently reports, with the failure reason.
Creates, changes or deletes records. A wrong change takes effect worldwide and stays cached for the TTL.
Failover routing with a health check, in Terraform (illustrative)
Not applied. Alias behaviour (allowed at the zone apex, no charge for queries to AWS resources, TTL set by the target) was checked against the Route 53 documentation on 11 November 2026.
Exercise
Read real DNS from your own machine. Nothing is changed.

items: Run dig +trace on a domain you know and identify the root, the TLD and the authoritative step.
Run dig with +noall +answer twice, a few seconds apart, and watch the TTL count down.
Find the name servers with dig NS, then ask one of them directly with dig @server.
Look up the same name through two public resolvers (for example @1.1.1.1 and @8.8.8.8) and compare.
Find a name that is a CNAME and one that returns A records at the zone apex, and say why the apex cannot be a CNAME.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state, for one domain, who is authoritative, what the TTL is, and how long a change to that record would take to reach everyone.
Troubleshooting

rows: A record was changed an hour ago and some users still reach the old address.
Resolvers cached the old answer for its TTL, and some clients and applications cache for longer still.
Wait for the old TTL. Next time, lower the TTL a day ahead of a planned change, then raise it again afterwards.
The domain does not resolve at all after creating the hosted zone.
The name servers at the registrar are not the four assigned to this hosted zone, often after the zone was deleted and recreated.
Copy the zone's NS values to the registrar. Confirm with dig +trace.
A name resolves inside the VPC to a different address than outside, or not at all.
A private hosted zone with the same domain name is attached to the VPC and overrides the public zone there.
Add the missing record to the private zone, or use a different internal domain.
Failover did not happen during an outage.
The health check was probing something that stayed up, such as a static page, or the record had no health check attached.
Health-check an endpoint that reflects the real dependency chain, attach it to the primary record, and rehearse the failover.
Creating a CNAME for the bare domain is rejected.
DNS does not allow a CNAME at the zone apex, because the apex must also hold NS and SOA records.
Use an alias record of type A (and AAAA) pointing at the load balancer or CloudFront distribution.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Use alias records for AWS targets. They work at the apex, follow address changes and their queries are not charged.
Manage records as code and review changes like any other deployment.
Keep TTLs moderate (for example 60 to 300 seconds) on records you may need to move quickly, and long on those that never change.
Rehearse DNS failover. An untested failover policy is a hope, not a plan.
Use weighted records for gradual migrations and keep the old target until the weight has been zero for longer than the TTL.
Remove records when the resource behind them is deleted.

blocks.text: Security

items: A record left pointing at a deleted bucket, load balancer or external service can be claimed by someone else, who then serves content on your domain. Audit for dangling records.
Restrict who may change hosted zones. A DNS change can redirect all traffic and obtain valid certificates for the domain.
Lock the domain at the registrar and protect that account with strong multi-factor authentication. It outranks everything else.
Add CAA records to limit which certificate authorities may issue for the domain.
Do not publish internal host names in a public zone. Use a private hosted zone.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between an alias record and a CNAME?
blocks.text: A CNAME is standard DNS: it says this name is another name, cannot exist at the zone apex, and the resolver makes a second lookup. An alias is a Route 53 extension: it is created as an A or AAAA record whose value Route 53 fills in with the current addresses of an AWS resource such as a load balancer or CloudFront distribution. It works at the apex, follows the resource when its addresses change, and queries for it are not charged. From the outside it looks like an ordinary A record.

blocks.title: Which Route 53 routing policies do you know and when would you use each?
blocks.text: Simple returns one answer. Weighted splits traffic by proportion, for gradual migrations or testing a new stack. Latency sends users to the region that responds fastest for them. Failover returns a primary while its health check passes and a secondary otherwise, for active-passive disaster recovery. Geolocation answers by the user's country or continent, for legal or content reasons, and geoproximity shifts traffic by distance with a bias. Multivalue answer returns several healthy records for simple client-side spreading.

blocks.title: You need to move a service to a new load balancer with no downtime. How do you use DNS?
blocks.text: A day or more before, lower the record's TTL so that caches turn over quickly. Bring up the new load balancer and verify it directly. Add it as a weighted record with a small weight, watch error rates, and raise the weight in steps. When it is at 100%, keep the old target running for longer than the old TTL plus a margin, because some clients cache beyond it. Then remove the old record and raise the TTL again.

blocks.title: Why is DNS failover not instant, and what can you do about it?
blocks.text: Three delays add up: the health check must fail several times before Route 53 changes its answer, resolvers keep serving the cached answer until the TTL runs out, and some clients ignore TTLs or hold open connections. With a 30-second check, three failures and a 60-second TTL, expect around two to three minutes. For faster failover, use shorter intervals and TTLs, or move the switch below DNS with a global load balancer or anycast service such as Global Accelerator, which changes routing without waiting for caches.

blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which record type can point the bare domain shop.example at a load balancer?
quiz.why: A CNAME is not allowed at the zone apex.

quiz.q: A record has a TTL of 300. After you change it, worst-case time for resolvers to pick it up is about…
quiz.why: Resolvers may serve the cached answer until the TTL expires.

quiz.q: Which policy suits active-passive disaster recovery?
quiz.why: It answers with the secondary when the primary's health check fails.

quiz.q: dig +trace shows delegation stopping before your name servers. The likely fault is…
options: wrong NS records at the registrar
quiz.why: The parent zone must point at your hosted zone's name servers.

modules.title: Azure and Google Cloud
modules.summary: The same jobs under different names, and the structural differences that matter. A mapping lesson, then one lesson each on Azure and Google Cloud: hierarchy, identity, networking and Kubernetes. Their commands were not run or checked line by line against provider documentation.

lessons.title: Azure and Google Cloud: the same jobs, different names

blocks.text: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud all sell the same building blocks: virtual machines, private networks, load balancers, object storage, managed databases, managed Kubernetes and an identity system. The names and some rules differ. If you understand the job each block does, moving between clouds is mostly a matter of translation, plus a short list of real differences to watch for.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Driving in another country. The car has a steering wheel, brakes and indicators wherever you are. The signs are in another language and a few rules differ, such as which side of the road to use. You do not relearn driving. You learn the signs and take care with the rules that changed.
Why it matters

Companies choose clouds for commercial, historical and regulatory reasons, and engineers change companies. Knowing one cloud deeply and being able to map it to the others is worth more than shallow knowledge of all three. It also lets you read architecture write-ups from any company.
Where you meet it

Reading another team's architecture, joining a company on a different provider, an acquisition that brings a second cloud, or an interview where the question is asked in terms of a cloud you have not used.
Scenario

checkout-api is a container image, a Helm chart and a Terraform configuration. To run it on Google Cloud: the cluster becomes GKE, the registry Artifact Registry, the bucket Cloud Storage, the database Cloud SQL, and the pod's permissions come from a Google service account. The image and the chart do not change. The Terraform resources are rewritten for a different provider, and the network design changes most, because the rules for networks differ.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TB subgraph SAME["Unchanged in every cloud"] IMG["Container image"] CHART["Helm chart / manifests"] PIPE["Pipeline stages"] ARGO["Argo CD"] end subgraph AWS["AWS"] A1["EKS"] --- A2["ECR"] --- A3["S3"] --- A4["RDS"] --- A5["IAM role +
Pod Identity"] end subgraph AZ["Azure"] B1["AKS"] --- B2["Container Registry"] --- B3["Blob Storage"] --- B4["Azure Database
for PostgreSQL"] --- B5["Managed identity +
Workload ID"] end subgraph GCP["Google Cloud"] C1["GKE"] --- C2["Artifact Registry"] --- C3["Cloud Storage"] --- C4["Cloud SQL"] --- C5["Service account +
Workload Identity"] end SAME --> AWS SAME --> AZ SAME --> GCP TF["Terraform: same language and workflow,
different provider and resource types"] --> AWS TF --> AZ TF --> GCP

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Azure: signs you in through the browser and stores a token for the CLI.
Azure: which subscription the CLI is pointing at. The equivalent of aws sts get-caller-identity.
Azure: resource groups in the subscription. Every Azure resource lives in exactly one.
Azure: adds an AKS cluster to your kubeconfig. The equivalent of aws eks update-kubeconfig.
Google Cloud: signs you in through the browser.
Google Cloud: the active account, project and default region.
Google Cloud: projects you can see. The project is the unit that holds resources and is billed.

blocks.code: gcloud container clusters get-credentials shop --region asia-south1
blocks.caption: Changes the local environment

blocks.text: Google Cloud: adds a GKE cluster to your kubeconfig.
Azure: deletes a resource group and every resource inside it. Convenient for cleaning up a lab; catastrophic if pointed at the wrong group.
Google Cloud: schedules a whole project and everything in it for deletion.
Exercise
Translate the checkout-api architecture from AWS into Azure and Google Cloud using the service map.

items: In the service map, find the Azure and Google Cloud names for: EKS, ECR, S3, RDS, Secrets Manager, SQS, CloudWatch
Search for "subnet" and read the note. How does the three-zone network design from the VPC lesson change on Google Cloud?
Search for "identity". Describe in one sentence each how a pod gets cloud permissions on the three providers
Which parts of the checkout-api delivery pipeline do not change at all when moving cloud?
Find two rows where the note warns that the services are not drop-in replacements, and say why that matters for a migration
What does an Azure resource group give you that AWS has no direct equivalent for?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Given a service name from any of the three clouds, you can say what job it does and name its counterparts.
Troubleshooting

rows: CLI commands affect the wrong environment
The active subscription (Azure) or project (Google Cloud) is not the one you meant.
az account show or gcloud config list before anything that changes resources.
A design copied from AWS does not fit
A structural difference: subnets that span zones, a global VPC, or a different identity model.
Translate the intent (isolation, redundancy), not the diagram.
Permission denied although a role was assigned
Azure and Google Cloud bind roles at a scope. The role was granted on a different subscription, resource group or project, or has not propagated yet.
Check the scope of the role assignment or binding.
Terraform code will not run against the other cloud
Resource types belong to a provider. aws_instance does not exist in the azurerm or google provider.
Keep module interfaces (inputs and outputs) the same and write one implementation per cloud.
The bill differs sharply from the estimate
Pricing units differ: data transfer between zones or regions, NAT, load balancer rules and logging are charged differently by each provider.
Use each provider's pricing calculator and cost reports; do not assume parity.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Learn one cloud deeply, then map the others onto it.
Keep the portable parts portable: containers, Kubernetes manifests, Terraform workflow, open observability standards.
Do not pursue multi-cloud for its own sake. Running one system on two clouds roughly doubles the operational work.
Use managed services where they save real effort, knowing each one is a tie to the provider.
Standardise names, tags or labels, and environments across clouds.
Check current documentation: services are renamed and replaced more often than you would expect.

blocks.text: Security

items: The identity model is the first thing to learn in a new cloud, and the most dangerous to guess at.
Each cloud has its own way to make storage public by accident. Learn the provider's public-access controls.
Use workload identities everywhere instead of exported keys: managed identities on Azure, attached service accounts on Google Cloud.
Central identity for people (one company directory, single sign-on, MFA) across all clouds.
Turn on each provider's audit log and send it somewhere the workload teams cannot alter.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you compare AWS, Azure and Google Cloud?
blocks.text: They offer equivalent core services with different names and some structural differences: how accounts are organised, whether networks and subnets are regional or global, and how identity and permissions are modelled. Strengths vary by area and change over time, so I compare for the specific workload rather than in general.

blocks.title: What are the equivalents of EC2, S3 and EKS?
blocks.text: Virtual Machines, Blob Storage and AKS on Azure; Compute Engine, Cloud Storage and GKE on Google Cloud.

blocks.title: Should a company go multi-cloud?
blocks.text: Only for a concrete reason: regulation, an acquisition, a service that exists on one provider, or negotiating position. The costs are duplicated tooling and skills, harder networking and security, and using the lowest common denominator. Many who say multi-cloud mean different systems on different clouds, which is far easier than one system on two.

blocks.title: What makes a workload portable between clouds?
blocks.text: Containers and Kubernetes for running it, infrastructure as code for creating its environment, open protocols for data (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, S3-compatible APIs) and open standards for telemetry. Identity, networking and proprietary managed services are what must be redone.

blocks.title: You know AWS and join a team on Google Cloud. What do you learn first?
blocks.text: The resource hierarchy and IAM, then networking (global VPC, regional subnets, firewall rules), then GKE and how workloads get permissions. After that the service names, which are a lookup.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: The Google Cloud counterpart of an AWS account is closest to…
quiz.why: A project holds resources and is the unit of billing and isolation.

quiz.q: Which usually needs the most rework when moving a containerised service to another cloud?
quiz.why: Images and manifests are portable; network and permission models are provider-specific.

quiz.q: In Azure, every resource belongs to…
quiz.why: The resource group is a required container, and a unit of access control and deletion.

lessons.title: Azure for someone who knows AWS

blocks.text: Azure offers the same building blocks as AWS, organised differently. Everything you create lives in a resource group, which lives in a subscription, which belongs to a tenant of Microsoft Entra ID. Access is granted by assigning a role to an identity at one of those levels, and it flows downwards. Once that shape is clear, the services map across easily: virtual networks, virtual machines and scale sets, storage accounts, managed databases and AKS for Kubernetes.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: An office building. The tenant is the company that holds the lease. Subscriptions are floors, each with its own budget. Resource groups are rooms on a floor, and resources are the furniture. Give someone a key to a floor and they can enter every room on it. When a project ends you can empty one room in a single move.
Why it matters

Many companies run on Azure, often because they already use Microsoft 365 and Entra ID. A DevOps engineer who knows one cloud is expected to become productive in another quickly, and that depends on knowing which ideas carry over and which do not.
Where you meet it
Enterprises with Microsoft agreements, .NET and Windows estates, and organisations that want one identity system for staff and cloud. The patterns here are the starting point for any Azure platform.
Scenario

The shop's parent company standardises on Azure for a new region. The team recreates the staging stack: a resource group per environment, a virtual network with a subnet for AKS, an AKS cluster with a managed identity, Azure Container Registry for images and Key Vault for secrets. checkout-api reads its database password through workload identity, with no secret stored in the cluster.
Architecture

(users, groups, service principals, managed identities)"] --> MG["Management groups
(policy across subscriptions)"] MG --> S1["Subscription: shop-staging
(billing and quota boundary)"] MG --> S2["Subscription: shop-production"] S1 --> RG["Resource group: rg-shop-staging"] RG --> VNET["Virtual network 10.20.0.0/16"] VNET --> SN1["Subnet snet-aks + NSG"] VNET --> SN2["Subnet snet-data + NSG"] SN1 --> AKS["AKS cluster

Commands

A resource group, a network and an AKS cluster with the Azure CLI (illustrative)

Draw the hierarchy tenant, subscription, resource group for a company with staging and production.

Write down how checkout-api in AKS would read a secret without a stored credential.
List two things that have no direct AWS equivalent (resource groups and tenant-wide identity are good candidates).

blocks.text: Your answer uses a subscription per environment, role assignments at resource group scope, and workload identity with Key Vault for the secret.
Troubleshooting

rows: A user with Contributor on the storage account cannot read blobs.
Contributor is a management role. Reading data needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader.
Assign the data role at the container or account scope.
Commands succeed but the resources appear in the wrong place.
The CLI was pointed at a different subscription.
Run az account show first, and pass --subscription explicitly in scripts.
AKS pods fail with ImagePullBackOff from Azure Container Registry.
The cluster's kubelet identity has no AcrPull role on the registry.
Attach the registry with az aks update --attach-acr, or assign AcrPull to the kubelet identity.
A resource cannot be deleted even by an owner.
A resource lock (CanNotDelete or ReadOnly) is set on it or on its group.
Remove the lock deliberately, make the change, and put the lock back.
Creating a resource is refused with "RequestDisallowedByPolicy".
An Azure Policy assigned at the management group or subscription forbids that location, size or configuration.
Read the policy named in the error and comply, or request an exemption.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Use a separate subscription per environment so that budgets, quotas and access are separated by default.
Group resources that share a lifecycle in one resource group, so that they can be deployed and removed together.
Assign roles to groups, not to individuals, at the narrowest scope that works.
Prefer managed identities to service principal secrets wherever Azure supports them.
Tag resources for owner, environment and cost centre, and enforce the tags with policy.
Define infrastructure with Terraform or Bicep rather than through the portal.

blocks.text: Security

items: Owner and User Access Administrator can grant access to others. Keep them rare and time-limited through Privileged Identity Management.
Use private endpoints for databases, storage and Key Vault so that they are not reachable from the internet.
Storage account keys grant full access and bypass role assignments. Disable shared-key access where you can.
Require multi-factor authentication and conditional access for anyone who can reach production.
Turn on Microsoft Defender for Cloud recommendations and review them. They surface open management ports and public storage.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain the Azure hierarchy from tenant to resource.
blocks.text: A tenant is an instance of Microsoft Entra ID: the directory of users, groups and application identities. Under it, management groups organise subscriptions and carry policy. A subscription is the billing and quota boundary and the usual unit for an environment. Inside a subscription, resource groups hold resources that share a lifecycle. Role assignments and policies set at a higher level are inherited by everything below.

blocks.title: What is a managed identity and how does it compare with an AWS IAM role?
blocks.text: A managed identity is an identity in Entra ID that Azure creates and rotates for a resource such as a virtual machine or an AKS workload. Code on that resource asks a local endpoint for a token and uses it to call other Azure services, so no secret is stored. It plays the same part as an IAM role attached to an EC2 instance or a pod. System-assigned identities live and die with one resource; user-assigned ones are separate objects that several resources can share.

blocks.title: How does Azure role-based access control decide whether a request is allowed?
blocks.text: Each role assignment joins three things: a principal, a role definition listing allowed actions, and a scope. Azure collects the assignments that apply at the resource's scope and above, and allows the request if any of them includes the action and no deny assignment blocks it. Management actions and data actions are separate, so a role that can configure a storage account does not necessarily read its contents. Azure Policy is evaluated as well and can refuse a compliant-looking request.

blocks.title: What differs between an Azure virtual network and an AWS VPC?
blocks.text: Both are private address spaces divided into subnets. In Azure a subnet spans all availability zones in the region rather than sitting in one, and outbound internet access has historically been available by default rather than needing a gateway, though explicit outbound through a NAT gateway is the recommended design. Network security groups attach to subnets or network interfaces and have numbered priority rules with both allow and deny, unlike AWS security groups, which only allow.

quiz.q: What is the billing and quota boundary in Azure?
quiz.why: Environments are usually separated by subscription.

quiz.q: Deleting a resource group…
quiz.why: A group is a lifecycle unit.

quiz.q: Azure's closest equivalent of an IAM role on an EC2 instance is…
quiz.why: An identity Azure issues and rotates for the resource.

quiz.q: Contributor on a storage account lets you…
options: manage the account, but not necessarily read its data
quiz.why: Data access needs a data role.

lessons.title: Google Cloud for someone who knows AWS

blocks.text: Google Cloud organises everything into projects. A project holds resources, has its own billing link, its own enabled APIs and its own access rules; folders and an organisation sit above it. Access is granted by binding a role to a member on a resource, and it is inherited downwards. Two differences from AWS matter most: a VPC network is global with regional subnets, and workloads act through service accounts rather than roles.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A workshop building where every job gets its own locked bay. The bay (project) has its own tools switched on, its own meter and its own key list. Close the job and you clear the bay. A single set of corridors (the global VPC) can connect bays in different cities without building a bridge between them.
Why it matters

Google Cloud is common in data-heavy companies and anywhere GKE is the Kubernetes of choice. Its project model makes isolation simple, but people arriving from AWS trip over the global network, the API-enablement step and the way service accounts are both identities and resources.
Where you meet it
Analytics and machine-learning platforms built on BigQuery, companies running GKE, and multi-cloud organisations. The patterns here are the starting point for any Google Cloud platform.
Scenario

The shop's analytics team runs on Google Cloud. They create a project per environment under a folder, one custom VPC with a subnet in Mumbai, and a GKE Autopilot cluster. A reporting service in GKE reads invoices from a Cloud Storage bucket: its Kubernetes service account is linked to a Google service account that holds only the object viewer role on that bucket.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TD ORG["Organisation: shop.example"] --> F1["Folder: analytics"] F1 --> P1["Project: shop-staging
(billing, APIs, IAM, quotas)"] F1 --> P2["Project: shop-production"] P1 --> VPC["VPC network (global)"] VPC --> SN1["Subnet asia-south1 10.30.0.0/20"] VPC --> SN2["Subnet europe-west1 10.31.0.0/20"] VPC --> FW["Firewall rules
(target by tag or service account)"] SN1 --> GKE["GKE cluster"] SN1 --> SQL["Cloud SQL (private IP)"] P1 --> GCS["Cloud Storage bucket"] P1 --> AR["Artifact Registry"] GKE --> KSA["Kubernetes service account"] KSA -->|"Workload Identity"| GSA["Google service account"] GSA -->|"roles/storage.objectViewer"| GCS IAM["Allow policy =
member + role, on a resource"] -. "inherited downwards" .-> P1

Commands

Switches the project that later commands act on.
Projects you can see, with their IDs and numbers.

Draw organisation, folders and projects for a company with two teams and two environments each.

Write down how a pod in GKE would read a bucket without a key file.
