Troubleshooting

rows: The first call to a service fails with "API has not been used in project … or it is disabled".
Each project must enable each service API before use.
Enable it with gcloud services enable, or declare it in Terraform.
A pod gets 403 from Cloud Storage although the Google service account has the role.
The pod is not running as that identity: the Kubernetes service account is not linked, or the pod uses the default one.
Check the pod's serviceAccountName and the Workload Identity binding between the two accounts.
Two virtual machines in the same VPC cannot reach each other.
A custom VPC has no allow rules for internal traffic; ingress is denied by default.
Add a firewall rule that allows the needed ports between the right tags or service accounts.
Resources were created in the wrong project.
gcloud was still set to another project.
Run gcloud config list first, and pass --project explicitly in scripts.
Creating an external IP or a key is refused by a constraint.
An organisation policy forbids it across the folder or organisation.
Read the constraint named in the error and comply, or request an exception.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Use a project per environment and per team boundary. Projects are cheap and are the strongest isolation unit.
Grant predefined roles on the narrowest resource. Avoid the basic roles Owner, Editor and Viewer.
Use custom-mode VPCs so that you choose every subnet range.
Give each workload its own service account with only the roles it needs.
Label resources for owner, environment and cost centre, and export billing data to BigQuery for analysis.
Define infrastructure with Terraform and enable APIs there, so that a new project is reproducible.

blocks.text: Security

items: A downloaded service account key is a long-lived password in a file. Prefer Workload Identity and short-lived credentials, and block key creation by organisation policy.
The default Compute Engine service account has historically been granted the broad Editor role. Do not run workloads as it.
The role that lets a user act as a service account (Service Account User or Token Creator) is a path to that account's full power. Grant it sparingly.
Buckets can be made public with a single binding to allUsers. Enforce public access prevention.
Use private clusters and private IPs for databases, and reach them through Identity-Aware Proxy rather than open management ports.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is a Google Cloud project and why does it matter?
blocks.text: A project is the container that owns resources and the boundary for billing, enabled APIs, quotas and access policy. Every resource belongs to exactly one. Because projects are cheap and isolated by default, the normal design is one per environment per team, arranged in folders under the organisation, with shared policy inherited from above. It plays the part that an AWS account plays, but is lighter to create.

blocks.title: How does a Google Cloud VPC differ from an AWS VPC?
blocks.text: A Google Cloud VPC network is a global resource: one network can have subnets in many regions and they route to each other privately without peering. Subnets are regional and span all zones in the region, whereas an AWS subnet sits in one availability zone and a VPC is confined to one region. Firewall rules belong to the network and select targets by network tag or service account rather than being attached to instances as security groups are.

blocks.title: What is a service account, and how does a GKE pod use one safely?
blocks.text: A service account is an identity for software rather than a person. It is also a resource, so there are roles about who may use or impersonate it. With Workload Identity, a Kubernetes service account in a namespace is linked to a Google service account; pods running under it receive short-lived Google credentials from the metadata server. No key file is created or mounted, access is specific to that workload, and credentials rotate on their own.

blocks.title: How are permissions granted in Google Cloud IAM?
blocks.text: Permissions are grouped into roles, and an allow policy on a resource binds roles to members such as users, groups or service accounts. Policies are inherited from organisation to folder to project to resource, and the effective access is the union of all of them, so a broad grant high up cannot be narrowed lower down except by deny policies or conditions. That is why grants should be made at the lowest level that works, using predefined roles instead of the old basic ones.

quiz.q: In Google Cloud, a VPC network is…
quiz.why: One network can span regions without peering.

quiz.q: The first call to a new service in a project fails. The first thing to check is…
quiz.why: APIs are enabled per project.

quiz.q: The safe way for a GKE pod to call Google APIs is…
options: a key file in the image
quiz.why: Short-lived credentials, scoped to one workload.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest default isolation unit?
quiz.why: Billing, APIs, quotas and IAM are all scoped to it.

modules.title: Databases in Production
modules.summary: PostgreSQL connections, pooling, slow queries and locks; replication, failover, RPO and RTO; backups, restores and zero-downtime schema changes. Not yet covered: MySQL specifics, sharding, NoSQL operations.

lessons.title: PostgreSQL in production: connections, slow queries and locks

blocks.text: A production database fails in a few well-known ways long before its disk or CPU gives out. It runs out of connections, one slow query holds everything up, or a long transaction holds a lock that every other request waits behind. Operating a database is mostly knowing how to see these three things and what to do about each.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A bank branch with ten counters. Each counter is a connection. If every customer takes a ticket and then stands at a counter filling in forms (an idle transaction), the queue goes out of the door although the staff are doing nothing. One customer with a complicated request (a slow query) blocks a counter for an hour. And if someone locks the vault door open to count the cash, nobody else can use the vault at all.
Why it matters

Stateless services can be restarted and scaled without thought. The database cannot: it is the one component that holds the truth, and every service depends on it. Most serious outages of a healthy application are database outages, and most of those are caused by the application's own behaviour, not by hardware.
Where you meet it
Any service with a relational database: PostgreSQL or MySQL, self-managed or as RDS, Cloud SQL or Azure Database. The commands here are PostgreSQL; the ideas carry over.
Scenario

checkout-api scales from 6 pods to 12 for a sale. Each pod keeps a pool of 10 connections, so 120 are wanted against a limit of 100. New pods fail their readiness check with "too many clients", the rollout stalls, and the pods that did get connections slow down under the extra load. The fix on the day is fewer connections per pod; the lasting fix is a connection pooler.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph PODS["checkout-api pods"] P1["pod 1
pool: 10"] P2["pod 2
pool: 10"] P3["pod N
pool: 10"] end PGB["Connection pooler
PgBouncer / RDS Proxy
transaction mode"] subgraph PG["PostgreSQL primary"] MAX["max_connections = 100
one server process each"] QP["Query planner
uses indexes and statistics"] WAL["Write-ahead log"] AV["autovacuum"] end P1 --> PGB P2 --> PGB P3 --> PGB PGB -->|"40 real connections"| MAX MAX --> QP QP --> DISK[("Tables and indexes")] QP --> WAL AV --> DISK MON["pg_stat_activity
pg_stat_statements"] -. "what is running, what is slow" .-> PG

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Checkout is slow or failing,
and the database is suspected"] --> B{"Can you connect at all?"} B -->|"no: too many clients"| C["Connections exhausted.
Count them by state and by application"] C --> C1{"Mostly idle or
idle in transaction?"} C1 -->|"yes"| C2["An application is holding connections
without using them. Fix the pool or add a pooler"] C1 -->|"no, active"| D B -->|"yes"| D["List active queries, longest first"] D --> E{"Are queries waiting on a lock?"} E -->|"yes"| F["Find the blocking session.
Usually a long transaction or a schema change"] F --> F1["Cancel or terminate the blocker,
then find out why it ran"] E -->|"no"| G{"One query, or many copies of it,
running for a long time?"} G -->|"yes"| H["EXPLAIN it. Look for a sequential scan
on a big table or a bad row estimate"] H --> H1["Add the index concurrently,
or fix the query"] G -->|"no"| I["Look at resources: CPU, memory,
disk I/O, replication, autovacuum"]

blocks.text: Commands

blocks.code: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "SELECT count(*), state FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state ORDER BY 1 DESC;"
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: How many connections exist and what they are doing. "idle" is a pooled connection waiting; "active" is running a query; "idle in transaction" has begun a transaction and stopped, which holds locks and blocks cleanup.

blocks.code:
count |        state
-------+---------------------
    61 | idle
    14 | active
     9 | idle in transaction
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: The connection limit. The default is 100.

blocks.code: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS running, state, wait_event_type, left(query, 60) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle' ORDER BY running DESC LIMIT 10;"
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: The ten longest-running statements, with what each is waiting for. wait_event_type "Lock" means it is blocked by another session.

blocks.code: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time) AS total_ms, round(mean_exec_time) AS mean_ms, left(query, 70) FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;"
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: The queries that cost the most time in total since statistics were reset. A fast query called a million times can matter more than one slow report. Needs the pg_stat_statements extension.

blocks.code: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM cart_items WHERE user_id = 48211;"
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Shows the plan the database would use, without running the query. "Seq Scan" on a large table for a query that returns a few rows usually means a missing index.

blocks.code:
Seq Scan on cart_items  (cost=0.00..185432.00 rows=3 width=64)
  Filter: (user_id = 48211)
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.code: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM cart_items WHERE user_id = 48211;"
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Runs the query for real and reports actual times and rows. Accurate, but it executes the statement: a slow query is slow again, and an UPDATE or DELETE really changes data.

blocks.code: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_cart_items_user ON cart_items (user_id);"
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Builds an index without blocking writes to the table. Slower than a plain CREATE INDEX and cannot run inside a transaction. If it fails it leaves an invalid index that must be dropped.
Cancels the statement a session is running. The session and its transaction stay open.
Closes a session. Its open transaction is rolled back. The way to remove a blocker that will not finish; the application sees a dropped connection.
pgbouncer.ini (illustrative)

blocks.code:
; pgbouncer.ini: a connection pooler between checkout-api and PostgreSQL.
[databases]
shop = host=shop-orders.internal port=5432 dbname=shop

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt

; A server connection is lent for one transaction, then returned.
pool_mode = transaction

; Clients (application connections) the pooler accepts.
max_client_conn = 2000

; Real PostgreSQL connections per database and user. This is the number
; that must stay under the database's max_connections.
default_pool_size = 40

; Close server connections that sat unused this long (seconds).
server_idle_timeout = 600

blocks.text: With this in place 12 pods with 10 connections each open 120 connections to the pooler, which serves them from 40 real ones. Try the same numbers in the Database lab.
Exercise
Reproduce the checkout-api connection outage in the Database lab and fix it two ways.

items: Start from the defaults and note how many more pods would fit
Press "Scale out to 12 pods". Read the error the new pods would see
Fix it without a pooler: what pool size per pod makes 12 pods fit? What does that cost during a burst?
Press "12 pods with a pooler". Which number now has to stay under max_connections?
Press "A slow query appears". Connections fit, but requests queue. Why does raising the pool size not help?
A deploy runs old and new pods side by side for a few minutes. Work out the peak number of connections for 12 pods and a 25 percent surge

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can calculate connection demand from pods and pool size, explain what a transaction-mode pooler changes, and tell exhaustion from saturation.
Troubleshooting

rows: FATAL: sorry, too many clients already
More connections are requested than max_connections allows: scale-out, a deploy overlap, or a connection leak.
Count connections by application and state. Reduce pool sizes, add a pooler, fix leaks. Raising max_connections costs memory and usually postpones the problem.
Queries that were fast are suddenly slow
The plan changed: statistics are stale after a bulk load, the table grew past a threshold, or an index was dropped.
EXPLAIN the query, run ANALYZE on the table, and compare with pg_stat_statements history.
Everything touching one table hangs
A session holds a lock: often a schema change waiting behind a long transaction, with all other queries queued behind the schema change.
Find sessions with wait_event_type Lock and what blocks them. Terminate the long transaction. Use lock_timeout on schema changes so they fail fast instead.
Many connections "idle in transaction"
The application opens a transaction and then does slow work (an HTTP call, a sleep) before committing.
Keep transactions short and free of network calls. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout as a safety net.
Disk usage grows although row counts are stable
Dead row versions are not being cleaned up: autovacuum cannot keep up, or a long transaction prevents cleanup.
Check for old transactions and replication slots holding back cleanup; tune autovacuum for the busy tables.
CPU at 100 percent on the database
Usually one inefficient query run very often.
pg_stat_statements ordered by total time. Fix the top entry before considering a larger instance.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Know your connection arithmetic: pods x pool size, at peak and during deploys.
Put a pooler in front of the database once pods scale automatically.
Set timeouts everywhere: statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and in the client.
Keep pg_stat_statements on and review the top queries regularly.
Build indexes concurrently on live tables.
Keep transactions short; never hold one across a network call.
Test with production-sized data. A query that is instant on a thousand rows tells you nothing.

blocks.text: Security

items: One database user per service with only the privileges it needs; the application never connects as a superuser.
The database is reachable only from the application's network, never from the internet.
Require TLS for connections.
Credentials come from a secret store and are rotated; they are not in the image or the repository.
Query text in logs and in pg_stat_activity can contain personal data. Restrict who can read them.
Audit who can run arbitrary SQL against production, and log when they do.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: An application starts failing with "too many connections". How do you handle it?
blocks.text: Confirm with pg_stat_activity: how many, from which application, in what state. If a scale-out or deploy caused it, reduce pool sizes or scale back to restore service. If connections are idle in transaction, find the leak. Longer term add a transaction-mode pooler so application scale is decoupled from database connections.

blocks.title: Why not simply raise max_connections?
blocks.text: Each connection is a server process with memory, and many active connections contend for CPU and locks. Past a point throughput falls. A database serves a few hundred queries at once well; thousands of mostly idle client connections are better multiplexed by a pooler.

blocks.title: How do you find and fix a slow query?
blocks.text: Find it by total time in pg_stat_statements or by duration in pg_stat_activity. EXPLAIN it, with ANALYZE if it is safe to run. Look for sequential scans on large tables, wrong row estimates and sorts on disk. Fix with an index built concurrently, a rewritten query or fresh statistics, and measure again.

blocks.title: What does "idle in transaction" mean and why is it harmful?
blocks.text: A session began a transaction and is not running anything. It holds its locks, occupies a connection and stops vacuum from removing dead rows newer than its snapshot. A few of them can stall a busy database.

blocks.title: What does a connection pooler change, and what does it break?
blocks.text: Many client connections share a few server connections, lent per transaction. Applications can scale without touching the server limit. Anything that depends on one session persisting, such as session-level settings, advisory locks or some prepared statement usage, needs care.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: 12 pods, pool size 10, max_connections 100 with 5 reserved. What happens?
options: 25 connections are refused once pools fill
quiz.why: 120 wanted, 95 available. There is no sharing without a pooler.

quiz.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE differs from EXPLAIN because it…
quiz.why: Which makes it accurate, and dangerous for statements that change data.

quiz.q: Requests queue for a connection although the pool is within limits. The usual cause is…
quiz.why: Each query holds a connection for its duration. Slow queries exhaust the pool.

lessons.title: Replication, failover, RPO and RTO

blocks.text: Replication keeps one or more copies of the database up to date on other machines. If the primary fails, a copy takes over: that is failover. Two numbers describe how well you survive it. RTO is how long you are down. RPO is how much recent data you lose. Synchronous copies lose nothing but slow every write a little; asynchronous copies are free of that cost but are always slightly behind.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A meeting with a note-taker. Synchronous: the speaker waits after every sentence until the note-taker says "got it". Nothing is ever missing from the notes, but the meeting is slower, and if the note-taker leaves the room the speaker must stop or carry on unrecorded. Asynchronous: the speaker talks at full speed and the note-taker is a sentence or two behind. If the speaker is suddenly called away, the last sentence is not in the notes.
Why it matters

Machines, disks and whole data centres fail. With one copy, the service is down until that machine is repaired or a backup is restored, which can take hours. Replication turns that into seconds or minutes. The design choices are about what you are willing to pay, in speed and money, for how little downtime and data loss.
Where you meet it

Every production database that matters. Managed services package it as options: Multi-AZ on RDS, high availability on Cloud SQL and Azure. Self-managed PostgreSQL uses streaming replication with a tool such as Patroni to decide who is primary.
Scenario

The zone holding the orders database loses power at 21:00 on a sale day. With a synchronous standby, checkout fails for about a minute and no paid order is lost. With only an asynchronous replica, an engineer must be paged and decide to promote it, and the last few seconds of paid orders are missing from the new primary: customers were charged for orders the system no longer knows about.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TB APP["checkout-api"] -->|"writes and consistent reads"| EP["Database endpoint name"] EP --> PRI[("Primary
zone a")] PRI -->|"synchronous: commit waits"| SBY[("Standby
zone b")] PRI -->|"asynchronous: may lag"| RR[("Read replica
zone c")] REP["Reporting, search indexing"] -->|"reads that tolerate lag"| RR PRI -->|"write-ahead log archive"| ARCH["Object storage:
base backups + log"] HA["Failover controller
(managed service, or Patroni
with a consensus store)"] -. "health checks,
decides who is primary" .-> PRI HA -.-> SBY ARCH -. "point-in-time restore" .-> NEW[("New instance")]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Primary stops answering"] --> B{"Is it really dead, or only
unreachable from here?"} B -->|"cannot tell"| C["Danger: if both sides think they are primary
and accept writes, the data diverges (split brain)"] C --> D["The old primary must be fenced:
shut down or cut off before another takes over"] B -->|"confirmed down"| D D --> E{"Is there a synchronous standby?"} E -->|"yes"| F["Promote it. RPO is zero"] E -->|"no"| G{"An asynchronous replica?"} G -->|"yes"| H["Promote it. Writes not yet
replicated are lost: RPO = lag"] G -->|"no"| I["Restore from backup and replay the log.
RPO = age of the last archived log. RTO = hours"] F --> J["Clients are redirected: endpoint or DNS switches"] H --> J I --> J J --> K{"Do applications reconnect
and retry on their own?"} K -->|"no"| L["Restart them. The outage lasts until someone does"] K -->|"yes"| M["Service resumes. Rebuild a new standby"]

blocks.text: Commands
false on a primary, true on a standby or replica. The quickest way to learn which one you are connected to.

blocks.code: psql "$PRIMARY_URL" -c "SELECT client_addr, state, sync_state, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;"
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Run on the primary: each replica, whether it is synchronous, and how far behind it is.
Run on a replica: how old the newest change it has applied is. On an idle primary this grows although nothing is missing.
Turns a replica into a primary that accepts writes. It never goes back to following the old primary. Only after the old primary is confirmed down and fenced.
On RDS Multi-AZ: forces a failover to the standby. Causes a short outage on purpose. This is how you rehearse failover and find out whether your applications reconnect.
On RDS: makes a read replica a standalone primary. Replication from the old primary stops for good.
Whether a standby exists and which zones the primary and standby are in.
Exercise
Compare three levels of protection in the "When the primary fails" part of the Database lab and put a price on each.

items: Select the synchronous standby and read the timeline. Which step takes longest?
Untick "The application reconnects and retries by itself". How much longer is the outage, and whose fault is the extra time?
Select the asynchronous replica with 8 seconds of lag. What exactly was lost, and what would support have to do about it?
Set the lag to 0. Is the result now as good as the synchronous standby? What is still different?
Select backups only with a 5-minute restorable point. Read the RTO. What would it be for a database ten times larger?
For checkout orders, a product catalogue and an analytics store, choose a level for each and justify the cost

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can define RPO and RTO, say what each replication mode guarantees, and name the part of failover that depends on the application.
Troubleshooting

rows: Replica lag keeps growing
The replica cannot apply changes as fast as the primary makes them: a burst of writes, a smaller replica instance, or long queries on the replica delaying replay.
Size replicas like the primary, look for long-running queries on the replica, and check network and disk throughput.
A user saves something and then does not see it
The write went to the primary and the next read went to a lagging replica.
Read your own writes from the primary, or route a user's reads to the primary for a short time after they write.
After failover the application stays broken
It holds dead connections or cached the old address.
Connect through the endpoint name, set a maximum connection lifetime and connect timeouts, and retry failed transactions. Rehearse failover to find this before an incident does.
Primary disk fills with write-ahead log
A replication slot for a replica that is gone or stuck forces the primary to keep log files for it.
Find inactive slots and drop them; alert on slot lag.
Two nodes both accept writes
Split brain: a network partition and a failover without fencing the old primary.
Stop writes to one side at once and reconcile by hand. Prevent it with a failover controller that uses a quorum and fences the old primary.
Writes hang when the standby is down
Strict synchronous replication waits for a standby that is not there.
Managed services fall back automatically. Self-managed setups need more than one synchronous candidate, or a deliberate rule for degrading to asynchronous.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Decide RPO and RTO per data set with the business, then choose the design. Do not start from the technology.
A synchronous standby in another zone for data you cannot lose.
Read replicas for scaling reads, never counted as your backup or your only failover target.
Rehearse failover on a schedule, in production if you can.
Make applications reconnect and retry, with idempotent writes.
Alert on replication lag and on missing standbys.
Automate failover with a tool that understands quorum; do not script it yourself.

blocks.text: Security

items: Replication traffic carries all your data: encrypt it and restrict which hosts may connect as a replica.
Replicas and standbys hold a full copy. Protect them exactly like the primary.
The replication role is powerful. Give it its own credentials and nothing else.
Cross-region replicas may move personal data to another jurisdiction. Check that this is allowed.
Promotion is a production change with data-loss risk: restrict who can do it and record it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Define RPO and RTO.
blocks.text: Recovery Point Objective: the maximum amount of recent data, measured in time, that may be lost in a failure. Recovery Time Objective: the maximum time the service may be unavailable. They are set by the business and drive the choice between backups, asynchronous replicas and synchronous standbys.

blocks.title: Synchronous versus asynchronous replication?
blocks.text: Synchronous: a commit is acknowledged only after a standby has it, so a failover loses nothing, at the cost of latency on every write and of availability if the standby is unreachable. Asynchronous: the primary does not wait, so writes are fast, but the replica lags and a failover loses whatever had not arrived.

blocks.title: What is split brain and how is it prevented?
blocks.text: Two nodes each believing they are the primary and accepting writes, so the data diverges. It is prevented by requiring a quorum to elect a primary and by fencing: making sure the old primary is stopped or isolated before a new one is promoted.

blocks.title: A replica is 30 seconds behind. Who is affected?
blocks.text: Anything reading from it sees old data: a customer may not see an order just placed. If it is the failover target, a failover now would lose 30 seconds of writes. Reporting usually does not care.

blocks.title: How do you test your high availability setup?
blocks.text: Trigger a real failover on a schedule, in staging and then production, and measure the time until the application is healthy again and whether any acknowledged write is missing. A setup that has never failed over is an assumption.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: RPO measures…
options: how much recent data can be lost
quiz.why: Recovery point: how far back in time you land.

quiz.q: An asynchronous replica is promoted while 8 seconds behind. Those 8 seconds of writes are…
quiz.why: They never reached the replica. That is the price of not waiting.

quiz.q: The database is ready a minute after failover, but the service stays down for ten more. The likely cause is…
quiz.why: Dead connections and no retry. This is the application's part of failover.

lessons.title: Backups you can restore, and schema changes without downtime

blocks.text: A backup is only real once you have restored it. Good backups let you go back to any moment in the recent past, not just to last night. Schema changes are the other routine danger: changing a table while the application is using it. The safe way is in small steps, where at every step the old and the new version of the code both still work.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Backups are a fire drill: owning extinguishers proves nothing until people have used one. Schema changes are replacing a bridge that traffic is using: build the new span beside the old one, move the lanes across one at a time, and take the old span down only when nothing drives on it.
Why it matters

Replication copies mistakes instantly. A bad deploy that deletes rows deletes them on every replica within milliseconds. Only a backup lets you go back in time. And because the application and the database change in separate steps during a rolling deploy, a schema change that assumes they switch at the same instant causes errors or locks the table for everyone.
Where you meet it
Every release that touches the database, and every incident involving wrong or missing data. Migrations usually run as a step in the pipeline or as a Kubernetes Job before the new version rolls out.
Scenario

A release renames a column that checkout-api reads. Done in one step, pods on the old version crash the moment the column is renamed, for the whole length of the rollout, and a rollback makes the new pods crash instead. Done as expand and contract over four releases, nothing ever breaks. Separately: a bad script wipes addresses from 4,000 orders at 09:00. Point-in-time recovery restores a copy of the database as of 08:59, and the lost column is copied back.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR PRI[("Primary database")] -->|"nightly base backup"| OBJ["Object storage
versioned, in another account"] PRI -->|"continuous write-ahead log archive"| OBJ OBJ -->|"base backup + log replayed
to a chosen second"| REST[("Restored copy
as of 08:59")] REST -->|"copy the damaged rows back"| PRI OBJ -->|"scheduled restore test"| TEST[("Throwaway instance:
does it start? row counts?")] subgraph REL["A release with a schema change"] M["Migration job
(expand step)"] --> R["Rolling deploy
old and new code run together"] end M --> PRI R --> PRI

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["You need to change a column that code uses"] --> B["Expand: add the new structure.
Old code keeps working unchanged"] B --> C["Deploy code that writes old and new,
and still reads old"] C --> D["Backfill existing rows in small batches"] D --> E["Deploy code that reads new"] E --> F{"Is anything still reading
or writing the old structure?"} F -->|"yes"| G["Wait. Check query statistics and logs"] G --> F F -->|"no"| H["Contract: remove the old structure"] B -.-> RB["At every step: the previous release
still works against the current schema,
so rolling back the code is safe"] C -.-> RB E -.-> RB

blocks.text: Commands
A logical backup of one database in PostgreSQL's compressed custom format. Consistent as of the moment it started. Reads the whole database, so it adds load; run it against a replica when you can.
Lists what a dump contains without restoring anything. A first check that the file is readable.
Restores the dump into a new, separate database. This is the restore rehearsal: time it, then compare row counts with production.
On RDS: how many days of backups are kept and the most recent moment you could restore to. If that moment is more than a few minutes old, log archiving is behind.
Creates a new database instance as it was at that second. The original is untouched. You then copy the needed data across or switch the application.

blocks.code: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "SET lock_timeout = '3s'; ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN shipping_address text;"
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Adds a nullable column. Fast, but it needs a brief exclusive lock; lock_timeout makes it give up after three seconds instead of queueing behind a long transaction and blocking every other query on the table.

blocks.code: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN address;"
blocks.caption: Destructive, high risk

blocks.text: Removes a column and its data. The contract step: only after confirming nothing reads or writes it, and with a backup you have tested.
Deletes the rehearsal database. Read the name twice before pressing Enter.
A zero-downtime column rename (illustrative SQL)

blocks.code:
-- Renaming orders.address to orders.shipping_address with no downtime.
-- Four separate releases. Each one is safe to roll back on its own.

-- Release 1 (expand): add the new column. Old code ignores it.
SET lock_timeout = '3s';            -- give up rather than block traffic
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN shipping_address text;

-- Release 2 (application): write to both columns, read the old one.
-- Then copy existing rows in small batches, not one giant UPDATE:
UPDATE orders SET shipping_address = address
 WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM orders
               WHERE shipping_address IS NULL AND address IS NOT NULL
               LIMIT 5000);         -- repeat until no rows are updated

-- Release 3 (application): read the new column, still write both.

-- Release 4 (contract): once nothing reads the old column, drop it.
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN address;

-- Indexes on a busy table: build without blocking writes.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_created
    ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

blocks.text: The rule behind every step: the schema must work with both the version of the code that is running and the one about to be deployed. A rename in one statement breaks that rule.
Exercise
Plan a restore and a safe schema change for the orders table.

items: In the Database lab choose "Backups only" and set the restorable point to 5 minutes. Read RTO and RPO
Change the restorable point to 1440 minutes (a nightly dump with no log archive). What is lost now?
A script corrupts data at 09:00 and is noticed at 09:40. Write the steps to recover the damaged rows without losing the orders placed between 09:00 and 09:40
Why can a standby not help with that incident?
Take the rename in the example and say what breaks if release 4 is deployed before release 3
You must add a NOT NULL column to a table with 200 million rows. Split it into safe steps

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain point-in-time recovery, why untested backups do not count, and the expand and contract sequence with the rollback property at each step.
Troubleshooting

rows: A restore fails or produces a database that will not start
The backup was incomplete, a needed log file was never archived, or versions do not match.
This is why restores are rehearsed. Automate a regular restore into a throwaway instance and alert when it fails.
A migration hangs and the whole application freezes
The ALTER TABLE is waiting for a lock held by a long transaction, and every other query on that table is queued behind the ALTER.
Cancel the migration. Set lock_timeout so it fails fast, retry it, and deal with the long transaction.
Errors during a rolling deploy that vanish once it completes
Old and new code ran together against a schema that only one of them understands.
Split the change into expand and contract releases.
A backfill makes the database slow
One huge UPDATE rewrites millions of rows in a single transaction: long locks, a flood of log, replica lag.
Update in small batches with pauses, and watch replication lag while it runs.
Rollback of the application fails after a migration
The migration removed or changed something the previous version needs.
Never combine a destructive schema change with the release that stops using it. Contract one release later.
Backups exist but restoring takes far longer than the business expects
RTO was never measured.
Time a full restore and tell the business the number, or invest in a standby.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Continuous log archiving, so you can restore to any second within the retention period.
Restore tests on a schedule, automated, with a check that the data is plausible.
Backups in a different account and region from the database, with deletion protection.
Every schema change backwards compatible with the previous release.
Migrations in version control, applied by the pipeline, never by hand in production.
lock_timeout on every DDL statement; indexes built concurrently.
Take a manual snapshot before any risky change.

blocks.text: Security

items: A backup is a full copy of the data. Encrypt it and restrict access as tightly as the database itself.
Whoever can delete backups can make an attack unrecoverable. Use immutable or versioned storage and a separate account.
Restored copies in test environments still contain real customer data. Mask it or do not copy it there.
The migration role needs rights to alter tables; the application role should not have them.
Keep an audit trail of who ran which migration and when.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you know your backups work?
blocks.text: By restoring them, regularly and automatically, into a fresh instance, checking it starts and that key tables have plausible contents, and timing the whole process. The measured time is the real RTO.

blocks.title: What is point-in-time recovery?
blocks.text: Restoring a base backup and replaying the archived write-ahead log up to a chosen moment. It lets you go back to just before a mistake, which neither a nightly dump nor a replica can do.

blocks.title: Is a replica a backup?
blocks.text: No. A replica reproduces every change, including destructive ones, almost immediately. It protects against losing a machine, not against losing data through error or attack.

blocks.title: How do you rename a column with zero downtime?
blocks.text: Expand and contract: add the new column; deploy code that writes both; backfill in batches; deploy code that reads the new one; when nothing uses the old column, drop it. At each step the previous release still works, so code rollback is always safe.

blocks.title: Why can a simple ALTER TABLE take down a busy site?
blocks.text: It needs an exclusive lock on the table. If a long transaction holds any lock on it, the ALTER waits, and every later query on that table queues behind the ALTER. A lock timeout turns that pile-up into a quick, retryable failure.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A script deletes rows from production at 09:00. Which protects you?
quiz.why: Replicas applied the delete too. Only going back in time recovers the rows.

quiz.q: During a rolling deploy, the schema must work with…
quiz.why: Old and new pods run side by side for the length of the rollout.

quiz.q: A backup that has never been restored is…
quiz.why: Until a restore succeeds you do not know that it can.

modules.title: Redis, Kafka and RabbitMQ Operations
modules.summary: Caching, expiry and eviction; partitions, consumer groups and lag; queues, acknowledgements and dead-lettering. Not yet covered: running the clusters themselves (Redis Cluster, Kafka brokers).

lessons.title: Redis: caching, expiry, eviction and what happens when it is gone

blocks.text: Redis keeps data in memory, so reading it takes well under a millisecond. The most common use is a cache: keep a copy of something that is slow to compute or fetch, with an expiry time, and serve the copy instead. A cache makes things fast. It also hides how much load the database would get without it, which matters on the day the cache is empty.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A chef's prep counter. Chopped onions and sauces within arm's reach, instead of walking to the store room for every order. The counter is small, so only what is used most stays on it, and things are thrown out after a while so nothing goes stale. If the counter is swept clean at the height of dinner service, every order needs a trip to the store room at once and the kitchen stops.
Why it matters

Many requests ask for the same things: the product page of a best-seller, a user's session, a price list. Computing each answer once and reusing it removes most of the work from the database and most of the latency from the response. The costs are staleness, and a new way to fail.
Where you meet it

Sessions and carts, product and price lookups, rate limiting, feature flags, queues for background jobs, leaderboards, distributed locks. As a service: ElastiCache, Memorystore, Azure Cache for Redis. Valkey is an open-source fork with the same commands.
Scenario

checkout-api looks up each product in the basket. With Redis in front, nine out of ten lookups never reach PostgreSQL, and the database was sized accordingly. One evening Redis restarts and comes back empty. Every lookup is now a miss, the database receives ten times its normal load, and checkout goes down, not because the cache is needed for correctness, but because the database can no longer carry the traffic alone.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR APP["checkout-api"] -->|"1. GET product:812"| R["Redis
in memory, sub-millisecond"] R -->|"2a. hit: return it"| APP R -. "2b. miss" .-> APP APP -->|"3. on a miss: SELECT ..."| DB[("PostgreSQL
source of truth")] DB --> APP APP -->|"4. SET product:812 ... EX 300"| R ADMIN["Price update"] -->|"write"| DB ADMIN -->|"then DEL product:812"| R subgraph RED["Redis"] R MEM["maxmemory + eviction policy"] REP["Replica (asynchronous)"] end R -.-> REP

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Request needs product 812"] --> B{"Is Redis reachable
within the timeout?"} B -->|"no"| DBQ["Read the database"] B -->|"yes"| C{"Is the key present
and not expired?"} C -->|"hit"| RET["Return the cached value"] C -->|"miss"| DBQ DBQ --> D{"Did the database answer?"} D -->|"no"| ERR["Fail the request, or serve
a stale copy if one is kept"] D -->|"yes"| E["Try to store it with a TTL"] E --> F{"Is memory full?"} F -->|"no"| OK["Stored"] F -->|"yes, allkeys-lru"| EV["Least recently used key evicted,
new value stored"] F -->|"yes, noeviction"| REJ["Write refused. Value not cached.
The request still succeeds"] OK --> RET2["Return the value"] EV --> RET2 REJ --> RET2

blocks.text: Commands
Checks that Redis answers.
Counters since start: hits, misses and evictions. Hit ratio is hits divided by hits plus misses. A rising evicted_keys means memory is full.
Memory in use, the limit, and what happens when the limit is reached.
Seconds until a key expires. -1 means it has no expiry; -2 means it does not exist.
Lists keys matching a pattern a little at a time, without blocking the server. Use this, never KEYS, on a production instance.
The ten most recent commands that took longer than the configured threshold. Redis runs commands one at a time, so one slow command delays every client.
Stores a value that expires in 300 seconds. On a production cache this changes what customers see until it expires.
Removes one key. The next read is a miss and repopulates it from the database. The normal way to invalidate after an update.
Returns every key in one blocking operation. On a large instance it freezes all clients for seconds. Do not run it in production.
Deletes everything in every database of this Redis. For a cache this is a self-inflicted stampede; for Redis used as a store it is data loss.
Cache-aside in checkout-api (illustrative Python)
Three details carry most of the reliability: a short timeout so a slow Redis cannot hold requests, treating every Redis error as a miss, and a random spread on the expiry.
Exercise
Find the settings that decide the hit ratio in the Cache lab, then take Redis away.

items: Note the hit ratio and the peak database load with the starting settings
Press "TTL of 2 seconds". Why did the hit ratio fall although nothing else changed?
Press "Cache holds 100 items", then "Full, with noeviction". Compare the two. Which policy suits a cache, and why is the other the default?
Press "Every item equally popular". What does this say about which data is worth caching?
Press "Redis is down". Then raise "Database capacity" until the database copes. What does that number mean for capacity planning?
In the last section, switch protection from none to a lock. How many identical queries does one expiry cause in each case?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain the hit ratio in terms of TTL, memory and popularity, choose an eviction policy, and describe what a cache outage does to the database.
Troubleshooting

rows: Low hit ratio
TTLs shorter than the gap between requests for the same key, keys that are too specific (a user id in a key for shared data), or frequent invalidation.
Look at which keys miss. Lengthen TTLs where staleness is acceptable and make keys as general as the data.
OOM command not allowed when used memory > maxmemory
Memory is full and the policy is noeviction.
For a cache set an eviction policy such as allkeys-lru. For a store, add memory or remove data; evicting would lose it.
Latency spikes on every client at once
A slow command blocks the single command thread: KEYS, a huge collection read in one go, or a large delete.
Check SLOWLOG. Use SCAN, read large structures in pages, and UNLINK instead of DEL for big keys.
The database falls over when the cache restarts
The database was sized for traffic after caching, and an empty cache sends it everything.
Keep database headroom, warm the cache before taking traffic, limit concurrency towards the database, and use replicas and persistence so a restart is not an empty start.
Customers see old prices
The database was updated and the cached copy was not invalidated, or the invalidation raced with a concurrent read.
Delete the key after the database write and keep TTLs as a backstop. Accept that a cache means bounded staleness, and choose the bound.
A burst of identical slow queries at regular intervals
A popular key expires and many requests rebuild it at once.
A lock or single-flight around the rebuild, serve-stale-while-refreshing, and random spread on TTLs.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Every cached key has a TTL.
Treat the cache as optional: any Redis error is a miss, and the request still succeeds.
Set short client timeouts so a slow cache cannot make everything slow.
Cache what is read often and changes rarely. Measure the hit ratio; do not assume it.
allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for caches; keep data that must not be lost in a separate instance with noeviction and persistence.
Know what your database can carry with a cold cache, and test it.
Namespace keys (product:812, cart:u-48211) and keep values small.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never expose Redis to the internet. It was designed for trusted networks.
Require authentication and TLS, and use ACLs to limit commands per application.
Disable or rename dangerous commands such as FLUSHALL and KEYS for application users.
Cached values are copies of your data: sessions, tokens and personal details sit in memory and in persistence files.
Do not cache one user's private data under a key another user can reach: include the user in the key.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain the cache-aside pattern.
blocks.text: The application reads the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL and returns it. On updates it writes the database and deletes the cached key. The cache holds only what was asked for, and the application keeps working, more slowly, if the cache is unavailable.

blocks.title: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
blocks.text: When a hot key expires or the cache is emptied, many requests miss at once and all run the same expensive query, overloading the database. Prevent it with a lock so one request rebuilds, by serving the stale value while refreshing, by spreading TTLs randomly, and by limiting concurrency towards the database.

blocks.title: Which eviction policy would you choose?
blocks.text: For a cache, allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu: when memory is full, drop what is least useful. noeviction refuses writes, which is right when Redis holds data that must not vanish, such as a job queue. Mixing both uses in one instance forces a bad compromise, so separate them.

blocks.title: Redis is single-threaded. What does that mean in operation?
blocks.text: Commands execute one at a time, so each is atomic and there are no locks, but one slow command delays everyone. Avoid KEYS, huge range reads and big blocking deletes; use SCAN, paging and UNLINK; watch SLOWLOG.

blocks.title: Your Redis cache is lost. What happens and how should the system be designed for it?
blocks.text: All reads fall through to the database. If it was sized assuming a 90 percent hit ratio it gets ten times the load and may fail, turning a cache outage into a full outage. Design with database headroom, concurrency limits, cache warming, replicas with failover, and load tests with a cold cache.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: The cache has a 90% hit ratio and then restarts empty. Database load…
options: jumps to roughly ten times normal
quiz.why: The database was serving one request in ten. Now it serves all of them.

quiz.q: For a pure cache, the sensible maxmemory-policy is…
quiz.why: When full, drop the least recently used entry and keep working.

quiz.q: On a production Redis, to list keys by pattern you use…
quiz.why: SCAN iterates in small steps. KEYS blocks every client until it finishes.

lessons.title: Kafka: partitions, consumer groups and lag

blocks.text: Kafka is a durable log of events. Producers append events to a topic. Consumers read them at their own pace and remember how far they have got. A topic is split into partitions so several consumers can share the work. Consumer lag is the number of events written but not yet processed: the one number that tells you whether consumers are keeping up.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A row of conveyor belts in a parcel depot. Each belt is a partition. Parcels with the same postcode always go on the same belt, so they arrive in order. Each belt is unloaded by exactly one worker at a time, though one worker may tend several belts. Lag is the parcels sitting on the belts. More workers than belts means some stand idle. If one postcode ships half of all parcels, its belt backs up no matter how many workers you hire.
Why it matters

When checkout calls email, inventory, analytics and fraud checks directly, checkout is as slow and as fragile as the worst of them. Publishing one "order placed" event and letting each team consume it decouples them: checkout stays fast, a consumer that is down catches up later, and new consumers can be added without touching checkout.
Where you meet it

Order and payment events, activity streams, change data capture from databases, log and metric pipelines, feeding search indexes and data warehouses. As a service: Amazon MSK, Confluent Cloud, Azure Event Hubs with its Kafka endpoint.
Scenario

During a sale the order rate doubles. The order-worker group cannot keep up and lag grows: confirmation emails arrive ten minutes late, then thirty. Adding consumers helps until there are as many consumers as partitions. Then one large corporate customer places 60 percent of all orders; every one of its events lands in the same partition, and that partition falls behind while the others are idle.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR P["checkout-api
(producer)"] -->|"key = customer id"| T subgraph T["Topic order-events (replication factor 3)"] P0["partition 0
leader on broker 1"] P1["partition 1
leader on broker 2"] P2["partition 2
leader on broker 3"] end subgraph G1["Consumer group order-worker"] C1["consumer 1"] C2["consumer 2"] end subgraph G2["Consumer group analytics"] A1["consumer"] end P0 --> C1 P1 --> C1 P2 --> C2 P0 --> A1 P1 --> A1 P2 --> A1 C1 -->|"commit offsets"| OFF["__consumer_offsets"] C2 --> OFF CTRL["Controller quorum (KRaft)
cluster metadata, leader election"] -. manages .-> T

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Partitions of a topic with the leader, the replicas and which replicas are in sync (ISR). A partition whose ISR is smaller than its replica list is under-replicated.

blocks.code:
Topic: order-events  PartitionCount: 6  ReplicationFactor: 3
  Partition: 0  Leader: 1  Replicas: 1,2,3  Isr: 1,2,3
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: The key command for lag. Per partition: the committed offset, the end of the log, the difference (LAG) and which consumer owns it.

blocks.code:
TOPIC         PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG    CONSUMER-ID
order-events  0          1048210         1069433         21223  worker-7c9f-1
order-events  1          1050117         1050119         2      worker-7c9f-1
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: Every consumer group known to the cluster.
Prints the next five events from one partition without joining a group, so it does not disturb real consumers. Event bodies may contain customer data.
Creates a topic that survives the loss of one broker with no data loss when producers use acks=all.
Adds partitions. They can never be removed, and events for the same key may now go to a different partition than before, which breaks per-key ordering across the change.
Moves the group's position to the end of the log: every unprocessed event is skipped for this group. Works only while the group is stopped. Run it with --dry-run first.
Deletes the topic and all its events for every consumer.
A consumer that commits after the work (illustrative Python)

blocks.code:
from confluent_kafka import Consumer

consumer = Consumer({
    "bootstrap.servers": "kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092,kafka-3:9092",
    "group.id": "order-worker",
    "enable.auto.commit": False,        # commit only after the work is done
    "auto.offset.reset": "earliest",    # a brand new group starts from the oldest message
})
consumer.subscribe(["order-events"])

while True:
    msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
    if msg is None:
        continue
    if msg.error():
        log.error("consume failed: %s", msg.error())
        continue

    order = json.loads(msg.value())

    # The same message can arrive twice (a crash before the commit below).
    # Make the work safe to repeat: skip orders already handled.
    if already_processed(order["order_id"]):
        consumer.commit(msg)
        continue

    send_confirmation_email(order)
    mark_processed(order["order_id"])
    consumer.commit(msg)                # "I am done up to here"

blocks.text: Committing after processing gives at-least-once delivery: a crash between the work and the commit means the event is delivered again. That is why the handler checks whether the order was already processed.
Exercise
Create and cure three different kinds of lag in the Kafka lab.

items: Step a few times and confirm lag stays at zero. What is the group's capacity compared with the arrival rate?
Double the order rate and step five times. By how much does lag grow per step, and why exactly that much?
Add consumers one at a time, stepping in between. What happens to lag during each rebalance? When does a consumer become idle?
Reset. Press "One customer sends 60% of events" and run. Where is the lag? Add a consumer. Did it help?
Reset. Crash a consumer and read the log. Where do the redelivered messages come from, and why were none lost?
Slow down a consumer. Which partitions lag? What would an alert on total lag miss here?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can read a lag table, say whether adding consumers will help, and explain redelivery after a crash.
Troubleshooting

rows: Lag grows steadily
Events arrive faster than the group processes them.
Add consumers up to the partition count, speed up processing, or add partitions. Check first whether the lag is in one partition.
The group rebalances over and over and makes no progress
Processing a batch takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so the consumer is considered dead and removed, which triggers a rebalance, and so on.
Reduce max.poll.records, raise the interval, or move slow work off the polling thread.
The same event is processed twice
A consumer crashed or was rebalanced after doing the work and before committing. This is normal at-least-once behaviour.
Make handlers idempotent: record processed ids, or use upserts.
Producers get NotEnoughReplicas errors
With acks=all, fewer replicas are in sync than min.insync.replicas requires, usually because brokers are down.
Restore the brokers. The error is Kafka refusing to accept writes it could lose.
Events for one customer arrive out of order
They were produced with different keys or no key, so they went to different partitions. Order is guaranteed only within a partition.
Use the entity id as the key for everything that must stay in order.
A consumer that was offline for a week finds its events gone
They were older than the topic's retention and were deleted.
Retention must exceed the longest outage you intend to survive. Alert on lag measured in time, not only in messages.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Choose the key deliberately: it decides ordering and how evenly load spreads.
Size partitions for the consumer parallelism you will need; adding them later breaks key ordering.
Replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 2 and acks=all for events you cannot lose.
Commit after processing and make consumers idempotent.
Alert on lag per partition and on its trend, not on a fixed total.
Send events that repeatedly fail to a dead-letter topic so one bad event cannot block a partition.
Version event schemas and keep changes backwards compatible.

blocks.text: Security

items: Encrypt connections with TLS and authenticate clients (SASL or mutual TLS).
Use ACLs so each service can read or write only its own topics and groups.
Events often carry personal data and are kept for days. Minimise what goes in and set retention accordingly.
Anyone who can reset a group's offsets can make it skip or replay everything. Restrict that right.
Brokers belong in private networks.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is consumer lag and how do you reduce it?
blocks.text: The difference, per partition, between the latest offset written and the offset the group has committed. Reduce it by adding consumers up to the number of partitions, making each event cheaper to process, fixing slow downstream calls, or adding partitions. If lag is concentrated in one partition the cause is a hot key or a slow consumer and more consumers do not help.

blocks.title: How do partitions and consumer groups relate?
blocks.text: Within a group each partition is read by exactly one consumer, and a consumer may read several partitions. So the partition count is the upper limit on parallelism for a group. Different groups read the same topic independently, each with its own offsets.

blocks.title: What delivery guarantees does Kafka give?
blocks.text: At-least-once by default when you commit after processing: nothing is lost, duplicates are possible. At-most-once if you commit before processing. Exactly-once processing is available within Kafka through idempotent producers and transactions, but effects outside Kafka still need idempotent handling.

blocks.title: What happens during a rebalance?
blocks.text: When consumers join, leave or time out, the group coordinator reassigns partitions. With the classic protocol all consumers stop and resume; with cooperative rebalancing only the partitions that move are paused. Frequent rebalances stall consumption.

blocks.title: How do you avoid losing events when a broker dies?
blocks.text: Replication factor of at least 3, producers with acks=all, and min.insync.replicas of 2, so a write is acknowledged only when it is on at least two brokers. Then losing one broker loses nothing, and losing two stops writes rather than silently losing them.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A topic has 6 partitions. A group has 8 consumers. How many do useful work?
quiz.why: One consumer per partition at most. The other two are idle.

quiz.q: Lag is large in partition 0 and zero elsewhere. Adding consumers…
quiz.why: One partition is read by one consumer. The cause is a hot key or a slow consumer.

quiz.q: A consumer crashes after processing an event and before committing. That event is…
quiz.why: At-least-once: the next owner of the partition starts from the last commit.

lessons.title: RabbitMQ and choosing between a queue and a log

blocks.text: RabbitMQ is a message broker built around queues of work. A producer sends a message to an exchange, which routes it into one or more queues. A worker takes a message, does the job and acknowledges it, and only then does the broker delete it. If the worker dies first, the message goes back in the queue. It differs from Kafka in one important way: a message is a task to be done once and then removed, not an entry in a log that many readers can replay.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A restaurant kitchen's ticket rail. The waiter (producer) hands an order to the pass (exchange), which clips it to the right station's rail (queue): grill, salads or both. A cook takes a ticket, cooks, and spikes the ticket when the plate goes out (acknowledge). If the cook walks off mid-order, the ticket goes back on the rail. A ticket nobody can cook after several tries goes to the manager's tray (dead-letter queue).
Why it matters

Some work should not happen inside a web request: sending an email, generating an invoice PDF, calling a slow partner API. Putting a message on a queue lets the request return at once, lets workers retry failures, and lets you add workers when the queue grows. The broker guarantees the job is not forgotten if a worker crashes.
Where you meet it

Background jobs, email and notification sending, task distribution to workers, request buffering in front of slow systems, routing by topic or type. Managed alternatives in the same role: Amazon SQS, Azure Service Bus, Google Cloud Tasks.
Scenario

After an order is paid, checkout-api publishes an "order.paid" message. The exchange routes a copy to the email queue and a copy to the invoice queue. The email provider has an outage: email workers fail and requeue their messages, the email queue grows to 40,000, and invoices are unaffected because they have their own queue. One malformed message crashes every worker that picks it up; after five deliveries it is moved to the dead-letter queue and the rest flow again.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR P["checkout-api
(publisher)"] -->|"routing key order.paid"| X{{"Exchange: orders
type topic"}} X -->|"binding order.*"| Q1["Queue email.send
quorum, replicated"] X -->|"binding order.paid"| Q2["Queue invoice.create"] Q1 --> W1["Email worker 1
prefetch 10"] Q1 --> W2["Email worker 2
prefetch 10"] Q2 --> W3["Invoice worker"] W1 -->|"ack: delete"| Q1 W1 -. "nack or crash: requeue" .-> Q1 Q1 -. "delivery limit reached" .-> DLX{{"Dead-letter exchange"}} DLX --> DLQ["Queue email.failed
for a person to inspect"]

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Confirms the broker application is running on this node.
Version, memory and disk use against their alarm thresholds, listeners and uptime.

blocks.code: rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages_ready messages_unacknowledged consumers
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: The first thing to look at. Ready: waiting for a worker. Unacknowledged: handed to a worker and not finished. Consumers: how many workers are attached.

blocks.code:
name            messages_ready  messages_unacknowledged  consumers
email.send      40213           20                       2
invoice.create  0               1                        1
email.failed    3               0                        0
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: Client connections. A state of "blocked" or "blocking" means the broker is holding publishers back because memory or disk is short.
Which exchanges feed which queues, and with what routing keys. A message published where nothing is bound is silently dropped unless it is marked mandatory.
Shows one message from a queue through the management API. By default the message is requeued afterwards, but its redelivered flag changes. Bodies can hold customer data.
Deletes every ready message in a queue. Those jobs will never be done.
Deletes the queue, its messages and its bindings.
A worker with acknowledgements, prefetch and a dead-letter queue (illustrative Python)

blocks.code:
import pika

conn = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.URLParameters(AMQP_URL))
ch = conn.channel()

# Messages that fail repeatedly go here instead of looping forever.
ch.exchange_declare("dlx", exchange_type="fanout", durable=True)
ch.queue_declare("email.failed", durable=True)
ch.queue_bind("email.failed", "dlx")

ch.queue_declare(
    "email.send",
    durable=True,                                # the queue survives a broker restart
    arguments={
        "x-queue-type": "quorum",                # replicated across nodes
        "x-dead-letter-exchange": "dlx",
        "x-delivery-limit": 5,                   # after 5 failed deliveries, dead-letter it
    },
)

ch.basic_qos(prefetch_count=10)                  # at most 10 unacknowledged messages per worker

def handle(ch, method, properties, body):
    try:
        send_email(json.loads(body))
        ch.basic_ack(method.delivery_tag)        # done: the broker deletes the message
    except TemporaryFailure:
        ch.basic_nack(method.delivery_tag, requeue=True)    # try again later
    except Exception:
        ch.basic_nack(method.delivery_tag, requeue=False)   # poison message: dead-letter it

ch.basic_consume("email.send", on_message_callback=handle)
ch.start_consuming()

blocks.text: Prefetch is back-pressure: a worker is never handed more than ten unfinished jobs, so a slow worker cannot hoard the queue and a crash requeues at most ten.
Exercise
Read the state of the email queue from the lesson's example output and decide what to do, then compare the model with Kafka.

items: From the list_queues output: how many messages wait, how many are in progress, and how many workers are there?
Ready is high and unacknowledged equals workers times prefetch. What does that tell you about the workers?
Ready is zero and unacknowledged keeps growing. What is different, and what would you check?
A message crashes every worker that receives it. Trace it through the architecture diagram until it stops causing harm
Use the decision flowchart for: sending emails; an audit trail every team reads; resizing uploaded images; feeding a search index and analytics from the same order events
In the Kafka lag lab, name two things the consumer group does that a RabbitMQ queue does differently

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain exchange, queue, binding, acknowledgement, prefetch and dead-lettering, and justify choosing a queue or a log for a given job.
Troubleshooting

rows: A queue grows without limit
Workers are down, too few, or slower than the publishing rate. Sometimes one poison message keeps crashing them.
Check the consumers column and worker logs. Add workers, fix the downstream system, and make sure a delivery limit and dead-letter queue exist.
Messages stay unacknowledged for a long time
Workers took them and are stuck, or the code never acknowledges.
Check worker health and that every path acknowledges or rejects. Unacknowledged messages return to the queue when the worker's connection closes.
Publishers hang
A memory or disk alarm: the broker blocks publishers to protect itself, usually because queues have grown too large.
Drain the queues (more workers), free disk, and set queue length limits so this cannot recur.
Published messages vanish
No queue is bound for that routing key, or the queue or message was not durable and the broker restarted.
Check bindings. Use durable queues, persistent messages and publisher confirms.
The same job runs twice
A worker finished the job but the acknowledgement was lost, so the message was delivered again.
Make jobs idempotent, exactly as with Kafka.
One worker has all the messages and the others idle
No prefetch limit: the broker pushed everything to the first worker to connect.
Set a prefetch count.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Acknowledge manually, after the work is done.
Set a prefetch count on every worker.
Give every queue a delivery limit and a dead-letter queue, and alert when the dead-letter queue is not empty.
Durable, replicated (quorum) queues and persistent messages for work that must not be lost.
Use publisher confirms so the producer knows the broker has the message.
Keep queues short. A broker is a buffer, not a database: alert on depth and on message age.
One queue per kind of work, so a problem in one does not delay the others.

blocks.text: Security

items: Remove the default guest account; one user per application with rights to its own exchanges and queues only.
TLS on client connections and between nodes.
The management interface is an admin console: never on the internet, behind single sign-on where possible.
Messages can contain personal data and sit on disk. Keep payloads minimal and queues short.
Whoever can purge queues can destroy work silently. Limit that permission.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does RabbitMQ differ from Kafka?
blocks.text: RabbitMQ is a queue broker: it routes messages to queues, pushes them to workers, and deletes each one when acknowledged. It offers flexible routing, per-message acknowledgement and retries. Kafka is a partitioned log: events are kept for a retention period, consumers track their own position and can replay, and many groups read the same events. Queues suit tasks; logs suit event streams and high throughput.

blocks.title: What are exchanges, queues and bindings?
blocks.text: Producers publish to an exchange with a routing key. Bindings connect exchanges to queues with a pattern. The exchange type decides matching: direct matches the key exactly, topic matches patterns, fanout copies to every bound queue. Consumers read from queues.

blocks.title: What does prefetch do?
blocks.text: It limits how many unacknowledged messages the broker will give one consumer. It spreads work fairly, provides back-pressure, and bounds how much is redelivered if a worker crashes.

blocks.title: What is a dead-letter queue for?
blocks.text: A place for messages that cannot be processed: rejected without requeue, expired, or delivered too many times. It stops a poison message from blocking the queue forever and keeps it for inspection.

blocks.title: A queue has two million messages. What do you do?
blocks.text: Find out why consumption fell behind: consumers missing, slow, or crash-looping on a poison message. Restore consumption and scale workers. Decide with the owners whether old messages are still worth processing. Afterwards add length limits, message TTLs and alerts on depth and age.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A worker crashes after receiving a message and before acknowledging it. The message is…
quiz.why: Unacknowledged messages are requeued when the worker's connection closes.

quiz.q: Several teams need to consume the same order events, and a new team must be able to process last week's as well. Choose…
quiz.why: Replay and independent consumers are what a log provides.

quiz.q: A message that fails every time should end up…
quiz.why: Out of the way of healthy messages, and kept for someone to look at.

modules.summary: Metrics and Prometheus, RED and USE, dashboards, alert rules, Alertmanager and burn rate. Not yet covered: Grafana dashboards as code, long-term storage in depth.

lessons.title: Metrics and Prometheus: rate, errors, duration

blocks.text: A metric is a number measured over and over: requests served, errors returned, memory used. Prometheus collects these numbers from every service every few seconds and stores them with a timestamp, so you can ask "how many requests per second, how many failed, and how slow were they" for any moment. For a service, those three questions, rate, errors and duration, tell you most of what you need.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A car dashboard. Speed, fuel, engine temperature: a few numbers, read constantly, that tell you whether things are fine without opening the bonnet. They do not tell you why the engine is hot. They tell you that you need to stop and look, and roughly where.
Why it matters

Without measurements you learn about problems from customers. With them you see an error rate rise within a minute of a bad deploy, can prove that a change made things faster, and know how close the system is to its limits before it reaches them. Metrics are cheap to keep because they are numbers, not text, so you can keep all of them.
Where you meet it

Every service, node, database and queue in production. In Kubernetes, Prometheus discovers pods automatically and scrapes them; node and cluster state come from exporters. Managed versions exist in every cloud.
Scenario

checkout-api exposes a /metrics page with a request counter and a histogram of response times, both labelled with route and status code. Prometheus scrapes it every 15 seconds. A release at 14:00 breaks one code path. On the dashboard the error line leaves the floor at 14:01, the rate stays flat and the duration is unchanged: within a minute you know it is errors, not load and not slowness, and that it began with the deploy.
Architecture

flowchart LR subgraph TARGETS["Things that expose /metrics"] APP["checkout-api pods
counters, histograms"] NODE["node_exporter
CPU, memory, disk"] KSM["kube-state-metrics
pods, deployments"] PG["postgres_exporter"] end SD["Service discovery
(Kubernetes API)"] --> PROM PROM["Prometheus
scrapes every 15 s,
stores time series"] -->|"pull: HTTP GET /metrics"| APP PROM --> NODE PROM --> KSM PROM --> PG PROM -->|"evaluates rules"| AM["Alertmanager"] GRAF["Grafana dashboards"] -->|"PromQL queries"| PROM PROM -->|"remote write"| LTS["Long-term storage
(Mimir, Thanos, a managed service)"]

and stores value + timestamp"] B --> C["A counter only goes up.

Shows what a service exposes: plain text, one line per time series, with a HELP and TYPE comment for each metric.
Validates the Prometheus configuration file and any rule files it names, before you deploy it.

blocks.code: SUCCESS: prometheus.yml is valid prometheus config file syntax
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: Every scrape target with its health and the last error. The same information as the Status, Targets page. Needs jq.
Runs a PromQL query through the HTTP API. "up" is 1 for each target that answered its last scrape and 0 for each that did not.
Requests per second across all checkout-api pods, averaged over five minutes.
Makes an in-cluster Prometheus reachable at localhost:9090 while the command runs. The service name depends on how Prometheus was installed.
How many distinct metric names Prometheus holds. A quick view of how much is being collected.
