examples/monitoring/lab10/prometheus.yml

blocks.code:
# What to scrape, and how often. Each target must serve metrics at /metrics.
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
  evaluation_interval: 15s

rule_files:
  - /etc/prometheus/rules.yml

scrape_configs:
  # Prometheus measures itself: its own HTTP requests, memory and scrapes.
  - job_name: prometheus
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["localhost:9090"]

  # Grafana also exposes metrics. "grafana" is its service name on the Compose network.
  - job_name: grafana
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["grafana:3000"]

blocks.text: The file from Lab 10. In Kubernetes the static target lists are replaced by service discovery, but the idea is identical: a list of jobs, each a set of addresses to scrape.
Exercise
Read rate, errors and duration for five different hours of checkout-api in the Metrics lab.

items: Select "A normal hour". Read the three charts and write down what normal looks like
Select the bad deploy. Which of the three charts moves? At which minute does it start to move, and when does it reach its plateau?
The fault began at minute 20 exactly. Why does the line rise gradually over five minutes?
Select "Slow database". Which chart moves now, and which stay flat?
Select the traffic surge. All three move. In what order would you explain cause and effect?
Why are the first five minutes of every chart empty?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can say what rate() does to a counter, read an error ratio and a 95th percentile from a chart, and tell load, errors and slowness apart.
Troubleshooting

rows: A target shows as DOWN
Prometheus cannot reach the address, the path is not /metrics, or a network policy or firewall blocks the scrape.
Read the error on the Targets page. Curl the same URL from inside the Prometheus pod.
A query returns nothing
A label does not match (job name, namespace), the range is shorter than two scrapes, or the metric name is different from what you assumed.
Query the bare metric name first, look at the labels it really has, then add filters one at a time.
Prometheus uses more and more memory
High cardinality: a label with many distinct values, such as a user id or a full URL path, creates one time series per value.
Find the largest metrics, remove or bound the offending label. Never put unbounded values in labels.
Graphs show a sudden dip to zero or a huge spike
A counter reset when a pod restarted, read without rate(), or a gap in scraping.
Always wrap counters in rate() or increase(), which handle resets.
The 95th percentile is a suspiciously round number
It is the upper edge of a histogram bucket. The real value is somewhere inside that bucket.
Choose bucket boundaries around the latencies you care about, or use native histograms.
Data older than two weeks is gone
Local storage keeps data for a limited time, 15 days by default.
Send data to long-term storage with remote write, or raise the retention with matching disk.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Instrument every service with the same three: request rate, error rate, duration histogram.
For resources (CPU, disk, connection pools) track utilisation, saturation and errors.
Keep label values bounded: route templates, not raw URLs; status class, not user id.
Use histograms for latency, never averages. An average hides the slow tail that customers feel.
Name metrics with units and the _total suffix for counters: http_request_duration_seconds, http_requests_total.
Build one dashboard per service with the same layout, so anyone on call can read any of them.
Monitor the monitoring: alert when Prometheus cannot scrape or is itself down.

blocks.text: Security

items: The /metrics page can reveal internal names, versions and traffic volumes. Do not expose it to the internet.
Never put secrets, tokens or personal data in metric names or label values.
Restrict who can reach Prometheus and Grafana; both show the shape of your whole system.
Protect the reload and admin APIs.
In a shared Prometheus, one team's high-cardinality metric can take monitoring down for everyone. Set per-target sample limits.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What are the metric types in Prometheus?
blocks.text: Counter: only increases, such as requests served; read it with rate(). Gauge: goes up and down, such as memory in use. Histogram: counts observations into buckets, such as response times, from which quantiles are estimated and which can be aggregated across instances. Summary: quantiles computed in the client, which cannot be aggregated.

blocks.title: Why does Prometheus pull instead of having services push?
blocks.text: Prometheus decides what to scrape and how often, so it knows at once when a target is missing ("up" becomes 0), services need no knowledge of the monitoring system, and you can open any target's /metrics page in a browser to debug. Short-lived jobs that cannot be scraped push to a gateway instead.

blocks.title: What are RED and USE?
blocks.text: RED is for request-driven services: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE is for resources: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors. RED tells you whether users are affected; USE helps find which resource is the cause.

blocks.title: How is a 95th percentile computed from a histogram?
blocks.text: The histogram counts requests under each bucket boundary. Take the rate of each bucket, find the bucket where the cumulative count crosses 95 percent, and interpolate linearly inside it. It is an estimate whose accuracy depends on the bucket boundaries.

blocks.title: What is cardinality and why does it matter?
blocks.text: The number of distinct time series, which is the product of the distinct values of every label. Each series costs memory. One unbounded label, such as a user id, can create millions of series and bring Prometheus down.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: http_requests_total is a counter. To see requests per second you use…
quiz.why: rate() turns an ever-growing count into a per-second speed and handles restarts.

quiz.q: Why is an average response time a poor signal?
options: It hides the slow requests some customers get
quiz.why: A few very slow requests barely move the average. Percentiles show the tail.

quiz.q: Which label is dangerous to add to a metric?
quiz.why: One time series per user: unbounded cardinality.

lessons.title: Dashboards and alerts that page for the right reasons

blocks.text: A dashboard is for looking at when you already suspect something. An alert is for when nobody is looking. A good alert means a person must do something now, says what is wrong for customers, and links to what to do. Everything else belongs on a dashboard or in a ticket. The hardest part is not making alerts fire; it is making them fire only when they should.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A smoke alarm. One that goes off every time you make toast gets its battery taken out, and then it is silent in a real fire. One that waits ten minutes to be sure is useless. A good one is quiet for toast, loud for fire, and everyone in the house knows what to do when it sounds.
Why it matters

People who are paged at night for things that fix themselves, or that they cannot act on, stop trusting pages. That is alert fatigue, and it is how real incidents get missed. Good alerting protects both the customers and the people on call.
Where you meet it

Prometheus evaluates alert rules and sends firing alerts to Alertmanager, which groups them, silences what should be silent, and routes them to chat, email or a paging service. Grafana shows the dashboards and can alert as well.
Scenario

checkout-api has two rules. The first pages when more than 2 percent of requests fail for five minutes. The second opens a ticket when the 95th percentile stays above 800 ms for ten minutes. A dependency restarts and errors spike for three minutes: the first rule goes pending and then clears, and nobody is woken. A bad deploy raises errors to 8 percent and keeps them there: after five minutes someone is paged, with a link to the runbook.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR PROM["Prometheus
evaluates rules every 15 s"] -->|"firing alerts"| AM["Alertmanager"] subgraph AMX["Alertmanager"] AM --> GRP["Group: one notification
for 40 pods with the same problem"] GRP --> INH["Inhibit: cluster down
silences its consequences"] INH --> SIL["Silences: planned maintenance"] SIL --> RT{"Route by labels"} end RT -->|"severity=page"| PAGER["Paging service
on-call phone"] RT -->|"severity=ticket"| TICKET["Ticket queue"] RT -->|"everything"| CHAT["Team chat channel"] PAGER --> ONCALL["On-call engineer"] ONCALL --> RB["Runbook linked
from the alert"] ONCALL --> DASH["Grafana dashboard
for the service"]

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Validates a rule file: YAML structure and every PromQL expression.
Alerts that are pending or firing right now, with when each became active.
Every rule with its health (did the expression evaluate) and state.
What Alertmanager currently holds.
Active silences, who created them and when they end.

blocks.code: amtool --alertmanager.url=http://localhost:9093 silence add alertname=CheckoutSlowP95 --duration=2h --comment="database maintenance, change 4821"
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Stops notifications for matching alerts for two hours. The alert still fires and is recorded. Always give a duration and a reason.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: A silence that is too broad hides real incidents. Match on the specific alert and service.

blocks.code: amtool --alertmanager.url=http://localhost:9093 config routes test severity=page service=checkout-api
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Shows which receiver an alert with these labels would be routed to, without sending anything.
examples/monitoring/alerts.yaml

blocks.code:
# Prometheus alerting rules for checkout-api.
groups:
  - name: checkout-api
    rules:
      - alert: CheckoutHighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
            /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api"}[5m])) > 0.02
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "checkout-api is returning more than 2% errors"
          runbook: "https://runbooks.example.com/checkout-high-error-rate"
      - alert: CheckoutSlowP95
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout-api"}[5m]))) > 0.8
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: ticket
        annotations:
          summary: "checkout-api p95 latency is above 800ms"

blocks.text: Both rules alert on what customers experience, not on a cause such as CPU. Each has a "for" so brief blips do not notify, a severity label that Alertmanager routes on, and the page carries a runbook link.
Exercise
Tune the two alert rules in the Metrics lab until they notify for the right hours and stay quiet for the others.

items: Run all five hours with the original rules. For each, note which alert fired and how many minutes after the fault began
Select the 3-minute blip. The page stays pending. Change "for: 5m" to "for: 1m". What happens, and is that better or worse?
Restore. Select the bad deploy and raise the error threshold to 0.1. What have you just done to your customers?
Select "Slow database". The latency rule takes a long time to fire. Add up where the delay comes from: the rate window, the "for", the evaluation
Use the error budget readout: at the peak of the bad deploy, how fast is a 99.9 percent target's budget being spent?
Write a one-line summary and a first runbook step for CheckoutHighErrorRate

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain pending versus firing, the trade-off in the "for" duration, and why these rules measure symptoms.
Troubleshooting

rows: People are paged for things that resolve themselves
No "for" duration, thresholds too tight, or alerts on causes rather than customer impact.
Add or lengthen "for", alert on error ratio and latency, and move the rest to tickets or dashboards.
An outage happened and no alert fired
The rule matched nothing (a label changed), the expression returns no data when the service is completely down, or the alert was silenced.
Add an alert for absent data and for "up == 0". Validate rules in CI. Review silences.
Forty notifications for one incident
No grouping: each pod's alert is sent separately.
Group by alert name and service in Alertmanager.
An alert flaps between firing and resolved
The value hovers around the threshold.
A longer "for", a longer rate window, or separate thresholds for firing and clearing.
The alert says something is wrong but not what to do
No summary, no runbook, no dashboard link.
Every page needs a summary in plain words, the affected service and a runbook URL.
A silence from last month is still active
Created with a very long duration and forgotten.
Short durations by default, a required comment, and a periodic review of active silences.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Page only when a person must act now. Everything else is a ticket or a dashboard.
Alert on symptoms customers feel: error ratio, latency, availability. Use causes for diagnosis.
Every page links to a runbook and a dashboard.
Alert on error budget burn rate: fast burn pages, slow burn opens a ticket.
Review every page after it happens: was it actionable? If not, fix the alert.
Keep alert rules in Git, validated in CI, and deployed like code.
A standard dashboard per service: rate, errors, duration on top, resources below, deploy markers on every graph.

blocks.text: Security

items: Alert text goes to chat and phones. Do not put secrets or personal data in labels or annotations.
Whoever can silence alerts can hide an attack in progress. Restrict and audit silences.
Webhook receivers are an outbound path from your monitoring. Limit where they can send.
Protect Alertmanager and Grafana with single sign-on; neither should be on the internet without it.
Alert on security signals too: a spike in 401 and 403 responses, or unexpected changes to permissions.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What makes a good alert?
blocks.text: It is actionable, urgent and about real or imminent user impact. It fires on a symptom, waits long enough to skip blips, says in plain words what is wrong, and links to a runbook. If the response is "ignore it" or "wait", it should not page.

blocks.title: What does the "for" clause do?
blocks.text: The expression must stay true for that long before the alert moves from pending to firing. It filters short spikes at the cost of slower detection, so its value is a deliberate trade between noise and delay.

blocks.title: What does Alertmanager do that Prometheus does not?
blocks.text: Prometheus decides that an alert is firing. Alertmanager decides who hears about it: it deduplicates and groups related alerts, inhibits consequences of a known bigger failure, applies silences, and routes by labels to the right receiver with retries.

blocks.title: What is burn-rate alerting?
blocks.text: Alerting on how fast the error budget of an SLO is being consumed. A burn rate of 1 uses the budget exactly over the SLO period. Page on a high rate over a short window, for example 14 times over an hour, and open a ticket for a low rate over days. It ties alerts directly to user impact and keeps them quiet when impact is small.

blocks.title: How do you reduce alert fatigue?
blocks.text: Delete or downgrade every alert that is not actionable, alert on symptoms, group and inhibit, add "for" durations, review each page in a weekly meeting, and measure pages per shift as a number the team owns.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: An alert is "pending". That means…
options: the condition is true but has not lasted the full "for" duration
quiz.why: Nobody is notified until it has stayed true long enough to fire.

quiz.q: Which is the better thing to page on?
options: More than 2 percent of checkout requests failing
quiz.why: It is what customers experience. The others are causes, and may harm nobody.

quiz.q: Grouping in Alertmanager is for…
options: sending one notification for many related alerts
quiz.why: Forty pods with the same problem should produce one message.

modules.title: Logging and Distributed Tracing
modules.summary: Structured, centralised logs with Loki and LogQL; traces, spans, context propagation, sampling and OpenTelemetry.

lessons.title: Centralised, structured logging

blocks.text: A log line records one thing that happened. With dozens of pods that come and go, logs on each machine are useless: they must be collected in one place and searchable. Writing each line as structured data, a JSON object with named fields, instead of a sentence, lets you filter by service, level, order or request the way you filter a spreadsheet.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A ship's logbook versus scraps of paper. If every sailor scribbles notes and keeps them in a pocket, nobody can reconstruct the voyage, and the notes of anyone who goes overboard are lost. One logbook, with the time, the watch and the event in fixed columns, can be read by anyone and searched for "all entries from the night watch about the engine".
Why it matters

Metrics tell you that the error rate rose. Logs tell you which order failed and with what message. In Kubernetes a pod's logs disappear when the pod does, usually exactly when you want them. Shipping them off the node as they are written is the only way to have them after a crash.
Where you meet it

Applications write to standard output. An agent on every node (Grafana Alloy, Fluent Bit, Vector or the OpenTelemetry Collector) reads the container log files, attaches labels such as namespace and pod, and sends them to a store: Loki, OpenSearch or Elasticsearch, or a cloud service.
Scenario

A customer says their payment was taken but no order appears. Support has the order reference. In the log store you search for it across all services and find one line from checkout-api with a trace id. Filtering on that trace id shows the whole story in eight lines from three services: payment succeeded, the order insert timed out, the retry was never attempted. Without central, structured logs that would have meant opening shells on pods that no longer exist.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph NODE["Each Kubernetes node"] P1["checkout-api pod
writes JSON to stdout"] P2["other pods"] F["Container log files
/var/log/pods/..."] AG["Log agent (DaemonSet)
adds namespace, pod, app labels"] P1 --> F P2 --> F F --> AG end AG -->|"batches over HTTP"| STORE subgraph STORE["Log store"] L["Loki: indexes labels only,
stores compressed chunks in object storage"] OS["or OpenSearch: indexes every word,
faster search, costs more to run"] end STORE --> G["Grafana / search UI"] STORE --> RET["Retention: 14 days hot,
older to cheap storage or deleted"] G --> ENG["Engineer"] STORE -->|"log-based alert rules"| AM["Alertmanager"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["You have one clue: an order id,
a user id or an error message"] --> B["Narrow by label first:
namespace, application, time range"] B --> C["Filter by text or by a parsed field"] C --> D{"Too many lines?"} D -->|"yes"| E["Add the level, a tighter time range,
or a more specific field"] E --> C D -->|"no"| F["Find a line for the failing request"] F --> G{"Does it carry a trace id
or request id?"} G -->|"no"| H["You can only guess which lines belong together.
Fix the logging"] G -->|"yes"| I["Search every service for that id"] I --> J["Read the lines in time order:
the story of one request"] J --> K["Open the trace for timing,
the metrics for how widespread it is"]

blocks.text: Commands
Recent logs from one pod of a Deployment. Useful for a quick look; it reads from the node, so it shows nothing for pods that are gone.
Logs from the previous run of a container that restarted. Often the only place the crash message survives.
The last lines from every pod with that label, each prefixed with its pod name.
Filters structured logs on a field and prints three fields. Works only because each line is JSON.
Loki's command-line client: lines from one application containing a text, over the last hour. The part in braces selects streams by label; what follows the pipe filters lines.
Every line from any service in the namespace that carries one trace id: one request, end to end.
A metric computed from logs: errors per application over five minutes. The basis for log-based alerts.
Deletes a pod. Its logs on the node go with it. If logs are not shipped centrally, read them before you restart anything.
Structured logging in checkout-api (illustrative Python)

blocks.code:
import json, logging, sys, time
from contextvars import ContextVar

# Set once per request by middleware, from the incoming traceparent header.
trace_id: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("trace_id", default="-")

class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        line = {
            "ts": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S", time.gmtime(record.created)) + f".{int(record.msecs):03d}Z",
            "level": record.levelname.lower(),
            "service": "checkout-api",
            "trace_id": trace_id.get(),
            "msg": record.getMessage(),
        }
        # Extra fields become their own keys, so they can be filtered on.
        line.update(getattr(record, "fields", {}))
        return json.dumps(line)

handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)   # stdout: the platform collects it
handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())
log = logging.getLogger("checkout")
log.addHandler(handler)
log.setLevel(logging.INFO)

# One event per line, with numbers as numbers:
log.info("order placed", extra={"fields": {"order_id": "ORD-7781", "total": 1299, "duration_ms": 142}})
# {"ts":"2026-11-11T12:00:03.142Z","level":"info","service":"checkout-api",
#  "trace_id":"4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736","msg":"order placed",
#  "order_id":"ORD-7781","total":1299,"duration_ms":142}

blocks.text: One line per event, written to standard output, with the same field names in every service. The trace id is what joins a log line to a trace and to the lines of other services.
Exercise
Follow one failed checkout through the logs in the Trace and log lab.

items: Select "Failed: payment provider down" and scroll to the Logs section. How many lines are there in total?
Set Level to "error". How many lines remain, and from which services?
Clear the level and press "Only this trace". Read the remaining lines in order and tell the story of the request
Read the LogQL shown above the log. Which part selects by label and which part filters by field?
Type "ORD" in Contains with all filters cleared. Which requests succeeded while this one failed?
Remove the trace id from every line in your head. How would you find the lines belonging to the failed request?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain why logs are structured and centralised, write a query that narrows by label, text and field, and use a trace id to isolate one request.
Troubleshooting

rows: Logs from a crashed pod are missing
They were only on the node, or the agent had not shipped the last lines before the pod was removed.
Check with kubectl logs --previous at once. Make sure the agent runs on every node and that applications flush on exit.
A multi-line stack trace appears as twenty separate lines
Each newline is treated as a new log entry.
Log the stack trace as one field of a JSON line, or configure multi-line parsing in the agent.
Queries are slow or time out
The query scans too much: a wide time range or no label selector.
Select by labels and a narrow time range first, then filter. In Loki the labels are the index.
The log store rejects data or runs out of resources
Too many label combinations, for example a request id used as a label.
Labels are for a small set of values: namespace, application, level. High-cardinality values belong inside the line.
The logging bill is far higher than expected
Debug logging left on, health checks logged on every probe, or retention longer than needed.
Info level in production, drop or sample noisy lines at the agent, and set retention by how long logs are useful.
Lines are present but cannot be filtered by field
They are free text, or services use different field names for the same thing.
Agree one schema: ts, level, service, trace_id, msg, plus named fields.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Write to standard output and let the platform collect. The application should not know where logs go.
One event per line, as JSON, with the same core fields in every service.
Put a trace id or request id on every line.
Log what happened and its identifiers, not long narratives. Numbers as numbers.
Use levels consistently: error means someone should look; info is normal business events; debug is off in production.
Do not log successful health checks.
Decide retention on purpose, and send audit logs to a separate, longer-lived, access-controlled store.

blocks.text: Security

items: Never log passwords, tokens, card numbers or full personal details. Mask them in code, and again at the agent as a backstop.
Logs are a copy of your data. Restrict who can read production logs.
Request and response bodies almost always contain something sensitive. Do not log them wholesale.
Audit logs must be tamper-resistant: a separate account, append-only storage.
User-supplied text in logs can forge lines or exploit viewers. Encoding lines as JSON neutralises most of that.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Why structured logging?
blocks.text: Each line is machine-readable with named fields, so it can be filtered, aggregated and joined reliably: all errors for one order, counts by status, lines for one trace. Free text needs fragile pattern matching and breaks when wording changes.

blocks.title: How do logs get from a pod to a central store in Kubernetes?
blocks.text: The container writes to standard output. The container runtime writes that to files on the node. An agent running as a DaemonSet tails those files, enriches lines with pod metadata and ships them to the store. The application is unaware of any of it.

blocks.title: Loki versus Elasticsearch or OpenSearch?
blocks.text: Loki indexes only labels and stores log content compressed in object storage, so it is cheap to run and you query by selecting streams then filtering. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch index the content of every line, so arbitrary text search is fast, at a much higher storage and operating cost.

blocks.title: How do you correlate logs across services for one request?
blocks.text: Generate or accept an id at the edge, propagate it on every downstream call (the W3C traceparent header does this), and include it in every log line. Searching for that id returns the request's lines from every service.

blocks.title: What should never be in logs?
blocks.text: Credentials, tokens, payment card data, and personal data beyond what is needed. Logs are copied widely, kept for a long time and read by many people, so they are a common source of leaks.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: In Kubernetes, an application should write its logs to…
quiz.why: The platform collects standard output. Files inside the container vanish with it.

quiz.q: A request id used as a Loki label causes…
quiz.why: One stream per distinct value. Keep such ids inside the log line.

quiz.q: What lets you pull one request's lines out of thousands, across services?
options: A trace id on every line
quiz.why: It is the one value all lines of the same request share.

lessons.title: Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry

blocks.text: One click by a customer can pass through a gateway, three services, a cache, a database and an outside provider. A trace records that whole journey as a tree of timed steps called spans. Looking at it, you see at once which step took the time or failed. OpenTelemetry is the standard way to produce this data, and to carry the request's identity from one service to the next.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Tracking a parcel. Each depot scans it and records when it arrived and left. Looking at the scans you see the parcel spent ten minutes at each depot and two days at one of them. Without the tracking number on the label, each depot would have its own records and nobody could put them together.
Why it matters

When a request is slow, each team's metrics say their own service is fine. The time is lost between and inside services, in a call nobody suspected. A trace shows the whole request in one picture, and answers "where did the two seconds go" in seconds instead of in a meeting.
Where you meet it

Any system with more than a couple of services. Libraries add spans automatically for web frameworks, HTTP clients, database drivers and message queues. Data goes to a collector and on to a backend such as Jaeger or Grafana Tempo, or a commercial service.
Scenario

Checkout takes 2.4 seconds for some customers. The trace of one slow request shows checkout-api calling the payment provider, waiting 2,000 ms for a timeout, retrying, and succeeding in 120 ms. Nothing is wrong with the database or the service's own code. The fix is a shorter timeout and a look at the provider's status, and it took one trace to find.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR C["Mobile app"] -->|"request"| GW["API gateway
starts the trace"] GW -->|"header: traceparent"| API["checkout-api
OpenTelemetry SDK"] API -->|"traceparent"| PAY["payment-service"] API --> DB[("PostgreSQL
driver creates spans")] API --> K["Kafka
trace context in message headers"] K --> W["order-worker
continues the same trace"] GW -. "spans (OTLP)" .-> COL API -. "spans" .-> COL PAY -. "spans" .-> COL W -. "spans" .-> COL COL["OpenTelemetry Collector
batch, sample, export"] --> BE["Tracing backend
Jaeger / Tempo"] BE --> UI["Trace view:
waterfall of spans"] MET["Metrics"] -. "exemplar: a trace id
on a slow bucket" .-> UI LOGS["Logs with trace_id"] -. "jump to trace" .-> UI

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Request arrives at a service"] --> B{"Does it carry a traceparent header?"} B -->|"no"| C["Start a new trace:
new trace id, root span"] B -->|"yes"| D["Continue the trace: same trace id,
the caller's span becomes the parent"] C --> E["Do the work. Each outgoing call
gets a child span"] D --> E E --> F["Inject traceparent into every outgoing
HTTP call and message"] F --> G["Span ends: name, start, duration,
status, attributes"] G --> H{"Sampling decision"} H -->|"head sampling: decided at the start,
for example keep 10 percent"| I["Kept or dropped as a whole trace"] H -->|"tail sampling: decided in the collector
after the trace is complete"| J["Keep all errors and slow traces,
a small share of the rest"] I --> K["Exported to the backend"] J --> K

blocks.text: Commands

blocks.code: pip install opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp && opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install
blocks.caption: Changes the local environment

blocks.text: Installs the OpenTelemetry SDK for Python and then the instrumentation packages that match the libraries already installed (FastAPI, the HTTP client, the database driver).
Runs the application with automatic instrumentation: no code changes, spans for every request and outgoing call, sent to a collector on the standard OTLP gRPC port.

Sends a request that claims to be part of an existing trace. The four parts are version, trace id (32 hex digits), parent span id (16 hex digits) and flags, where 01 means sampled. A quick way to check that a service continues a trace instead of starting a new one.
The collector's own logs: export failures, dropped data and refused connections show up here. The namespace and name depend on your install.

blocks.code: kubectl set env deployment/checkout-api -n staging OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Keeps one trace in ten that starts at this service, and follows the caller's decision otherwise. Changing environment variables restarts the pods.
Opens the Jaeger interface at localhost:16686 while the command runs. The service name depends on how Jaeger was installed.
examples/monitoring/otel-collector.yaml

blocks.code:
# OpenTelemetry Collector: one place that receives telemetry from every service
# and forwards it to the backends. Services only need to know the collector's address.
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  # Refuse data before the collector runs out of memory.
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_percentage: 80
    spike_limit_percentage: 20
  # Send in batches instead of one request per span.
  batch:
    timeout: 5s

exporters:
  # Traces to a tracing backend that accepts OTLP (Jaeger, Tempo and others do).
  otlp/traces:
    endpoint: jaeger:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true # plain text inside a private network; use TLS across networks
  # Prints what it receives. For debugging the pipeline itself.
  debug:
    verbosity: basic

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlp/traces]
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [debug]

blocks.text: Receivers take data in, processors change it, exporters send it on, and pipelines connect them per signal. Services send to the collector and never need to know which backend is in use, so the backend can change without redeploying them.
Exercise
Diagnose four slow or failed checkouts from their traces in the Trace and log lab.

items: Select "A healthy checkout". Read the waterfall top to bottom and name each step. How long is the whole request?
Select "Slow: one query". Which span is long? Click it and read its attributes. What would you do next, using the database lesson?
Select "Slow: many small queries". No single span is slow. Use "Where the time went" to find the problem. What is this pattern called?
Select "Slow: a timeout and a retry". How long was the first attempt allowed to wait? Is the customer charged twice? Which attribute says why not?
Select "Failed: payment provider down". Which spans are missing compared with the healthy trace, and why is that good?
For each case, which of metrics, logs or traces would have told you first that something was wrong, and which told you where?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can read a waterfall, tell a slow span from many fast ones, explain parent and child spans and own time, and describe how the trace id travels between services.
Troubleshooting

rows: Each service shows its own separate trace
The trace context is not propagated: a proxy strips the header, an HTTP client is not instrumented, or services use different propagation formats.
Check that traceparent leaves one service and arrives at the next. Standardise on W3C trace context.
No traces arrive at all
A wrong collector address or port, a network policy, or a mismatch between gRPC (4317) and HTTP (4318).
Read the application's start-up output and the collector's logs. Use the debug exporter in the collector to see what it receives.
Traces have gaps where a queue or background job sits
Context was not carried in the message, so the consumer started a new trace.
Use messaging instrumentation that injects and extracts context from message headers.
The interesting trace was not kept
Head sampling dropped it before anyone knew it would be slow or fail.
Tail sampling in the collector: keep every error and slow trace, and a small share of the rest.
Tracing costs too much
Every span of every request is exported and stored.
Sample, shorten retention, and drop noisy spans such as health checks at the collector.
Span names like GET /orders/8812 flood the interface
High-cardinality span names: the raw path instead of the route template.
Name spans by route, GET /orders/{id}, and put the id in an attribute.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Start with automatic instrumentation; add manual spans only around business steps that matter.
Propagate context on every hop, including messages and background jobs.
Send everything through a collector, so sampling and backends can change in one place.
Put the trace id in every log line and attach exemplars to latency histograms: then metrics, logs and traces link to one another.
Keep all errors and slow traces; sample the ordinary ones.
Name spans with low-cardinality names and record details as attributes.
Set timeouts on every outgoing call. A trace makes a missing timeout obvious, but only after it has hurt.

blocks.text: Security

items: Span attributes can capture query text, URLs and headers. Make sure passwords, tokens and personal data are not recorded.
Do not trust a traceparent header from the internet for anything but correlation, and consider starting a fresh trace at the edge.
The tracing backend shows the internal structure of your system. Restrict access.
Baggage travels to every downstream service, including third parties. Never put sensitive values in it.
The collector receives data from everything: keep it inside the private network and authenticate senders where you can.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What are a trace and a span?
blocks.text: A span is one timed operation with a name, start, duration, status and attributes. A trace is the set of spans for one request, linked by a shared trace id and parent-child relationships, forming a tree that shows the request's path and timing across services.

blocks.title: How does trace context travel between services?
blocks.text: In request metadata. The W3C traceparent header carries the trace id, the calling span's id and a sampled flag. Instrumentation injects it into outgoing calls and extracts it from incoming ones; for messaging it goes in message headers.

blocks.title: Metrics, logs and traces: when do you use which?
blocks.text: Metrics tell you that something is wrong and how widespread it is, cheaply and for everything. Traces tell you where in the request path the time or the failure is. Logs tell you the detail of what happened at that point. They are most useful linked by a shared trace id.

blocks.title: Head sampling versus tail sampling?
blocks.text: Head sampling decides when the trace starts, so it is cheap and simple but blind: it may drop the one trace you needed. Tail sampling decides after the trace is complete, usually in the collector, so it can keep all errors and slow requests, at the cost of buffering whole traces.

blocks.title: What is OpenTelemetry?
blocks.text: A vendor-neutral standard and toolkit for telemetry: APIs and SDKs for traces, metrics and logs in many languages, automatic instrumentation for common libraries, the OTLP wire protocol and a collector. It separates how you instrument from which backend stores the data.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A request is slow and every service's dashboard looks normal. The best tool is…
options: a trace of one slow request
quiz.why: A trace shows the whole path and where the time went.

quiz.q: Two services show separate traces for the same request. The likely cause is…
options: the trace context header is not being passed on
quiz.why: Without the header, the second service starts a new trace.

quiz.q: Forty 9 ms spans of the same query in one request suggests…
quiz.why: One query per item instead of one query for all of them.

modules.title: DevSecOps
modules.summary: Security checks in the pipeline, SBOMs and signing; secrets management, rotation and leak response; hardening workloads with Pod Security Standards, network policy and least privilege. Not yet covered: threat modelling, compliance frameworks, runtime detection.

lessons.title: Security in the pipeline: scanning, SBOMs and signing

blocks.text: DevSecOps means the pipeline checks security automatically on every change, the same way it runs the build. Different checks catch different problems: a leaked password, a dangerous line of code, a library with a known hole, an insecure cloud setting, a vulnerable base image. A final check at deploy time makes sure the cluster only runs images that your own pipeline built and signed.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Airport security. A ticket check at the door, a bag scanner, a metal detector, a passport desk, a last look at the gate. Each stage looks for something different and none is perfect, but getting something dangerous through all of them is hard. And the earlier a problem is found, the less disruption: a wrong ticket at the door costs a minute; at the gate it delays the flight.
Why it matters

Most of what runs in production was not written by your team: base images, libraries, and their libraries. Attackers go for that chain because one compromised package reaches thousands of companies. A human reviewer cannot check it by reading. Automated checks on every change, and proof of where each image came from, are the only approach that scales.
Where you meet it

In pull requests (secrets, your code, dependencies, infrastructure code), in the build (the image), in the registry (repeat scans, because new vulnerabilities are published for old images), and at admission to the cluster (signatures and policy).
Scenario

A developer adds a feature to checkout-api. The pull request brings in a library with a published critical flaw, and the Dockerfile still uses an old base image. Dependency scanning stops the first in the pull request, where the fix is a one-line version bump. The second is caught by the image scan at build. During an incident weeks later, someone pushes an image from their laptop to skip the queue: the cluster refuses it because it carries no signature from the pipeline.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR DEV["Developer"] -->|"commit"| PC["Pre-commit hook
secret scan"] PC --> PR["Pull request"] subgraph PRC["Checks on the pull request"] S1["Secret scanning"] S2["Static analysis
of your code (SAST)"] S3["Dependency scanning (SCA)"] S4["Infrastructure code scan
Terraform, manifests, Dockerfile"] end PR --> PRC PRC -->|"merge"| B["Build image"] B --> IS["Image scan
OS packages + libraries"] IS --> SB["SBOM: list of everything inside"] SB --> SG["Sign the image digest"] SG --> REG[("Registry
re-scanned daily")] REG --> ADM{"Admission policy:
signed by our pipeline?"} ADM -->|"yes"| K["Cluster runs it"] ADM -->|"no"| X["Rejected"]

blocks.text: Flow
Commands

Scans the repository, including its whole history, for things that look like keys, tokens and passwords. --redact keeps the values out of the output. Newer versions of gitleaks call this command "gitleaks git".

blocks.code:
Finding:     AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=REDACTED
File:        settings.py
Commit:      e91b7c3…
1 leak found
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: Reads the dependency lock files in a project and lists libraries with known high or critical vulnerabilities, with the version that fixes each.
Checks Terraform, Kubernetes manifests and Dockerfiles for insecure settings: public buckets, containers running as root, open security groups.
Scans a built image: operating system packages from the base image as well as application libraries. --ignore-unfixed hides problems for which no fixed version exists yet.

rows: `--exit-code 1`
fail the pipeline step when something is found
`--format cyclonedx --output sbom.json`
write a bill of materials instead of a report

blocks.text: Writes a software bill of materials: every package and library in the image with its version. When a new vulnerability is announced you can search these files instead of rescanning everything.
Signs an image digest. In a pipeline this uses the job's short-lived identity, so there is no signing key to store or leak. The signature is stored in the registry next to the image.
Checks that the image was signed by that exact workflow on that branch. This is the question an admission policy asks before letting a pod start.
An alternative scanner built into recent Docker Desktop versions. Results differ slightly between scanners because their vulnerability databases differ.
A build that scans, records and signs (illustrative)

blocks.code:
# .github/workflows/secure-build.yml (illustrative)
name: secure-build
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write      # short-lived identity for signing and for the registry
  packages: write

jobs:
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0                       # full history, so secrets in old commits are seen

      - name: Secrets in the change
        run: gitleaks detect --source . --redact

      - name: Vulnerable dependencies and insecure configuration
        run: |
          trivy fs --scanners vuln --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 .
          trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 .

  image:
    needs: checks
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build
        run: docker build -t "$IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA" .

      - name: Scan the built image, base image included
        run: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 "$IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA"

      - name: Push, then record exactly what was pushed
        run: |
          docker push "$IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA"
          echo "DIGEST=$(docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA")" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Software bill of materials
        run: syft "$DIGEST" -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json

      - name: Sign the digest with the workflow's own identity (no stored key)
        run: cosign sign --yes "$DIGEST"

blocks.text: The order is the lesson: cheap checks on the pull request, the image scan after the build, the signature last and on the digest, never on a tag that can be moved.
Exercise
Find out what each gate is for by switching it off in the Pipeline security gates lab.

items: With every gate on, try each of the seven changes. Note which gate stops each one and at which stage
Switch off dependency scanning and try the vulnerable library again. What catches it now, and why is that later and more expensive?
Press "Only an image scan". How many of the six dangerous changes reach production? Which kinds of problem can an image scan never see?
Select the committed AWS key with all gates on. It is stopped. Read the note: what must still happen?
Switch off the signature check and try the hand-pushed image. Why can no scanner earlier in the pipeline catch this one?
Pick the one gate you would add first to a pipeline that has none, and justify it

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can name the six kinds of check, what each can and cannot see, and explain why the signature check is at the cluster and not in the pipeline.
Troubleshooting

rows: The scanner reports hundreds of findings and nobody reads them
Everything is reported at once with no threshold, including problems with no available fix.
Fail the build only on high and critical findings that have a fix. Report the rest to a backlog. Start strict on new code and work the old findings down.
A release is blocked by a vulnerability in something the service does not use
Scanners report by presence, not by whether the vulnerable code can be reached.
Record an exception with a reason and an expiry date in the scanner's ignore file, reviewed like code. Better, remove the unused package.
An image that passed last month now fails the scan
A vulnerability was published since. The image did not change; knowledge about it did.
This is expected. Rebuild on a current base image. Rescan what is running on a schedule, not only at build time.
Signature verification fails for a legitimately built image
It was signed by tag and the tag moved, or the expected identity in the policy does not match the workflow path or branch.
Sign and deploy by digest. Compare the identity in the signature with the one the policy expects.
Developers bypass the checks
The checks are slow, noisy or block on false alarms.
Treat this as a defect in the pipeline. Make checks fast, precise and visible in the pull request, with a documented exception path.
A secret was found in history although the file was deleted
Deleting a file does not remove it from earlier commits.
Revoke the secret first. Rewriting history is optional clean-up afterwards.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Scan on every pull request, and fail on high and critical findings that have a fix.
Use small, current base images. Fewer packages means fewer vulnerabilities to manage.
Pin dependencies with lock files and let a bot propose upgrades continuously.
Build once, sign the digest, and deploy that digest to every environment.
Keep an SBOM for every released image.
Rescan images that are running, because new vulnerabilities appear for old code.
Exceptions live in the repository with a reason, an owner and an expiry date.

blocks.text: Security

items: The pipeline can deploy to production, so it is itself a prime target. Protect who can change workflows, and pin third-party actions to a commit.
Pull requests from forks must not receive secrets or signing identity.
Prefer keyless signing with short-lived identities over a long-lived private key.
Pull base images from registries you trust, by digest.
A scanner finding nothing does not mean safe. It means no known vulnerability in the components it recognised.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What security checks belong in a CI/CD pipeline, and where?
blocks.text: On the pull request: secret scanning, static analysis of the code, dependency scanning and infrastructure-code scanning, because fixes are cheapest there. At build: image scanning, an SBOM, and signing the image digest. At deploy: an admission policy that accepts only signed images that meet pod security rules. In operation: periodic rescans of what is running.

blocks.title: SAST, SCA and image scanning: what is the difference?
blocks.text: SAST analyses your own source code for dangerous patterns such as injection. SCA checks the libraries you depend on against databases of known vulnerabilities. Image scanning does the same for everything inside the built image, including operating system packages from the base image.

blocks.title: What is an SBOM and why keep one?
blocks.text: A software bill of materials: a machine-readable list of every component and version in an artifact. When a new vulnerability is announced you can tell in minutes which of your services contain the affected component, instead of scanning everything again.

blocks.title: Why sign container images?
blocks.text: So the cluster can verify that an image was produced by your pipeline from reviewed code and has not been altered. Without it, anyone who can push to the registry, or tamper with it, can run arbitrary code in production.

blocks.title: A critical CVE is announced in a library you use. Walk through your response.
blocks.text: Find where it is, from SBOMs or a scan. Judge exposure: is the vulnerable function used and reachable? If a fix exists, upgrade, rebuild and redeploy, most exposed services first. If not, mitigate by configuration, filtering or disabling the feature. Track until fixed, and check logs for signs of exploitation.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A library you import has a known critical flaw. Which check finds it earliest?
options: Dependency scanning on the pull request
quiz.why: It reads the lock file before anything is built.

quiz.q: An image that passed scanning last month fails today, unchanged. Why?
quiz.why: The image is the same. What is known about it has changed.

quiz.q: You should sign and deploy images by…
quiz.why: A digest identifies exact content. A tag can be pointed at something else.

lessons.title: Secrets: storing, delivering, rotating, and what to do when one leaks

blocks.text: A secret is anything that grants access: a database password, an API key, a private key. The rules are short. Keep secrets out of code and images. Store them in a system built for the purpose, which controls and records who reads them. Give each service only its own. Change them regularly, automatically. And when one is exposed, replace it first and investigate second.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: House keys. You do not tape the key to the front door (a secret in the repository) or hide one under the mat (a secret in the image). You do not give the plumber a key to every room. You keep a record of who holds a copy. And if a key is lost, you change the lock straight away. You do not first spend a day working out where it fell.
Why it matters

A leaked credential is the most common way into a company's systems, and the cheapest for the attacker. Repositories, images, logs and chat messages are copied, cached and backed up far beyond where you can see. Once a secret has been written into any of them it should be considered public.
Where you meet it

Database passwords, keys for payment and messaging providers, cloud credentials, TLS private keys, signing keys, tokens between services. In practice: a cloud secret manager or Vault as the store, delivered to pods as files or environment variables, and short-lived identities in place of stored keys wherever the platform allows.
Scenario

checkout-api needs a database URL and a payment provider key. Both live in AWS Secrets Manager. An operator in the cluster syncs them into Kubernetes Secrets that only the checkout-api service account can read, and the pods get them as environment variables. The database password is rotated automatically every month. One day a developer pastes the payment key into a debugging script and commits it. Secret scanning blocks the push; the key is replaced within the hour anyway, because it had left the secret store.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph STORE["Secret store (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault)"] S1["checkout/db-url"] S2["checkout/payment-key"] AUD["Audit log:
who read what, when"] ROT["Rotation function"] end ROT -->|"new password"| DB[("Database")] ROT --> S1 ESO["External Secrets operator
(its own narrow IAM role)"] -->|"read"| S1 ESO -->|"read"| S2 ESO -->|"create and refresh"| KS["Kubernetes Secret checkout-db
(encrypted at rest in etcd)"] KS -->|"env or mounted file"| POD["checkout-api pod"] RBAC["RBAC: only this service
account may read it"] -.-> KS GIT["Git repository"] -. "holds the ExternalSecret,
never the value" .-> ESO CI["CI pipeline"] -. "OIDC: short-lived
credentials, no stored key" .-> STORE

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["A secret has been exposed:
committed, logged, pasted in chat"] --> B["Assume it is compromised.
Do not wait for proof"] B --> C["Revoke or rotate it NOW"] C --> D{"Can the old one be disabled
without an outage?"} D -->|"yes"| E["Disable the old credential"] D -->|"no"| F["Issue the new one, deploy it,
then disable the old one. Minutes, not days"] E --> G["Check the audit log:
was it used by anyone else?"] F --> G G --> H{"Signs of misuse?"} H -->|"yes"| I["Security incident: contain,
find what was accessed or created"] H -->|"no"| J["Record the exposure window"] I --> K["Remove the secret from where it leaked
(history, logs). Clean-up, not a fix"] J --> K K --> L["Prevent the repeat: scanning at commit and push,
and replace stored keys with short-lived identity"]

blocks.text: Commands
Every secret with whether rotation is switched on and when it last happened. Names only, no values.

blocks.code: aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id checkout/db-url --query SecretString --output text
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Prints a secret's value. The read is recorded in the audit log, and the value is now in your terminal scrollback. Rarely needed by a person.
Starts a rotation now: a function creates a new password in the database and stores it. Services must pick up the new value, so know how they do before running this.

blocks.code: kubectl -n production get secret checkout-db -o jsonpath='{.data.url}' | base64 -d
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Shows that a Kubernetes Secret is only base64-encoded, not encrypted: anyone allowed to read the Secret object can read the value. Run it once in a lab to be convinced, not in production.

blocks.code: kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n production --as=system:serviceaccount:production:cart-api
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Asks whether another service's identity may read secrets in the namespace. The answer should be no.
With the External Secrets operator: each synced secret and whether the last sync succeeded.

blocks.code:
NAME         STORE                REFRESH  STATUS
checkout-db  aws-secrets-manager  1h       SecretSynced
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: Finds every commit, on any branch, that added or removed the text AKIA (how AWS access key ids begin). Useful to learn when and where a key leaked.

blocks.code: aws iam update-access-key --user-name ci-deploy --access-key-id AKIAEXAMPLEKEYID0000 --status Inactive
blocks.caption: Production change

blocks.text: Disables an access key at once. The first action when one is exposed. Anything still using it stops working, which is the intention.
Deletes the key for good, after you have confirmed nothing legitimate still needs it.
ExternalSecret for checkout-api (illustrative)

blocks.code:
# The secret's value lives in AWS Secrets Manager. This object only says where.
# It is safe to keep in Git: it contains no secret.
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1          # older installations use v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: checkout-db
  namespace: production
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h                       # pick up rotations within the hour
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
    name: aws-secrets-manager
  target:
    name: checkout-db                       # the Kubernetes Secret to create and keep in sync
  data:
    - secretKey: url
      remoteRef:
        key: checkout/db-url

blocks.text: Git holds a pointer to the secret, the store holds the value, and the operator joins them. Rotating the value in the store reaches the cluster within the refresh interval; pods that read it as an environment variable still need a restart to see it.
Exercise
Handle a leaked cloud key in the incident simulator, then a credential that expired.

items: In the scenario shown, read the page. Before investigating, say what your first action would be and why
Check what the key can do and what it has done. What makes this leak as bad as it can be?
Take the action you believe is right. Read the outcome of the others afterwards by running the scenario again
Why is removing the commit from history the wrong first move?
Open the Incident simulator and run scenario 13 (payments failing with 401). What do the two incidents have in common?
For checkout-api, list every secret it needs and, for each, whether a short-lived identity could replace it

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state the order of response to a leak, explain why base64 is not protection, and describe how a secret reaches a pod without being in Git.
Troubleshooting

rows: A pod still uses the old password after rotation
Environment variables are read once at start. The Secret changed; the running process did not.
Restart the pods as part of rotation, or mount the secret as a file and have the application re-read it.
Rotation happened and the service lost access
The store has the new value but the database or provider does not, or the other way round.
Rotate in steps that are each checked: create the new credential, verify it works, switch, then remove the old one.
ExternalSecret shows SecretSyncedError
The operator's role may not read that secret, or the name or key is wrong.
kubectl describe the ExternalSecret for the message. Check the IAM policy and the exact secret name.
A secret appears in CI logs
A command echoed it, or debug output printed the environment.
Rotate it. Then stop printing environments, and rely on the CI system's masking only as a backstop.
Many services share one database password
It was easier at the start.
One credential per service. Otherwise a leak anywhere is a leak everywhere, and you cannot tell from the audit log who did what.
Nobody knows whether an old key is still in use
No record of consumers.
Check last-used information in the provider, disable (do not delete) the key, wait, then delete.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: No secrets in source code, images, or infrastructure state that people can read.
One store for secrets, with access control and an audit log.
One credential per service and per environment.
Prefer short-lived identity (roles, workload identity, OIDC) over any stored key.
Rotate automatically, and make every consumer able to pick up a new value.
Scan for secrets before commit and at push.
Practise the leak response, so the first time is not a real one.

blocks.text: Security

items: A Kubernetes Secret is base64, not encryption. Enable encryption at rest for etcd and restrict who can read Secret objects.
Anyone who can create a pod in a namespace can mount any secret in it. Namespace boundaries matter.
Secrets passed as environment variables show up in crash dumps and debugging tools. Files are a little safer.
Terraform state contains the secrets of resources it manages. Protect the state as a secret store.
Break-glass admin credentials should be locked away, alert when used, and be rotated after every use.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you manage secrets for an application on Kubernetes?
blocks.text: Values live in a secret manager with access control, audit and rotation. An operator such as External Secrets, or a CSI driver, brings them into the cluster, so Git holds only references. RBAC limits each secret to its service account, etcd is encrypted at rest, and where possible the application uses a workload identity instead of any stored secret.

blocks.title: A developer committed an API key to a public repository. What do you do?
blocks.text: Revoke or rotate the key immediately; that is the only step that removes the risk. Then check the provider's audit log for use by anyone else and handle that as an incident if found. Afterwards clean the history and add scanning with push protection. Deleting the commit first achieves nothing, because the key was copied the moment it was public.

blocks.title: Are Kubernetes Secrets secure?
blocks.text: Not by themselves. They are base64-encoded objects in etcd: readable by anyone with get on secrets or the ability to run a pod in the namespace, and stored in plain form unless encryption at rest is configured. They are a delivery mechanism; security comes from RBAC, encryption, and keeping the source of truth elsewhere.

blocks.title: How do you rotate a database password without downtime?
blocks.text: Use two valid credentials during the change. Create a new user or password, store it, roll the application to it, confirm nothing uses the old one, then remove the old one. Managed rotation with alternating users does exactly this.

blocks.title: Why are short-lived credentials better than long-lived keys?
blocks.text: They expire on their own, so a leak is useful to an attacker for minutes or hours, not years. They are issued to an identity at run time, so nothing needs to be stored, distributed or rotated by hand.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A secret was pushed to a repository. The first action is…
quiz.why: Only replacing it removes the risk. Everything else is clean-up.

quiz.q: A Kubernetes Secret's data is…
quiz.why: Encoding, not encryption. Anyone who can read the object can read the value.

quiz.q: After rotating a password, pods still use the old one because…
options: environment variables are read at start
the Secret is cached in Git
quiz.why: The process keeps what it read when it started. Restart it or read from a file.

lessons.title: Hardening workloads on Kubernetes

blocks.text: By default a container may run as root, a pod may talk to every other pod, and every pod carries a token for the Kubernetes API. Hardening means switching each of those defaults to the safe side: run as an ordinary user with no extra privileges, allow only the network connections the service needs, and give its identity only the permissions it uses. Kubernetes can then enforce those rules for a whole namespace.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A hotel with a new guest. By default they get a key card that opens every door, the kitchen and the server room. Hardening is issuing a card for their own room only (least privilege), closing the corridors they have no reason to walk (network policy), and having the lock, not a polite notice, refuse everything else (admission control).
Why it matters

Applications get compromised: a vulnerable library, a bug in input handling. What matters then is how far the intruder can go. In a hardened pod they are an unprivileged user in a read-only filesystem, with no route to other services and no useful API permissions. In a default pod they may be one step from the node and everything on it.
Where you meet it

The securityContext of every workload, a default-deny NetworkPolicy and Pod Security Standards labels on every namespace, minimal RBAC for every service account, and a policy engine at admission for the rules that are specific to your organisation.
Scenario

A flaw in an image-processing library lets an attacker run commands inside a catalogue-api pod. Because the pod runs as a non-root user with all capabilities dropped and a read-only filesystem, they cannot install tools or change the application. A default-deny network policy stops them reaching the orders database or the cloud metadata address. The service account token is not mounted, so there is nothing to call the Kubernetes API with. The break-in ends where it began.
Architecture
