flowchart TB DEV["Manifest applied"] --> API["Kubernetes API server"] subgraph ADM["Admission: the gate before anything is stored"] PSA["Pod Security admission
namespace label: enforce=restricted"] POL["Policy engine (Kyverno, Gatekeeper)
signed images only, approved registries"] end API --> ADM ADM -->|"allowed"| POD ADM -->|"denied"| REJ["Rejected with a reason"] subgraph NS["Namespace production"] POD["checkout-api pod
non-root, no capabilities,
read-only filesystem, seccomp"] NP["NetworkPolicy:
default deny, then allow
ingress controller in, database out"] SA["ServiceAccount with no
API permissions, token not mounted"] end NP -.-> POD SA -.-> POD POD -->|"allowed"| DB[("orders database")] POD -. "blocked" .-> OTHER["other services,
cloud metadata address"]

blocks.text: Flow
Commands
Shows which Pod Security level the namespace enforces, if any, through its pod-security.kubernetes.io labels.
Asks the API server what would happen if the namespace enforced "restricted", without changing it. It prints a warning for every existing workload that would be rejected.

blocks.code:
Warning: existing pods in namespace "production" violate the new PodSecurity enforce level "restricted:latest"
Warning: checkout-api-7c9f-a: unrestricted capabilities, seccompProfile
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: Turns on warnings and audit records for the restricted level without blocking anything. The safe first step: people see what they need to fix.
From now on, new pods in the namespace that do not meet the restricted level are rejected. Existing pods keep running until they are recreated, and then fail if they have not been fixed.
Lists network policies. An empty list means every pod can reach every other pod in the cluster.
Everything a service account may do in the namespace. For an application that never calls the Kubernetes API, the list should be almost empty.
Shows which user the container really runs as. uid=0 is root.
Tries to write to the container's filesystem. With a read-only root filesystem it must fail.
examples/kubernetes/deployment-hardened.yaml

blocks.code:
# checkout-api with every setting the "restricted" Pod Security Standard asks for,
# plus three that it does not require but that are worth having.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: production
  labels:
    app: checkout-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout-api
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: checkout-api
      automountServiceAccountToken: false   # the app never calls the Kubernetes API
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault              # the container runtime's default system-call filter
      containers:
        - name: checkout-api
          # Pinned by digest: the exact image that was scanned and signed.
          image: registry.example.com/shop/checkout-api@sha256:4f0c2c1d8f6a7b3e9d5a1c0b2e4f6a8c0d2e4f6a8b0c2d4e6f8a0b2c4d6e8f01
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tmp
              mountPath: /tmp               # the only writable path
      volumes:
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: {}

blocks.text: Compare it with the everyday Deployment in the Pod security checker. The everyday one already runs as a non-root user and still fails the restricted level, for two missing settings.
Exercise
Take a Deployment from "fails baseline" to "meets restricted" in the Pod security checker.

items: Select "Everyday Deployment". Which level does it meet, and which two settings hold it back?
Add those two settings by editing the YAML until the badge changes. Use the hardened example as a reference only if stuck
Select "Risky Deployment". List every finding under "Blocks baseline" and say what an intruder could do with each
Fix the risky Deployment one finding at a time and watch the level change. Which single line was the most dangerous?
Look at "Also worth fixing" on the everyday Deployment. Why are these not part of the standard, and why do them anyway?
Follow the attacker flowchart for the hardened Deployment and for the risky one. Where does each path end?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can list the settings the restricted level requires, explain what each prevents, and describe how a namespace enforces a level.
Troubleshooting

rows: Pod rejected: violates PodSecurity "restricted"
The manifest lacks a required setting. The message lists which.
Add the settings to the workload. Do not lower the namespace level to make the error go away.
CreateContainerConfigError: container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root
runAsNonRoot is set, but the image has no USER line or uses a named user Kubernetes cannot verify.
Set a numeric USER in the Dockerfile, or runAsUser in the manifest.
The application crashes with "Read-only file system"
It writes to a path inside the image: temporary files, caches, a PID file.
Mount an emptyDir volume at exactly those paths and keep the rest read-only.
After adding a default-deny policy, nothing can resolve names
DNS to the cluster DNS service is blocked along with everything else.
Allow egress to the DNS pods on port 53, UDP and TCP, in the same change as the default deny.
A NetworkPolicy has no effect at all
The cluster's network plugin does not enforce NetworkPolicy.
Check which CNI is installed. Policies are silently ignored without one that supports them.
The service cannot bind port 80 after dropping capabilities
Ports below 1024 need the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability for a non-root user.
Listen on a high port such as 8000 and let the Service map 80 to it. Or add back only NET_BIND_SERVICE.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Enforce the restricted Pod Security level on application namespaces; start with warn and audit.
Default-deny NetworkPolicy in every namespace, then allow what each service needs.
One service account per workload, no permissions unless it calls the API, token not mounted.
Images run as a numeric non-root user and keep working with a read-only filesystem.
Deploy images by digest from your own registry only, enforced at admission.
Keep nodes and the control plane patched and upgraded.
Check manifests for these rules in the pull request, long before admission rejects them.

blocks.text: Security

items: privileged: true, hostPath, hostNetwork and hostPID each give a path to the node. Allow them only for system components, in their own namespaces.
Block pod access to the cloud metadata address, or the node's cloud credentials are one HTTP request away.
The ability to create pods in a namespace is equivalent to reading every secret in it.
cluster-admin for people or pipelines should be rare, time-limited and logged.
Turn on API audit logs and alert on exec into production pods and on secrets being read.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you harden a pod?
blocks.text: Run as a non-root numeric user, set allowPrivilegeEscalation false, drop all capabilities, use the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile and a read-only root filesystem with emptyDir for scratch paths. Set resource limits, do not mount the service account token unless needed, and pin the image by digest. Then enforce it for the namespace with the restricted Pod Security level.

blocks.title: What are the Pod Security Standards?
blocks.text: Three policy levels defined by Kubernetes. Privileged is unrestricted. Baseline forbids known privilege escalations such as privileged containers, host namespaces and hostPath volumes. Restricted adds current hardening practice: non-root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped, a seccomp profile and a limited set of volume types. A built-in admission controller applies a level per namespace in enforce, warn or audit mode.

blocks.title: What does a NetworkPolicy do, and what is the default without one?
blocks.text: Without any policy every pod can talk to every pod in every namespace. A NetworkPolicy selects pods and lists the allowed inbound and outbound connections; once a pod is selected by any policy, everything not allowed is denied. It only works if the network plugin enforces it.

blocks.title: Why is running as root in a container dangerous if containers are isolated?
blocks.text: Isolation relies on kernel features, and root inside the container is the same user id as root on the node. A kernel or runtime vulnerability, a mounted host path or an extra capability can turn container root into node root. A non-root user removes most of those paths.

blocks.title: How do you roll out stricter pod security to a cluster that has none?
blocks.text: Measure first: dry-run the label or use warn and audit modes to list violations. Fix workloads team by team, with checks in pull requests to stop new ones. Then enforce baseline everywhere and restricted on application namespaces, with system components in exempt, tightly controlled namespaces.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: With no NetworkPolicy in a cluster, pods can reach…
quiz.why: The default is allow-all. Isolation has to be added.

quiz.q: Which is required by the restricted level?
quiz.why: The other three are good practice but not part of the standard.

quiz.q: The safest first step towards enforcing restricted on a busy namespace is…
options: set warn and audit to restricted
quiz.why: It shows what would break without breaking it.

modules.title: Site Reliability Engineering
modules.summary: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets and burn-rate alerts; toil, on-call health, readiness reviews and capacity planning.

lessons.title: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets

blocks.text: An SLI is a measurement of what users experience, such as the share of checkout requests that succeed. An SLO is the target for it: 99.9% over 30 days. The gap between the target and perfect, 0.1% here, is the error budget: the amount of failure you are allowed. While budget remains, ship features. When it is spent, stop and work on reliability. It turns an argument about "is it reliable enough" into a number both sides agreed in advance.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A monthly household budget. You decide in advance how much may be spent on eating out. While there is money left, you go out without a discussion. When it is gone, you cook at home until next month. Nobody has to argue about each meal, and nobody pretends the right amount is zero.
Why it matters

Perfect reliability is impossible and each extra "nine" costs roughly ten times more. Without a target, operations push for no change and developers push for speed, and every incident restarts the argument. A target with a budget gives both a shared rule, tells you when an alert should wake someone, and tells you when reliability work must take priority.
Where you meet it

Every user-facing service has a few SLOs: availability and latency at least. They drive paging alerts (burn rate), release decisions, capacity planning and conversations with the business. An SLA is the contractual promise to customers; the internal SLO is stricter so there is warning before the contract is broken.
Scenario

checkout-api has an SLO of 99.9% successful requests over 30 days: 43 minutes of budget. On day 10 a bad release causes 20 minutes of errors. Nearly half the month's budget is gone in a third of the month. At that pace it runs out on day 22, so the team slows risky releases and brings forward the work on automatic rollback. Nothing about this needed a meeting: the policy was agreed when the SLO was set.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR U["Customers"] --> LB["Load balancer"] LB --> SVC["checkout-api"] LB -. "request logs or metrics:
the SLI is measured here,
as close to the user as possible" .-> SLI["SLI = good requests / all requests"] SLI --> SLO{"SLO: 99.9%
over 30 days"} SLO --> EB["Error budget: 0.1%
= 43 minutes"] EB --> BR["Burn-rate alerts"] BR -->|"fast burn"| PAGE["Page on-call"] BR -->|"slow burn"| TICKET["Ticket"] EB --> POL["Error budget policy"] POL -->|"budget left"| SHIP["Ship features, take risks"] POL -->|"budget spent"| FIX["Freeze features,
work on reliability"] SLO -. "stricter than" .-> SLA["SLA: 99.5% promised
to customers, with penalties"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Choose what users care about:
did it work, was it fast"] --> B["Define the SLI precisely:
which requests count, what is 'good'"] B --> C["Measure it for a few weeks"] C --> D["Set the SLO a little below
what you achieve today"] D --> E["Budget = 100% minus the SLO"] E --> F["Agree the policy before you need it"] F --> G{"Each week: how much budget is left?"} G -->|"plenty"| H["Release normally. Consider
whether the SLO is too easy"] G -->|"burning fast"| I["Slow risky changes.
Prioritise the top reliability items"] G -->|"spent"| J["Stop feature releases until it recovers.
Postmortem items first"] H --> K{"Quarterly: do users still agree

blocks.text: Commands
The availability SLI over 30 days: the share of requests that did not fail with a server error. Compare it with the target.
The share of the 30-day error budget still unspent, for a 99.9% target. 1 means untouched, 0 means spent, negative means overspent.
The burn rate over the last hour. 1 is exactly on budget; 14.4 sustained for an hour is the usual threshold for a page.
A latency SLI: the response time 95% of requests beat. A latency SLO might say this stays under 800 ms.
Validates the recording and alerting rules for the SLO before they are deployed.
Installs the SLO rules where a Prometheus operator picks them up. From then on these alerts can page people, so review thresholds and routing first.
Error-budget alert rules (illustrative)

blocks.code:
# Error-budget alerts for checkout-api. SLO: 99.9% of requests succeed, over 30 days.
# The budget is 0.1% = 0.001. Each alert asks: are we spending it N times too fast?
groups:
  - name: checkout-api-slo
    rules:
      # Reusable: the share of requests failing, over several windows.
      - record: checkout:error_ratio:rate5m
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api"}[5m]))
      - record: checkout:error_ratio:rate30m
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api",status=~"5.."}[30m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api"}[30m]))
      - record: checkout:error_ratio:rate1h
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api",status=~"5.."}[1h])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api"}[1h]))
      - record: checkout:error_ratio:rate6h
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api",status=~"5.."}[6h])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout-api"}[6h]))

      # 14.4x for an hour spends 2% of the month's budget. Wake someone.
      - alert: CheckoutBudgetFastBurn
        expr: checkout:error_ratio:rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001) and checkout:error_ratio:rate5m > (14.4 * 0.001)
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "checkout-api is spending its error budget 14x too fast"
          runbook: "https://runbooks.example.com/checkout-error-budget"

      # 6x for six hours spends 5%. Still a page, less urgent.
      - alert: CheckoutBudgetSlowBurn
        expr: checkout:error_ratio:rate6h > (6 * 0.001) and checkout:error_ratio:rate30m > (6 * 0.001)
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "checkout-api is spending its error budget 6x too fast"

blocks.text: Each alert uses two windows. The long one shows the problem is significant; the short one shows it is still happening, so the alert stops soon after the fault does.
Exercise
Use the Error budget lab to make release decisions and to see which alert would fire for four different faults.

items: Set the target to 99.9%. How many minutes of failure does that allow in 30 days? What about 99.99%?
Press "One bad deploy". What is the verdict on day 10, and on which day would the budget run out?
Press "A long outage". What does the policy say now? Who needs to agree to that policy before the day it applies?
In the alerts section, press "Total outage, 30 min". How quickly does the fast-burn alert fire?
Press "2% errors, 10 min". Nothing fires. Is that a failure of alerting or the design working?
Press "0.3% errors, 3 days". Which alert notices? Why would a simple threshold at 2% never have seen this?
Change the target to 99.99% and repeat the 2-hour case. What changes, and what would it cost to live with that target?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can define SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget, compute a budget in minutes, and explain what a burn rate of 14.4 means.
Troubleshooting

rows: The SLO is always met and users still complain
The SLI does not measure what users experience: it is taken inside the service, ignores timeouts, or averages away a failing region or customer group.
Measure at the edge. Count slow responses as bad. Split by the dimensions users differ in.
The budget is always exhausted
The target is stricter than the system or its dependencies can deliver.
Either invest until it can be met, or lower the target to what users actually need. An SLO nobody can meet stops guiding decisions.
Budget is spent and features ship anyway
The policy was never agreed with product and leadership, so it has no force.
Write the policy, get it signed off while things are calm, and report budget status every week.
One long incident consumed the whole budget
Detection or recovery was slow.
The postmortem's priority is time to detect and time to mitigate: faster alerts, automatic rollback.
The SLI is 100% during an outage
When the service is completely down it serves no requests, so there are no failures to count.
Count from the load balancer or a synthetic probe, where failed and refused requests are still seen.
A dependency with a 99.9% SLA sits under a service promising 99.99%
Availability multiplies down a chain of hard dependencies.
Make the dependency optional (cache, fallback, queue), or accept a target no higher than the weakest hard dependency.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: A few SLOs per service, about what users experience. Availability and latency first.
Measure as close to the user as you can.
Set targets from user need and measured history, not from ambition.
Agree the error budget policy in writing before it is needed.
Page on burn rate; open tickets for slow burn.
Keep the internal SLO stricter than any external SLA.
Review targets every quarter. Spending no budget at all means you could be moving faster.

blocks.text: Security

items: Availability is part of security. A denial-of-service attack spends error budget like any outage.
SLO dashboards reveal traffic volumes and weaknesses. Limit who outside the company can see them.
Do not exclude "bad" traffic from the SLI too generously: attackers and real users can look alike, and excluded requests hide real failures.
A budget freeze should never block security patches. Say so in the policy.
Synthetic probes carry credentials. Give them accounts with no real privileges.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Define SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget.
blocks.text: SLI: a measured indicator of service quality, such as the proportion of successful requests. SLO: the internal target for it over a period, such as 99.9% over 30 days. SLA: a contract with customers, with consequences if missed, set looser than the SLO. Error budget: one minus the SLO, the amount of failure permitted, here about 43 minutes a month.

blocks.title: Why not aim for 100%?
blocks.text: It is unattainable and each step closer costs far more than the last. Users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% through their own network and devices. And a 100% target leaves no room to change anything, since change is the main cause of failure.

blocks.title: What happens when the error budget is exhausted?
blocks.text: By a policy agreed in advance, the team stops feature releases and works on reliability until the budget recovers, with exceptions for security and for fixes. The value is that the decision is made by a rule, not by whoever argues hardest that day.

blocks.title: How do you choose a good SLI?
blocks.text: Start from what users would call broken: the request failed or was too slow. Express it as good events over valid events, measured at the edge, on the operations that matter such as checkout. Avoid internal causes like CPU.

blocks.title: What is burn rate?
blocks.text: How fast the budget is being consumed relative to the rate that would use it exactly over the SLO period. A burn rate of 1 lasts the whole month; 14.4 uses 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. Alerts on burn rate over paired long and short windows page for real damage and stay quiet for blips.

quiz.q: A 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days allows about…
quiz.why: 0.1% of 43,200 minutes.

quiz.q: The error budget is spent on day 20. The usual policy says…
options: stop feature releases and work on reliability
quiz.why: That is what the budget is for: a pre-agreed trigger.

quiz.q: During a total outage the service reports 100% success. Why?
options: It serves no requests, so it counts no failures
quiz.why: Measure at the load balancer or with a probe, where failures are still seen.

lessons.title: Toil, on-call and capacity

blocks.text: Toil is operational work that is manual, repetitive and brings no lasting improvement: restarting the same service, clearing the same disk, approving the same request. It grows with the size of the system, so if nobody removes it, it eventually takes all the team's time. SRE treats operations as an engineering problem: limit toil, automate the repeats, keep on-call humane, and plan capacity before it runs out.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Bailing water out of a boat. You can bail faster and hire more people to bail, and the boat keeps floating. Or you can spend an afternoon finding and fixing the leak. A crew that only ever bails is busy, exhausted and one storm from sinking. A good crew sets aside time to fix leaks, even when there is water to bail.
Why it matters

A team drowning in manual work has no time to fix what causes it, and tired people on call make mistakes and leave. Systems that are only kept alive by heroics fail when the hero is on holiday. Capping toil and investing the rest in automation is what lets a small team run a system that keeps growing.
Where you meet it

Any team that operates what it builds. The practices are a toil budget (commonly at most half of each engineer's time), on-call rotations with limits, runbooks, production readiness reviews before launch, and capacity planning from measured growth.
Scenario

Every few weeks the orders database disk fills with old log files and someone is paged at night to delete them. It takes ten minutes and feels like a small thing. Over a year it is twenty pages, twenty interrupted nights, and one occasion when the alert was acknowledged and forgotten and the database stopped. The fix, a retention setting and an alert on growth rate, takes an afternoon. Nobody had the afternoon because they were busy answering the page.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TB subgraph WORK["Where an operations team's week goes"] T["Toil: manual, repetitive,
automatable, no lasting value"] E["Engineering: automation, reliability
fixes, tooling, capacity"] O["Overhead: meetings, planning"] end PAGES["Pages and tickets"] --> T T -->|"measured every sprint"| CAP{"Above the agreed cap?
(commonly 50%)"} CAP -->|"yes"| PUSH["Hand work back to the service's developers,
or stop taking on new services"] CAP -->|"no"| E E -->|"removes causes"| PAGES RR["Production readiness review"] -->|"before launch: SLOs, alerts,
runbooks, capacity, rollback"| NEW["New service"] NEW --> PAGES CAPP["Capacity plan:
growth forecast + headroom"] --> E

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["A page or ticket arrives"] --> B["Handle it. Restore service"] B --> C{"Have we seen this exact
thing before?"} C -->|"no"| D["Write down what was done:
the start of a runbook"] C -->|"yes"| E{"How many times this quarter?"} E -->|"once or twice"| F["Improve the runbook"] E -->|"again and again"| G{"Can the cause be removed?"} G -->|"yes"| H["Fix the cause. The page disappears"] G -->|"not yet"| I{"Can the response be automated safely?"} I -->|"yes"| J["Automate it, with limits and logging.
Alert only if automation fails"] I -->|"no"| K["Make it a ticket in working hours,
not a page at night, if users are not affected"] D --> L["Review all pages weekly:
was each one actionable and urgent?"] F --> L H --> L J --> L K --> L

blocks.text: Commands
Current CPU and memory use per node as a share of capacity. A first look at headroom.

blocks.code:
NAME    CPU(cores)  CPU%  MEMORY(bytes)  MEMORY%
node-a  2710m       68%   11.2Gi         71%
blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.text: What is reserved by pod requests on each node, which is what the scheduler uses. A node can be idle and still "full" if requests are oversized.
Asks Prometheus whether, at the growth rate of the last six hours, the disk will be full within four days. Alerting on this gives days of warning; alerting at 90% full gives hours.
Which alerts are firing most right now. Run over a longer range, this shows the noisiest alerts: the first candidates for fixing or deleting.
For each autoscaled service: current load against target, and current replicas against the maximum. A service sitting at its maximum has no room left to scale.
PodDisruptionBudgets: how many pods of each service may be taken down at once for maintenance. A service with none can lose all its pods in a node upgrade.
The classic piece of toil: "restart it and it works again". Fine as a mitigation. If you run it weekly, the real task is finding out why.
Exercise
Work the disk-full incident, then decide what should change so it never pages again.

items: Read the page. Notice the second sentence: what had already happened three hours earlier?
Investigate until you can say why the disk filled. Which check gave the most information?
Two actions restore service. Compare them: which removes the cause and which only buys time?
Read the review. Classify each prevention item: removes the cause, improves detection, or improves response
This incident took one night. Suppose it recurred monthly: estimate the yearly cost in pages and hours, and compare with the cost of the fix
Write a production readiness checklist of six questions you would ask before launching a new service

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can define toil, explain why it is capped, and describe what turns a recurring page into a fixed cause.
Troubleshooting

rows: The team has no time for improvements
Interrupt work fills the week and is not measured, so it cannot be argued about.
Track time spent on toil for a month. Use the number to reserve engineering time and to push recurring problems back to their owners.
The same alert pages every week
Each time it is fixed by hand and closed. Nobody owns removing the cause.
A weekly page review with one rule: every repeat gets an owner and a date, or the alert is deleted.
On-call engineers are exhausted and leaving
Too many pages, too few people in the rotation, pages for things that could wait.
Count pages per shift and set a limit. Move non-urgent alerts to tickets. Spread the rotation, and give time off after a bad night.
A new service launched and immediately caused incidents
No readiness review: no alerts, no runbook, unknown capacity, no rollback.
A short, required checklist before production, owned by the team that will be paged.
Capacity ran out during an event everyone knew about
Forecasts were not connected to marketing plans, or scaling limits were never checked against the forecast.
Plan for known peaks with the business, load test at the forecast, and check autoscaler maximums, quotas and database limits.
Automation made an outage worse
It acted without limits: restarted everything, scaled without bound, retried forever.
Automate with rate limits, a maximum blast radius, logging and an off switch. Page a human when the limit is reached.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Measure toil and cap it. Above the cap, stop and fix causes.
Every page must be urgent, actionable and about user impact. Review them weekly.
Runbooks for every alert, linked from the alert, tested by someone who did not write them.
On-call: at least six people per rotation where possible, a clear hand-over, a secondary, and no more than a couple of incidents per shift.
A production readiness review before launch.
Capacity planned from measured growth, with headroom for the loss of a zone and for the next peak.
Automate the response only after you understand the cause.

blocks.text: Security

items: On-call engineers hold powerful access. Make it time-limited, logged and reviewed, not permanent.
Runbooks must not contain passwords or keys. Reference the secret store.
Automation that can restart, scale or delete is a privileged identity. Scope it tightly.
Tired people skip steps. Excessive paging is a security risk as well as a human one.
Emergency "break-glass" access should exist, alert when used, and be reviewed afterwards.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is toil?
blocks.text: Work tied to running a service that is manual, repetitive, automatable, reactive, without lasting value, and that grows as the service grows. Restarting a stuck job by hand each morning is toil; writing the fix that stops it sticking is engineering.

blocks.title: Why cap toil at around 50%?
blocks.text: Because toil expands with the system. Without a cap, operations consumes all the time, nothing gets automated, and headcount must grow with load. The cap guarantees time to remove causes, and exceeding it is a signal to hand work back or stop taking on more.

blocks.title: What makes an on-call rotation sustainable?
blocks.text: Enough people that shifts are infrequent, few and meaningful pages, runbooks and clear escalation, a secondary on call, compensation or time off, and a team that reviews every page and fixes what caused it.

blocks.title: What do you check in a production readiness review?
blocks.text: SLOs and alerts tied to them, dashboards, runbooks, ownership and on-call, capacity and load test results, dependency failure behaviour and timeouts, deployment and rollback method, backups and restore tests, security review, and cost.

blocks.title: How do you plan capacity?
blocks.text: Measure current use and its drivers, forecast growth from history and business plans, load test to find the real limits, add headroom for failures and peaks, and remember the limits that are not CPU: database connections, quotas, IP addresses, partitions. Then let autoscaling handle the short-term variation inside those limits.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which of these is toil?
options: Deleting old log files by hand every month
quiz.why: Manual, repetitive, automatable, and it leaves the system no better.

quiz.q: An alert pages every week and is resolved by a restart. The best next step is…
options: find and remove the cause, or automate and stop paging
quiz.why: A recurring page is a defect in the system, not a duty to perform.

quiz.q: Alerting when a disk "will be full in four days" rather than "is 90% full" gives you…
options: time to act in working hours
quiz.why: A prediction turns a night-time emergency into a daytime ticket.

modules.title: Incident Management
modules.summary: Roles, severity, mitigation before diagnosis and communication; blameless postmortems, action items and runbooks. Fifteen incidents to practise on.

lessons.title: Incident response: the first thirty minutes

blocks.text: An incident is when the service is harming users and needs a coordinated response. The goal in the first minutes is not to understand what happened. It is to stop the harm: roll back, fail over, switch the feature off. Understanding comes later. One person coordinates, the others investigate and act, and everyone else is kept informed so they do not have to ask.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A kitchen fire in a restaurant. Nobody starts by working out which pan caused it. Someone takes charge, the fire is put out or the gas is cut, customers are told what is happening, and one person keeps notes. The investigation into why the oil was left unattended happens the next day, calmly, with the notes.
Why it matters

Under stress people do the opposite of what helps: everyone debugs the same thing, nobody tells customers, three people make changes at once and nobody knows which one had an effect. A simple agreed structure, practised in advance, is what keeps a ten-minute problem from becoming a two-hour one.
Where you meet it

Any outage or serious degradation, security events, and data problems. The tooling is ordinary: an alert, a chat channel or call for the incident, a status page, and a shared document for the timeline.
Scenario

At 14:08 the on-call engineer is paged: 41% of checkout requests are failing. She declares an incident, opens a channel and asks a colleague to handle communication. The rollout history shows a release six minutes before the errors began. She does not read the new code. She rolls back. By 14:16 the error rate is normal. The status page is updated twice in that time. Why the release failed is tomorrow's question, and the timeline in the channel will answer half of it.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TB ALERT["Alert or customer report"] --> ONCALL["On-call engineer"] ONCALL -->|"declares"| INC["Incident: one channel, one document"] subgraph ROLES["Roles (one person each; in a small incident one person holds several)"] IC["Incident commander
decides, coordinates, does not debug"] OPS["Operations lead
investigates and makes changes"] COMMS["Communications lead
status page, support, leadership"] SCRIBE["Scribe
timeline of what was seen and done"] end INC --> ROLES OPS -->|"proposes actions"| IC IC -->|"approves, one change at a time"| OPS COMMS --> SP["Status page and
stakeholder updates, on a timer"] SCRIBE --> DOC["Timeline: input to the postmortem"] IC -->|"needs more help"| ESC["Escalate: other teams, vendors"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Paged"] --> B["Acknowledge. Is it real, and how bad?"] B --> C{"Are users affected,
or about to be?"} C -->|"no"| D["Handle as a normal alert or ticket"] C -->|"yes"| E["Declare an incident. Assign roles.
Say the severity out loud"] E --> F["First update to users within minutes:
we know, we are working on it"] F --> G{"What changed recently?
Deploy, config, flag, traffic, dependency"} G -->|"a change lines up"| H["Undo it: roll back, switch the flag off"] G -->|"nothing obvious"| I["Mitigate by other means:
fail over, add capacity, shed load"] H --> J{"Is the harm stopping?"} I --> J J -->|"no"| K["One change at a time. Record each.
Escalate early, not late"] K --> G J -->|"yes"| L["Watch until stable. Tell users it is resolved"] L --> M["Close the incident. Keep the timeline.
Schedule the postmortem"]

blocks.text: Commands
The first question in most incidents: what changed, and when. Compare the time of the last revision with the time the graph bent.
The same question where deployments come from Git: each sync with its commit and time.
What the cluster has been doing in the last minutes: failed probes, kills, scheduling problems, image pull errors.

blocks.code: kubectl -n production get pods -o wide | grep -v Running
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Every pod that is not simply running, with its node. A quick view of how widespread the problem is and whether it is tied to one node or zone.

blocks.code: kubectl -n production logs deploy/checkout-api --since=10m | grep -ci error
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: A count of error lines in the last ten minutes. Run it again a minute later to see whether things are getting better or worse.
Returns the Deployment to its previous revision. The most common mitigation there is. With GitOps, revert the commit instead, or the controller will put the bad version back.
In the deployment repository: a new commit that undoes the last one. After it is published the GitOps controller rolls production back. The rollback is recorded and reviewed like any change.
Stops a component completely. Sometimes the right mitigation is to switch off the thing causing harm, such as a worker hammering a struggling database.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Know what stops when you do this, and write down the previous replica count.
Deletes every pod in the namespace at once. A panic move: it removes the evidence and takes down whatever was still working. Not a mitigation.
Exercise
Mitigate five incidents in the simulator with as little time and as few wrong moves as possible.

items: Start with "502 Bad Gateway from the API". Before touching anything, say which check you will make first and why
Mitigate it. Read the review: how many minutes, and how many pieces of evidence did you need?
Run it again and try each wrong action. What does each one cost?
Do "Latency doubled after a deploy" and "Database connections exhausted". In both, one tempting action makes things worse. What do those two actions have in common?
Do "TLS certificate expired". Why did the service's own dashboards show nothing?
Do one SEV1 of your choice and, as you go, write the two status page updates you would post
Across the five: which single question was most often the fastest route to the cause?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can describe the roles in an incident, state why mitigation comes before diagnosis, and name the first three things you check when paged.
Troubleshooting

rows: Ten people in the call, all investigating, nobody deciding
No incident commander.
Name one, out loud. Their job is to coordinate and decide, not to debug.
Several changes were made and nobody knows which helped
People acted in parallel without announcing it.
One change at a time, announced in the channel before it is made, with its result noted.
Support and leadership keep interrupting the engineers
They have no other source of information.
A communications lead who posts updates on a fixed timer, even when the update is "no change".
An hour spent finding the root cause while users were down
Diagnosis was put before mitigation.
Ask first: what is the fastest way to stop the harm? Roll back, fail over or switch off. Diagnose afterwards.
The rollback did not help
The deploy was a coincidence, or the change is not reversible (a data migration, a dependency), or the damage is in state, not code.
Widen the question: configuration, feature flags, traffic, dependencies, expiring things (certificates, credentials), and scheduled jobs.
The incident was declared 40 minutes after the first sign
Reluctance to "make a fuss".
Make declaring cheap and blameless. Standing down a false alarm costs minutes; a late start costs the whole outage.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Mitigate first. Roll back before you understand.
Declare early. It is easy to stand down.
One incident commander, one channel, one timeline.
One change at a time, announced and recorded.
Update users and stakeholders on a timer.
Keep evidence: note what you saw and when, and capture logs before restarting things.
Practise with drills, so the roles are familiar before a real incident.

blocks.text: Security

items: If there is any sign of an intrusion, involve security at once and preserve evidence: do not wipe or restart machines before they are captured.
Incident channels fill with screenshots and logs. Keep credentials and personal data out, and limit who can join.
Emergency access granted during an incident must be removed afterwards.
Attackers sometimes cause an outage as a distraction. An odd incident deserves a second look at access logs.
Status page wording should inform users without describing your internals in detail.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: You are paged for a major outage. What do you do in the first ten minutes?
blocks.text: Acknowledge and assess impact. Declare an incident, open a channel and get someone to handle communication. Check what changed recently. If a change lines up, roll it back; otherwise mitigate by failing over, adding capacity or shedding load. Post a first update for users. Make one change at a time and write down what is seen and done.

blocks.title: What does an incident commander do?
blocks.text: Owns the response: sets priorities, assigns roles, decides which action to take next, keeps people from colliding, calls for escalation, and ensures communication happens. They do not do the hands-on debugging, because someone must keep the whole picture.

blocks.title: Why mitigate before finding the root cause?
blocks.text: Because every minute of diagnosis is a minute of user harm, and most mitigations, such as rollback or failover, do not require knowing the cause. Diagnosis is easier and safer once the pressure is off, using the evidence collected.

blocks.title: How do you define severity levels?
blocks.text: By user impact and urgency, in terms anyone can apply: SEV1 is a critical function down or data at risk for many users and needs everyone now; SEV2 is serious degradation or a partial outage; SEV3 is minor impact with a workaround. Each level fixes who is paged and how often updates go out.

blocks.title: How should you communicate during an incident?
blocks.text: Early, regularly and plainly. A first acknowledgement within minutes, then updates on a fixed interval saying what users experience, what is being done and when the next update comes. No guesses about cause, no blame, no internal jargon.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Errors began two minutes after a release. The first action is usually…
quiz.why: Stop the harm. The diff will still be there tomorrow.

quiz.q: The incident commander's main job is to…
quiz.why: Someone must hold the whole picture while others work on the parts.

quiz.q: Three engineers each try a fix at the same time. The problem is…
options: nobody can tell what had which effect
quiz.why: One change at a time, announced and recorded.

lessons.title: Postmortems and runbooks: learning from incidents

blocks.text: After an incident, the team writes down what happened, why the system allowed it, and what will change. That document is a postmortem. It is blameless: it asks how a reasonable person, doing their job, could end up causing or missing the problem, and fixes that. A runbook is the other product of incidents: the steps for responding to a known alert, written so that someone half awake can follow them.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Aviation. After any serious event, investigators do not ask "which pilot is to blame". They ask why the instruments, checklists and training allowed it, and they change those for every aircraft. Pilots report their own mistakes freely because reporting is safe. That is a large part of why flying became as safe as it is.
Why it matters

Incidents are expensive lessons. Without a written review the same failure returns, and the knowledge of how it was fixed lives in one person's memory. With blame, people hide what they did and the real causes stay hidden. A blameless review turns one team's bad afternoon into an improvement for the whole organisation.
Where you meet it

After every significant incident and after near misses. Postmortems are shared widely and their action items are tracked like any other engineering work. Runbooks are linked from the alerts they belong to.
Scenario

The day after the checkout outage, the team meets for 45 minutes with the timeline from the incident channel. They find that the alert took five minutes to fire, that a required setting was only checked by deploying, and that the rollout did not stop itself. Nobody asks who forgot the setting. Four action items get owners and dates. Two weeks later a similar mistake in another service is stopped by the new pipeline check, and nobody is paged.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR INC["Incident"] --> TL["Timeline, logs, graphs,
chat history"] TL --> PM["Blameless postmortem
within a few days"] subgraph DOC["The document"] S["Summary and impact"] T["Timeline"] CF["Contributing factors:
why the system allowed it"] WW["What went well and badly"] AI["Action items:
owner and date each"] end PM --> DOC AI --> BL["Team backlogs,
tracked to done"] DOC --> SHARE["Shared with the whole
engineering organisation"] AI --> RB["Runbooks updated,
linked from alerts"] AI --> AL["Alerts fixed or added"] AI --> PIPE["Pipeline and platform changes"] BL --> REV["Monthly review: are
action items being closed?"] SHARE --> TREND["Patterns across incidents"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Something went wrong and a person was involved"] --> B{"Ask: who made the mistake?"} B --> C["Answer: a name. Outcome: that person is careful for a while.
The trap remains for the next person"] A --> D{"Ask: why did it make sense
to them at the time?"} D --> E["They had the information, tools and
pressures the system gave them"] E --> F{"Why did the system let
the action cause harm?"} F --> G["No check before the action"] F --> H["No early signal that it had gone wrong"] F --> I["No fast, safe way to undo it"] G --> J["Action: add a guard
(validation, review, policy)"] H --> K["Action: improve detection
(alert, canary, health check)"] I --> L["Action: improve recovery
(rollback, backup, runbook)"] J --> M["Each action: one owner, one date,
followed until closed"] K --> M L --> M

blocks.text: Commands
Cluster events with timestamps: raw material for a timeline. Events expire after about an hour by default, so collect them during or straight after the incident.
Exactly what one revision changed: image, environment, resources. Establishes what the triggering change was.
In the deployment or infrastructure repository: every change in the window around the incident, with time and author. Used to build the timeline, not to assign blame.
Error logs for the incident window from the central store, which still has them after the pods are gone.
The error rate over the incident window as data points. Gives precise times for "impact began" and "impact ended", and the size of the impact.
Silences that were active recently. A question for every postmortem: was an alert that should have fired silenced?
A postmortem (illustrative)

blocks.code:
# Postmortem: checkout errors after release 1.8.3

**Date:** 2026-11-11   **Duration:** 14 minutes   **Severity:** SEV1
**Author:** on-call engineer   **Status:** action items in progress

## Summary
For 14 minutes, 41% of checkout requests failed. A release needed a configuration
value that existed in staging but not in production. The new pods crashed at
start-up; a rollback restored service.

## Impact
About 2,300 failed checkout attempts. 31% of the month's error budget.
No data was lost and no customer was charged without an order.

## Timeline (UTC)
- 14:02  Release 1.8.3 starts rolling out.
- 14:03  New pods enter CrashLoopBackOff. Error rate begins to rise.
- 14:08  CheckoutHighErrorRate pages the on-call engineer.
- 14:10  Incident declared. Recent deploy identified from rollout history.
- 14:14  Rollback started.
- 14:16  Error rate back to normal. Incident mitigated.

## What went well
- maxUnavailable: 0 kept the old pods serving, so the outage was partial.
- The alert linked to the runbook, whose first step is "check recent changes".

## What went badly
- The alert took five minutes to fire for a 41% error rate.
- The missing setting was only discoverable by deploying.

## Contributing factors
- Configuration for staging and production is maintained in different places.
- The service starts without validating that required settings are present
  in the target environment before the rollout begins.
- The rollout does not stop itself when new pods fail to become ready.

## Action items
| Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Keep all environments' settings in one reviewed repository | platform team | 25 Nov |
| Pipeline step: fail if a required setting is missing in the target | checkout team | 18 Nov |
| Add a fast-burn error-budget alert (pages in about 2 minutes at 41%) | SRE | 15 Nov |
| Automatic rollback when a rollout makes no progress for 5 minutes | platform team | 2 Dec |

_Blameless: this document describes what the system allowed, not who made a mistake._

blocks.text: Short, specific and dated. The contributing factors describe the system, not people, and every action item has an owner and a date. "Be more careful" is not an action item.
Exercise
Work the data-loss incident, then write the core of its postmortem.

items: Mitigate the incident shown. Note the time you took and the evidence you used
From the review, write a three-sentence summary a non-engineer could follow
Write the timeline as five lines with times
The migration was written by a person. Without naming or blaming them, list three things the system could have done to prevent the damage
Turn those into action items. For each: is it a guard, better detection, or better recovery? Who would own it?
One prevention item says "replicas are not backups". Which earlier lesson explains why, and what saved the data here?
Write the first five steps of a runbook for the alert that should have existed

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain what blameless means in practice, name the sections of a postmortem, and tell a good action item from a vague one.
Troubleshooting

rows: Postmortems are written and the same incidents recur
Action items are not tracked, or they are vague ("improve monitoring").
Each item specific, owned and dated, in the team's normal backlog, and reviewed monthly until closed.
People are defensive or quiet in the review
They expect blame, from experience.
Leaders must model it: thank people for reporting, ask "how did the system allow this", and never use a postmortem in performance reviews.
The root cause is recorded as "human error"
The analysis stopped at the person.
Human error is where the investigation starts. Ask why the mistake was easy to make and hard to notice.
The review hunts for one root cause
A belief that incidents have a single cause.
List contributing factors. Serious incidents need several things to line up, and each is a place to add a defence.
Nobody can reconstruct the timeline
Nothing was recorded during the incident, and logs and events have expired.
A scribe during incidents, a channel with timestamps, and central retention of logs and metrics.
The runbook did not match reality
It was written once and never used.
Review runbooks after each use, and have someone unfamiliar follow them in a drill.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Write the postmortem within days, while memory and data are fresh.
Blameless, always, and visibly so from leadership.
Contributing factors, not a single root cause.
Record what went well too: those are defences worth keeping.
Action items that are specific, owned, dated and tracked.
Share postmortems widely and look for patterns across them.
Review near misses: they are free lessons.

blocks.text: Security

items: Postmortems for security incidents may need restricted distribution. Publish a redacted version rather than nothing.
Do not include secrets, customer data or exploitable detail in widely shared documents.
For security events, record what the attacker accessed and for how long: it determines legal and customer notification duties.
Evidence used in the review should be preserved unaltered.
An action item that weakens a control to make operations easier needs a security review of its own.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is a blameless postmortem?
blocks.text: A written review of an incident that assumes everyone acted reasonably with what they knew, and looks for the conditions in systems, tools and process that allowed the outcome. It covers impact, timeline, contributing factors and concrete actions, and names roles, not culprits, so people share what really happened.

blocks.title: Why blameless? Is nobody accountable?
blocks.text: People are accountable for taking part honestly and for completing the actions. Punishing mistakes makes people hide them, which removes the information needed to fix the system. Blamelessness is the price of that information, and it produces better outcomes than fear.

blocks.title: What makes a good action item?
blocks.text: It is specific, has one owner and a date, can be verified as done, and changes the system rather than asking people to try harder. "Add a pipeline check that fails when a required setting is missing in production" is good. "Be more careful with configuration" is not.

blocks.title: What goes in a runbook?
blocks.text: What the alert means in terms of user impact, how to confirm it, the first diagnostic steps with exact commands, the known mitigations in order of safety, when and whom to escalate to, and links to dashboards. It is written for someone woken at night who did not build the service.

blocks.title: Tell me about an incident you learned from.
blocks.text: Structure the answer like a postmortem: the impact, how it was detected, what you did to mitigate, the contributing factors, and what was changed afterwards. Interviewers listen for ownership without blame, for mitigation before diagnosis, and for a concrete improvement that outlived the incident.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which is a good postmortem action item?
options: Add a check that blocks the migration unless the backfill has finished; owner: data team; due 20 Nov
quiz.why: Specific, owned, dated, and it changes the system.

quiz.q: "Root cause: human error" means the analysis…
quiz.why: The useful question is why the error was possible and went unnoticed.

quiz.q: A runbook is written for…
options: the person who built the service
quiz.why: It must work for someone tired and unfamiliar with the service.

modules.title: Disaster Recovery
modules.summary: RTO and RPO by tier, the four recovery strategies, cross-region data, DNS failover, drills and failback. One lesson; no hands-on lab, because a real one needs two cloud regions.

lessons.title: Disaster recovery: surviving the loss of a region

blocks.text: High availability handles small failures automatically: a server, a zone. Disaster recovery is the plan for the big ones: a whole cloud region unavailable, or data destroyed by a mistake or an attack. The plan is defined by two numbers agreed with the business. RTO is how long the service may be down. RPO is how much recent data may be lost. The smaller those numbers, the more of the system must already be running somewhere else, and the more it costs.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A company deciding what to do if its office burns down. One option: copies of the files in a bank vault, and a plan to rent a new office (weeks). Another: an empty second office with desks ready (days). Another: a second office with a skeleton staff already working (hours). The most expensive: two full offices, each able to carry on alone (no gap). No option is wrong. Each is a price for a certain speed of recovery.
Why it matters

Regions do fail, rarely. More often the disaster is self-inflicted: a deletion, a bad migration, ransomware, a compromised account. An organisation that has never restored its systems elsewhere does not have a recovery plan; it has a hope. And the decision about how much to spend belongs to the business, which can only make it if engineering gives it honest numbers.
Where you meet it

Everything needed to run the service: data first, then the infrastructure definitions, container images, secrets, DNS and the pipeline itself. Different services get different tiers: checkout and payments need far more than internal reporting.
Scenario

The shop runs in Mumbai. Checkout is tier 1 with an RTO of 15 minutes and an RPO of 1 minute, so a scaled-down copy runs in Singapore with the database replicated continuously (warm standby). The catalogue is tier 2: its data is replicated and its servers would be started on demand (pilot light). Analytics is tier 3: backups copied across regions, rebuilt from code within a day. Twice a year the team fails checkout over to Singapore for real, on a quiet morning, and measures how long it actually takes.
Architecture

flowchart TB DNS["DNS with health checks
api.shop.example, TTL 60 s"] -->|"normally"| P DNS -. "when the primary is unhealthy" .-> S subgraph P["Primary region: Mumbai"] PA["checkout-api, full size"] PDB[("Orders database, primary")] PS3["Object storage"] end subgraph S["Recovery region: Singapore"] SA["checkout-api, small
(warm standby)"] SDB[("Orders database,
cross-region replica")] SS3["Object storage, replicated"] CAT["catalogue: data only,
servers off (pilot light)"] end PDB -->|"continuous replication,
seconds behind"| SDB PS3 -->|"replication"| SS3 subgraph BK["Separate backup account"] B["Immutable backups of everything,
copied across regions"] end PDB --> B IAC["Terraform + GitOps repositories,
images in a second-region registry"] -. "rebuild anything" .-> S

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["The primary region is failing"] --> B{"Is it really the region,
or our own change?"} B -->|"our change"| C["Ordinary incident: roll back. Do not fail over"] B -->|"region, confirmed"| D{"Will it be back
within our RTO?"} D -->|"probably"| E["Wait and watch. Failover has
its own risks and costs"] D -->|"no, or unknown"| F["Decide to fail over.
A named person makes the call"] F --> G["Stop writes in the primary if reachable,
so the two sides cannot diverge"] G --> H["Promote the database replica
in the recovery region"] H --> I["Scale the application up to full size"] I --> J["Point DNS at the recovery region"] J --> K["Verify with real requests.
Tell users"] K --> L["Later: plan failback as carefully
as the failover. Data now lives in the new region"]

blocks.text: Commands
Read replicas in the recovery region and what they replicate from. Confirms the copy exists and is healthy.

blocks.code: aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region ap-southeast-1 --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name ReplicaLag --dimensions Name=DBInstanceIdentifier,Value=shop-orders-sg --start-time 2026-11-11T12:00:00Z --end-time 2026-11-11T13:00:00Z --period 300 --statistics Maximum
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: How far behind the cross-region replica has been, in seconds. This number is your real RPO.
Shows whether a bucket's objects are being copied to another region, and to which bucket.
The most recent backups held in the recovery region's vault. If the newest is older than your RPO, the plan is already broken.
Where the public name points right now. Run it before, during and after a failover.
What each of Route 53's checkers thinks of the primary. DNS failover follows this.
Shows what would be created to bring the recovery region to full size. Running this regularly proves the code still works there.
Turns the cross-region replica into a standalone primary. Replication from the old primary ends permanently, and anything not yet replicated is lost. The point of no return in a failover.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Only on the decision of the named incident owner, after writes in the primary are stopped or the primary is confirmed unreachable.

Deletes every object in a bucket. Shown here as the kind of command, typed by a person or by ransomware, that replication copies faithfully to the other region. Only versioning and separate, immutable backups protect against it.
DNS failover between regions (Terraform, illustrative)

The health check and the short TTL together set a floor under the RTO: about 90 seconds to detect plus up to 60 for clients to notice. Automatic DNS failover suits stateless tiers; promoting a database is usually a human decision.
Exercise
Choose a recovery strategy for three kinds of service in the Disaster recovery planner, and put a price on each.

items: Press the tier 1 button. Which strategies meet the targets, and which only "on a good day"? What does the cheapest reliable one cost?
Relax the RTO to 30 minutes. What becomes possible, and how much is saved?
Press tier 2 and tier 3. Why would it be a waste to give analytics the same design as checkout?
Set both targets to "none at all". What does the planner say, and what would you tell a manager who asks for zero downtime and zero data loss?
Ransomware encrypts the primary database, and replication copies the damage to the recovery region within seconds. Which part of the architecture diagram saves you?
Using the flowchart, list who must be available and what must already exist for a failover to take 15 minutes
Design a twice-yearly drill for checkout: what do you fail, what do you measure, and how do you make it safe?

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can define RTO and RPO, describe the four strategies and their trade-offs, and explain why replication alone is not disaster recovery.
Troubleshooting

rows: The failover took hours, not the planned minutes
It had never been done. Steps were missing, people lacked access, quotas in the recovery region were too low.
Rehearse on a schedule. Every drill finds something; fix it and repeat.
The recovery region cannot start enough servers
Service quotas there were never raised, or capacity is short because everyone else is failing over too.
Raise quotas in advance. For tier 1, keep capacity running or reserved.
The application starts in the recovery region and cannot work
A dependency exists only in the primary: a secret, an image registry, a third-party allow-list, a license server.
Inventory dependencies and replicate each. Drills are how the missing ones are found.
After failover, some users still reach the dead region
Long DNS TTLs or clients that cache addresses.
Short TTLs on failover names, and clients that re-resolve.
Data was corrupted and the replica has the same corruption
Replication copies every change, good or bad.
Point-in-time recovery and versioned, immutable backups in a separate account. Replication is for losing a place, backups are for losing the data.
Nobody is sure whether to fail over
No named decision-maker and no criteria.
Write down who decides and on what evidence, before the day it is needed.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Set RTO and RPO per service with the business, in tiers. Do not give everything the top tier.
Infrastructure as code and GitOps for everything, so any environment can be rebuilt.
Backups in a separate account and region, immutable, and restore-tested.
Rehearse failover for real on a schedule, and measure it.
Include the things people forget: DNS, secrets, images, the pipeline, monitoring, and access for the people who must act.
Plan failback as carefully as failover.
Keep the plan short, current and reachable when the primary region, and your wiki in it, are down.

blocks.text: Security

items: Ransomware and compromised credentials are the likeliest disasters. Backups must be out of reach of the production account's administrators.
Use immutable storage (object lock) and deletion protection for backups.
The recovery region needs the same security controls as the primary: it will be production one day.
Data residency: check that replicating to another country is permitted.
Recovery credentials and procedures must not depend on systems that would be down in the disaster.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between high availability and disaster recovery?
blocks.text: High availability keeps a service running through expected, small failures such as a server or zone, usually automatically and without data loss. Disaster recovery restores service after a major event such as losing a region or the data itself, with defined recovery time and data-loss targets, often with human decisions involved.

blocks.title: Describe the common disaster recovery strategies.
blocks.text: Backup and restore: only backups elsewhere; hours to days to recover; cheapest. Pilot light: data replicated and minimal core running; servers started on demand. Warm standby: a scaled-down full copy running; scale up and switch. Multi-site active/active: both regions serve traffic; near-zero recovery time at roughly double the cost and with hard data consistency problems.

blocks.title: How do you choose between them?
blocks.text: From the RTO and RPO the business sets for each service, and their cost. Tier the services: revenue-critical ones justify warm standby or active/active; others are fine with pilot light or backups. Then validate the choice by measuring an actual recovery.

blocks.title: Your database is replicated to another region. Are you protected against data loss?
blocks.text: Against losing the region, yes, apart from replication lag. Against deletion, corruption or ransomware, no: those are replicated too. That needs point-in-time recovery and immutable backups in a separate account.

blocks.title: How do you test a disaster recovery plan?
blocks.text: In stages: restore backups regularly; run tabletop walk-throughs; then real failover drills for tier 1 services, first in staging and then in production at a quiet time, measuring time to recover and data lost against the targets. Each drill produces fixes, like an incident.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A scaled-down copy of the whole system runs in a second region. This is…
quiz.why: Running, but small. Scale it up and switch traffic.

quiz.q: Ransomware encrypts the production database. Cross-region replication…
options: copies the encrypted data to the other region
quiz.why: Replication copies every change. Immutable backups are what save you.

quiz.q: The only way to know your real RTO is to…
options: perform a recovery and time it
quiz.why: Everything else is an estimate that leaves out what you forgot.

modules.title: Performance and Scalability
modules.summary: Capacity, queueing, load testing and finding the bottleneck. One lesson.

lessons.title: Performance, load testing and finding the bottleneck

blocks.text: Every system has a maximum rate of work, set by its slowest part. Below that rate, response time is flat. Close to it, requests queue and response time climbs steeply. Past it, requests fail. A load test finds where that point is before your customers do, and tells you which part to fix: adding servers only helps if servers are the limit.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A motorway with a toll booth. Traffic flows freely until the booths are nearly full; then a small increase in cars produces a long queue. Adding lanes before the booths does nothing. Only more booths, or faster payment, moves the limit.
Why it matters

Teams scale the wrong thing all the time: more pods in front of a database that is already the limit makes it worse. Knowing the capacity and the bottleneck turns a sale day from a gamble into a plan.
Where you meet it

Before a known peak, after any change to architecture or dependencies, and as a regular check that capacity still exceeds forecast. Tools: k6, Locust, Gatling, JMeter, against an environment that resembles production.
Scenario

The annual sale is forecast at 600 checkouts per second. A load test shows checkout-api saturating at 400 with 6 pods. Doubling the pods raises the limit to 660, where the database's 40 connections become the limit and more pods change nothing. Fixing one slow query moves the wall further than any number of pods.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR LG["Load generator
k6, several machines"] -->|"ramping traffic"| LB["Load balancer"] LB --> APP["checkout-api pods
slots = pods x workers"] APP --> POOL["Connection pool"] POOL --> DB[("Database
limited connections")] APP --> EXT["Payment provider
(stubbed in tests)"] APP -. "metrics" .-> MON["Dashboards: rate, errors,
p95, saturation of each tier"] LG -. "results" .-> REP["Report: capacity,
bottleneck, headroom"]

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["Response time is rising with load"] --> B{"Is CPU high on the service?"} B -->|"yes"| C["The service is the limit.
Add pods, or profile and optimise"] B -->|"no: threads are waiting"| D{"Waiting on what?"} D -->|"a database connection"| E["Pool or max_connections.
Faster queries, or a pooler"] D -->|"the database itself"| F["Slow queries, locks, I/O.
EXPLAIN, index, cache"] D -->|"a downstream call"| G["That service is the limit.
Timeout, cache, or scale it"] C --> H["Change one thing"] E --> H F --> H G --> H H --> I["Run the same test again"] I --> J{"Did the limit move?"} J -->|"no"| A J -->|"yes"| K["A new bottleneck is now first.
Stop when capacity exceeds forecast plus headroom"]

blocks.text: Commands
Runs the load test against staging. It generates real traffic: point it only at an environment you own and have warned people about.

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: Never aim a load test at production or at a third party without agreement.
A small smoke run with 10 virtual users, to check the script works before the real test.
CPU and memory per pod during the test. High CPU means the service is the limit; low CPU with slow responses means it is waiting on something.
Watches the autoscaler react during the test: how quickly it adds pods and whether it reaches its maximum.

blocks.code: psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "SELECT count(*), state, wait_event_type FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 2,3 ORDER BY 1 DESC;"
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: During the test: how many connections are active, idle or waiting on locks. A pool at its limit shows here.
The 95th percentile as the service measured it. Compare with what the load generator saw: a gap means time lost in the network or the load balancer.
A ramping load test (k6, illustrative)
Thresholds make the test pass or fail by itself, so it can run in a pipeline. Stub the payment provider: you are testing your system, not theirs.
Exercise
Find the capacity and the bottleneck of checkout-api in the Load-test lab, and get it ready for 900 requests per second.

items: At the start settings, read the capacity and the safe rate for a 300 ms target. Why are they different numbers?
Press "Evening peak" then "Sale day". Describe what happens to response time and errors at each
Press "Double the pods". Which limit is now first?
Press "Quadruple the pods". Did capacity change? Why not?
Press "Fix the slow query". What moved, and by how much?
Find the cheapest combination of settings that handles 900 per second under 300 ms

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can read a latency-against-load curve, name the bottleneck from the evidence, and explain why scaling one tier can do nothing.
Troubleshooting

rows: Adding pods did not raise throughput
The limit is elsewhere: database connections, a downstream service, or a lock.
Find what requests are waiting on, using traces and saturation metrics for each tier.
The test shows great numbers that production never reaches
Unrealistic test: tiny data set, one hot cache key, no think time, no realistic mix of requests.
Use production-like data volumes and a traffic mix taken from real logs.
Errors start at a low rate during the test
The load generator is the bottleneck, or a rate limit or firewall is blocking it.
Watch the generator's own CPU and network; distribute it; allow-list it.
Latency is fine on average and customers complain
The tail is slow: a few requests take seconds.
Report the 95th and 99th percentiles, never the average.
The system fell over and stayed down after the load dropped
Retries and queued work kept it overloaded.
Limit retries with back-off, shed load early, and set queue limits.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Test for the forecast peak plus headroom, and for losing one zone at that peak.
Measure the tail, not the average.
Change one thing between runs.
Know the limit of every tier, including the ones you do not own.
Keep utilisation below about 70% at normal peak.
Protect the system past its limit: timeouts, limited retries, load shedding, a waiting room.
Re-run after significant changes; capacity drifts.

blocks.text: Security

items: A load test is indistinguishable from an attack. Announce it, and never run one against systems you do not own.
Test data must be synthetic. Do not replay real customer requests with real personal data.
Test accounts and stubs must not be reachable in production.
Rate limits are also a defence against abuse: test that they hold.
Results reveal your limits. Share them inside the company only.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you find the bottleneck in a slow system?
blocks.text: Measure where requests spend time. High CPU on the service means the service. Low CPU with slow responses means waiting: look at connection pools, database activity, locks and downstream calls, using traces. Fix the first limit, re-test, and expect a different one to appear next.

blocks.title: Why does latency rise sharply near capacity?
blocks.text: Requests arrive unevenly. As utilisation approaches 100%, the chance that all slots are busy rises fast, so requests queue. Waiting time grows without bound as utilisation nears one, which is why systems are run with headroom.

blocks.title: Load, stress, soak and spike tests?
blocks.text: Load: expected peak, to confirm targets are met. Stress: beyond peak, to find the limit and how it fails. Soak: hours at normal load, to find leaks. Spike: a sudden jump, to test autoscaling and recovery.

blocks.title: Horizontal versus vertical scaling?
blocks.text: Vertical means a bigger machine: simple, limited, and a single point of failure. Horizontal means more machines: needs stateless services and a load balancer, scales further and survives failures. Databases are usually scaled vertically first, then with replicas, caching and partitioning.

blocks.title: What happens when a system is pushed past capacity, and how do you protect it?
blocks.text: Queues grow, everything times out, and retries add load, so it can stay down after traffic falls. Protect it by rejecting excess early: rate limits, concurrency limits, short timeouts, retries with back-off and budgets, circuit breakers, and a queue in front for known peaks.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: CPU on the service is 20%, responses are slow. More pods will…
quiz.why: The service is waiting, not working. The limit is somewhere else.

quiz.q: A healthy utilisation target at normal peak is around…
quiz.why: It leaves room for bursts and for losing capacity.

quiz.q: Which number best describes user experience?
quiz.why: The tail is what the unlucky customers feel.

modules.title: Cost Optimization / FinOps
modules.summary: Tags and visibility, idle resources, scheduling, right-sizing, spot, commitments and unit cost. One lesson.

lessons.title: FinOps: understanding and reducing the cloud bill

blocks.text: In the cloud every engineer can spend money with one command, and the bill arrives a month later. FinOps is making cost visible to the people who cause it, removing what nobody uses, sizing what is used to what it needs, and paying the right price for what remains. The order matters: delete, schedule, right-size, then commit.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A household electricity bill. First you find the heater left on in the empty room. Then you stop heating the house while everyone is out. Then you replace the oversized boiler. Only then do you sign a fixed-price contract, for the amount you now know you need.
Why it matters

Cloud spending grows quietly: forgotten test clusters, machines sized for a launch years ago, staging running all night. Typical estates carry a large share of waste. Cutting it funds engineers, and the same visibility tells you whether growth is efficient.
Where you meet it

Tagging and budgets in Terraform, cost dashboards per team, regular reviews, and a few big levers: idle resources, non-production schedules, right-sizing, spot capacity for batch work, commitments for the steady base, storage classes and data transfer.
Scenario

The shop's bill is $18,600 a month. A review finds a load-test cluster from March still running, 9 TB of orphaned disks, staging on all night, nightly reports on machines that idle 18 hours a day, and checkout-api at a fifth of its CPU. Fixing those, then committing to the baseline, brings it under $4,000 with no effect on customers.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart LR RES["Cloud resources
tagged: team, service, env"] --> BILL["Billing data export"] BILL --> DASH["Cost dashboards
per team and service"] DASH --> TEAMS["Teams see their own spend"] BILL --> BUD["Budgets and anomaly alerts"] BUD --> TEAMS METRICS["Utilisation metrics"] --> REC["Right-sizing recommendations"] REC --> TEAMS TEAMS -->|"pull requests"| IAC["Terraform / manifests"] IAC --> RES BIZ["Business metric: orders"] --> UNIT["Unit cost: $ per order"] BILL --> UNIT

blocks.text: Flow
Commands

blocks.code: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Last month's cost by AWS service. The first look at where the money goes.

blocks.code: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=TAG,Key=team
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: The same, by team tag. A large "untagged" share means nobody owns that spend.
Disks attached to nothing. Usually left behind when an instance was deleted, and billed every month.
Actual CPU use per pod. Compare with requests: a pod requesting 2 cores and using 0.2 is reserving capacity nobody else can use.
Scales every Deployment in staging to zero, for example at night. Record the previous counts or let a scheduler restore them.
Deletes a disk and its data for good. Take a snapshot first and wait a while when in doubt; a snapshot costs a fraction of the disk.
Tags and a budget in Terraform (illustrative)
default_tags puts the same tags on every resource the provider creates. Without tags a bill is one number that nobody can act on.
Exercise
Cut the shop's bill in the Cloud cost lab and say what each saving risked.

items: With everything off, which three lines are largest? Which of them is doing useful work?
Switch on "Delete what nothing uses". How much was pure waste?
Add scheduling, then right-sizing. Which workloads changed, and which were left alone and why?
Add spot for batch work. Why is this the largest saving, and what must be true of the jobs?
Press "Only buy a commitment". Read the warning. Then add right-sizing and see it disappear
Compare the cost per order before and after, and at double the order volume

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can state the order of cost levers and why, and explain unit cost.
Troubleshooting
