rows: Nobody can say which team caused the increase
Resources are untagged.
Enforce tags in Terraform and with policy; report the untagged share until it is near zero.
The bill jumped overnight
A runaway autoscaler, a log or metric explosion, a data transfer loop, or a compromised credential mining crypto-currency.
Anomaly alerts on daily spend, and maximum sizes on everything that scales.
Right-sizing caused an outage
Sized from average CPU, ignoring memory, peaks or zone loss.
Size from peak with headroom, change gradually, and watch the SLO.
A commitment is being paid for and not used
It was bought before right-sizing, or the workload moved.
Commit only to a measured, stable baseline, and cover it partly, not fully.
Data transfer is a top line item
Traffic between zones or regions, or out through NAT gateways.
Keep chatty services in the same zone, use VPC endpoints, and cache at the CDN.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Tag everything: team, service, environment.
Show each team its own cost, weekly.
Delete, schedule, right-size, then commit. In that order.
Budgets and anomaly alerts for every account.
Track unit cost, such as dollars per order, not only the total.
Give every temporary environment an expiry date.
Treat cost as a non-functional requirement in design reviews.

blocks.text: Security

items: A sudden cost spike is often the first sign of a compromised account.
Cost tools need read access to billing only; keep them away from resources.
Cleaning up unused resources also removes forgotten, unpatched attack surface.
Never save money by removing backups, logs or a standby without an explicit decision by the owner.
Budget alerts should reach security as well as finance.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you reduce a cloud bill?
blocks.text: First visibility: tags and cost per team. Then in order: delete unused resources, schedule non-production, right-size from measured use, move interruptible work to spot, and commit to the steady baseline. Then storage classes and data transfer. Keep it going with budgets, alerts and regular reviews.

blocks.title: What is right-sizing and what are the risks?
blocks.text: Matching provisioned capacity to measured need. The risks are sizing from averages and missing peaks, ignoring memory, and removing the headroom needed to survive a zone failure. Do it gradually while watching the SLO.

blocks.title: When would you use spot instances?
blocks.text: For work that tolerates interruption: batch jobs, CI runners, stateless services with enough replicas across instance types. Not for databases or anything that cannot lose a node at two minutes' notice.

blocks.title: What is unit cost and why does it matter?
blocks.text: Cost divided by a business measure, such as per order or per active user. Total cost rising with the business is fine; unit cost rising means the system is getting less efficient.

blocks.title: How do you make engineers care about cost?
blocks.text: Show them their own spend next to their own services, make the cheap option the default in the platform, set budgets with alerts to the team, and celebrate savings like features. Blame and central policing do not work.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: Which comes first?
quiz.why: It is free money with the least risk.

quiz.q: Committing before right-sizing…
quiz.why: You commit to capacity you are about to stop needing.

quiz.q: The bill rose 20% and cost per order fell. That is…
quiz.why: More business, served more efficiently.

modules.title: Platform Engineering
modules.summary: Golden paths, self-service, guardrails and measuring a platform. One lesson.

lessons.title: Platform engineering: golden paths and self-service

blocks.text: A platform team builds the road other teams drive on: a standard way to create, build, deploy, observe and secure a service, offered as self-service. A team describes its service in one small file and gets a repository, a pipeline, a deployment, dashboards and alerts. The standard way is called a golden path: not compulsory, but so much easier than the alternatives that people choose it.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A city's roads, water and electricity. A shop owner does not dig a well or build a power station. They connect to what the city provides and get on with running the shop. The city's job is to make connecting easy and the service dependable.
Why it matters

This whole academy is what one service needs: a Dockerfile, a pipeline, manifests, probes, RBAC, secrets, dashboards, alerts, SLOs. Thirty teams each assembling that by hand produce thirty variations, uneven security and slow starts. A platform does it once, well, and lets product teams spend their time on the product.
Where you meet it

Companies with more than a handful of teams. The pieces: service templates, a shared pipeline, GitOps, a developer portal with a service catalogue (Backstage is a common one), and guardrails enforced as policy.
Scenario

A new team needs a service in production. Without a platform: three weeks of tickets and copied YAML. With one: they fill in a short service file, a pull request is opened for them, and an hour later a hardened, monitored service is running in staging with a pipeline, burn-rate alerts and a runbook stub. Everything from the earlier modules is there; they did not have to write it.
Architecture

blocks.code:
flowchart TB DEV["Product team"] -->|"service.yaml, or a form in the portal"| PORTAL["Developer portal
catalogue, templates, docs"] PORTAL --> TPL["Golden-path templates"] TPL --> REPO["Repository with code skeleton,
Dockerfile, pipeline"] TPL --> GITOPS["Deployment repository entry"] REPO --> CI["Shared pipeline:
build, scan, sign"] CI --> GITOPS GITOPS --> ARGO["Argo CD"] ARGO --> K8S["Clusters with guardrails:
pod security, network policy, quotas"] TPL --> OBS["Dashboards, SLO alerts,
on-call routing"] TPL --> INFRA["Terraform modules:
database, topic, bucket"] PLAT["Platform team"] -->|"builds and runs as a product"| PORTAL PLAT --> K8S DEV -. "feedback, adoption data" .-> PLAT

blocks.text: Flow

blocks.code:
flowchart TD A["A team needs something:
a service, a database, a topic"] --> B{"Is there a golden path for it?"} B -->|"yes"| C["Self-service: minutes, no ticket"] B -->|"no"| D{"Is the need common?"} D -->|"yes"| E["Platform team builds a path,
with the first team as a customer"] D -->|"no"| F["The team goes its own way,
and owns what it builds"] C --> G["Guardrails apply automatically:
security, cost tags, SLOs"] E --> G F --> H["Must still pass the same policies"] G --> I{"Do teams choose the path?"} I -->|"no"| J["Find out why. Fix the path,
do not mandate it"] I -->|"yes"| K["Measure: time to first deploy,
adoption, deploy frequency"]

blocks.text: Commands
How many workloads were created through the golden path. Adoption is the platform's main success measure.
Namespaces with their owning team and cost centre. A namespace without an owner is a gap in the platform.
The limits a team's namespace may use: a guardrail that stops one team consuming the cluster.
Every application the platform deploys, with its sync and health status.

blocks.code: helm template checkout ./platform-chart -f service-values.yaml | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -
blocks.caption: Safe, read-only

blocks.text: Renders what the platform would create for a service and asks the cluster whether it would be accepted, without applying it.
A guardrail applied to a team's namespace. On a platform this is set by the namespace template, not by hand.
A service definition on the platform (illustrative)

blocks.code:
# service.yaml: all a team writes to get a production service on the platform (illustrative).
# The platform turns this into a repository, a pipeline, a Helm release, dashboards and alerts.
apiVersion: platform.shop.example/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  team: checkout
spec:
  runtime: python-fastapi          # picks the template: Dockerfile, pipeline, base chart
  port: 8000
  replicas: { min: 3, max: 12 }
  resources: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
  slo:
    availability: 99.9             # creates burn-rate alerts routed to the team's on-call
    latencyP95Ms: 300
  dependencies:
    - postgres: orders             # provisions credentials through the secret store
    - kafka-topic: order-events
  exposure: public                 # ingress, TLS certificate and WAF rules

blocks.text: This API is invented for the lesson. The point is the ratio: twenty lines from the team, and hundreds of lines of correct, consistent configuration generated for them.
Exercise
Design the golden path for a new backend service using what this academy covered.

items: List everything checkout-api needed across the modules, from Dockerfile to burn-rate alert. Count the items
Mark each: the same for every service, or specific to this one
Write the smallest service file that captures only the specific parts
Which guardrails should be impossible to switch off, and which should be defaults a team can change?
A team wants a language the platform does not support. What do you tell them?
Choose three numbers that would tell you whether the platform is working

blocks.title: Verify
blocks.text: You can explain what a golden path is, why it is offered rather than forced, and how a platform team measures success.
Troubleshooting

rows: Teams avoid the platform
It is slower or more restrictive than doing it themselves, or was built without talking to them.
Treat teams as customers: interview them, fix the top friction, and make the path the fastest option.
The platform team is a ticket queue
Requests need a human.
Turn the most frequent tickets into self-service, one by one.
Every team has customised the template until nothing is shared
The template was copied once and never updated.
Templates as versioned dependencies (a base chart, a shared pipeline library) that teams upgrade, not copies.
A platform change broke thirty services at once
No staged rollout for the platform itself.
Version platform components, canary them on a few teams, and keep a rollback.
The abstraction hides too much and nobody can debug
Teams cannot see what was generated.
Make the generated manifests and pipelines visible and documented.

blocks.text: Best practices

items: Run the platform as a product, with users, a roadmap and feedback.
Pave the most common path first; do not try to cover everything.
Self-service by default. A ticket is a missing feature.
Build guardrails in: security, cost tags and SLOs come with the path.
Offer, do not mandate. Adoption is the test.
Share components as versioned dependencies, not copied templates.
Measure time to first deploy, adoption, deployment frequency and developer satisfaction.

blocks.text: Security

items: The platform is where security is applied once for everyone: pod security, network policy, signed images, least-privilege identities.
It is also a single point of compromise. Protect templates, pipelines and the deployment repository like production.
Guardrails enforced by policy, not by documentation.
Multi-tenancy needs real isolation: namespaces, quotas, network policy, separate secrets.
Every exception to a guardrail is recorded, owned and time-limited.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is platform engineering?
blocks.text: Building and running an internal product that gives development teams self-service access to everything needed to ship and operate software: templates, pipelines, infrastructure, observability and guardrails. Its goal is to reduce the effort and knowledge each team needs, while keeping standards consistent.

blocks.title: What is a golden path?
blocks.text: An opinionated, supported route for a common task, such as creating a production-ready service, with security, deployment and monitoring already built in. It is optional, and succeeds by being the easiest way.

blocks.title: How is platform engineering different from DevOps and SRE?
blocks.text: DevOps is the practice of teams owning both building and running software. SRE applies engineering to reliability with SLOs and error budgets. Platform engineering provides the shared tools that make both practical at scale, so each team does not rebuild them.

blocks.title: How do you measure a platform team?
blocks.text: Adoption of the golden path, time from idea to first production deploy, deployment frequency and lead time across teams, the volume of tickets, reliability of the platform itself, and what developers say in surveys.

blocks.title: What are common ways a platform fails?
blocks.text: Building what the platform team finds interesting instead of what users need, mandating use, becoming a ticket queue, hiding so much that teams cannot debug, and never updating templates so every team drifts.

blocks.title: Simulator
blocks.text: This lesson has a simulator in the interactive version of the course.

quiz.q: A golden path should be…
quiz.why: People choose it because it is better, which is how you know it works.

quiz.q: A frequent ticket to the platform team is…
quiz.why: Automate the repeat so nobody waits.

quiz.q: The main measure of a platform is…
quiz.why: An unused platform delivers nothing.

questions.topic: Lesson · What DevOps is, and the path from commit to customer
questions.q: What is DevOps?
questions.a: A way of working where development and operations share ownership of delivery and reliability, supported by automation (CI/CD, infrastructure as code, monitoring) so changes are small, frequent and reversible. It is a practice, not a job title or a tool.

questions.topic: Lesson · What DevOps is, and the path from commit to customer
questions.q: What are the DORA metrics?
questions.a: Deployment frequency and lead time for changes measure speed. Change failure rate and time to restore service measure stability. Strong teams improve both together.

questions.topic: Lesson · The filesystem and moving around
questions.q: What is the difference between an absolute and a relative path?
questions.a: An absolute path starts at / and means the same thing from anywhere. A relative path is resolved from the current directory, so its meaning changes with pwd.

questions.topic: Lesson · The filesystem and moving around
questions.q: What lives in /etc, /var and /tmp?
questions.a: /etc holds system-wide configuration, /var holds data that grows while the system runs (logs, databases, caches), /tmp holds scratch files that may be cleared on reboot.

questions.topic: Lesson · The filesystem and moving around
questions.q: How does the shell find the program when you type "ls"?
questions.a: It searches each directory listed in the PATH environment variable, in order, and runs the first executable named ls.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reading and searching text: logs are your evidence
questions.q: How would you find the top 5 client IPs in an nginx access log?
questions.a: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5. Extract the IP column, group identical values, count, sort by count descending, take five.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reading and searching text: logs are your evidence
questions.q: What is the difference between tail -f and less +F?
questions.a: Both follow a growing file. less +F lets you press Ctrl+C to stop following and scroll or search backwards, then F to resume.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reading and searching text: logs are your evidence
questions.q: What does a pipe actually connect?
questions.a: The standard output (file descriptor 1) of the left process to the standard input (file descriptor 0) of the right one, through a kernel buffer. Both processes run at the same time.

questions.topic: Lesson · Users, groups and permissions
questions.q: What does chmod 750 mean?
questions.a: Owner 7 = rwx, group 5 = r-x, others 0 = nothing. Typical for a directory the service owns and an ops group may browse.

questions.topic: Lesson · Users, groups and permissions
questions.q: A file is mode 644 but a user still cannot read it. Why?
questions.a: Reading a file also needs execute (x) permission on every directory in its path. Another cause is an ACL, SELinux or AppArmor policy.

questions.topic: Lesson · Users, groups and permissions
questions.q: Why should services not run as root?
questions.a: A bug or exploit in the service then has full control of the machine. As an unprivileged user the damage is limited to what that user can touch.

questions.topic: Lesson · Processes, signals and what "kill" really does
questions.q: Difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL?
questions.a: SIGTERM is a request the process can catch to shut down cleanly. SIGKILL is enforced by the kernel and cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, so no cleanup runs.

questions.topic: Lesson · Processes, signals and what "kill" really does
questions.q: A container exits with code 137. What happened?
questions.a: 137 = 128 + 9, so it received SIGKILL. Usually the kernel OOM killer (memory limit exceeded) or a stop whose grace period expired. Check for OOMKilled in kubectl describe pod or the kernel log.

questions.topic: Lesson · Processes, signals and what "kill" really does
questions.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
questions.a: A process has its own address space and file descriptors. Threads are execution paths inside one process sharing that memory. Linux schedules both as tasks.

questions.topic: Lesson · Disk, memory and ports: the three things that run out
questions.q: free shows only 400MB "free" on an 8GB server. Is it out of memory?
questions.a: Not necessarily. Linux uses spare RAM as page cache and counts it under buff/cache. The "available" column estimates what programs can still get. Low available plus swap activity or OOM kills is the real warning.

questions.topic: Lesson · Disk, memory and ports: the three things that run out
questions.q: What is the difference between binding to 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0?
questions.a: 127.0.0.1 accepts connections only from the same machine. 0.0.0.0 accepts on every network interface, including public ones.

questions.topic: Lesson · Disk, memory and ports: the three things that run out
questions.q: How do you find what is filling a disk?
questions.a: df -h to find the filesystem, then du -sh on its top-level directories and drill into the largest, or du -ah DIR | sort -rh | head.

questions.topic: Lesson · systemd services and logs
questions.q: Walk me through debugging a service that will not start.
questions.a: systemctl status for state and exit code, journalctl -u for the last error, then check the usual causes in order: config syntax, missing environment, permissions on files, port already in use, dependency not reachable. Fix, start, verify with a real request.

questions.topic: Lesson · systemd services and logs
questions.q: restart versus reload?
questions.a: restart stops the process and starts a new one, dropping open connections. reload asks the running process to re-read its configuration without exiting, if it supports that (nginx does).

questions.topic: Lesson · systemd services and logs
questions.q: What does "systemctl enable" do?
questions.a: It makes the unit start at boot by linking it into a target. It does not start it now; that is "start", or "enable --now" for both.

questions.topic: Lesson · Namespaces, cgroups and the OOM killer: what a container really is
questions.q: What is a container, at the kernel level?
questions.a: A normal process started in its own set of namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) so it sees an isolated system, attached to cgroups that cap its resources, with a root filesystem assembled from image layers by an overlay filesystem.

questions.topic: Lesson · Namespaces, cgroups and the OOM killer: what a container really is
questions.q: Container versus VM?
questions.a: A VM virtualises hardware and runs its own kernel: strong isolation, heavier, slower to start. A container shares the host kernel and isolates at the process level: light and fast, but the kernel is a shared attack surface.

questions.topic: Lesson · Namespaces, cgroups and the OOM killer: what a container really is
questions.q: Why might a container be OOM-killed while the node has free memory?
questions.a: The limit is enforced per cgroup. The container hit its own memory.max regardless of what the node has free.

questions.topic: Lesson · IP addresses, subnets and CIDR
questions.q: How many usable hosts are in a /26?
questions.a: 32 - 26 = 6 host bits, 2^6 = 64 addresses, minus network and broadcast = 62 usable (59 on AWS, which reserves 5).

questions.topic: Lesson · IP addresses, subnets and CIDR
questions.q: What does NAT do?
questions.a: It rewrites the private source address of outgoing packets to a public one and remembers the mapping so replies return to the right machine. Private hosts can reach out but cannot be reached from outside.

questions.topic: Lesson · IP addresses, subnets and CIDR
questions.q: Public versus private subnet in a cloud VPC?
questions.a: A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway. A private subnet does not; its outbound traffic, if any, goes through a NAT gateway.

questions.topic: Lesson · DNS: turning names into addresses
questions.q: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter? Start with DNS.
questions.a: The browser checks its cache, the OS cache and /etc/hosts, then asks the configured resolver. The resolver walks root, TLD and authoritative servers, returns the address and caches it for the TTL. Then TCP, TLS and HTTP follow.

questions.topic: Lesson · DNS: turning names into addresses
questions.q: A record versus CNAME?
questions.a: An A record maps a name directly to an IPv4 address. A CNAME maps a name to another name, which is then resolved. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records on the same name, which is why the zone apex needs A or ALIAS records.

questions.topic: Lesson · DNS: turning names into addresses
questions.q: What is TTL and how does it affect failover?
questions.a: How long resolvers may cache the answer. A long TTL reduces lookups but means a change or failover takes up to that long to reach everyone.

questions.topic: Lesson · TCP, HTTP and TLS: what one API call is made of
questions.q: Difference between 502, 503 and 504?
questions.a: 502: the proxy got an invalid or no response from the upstream (crashed, refused). 503: no capacity or no healthy upstream. 504: the upstream accepted the request but did not answer within the proxy timeout.

questions.topic: Lesson · TCP, HTTP and TLS: what one API call is made of
questions.q: TCP versus UDP?
questions.a: TCP is connection-oriented with ordering, retransmission and congestion control. UDP sends independent datagrams with no guarantees and less overhead. DNS queries, streaming and QUIC (HTTP/3) use UDP.

questions.topic: Lesson · TCP, HTTP and TLS: what one API call is made of
questions.q: What does the TLS handshake establish?
questions.a: Server identity (a certificate chained to a trusted CA and matching the hostname), an agreed cipher, and shared session keys derived by key exchange, so later traffic is encrypted and tamper-evident.

questions.topic: Lesson · Network troubleshooting: a method, not guessing
questions.q: A service cannot reach its database. How do you debug it?
questions.a: From the service host or pod: resolve the name, test the port with nc, check credentials and TLS with the real client, then check the database side (listening address, max connections, firewall or security group, pg_hba). State what each result rules out.

questions.topic: Lesson · Network troubleshooting: a method, not guessing
questions.q: Refused versus timed out?
questions.a: Refused is an immediate TCP reset: the host is reachable and nothing listens. A timeout means packets vanish: firewall, routing or a dead host.

questions.topic: Lesson · Commits and the three areas
questions.q: What is the staging area for?
questions.a: It lets you compose a commit deliberately from part of your working changes, so each commit is one coherent change even when your working tree holds several.

questions.topic: Lesson · Commits and the three areas
questions.q: What does a commit contain?
questions.a: A snapshot of the whole tracked tree, a message, author and committer details, and the ID of its parent commit or commits. Its ID is a hash of all of that, so changing anything creates a different commit.

questions.topic: Lesson · Commits and the three areas
questions.q: How do you undo a change that is staged, and one that is not?
questions.a: git restore --staged FILE unstages and keeps the edit. git restore FILE discards an unstaged edit permanently.

questions.topic: Lesson · Branches, merging and conflicts
questions.q: Fast-forward merge versus three-way merge?
questions.a: Fast-forward is possible when the current branch is an ancestor of the other: Git just moves the pointer and creates no commit. Otherwise Git merges the two tips against their common ancestor and creates a merge commit with two parents.

questions.topic: Lesson · Branches, merging and conflicts
questions.q: When does Git report a conflict?
questions.a: When both sides changed the same region of the same file differently relative to the merge base, or one side deleted a file the other modified. Changes to different regions of one file merge automatically.

questions.topic: Lesson · Branches, merging and conflicts
questions.q: What is HEAD?
questions.a: A pointer to the current branch, and through it to the commit your working tree is based on. In a detached HEAD state it points straight at a commit instead of a branch.

questions.topic: Lesson · Rewriting and undoing: rebase, cherry-pick, revert, reset, tags
questions.q: Merge versus rebase: when do you use each?
questions.a: Rebase to update a private feature branch onto the latest main and keep history linear. Merge to integrate finished work into a shared branch, preserving what actually happened. Never rebase shared history.

questions.topic: Lesson · Rewriting and undoing: rebase, cherry-pick, revert, reset, tags
questions.q: A bad commit reached production. What do you do?
questions.a: Restore service first by rolling back the deployment. Then git revert the commit on main so the pipeline ships the corrected state, and follow up with a proper fix and a test. Do not rewrite main.

questions.topic: Lesson · Rewriting and undoing: rebase, cherry-pick, revert, reset, tags
questions.q: reset --soft, --mixed and --hard?
questions.a: All move the branch pointer. Soft keeps the staging area and files, so the changes are ready to recommit. Mixed (default) unstages them but keeps files. Hard overwrites files too, discarding uncommitted work.

questions.topic: Lesson · Rewriting and undoing: rebase, cherry-pick, revert, reset, tags
questions.q: What does cherry-pick do and when is it risky?
questions.a: It applies the diff of one commit as a new commit elsewhere. Useful for backporting a fix. It duplicates the change under a different ID, which can cause confusing conflicts if the branches later merge.

questions.topic: Lesson · Team workflows and how Git drives CI/CD
questions.q: Trunk-based development versus GitFlow?
questions.a: Trunk-based: one long-lived branch, short-lived feature branches merged at least daily, features gated by flags, releases cut from main. GitFlow: develop, feature, release and hotfix branches with scheduled releases. Trunk-based gives faster feedback and suits continuous delivery; GitFlow suits versioned products with slow release cycles, at the cost of late integration.

questions.topic: Lesson · Team workflows and how Git drives CI/CD
questions.q: How does a Git commit become a running container?
questions.a: The push sends a webhook to CI, which checks out that commit, tests it, builds an image tagged with the commit ID, pushes it to a registry and updates the deployment to that tag. The ID links production back to exact source.

questions.topic: Lesson · Team workflows and how Git drives CI/CD
questions.q: Monorepo versus many repositories?
questions.a: A monorepo makes cross-service changes atomic and tooling uniform, but needs path-based builds and scales poorly without investment. Many repos give teams independence and simple pipelines, but coordinated changes and shared-library upgrades become multi-step.

questions.topic: Lesson · Your first scripts: variables, quoting and exit codes
questions.q: What is an exit code and why does it matter?
questions.a: An integer from 0 to 255 returned by every process. 0 is success. Shells, CI systems, systemd and Kubernetes probes all decide what to do next from it, so a script that prints "error" but exits 0 is treated as a success.

questions.topic: Lesson · Your first scripts: variables, quoting and exit codes
questions.q: Single quotes versus double quotes?
questions.a: Single quotes keep everything literal. Double quotes allow variable and command substitution but still stop word splitting and globbing.

questions.topic: Lesson · Your first scripts: variables, quoting and exit codes
questions.q: What does the shebang do?
questions.a: When a file is executed, the kernel reads the first line and runs the named interpreter with the file as its argument. #!/usr/bin/env bash finds bash through PATH, which is more portable than a fixed path.

questions.topic: Lesson · Conditions, loops, functions and pipes
questions.q: What is the difference between [ and [[ in bash?
questions.a: [ is the portable test command: its arguments are ordinary words, so unquoted variables can break it. [[ is bash syntax: no word splitting inside, pattern and regex matching with == and =~, and && / || work inside. Use [[ in bash scripts and [ when the script must run under plain sh.

questions.topic: Lesson · Conditions, loops, functions and pipes
questions.q: What does 2>&1 mean?
questions.a: Redirect file descriptor 2 (stderr) to wherever descriptor 1 (stdout) currently points. Order matters: "> file 2>&1" sends both to the file; "2>&1 > file" sends only stdout to the file.

questions.topic: Lesson · Conditions, loops, functions and pipes
questions.q: Write a retry loop for a flaky command.
questions.a: for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do cmd && break; sleep $((i * 2)); done, then check whether it ultimately succeeded and exit non-zero if not. Mention backoff, a maximum and that only idempotent actions should be retried.

questions.topic: Lesson · Scripts you can trust in production: strict mode, idempotency, cron
questions.q: What does set -euo pipefail do, and what are its gotchas?
questions.a: -e exits on a failing command, -u errors on unset variables, pipefail makes a pipeline fail when any stage fails. Gotchas: -e does not apply inside conditions or before && and ||, grep returning 1 for "no match" will stop the script unless handled, and behaviour inside functions called from conditions surprises people.

questions.topic: Lesson · Scripts you can trust in production: strict mode, idempotency, cron
questions.q: What makes a script idempotent, and why does it matter?
questions.a: Running it any number of times produces the same end state. It checks before acting: create the directory only if missing, skip if already healthy. It matters because automation retries, and a retry of a non-idempotent step does the work twice.

questions.topic: Lesson · Scripts you can trust in production: strict mode, idempotency, cron
questions.q: How would you make sure a nightly backup is actually working?
questions.a: Exit non-zero on failure, log to a known file, send a heartbeat on success and alert when it is missing, monitor backup age and size, and run automated test restores.

questions.topic: Lesson · Scripts you can trust in production: strict mode, idempotency, cron
questions.q: Explain the cron expression */15 9-17 * * 1-5.
questions.a: Every 15 minutes during the hours 09 to 17, Monday to Friday.

questions.topic: Lesson · Python for automation: when a script outgrows Bash
questions.q: When do you choose Python over Bash for automation?
questions.a: When the task involves structured data, API calls, non-trivial error handling, or will be maintained and tested. Bash stays the right choice for short sequences of commands and for places where only a shell is available, such as a minimal container.

questions.topic: Lesson · Python for automation: when a script outgrows Bash
questions.q: How do you run a shell command from Python safely?
questions.a: subprocess.run with a list of arguments, check=True to raise on failure, a timeout, and capture_output when the output is needed. Avoid shell=True, and never interpolate untrusted input into a command string.

questions.topic: Lesson · Apache HTTP Server: virtual hosts and reverse proxying
questions.q: Apache versus Nginx?
questions.a: Both serve files, terminate TLS and reverse proxy. Nginx uses an event-driven design that handles many connections with little memory. Apache uses processes or threads per connection (with an event mode for keep-alive), has per-directory .htaccess files and a very large module ecosystem. New systems usually choose Nginx; Apache is common in existing ones.

questions.topic: Lesson · Apache HTTP Server: virtual hosts and reverse proxying
questions.q: How does Apache choose a virtual host?
questions.a: By the address and port the request arrived on, then by matching the Host header against ServerName and ServerAlias. If none match, the first virtual host defined for that port is used.

questions.topic: Lesson · Apache HTTP Server: virtual hosts and reverse proxying
questions.q: What is an MPM?
questions.a: A multi-processing module: how Apache handles connections. Prefork uses one process per connection, worker uses threads, event uses threads and hands idle keep-alive connections to a listener so they do not hold a worker.

questions.topic: Lesson · Apache HTTP Server: virtual hosts and reverse proxying
questions.q: What is .htaccess and why avoid it?
questions.a: A per-directory configuration file read at request time, which lets users without access to the main configuration change settings. It costs a file lookup on every request and scatters configuration, so prefer the main configuration when you control it.

questions.topic: Lesson · Apache HTTP Server: virtual hosts and reverse proxying
questions.q: How do you apply an Apache change with no downtime?
questions.a: apachectl configtest, then a graceful reload, which lets workers finish current requests before picking up the new configuration.

questions.topic: Lesson · Servers and SSH: getting onto a machine you cannot touch
questions.q: How does SSH key authentication work?
questions.a: The server holds the user's public key in authorized_keys. During login the client signs a session-specific challenge with the private key and the server verifies the signature with the public key. The private key is never transmitted, so nothing reusable can be captured.

questions.topic: Lesson · Servers and SSH: getting onto a machine you cannot touch
questions.q: Difference between a virtual machine and a bare-metal server?
questions.a: Bare metal is the whole physical machine: full performance and isolation, slow to provision. A VM is a slice presented by a hypervisor: created in seconds, resizable, shares hardware with others. Cloud instances are VMs.

questions.topic: Lesson · Servers and SSH: getting onto a machine you cannot touch
questions.q: What is a bastion host?
questions.a: The single hardened server with a public IP through which administrators reach machines in private subnets. It shrinks the attack surface to one audited entry point.

questions.topic: Lesson · The first hour on a new server: users, SSH hardening, firewall, updates
questions.q: You get a fresh Ubuntu server with a public IP. What do you do first?
questions.a: Create a personal sudo user with my key, verify I can log in, disable root and password logins, enable a default-deny firewall allowing only SSH and the service ports, apply updates and enable automatic security updates, and confirm from outside what is reachable. Then capture those steps as code.

questions.topic: Lesson · The first hour on a new server: users, SSH hardening, firewall, updates
questions.q: Security group versus host firewall?
questions.a: A security group is enforced by the cloud network before traffic reaches the instance and is managed through the provider API. A host firewall runs inside the OS. Using both gives defence in depth: one misconfiguration alone does not expose a service.

questions.topic: Lesson · The first hour on a new server: users, SSH hardening, firewall, updates
questions.q: Why bind a database to 127.0.0.1?
questions.a: It then accepts connections only from the same host, whatever the firewall says. It turns an exposure that would need one mistake into one that needs two.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running several applications on one server
questions.q: How can many websites share one IP address and port?
questions.a: The client sends the hostname in the HTTP Host header (and in the TLS SNI field). The web server picks the matching virtual host. That is name-based virtual hosting.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running several applications on one server
questions.q: When would you stop running everything on one server?
questions.a: When you need availability through a machine failure, independent scaling of components, isolation between workloads, or zero-downtime deploys. The first step is usually moving the database out, then adding a second app server behind a load balancer.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running several applications on one server
questions.q: What does a reverse proxy do that the app could not do itself?
questions.a: It terminates TLS, serves static files efficiently, routes by host and path, buffers slow clients, applies limits and logs every request in one consistent place, so each application stays simple and private.

questions.topic: Lesson · TLS certificates, Let's Encrypt and automatic renewal
questions.q: What does a client verify about a server certificate?
questions.a: That the chain of signatures leads to a root it trusts, that the current time is within the validity period, that the requested hostname appears in the subject alternative names, and that the server proves possession of the private key during the handshake. Revocation may also be checked.

questions.topic: Lesson · TLS certificates, Let's Encrypt and automatic renewal
questions.q: How does Let's Encrypt verify domain ownership?
questions.a: Through an ACME challenge. HTTP-01: the CA fetches a token from http://domain/.well-known/acme-challenge/. DNS-01: you publish a TXT record, which also allows wildcard certificates and works for servers not reachable on port 80.

questions.topic: Lesson · TLS certificates, Let's Encrypt and automatic renewal
questions.q: Why are certificate lifetimes getting shorter?
questions.a: Short lifetimes limit the damage of a leaked key and of mis-issuance, since revocation is unreliable in practice. Let's Encrypt issues 90-day certificates today and has published a schedule down to 64 days in February 2027 and 45 days in February 2028; industry rules cap all public certificates at 47 days from 2029. This only works with automation.

questions.topic: Lesson · TLS certificates, Let's Encrypt and automatic renewal
questions.q: A certificate expired in production. What do you do, in order?
questions.a: Renew and reload to restore service, verify from outside, then find why renewal failed (logs, challenge reachability, hook), add expiry alerting, and write it up. The lasting fix is monitoring the outcome, not the job.

questions.topic: Lesson · Pointing a domain at your server, and moving it without downtime
questions.q: How do you migrate a live site to a new IP without downtime?
questions.a: Lower the TTL in advance and wait out the old one, bring up and test the new target by IP, switch the record, keep both serving until the old one is idle, then raise the TTL and decommission. Keep a rollback at each step.

questions.topic: Lesson · Pointing a domain at your server, and moving it without downtime
questions.q: Why can the apex of a domain not be a CNAME?
questions.a: A CNAME must be the only record at its name, but the apex must also hold SOA and NS records. Providers offer ALIAS or ANAME records that behave like a CNAME but answer with addresses.

questions.topic: Lesson · Pointing a domain at your server, and moving it without downtime
questions.q: Registrar versus DNS provider?
questions.a: The registrar sells the name and tells the registry which name servers are authoritative. The DNS provider runs those name servers and holds the records. They can be the same company or different ones.

questions.topic: Lesson · Nginx configuration: server blocks and location matching
questions.q: How does nginx choose a location block?
questions.a: Exact match first. Otherwise it remembers the longest matching prefix; if that prefix has ^~ it is used. If not, regex locations are tested in the order they appear and the first match wins. If no regex matches, the remembered prefix is used.

questions.topic: Lesson · Nginx configuration: server blocks and location matching
questions.q: root versus alias?
questions.a: root appends the full request URI to the path. alias replaces the matched location part with the path. For location /img/ with root /data, /img/a.png maps to /data/img/a.png; with alias /data/, it maps to /data/a.png.

questions.topic: Lesson · Nginx configuration: server blocks and location matching
questions.q: reload versus restart?
questions.a: reload re-reads the configuration and gracefully replaces worker processes with no dropped connections, and is refused if the config is invalid. restart stops nginx and starts it again, dropping connections, and fails to come back if the config is broken.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reverse proxy and load balancing
questions.q: What happens to the URI with "proxy_pass http://backend/" versus "proxy_pass http://backend"?
questions.a: With a URI part (the trailing slash counts) nginx replaces the part of the request URI that matched the location with that URI. Without one, the original URI is passed unchanged. For location /api/, /api/health becomes /health in the first case and stays /api/health in the second.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reverse proxy and load balancing
questions.q: How does nginx load balance, and what happens when a backend dies?
questions.a: Round-robin by default, optionally weighted, or least_conn or ip_hash. Open-source nginx uses passive health checks: after failed attempts (max_fails within fail_timeout) a server is skipped for a while, and the failed request is retried on the next server per proxy_next_upstream.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reverse proxy and load balancing
questions.q: Forward proxy versus reverse proxy?
questions.a: A forward proxy acts for clients reaching out to the internet and hides the clients. A reverse proxy acts for servers, receiving requests from the internet and hiding the backends.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reverse proxy and load balancing
questions.q: Why might retrying a failed request at the proxy be dangerous?
questions.a: If the backend processed the request but the response was lost, a retry runs it twice: two orders, two charges. Retries are safe only for idempotent requests or when the application uses idempotency keys.

questions.topic: Lesson · CI/CD: from commit to a running release
questions.q: Continuous delivery versus continuous deployment?
questions.a: Delivery: every passing change is releasable and a human decides when. Deployment: every passing change is released automatically. The difference is the manual gate.

questions.topic: Lesson · CI/CD: from commit to a running release
questions.q: Why tag images with the commit SHA instead of "latest"?
questions.a: A SHA tag is immutable and traceable: you know exactly which code is running and can roll back to an exact prior image. "latest" moves, so two nodes can run different code under the same tag.

questions.topic: Lesson · CI/CD: from commit to a running release
questions.q: How do you make a deployment safe?
questions.a: Small change, automated tests, a staging run of the same artifact, gradual rollout (rolling or canary), readiness-gated traffic, automated health verification, and an automatic rollback path.

questions.topic: Lesson · Artifacts, environments and deployment strategies
questions.q: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments.
questions.a: Rolling replaces instances gradually with little extra capacity; rollback is gradual. Blue-green stands up a full copy and switches traffic at once; rollback is instant but capacity doubles. Canary shifts a small share of traffic, compares metrics and widens; it limits exposure best but needs traffic splitting and trustworthy metrics.

questions.topic: Lesson · Artifacts, environments and deployment strategies
questions.q: Why "build once, deploy many"?
questions.a: It guarantees that what was tested is what runs in production. Rebuilding can pull different dependency versions or base images, so the tested artifact and the deployed one are no longer the same thing.

questions.topic: Lesson · Artifacts, environments and deployment strategies
questions.q: How do you deploy a database schema change with zero downtime?
questions.a: Expand and contract. First add the new structure in a backward-compatible way. Deploy code that writes both and reads the new. Backfill. Only when no running version needs the old structure, remove it. Each step is independently reversible.

questions.topic: Lesson · Artifacts, environments and deployment strategies
questions.q: What is the difference between deploying and releasing?
questions.a: Deploying puts code on servers. Releasing exposes behaviour to users. Feature flags separate them, so code can ship dark, be enabled for a few users, and be turned off without a deploy.

questions.topic: Lesson · Jenkins architecture: controller, agents, jobs and credentials
questions.q: Explain the Jenkins controller and agent model.
questions.a: The controller schedules builds, stores configuration and credentials and serves the UI. Agents connect to it and execute builds in workspaces. Labels route builds to agents with the right tools; executors set how many builds an agent runs concurrently.

questions.topic: Lesson · Jenkins architecture: controller, agents, jobs and credentials
questions.q: Why should builds not run on the controller?
questions.a: Builds execute arbitrary code. On the controller that code sits beside all credentials and configuration and competes for the resources that scheduling needs, so one bad build can compromise or stall everything.

questions.topic: Lesson · Jenkins architecture: controller, agents, jobs and credentials
questions.q: How do you scale Jenkins?
questions.a: Add agents, preferably ephemeral ones provisioned on demand (Kubernetes pods, cloud VMs). Keep the controller small and stateless in configuration, and split very large installations into several controllers by team.

questions.topic: Lesson · Writing a Jenkinsfile: stages, parallelism, credentials and post actions
questions.q: Declarative versus scripted pipelines?
questions.a: Declarative has a fixed structure (pipeline, agent, stages, steps, post) that Jenkins validates before running; it is easier to read and covers most needs. Scripted is plain Groovy with full control flow and no enforced structure. A script block lets declarative pipelines drop into Groovy where needed.

questions.topic: Lesson · Writing a Jenkinsfile: stages, parallelism, credentials and post actions
questions.q: How do you handle secrets in a Jenkins pipeline?
questions.a: Store them in the credential store, bind them with withCredentials around only the steps that need them, reference them from single-quoted shell commands so they are not interpolated, rely on masking in logs but never print them, scope them to the folder or job, and rotate them.

questions.topic: Lesson · Writing a Jenkinsfile: stages, parallelism, credentials and post actions
questions.q: What is a shared library and when would you write one?
questions.a: A Git repository of Groovy code that pipelines import with @Library, exposing custom steps such as deployToKubernetes(...). Write one when several repositories repeat the same pipeline logic, so a fix is made once. Version it, because every pipeline depends on it.

questions.topic: Lesson · Writing a Jenkinsfile: stages, parallelism, credentials and post actions
questions.q: How would you speed up a 40-minute pipeline?
questions.a: Measure per stage first. Then run independent stages in parallel, cache dependencies and image layers, run only the tests affected by the change on pull requests, use bigger or more agents, and move slow suites to a later or nightly stage.

questions.topic: Lesson · When the pipeline is red: a method for build failures
questions.q: A pipeline that was green yesterday is red today with no code change. How do you approach it?
questions.a: No code change points outside the code: a dependency version that floated, an expired credential, a changed base image, an agent problem or an external service. I find the first error, classify it, check whether other pipelines fail the same way, and compare with the last green run's log.

questions.topic: Lesson · When the pipeline is red: a method for build failures
questions.q: How do you deal with flaky tests?
questions.a: Treat flakiness as a defect with an owner. Detect it by rerunning failures and recording pass-on-retry, quarantine the test so it stops blocking, fix the cause (timing, shared state, order dependence, real race conditions), and track the count over time.

questions.topic: Lesson · When the pipeline is red: a method for build failures
questions.q: The deploy stage timed out waiting for the rollout. What now?
questions.a: Check whether the automatic rollback ran and production is serving the old version. Then describe a new pod for events, read its previous logs, and compare configuration and secrets with the last good revision. Fix forward only after service is confirmed healthy.

questions.topic: Lesson · Jenkins shared libraries and secrets in pipelines
questions.q: What is a Jenkins shared library?
questions.a: A versioned Git repository of reusable pipeline code. Files in vars become steps callable from any Jenkinsfile, src holds helper classes and resources holds templates. It removes duplication and gives one place to change how everything is built.

questions.topic: Lesson · Jenkins shared libraries and secrets in pipelines
questions.q: How do you roll out a change to a shared library safely?
questions.a: Check it in the library's own pipeline, tag a new version, move a few pipelines to it, then the rest. Never have every pipeline follow the main branch.

questions.topic: Lesson · Jenkins shared libraries and secrets in pipelines
questions.q: How should secrets be used in a Jenkins pipeline?
questions.a: From the credentials store, bound with withCredentials around the smallest block, read by the shell from the environment. Better still, replace stored secrets with short-lived identities.

questions.topic: Lesson · Jenkins shared libraries and secrets in pipelines
questions.q: Why is "${SECRET}" in a double-quoted sh step a problem?
questions.a: Groovy substitutes the value before the shell runs, so it appears in the command line and can leak through process listings and logs. With single quotes the shell reads the environment variable itself.

questions.topic: Lesson · Jenkins shared libraries and secrets in pipelines
questions.q: What is the risk of a shared library?
questions.a: It concentrates power: a bad or malicious change affects every pipeline. It needs the same protection as production, and versioning so failures are contained.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitHub Actions: the same pipeline in workflow form
questions.q: How do GitHub Actions and Jenkins differ?
questions.a: Actions is a hosted service integrated with GitHub: runners are ephemeral, configuration is YAML in the repository, and reuse is through actions. Jenkins is self-hosted software you operate: long-lived or ephemeral agents, Groovy pipelines, plugins. Actions removes operations work; Jenkins gives more control over machines, networks and unusual build environments.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitHub Actions: the same pipeline in workflow form
questions.q: How do you deploy to a cloud from Actions without storing cloud keys?
questions.a: Use OpenID Connect. The workflow requests a signed identity token from GitHub; the cloud provider is configured to trust tokens from a specific repository and branch and exchanges it for short-lived credentials. Nothing long-lived is stored.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitHub Actions: the same pipeline in workflow form
questions.q: What is a matrix build?
questions.a: One job definition expanded into several jobs over combinations of variables, for example operating systems and language versions, run in parallel.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitHub Actions in depth: reuse, matrix, caching, environments and OIDC
questions.q: What is the difference between a reusable workflow and a composite action?
questions.a: A reusable workflow is a whole workflow called at the job level with uses:. It can contain several jobs, choose its own runners and use environments. A composite action is a bundle of steps called as one step inside a job, so it runs on the caller's runner. Share a complete pipeline with a reusable workflow; share a few repeated steps with a composite action.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitHub Actions in depth: reuse, matrix, caching, environments and OIDC
questions.q: How does OIDC replace stored cloud credentials in GitHub Actions?
questions.a: The job asks GitHub for a signed token that states which repository, branch or environment it is running for. It presents that token to the cloud provider, which has been told to trust GitHub as an identity provider. The provider checks the claims against the role's trust policy and returns credentials that expire in about an hour. Nothing long-lived is stored, so there is nothing to leak or rotate.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitHub Actions in depth: reuse, matrix, caching, environments and OIDC
questions.q: Why pin an action to a commit SHA rather than a version tag?
questions.a: A tag is a movable pointer. If the action's repository is compromised, the attacker can move v4 to malicious code and every workflow using that tag runs it on the next build, with access to your secrets. A commit SHA is immutable. Tools such as Dependabot can still propose updates to the pinned SHA.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitHub Actions in depth: reuse, matrix, caching, environments and OIDC
questions.q: A matrix job fails on one version and the others are cancelled. Why, and how do you change it?
questions.a: fail-fast defaults to true, so the first failure cancels the rest of the matrix to save minutes. Setting strategy.fail-fast: false lets every combination finish, which is what you want when you need to know whether the failure is specific to one version.

questions.topic: Lesson · Volumes and container networking
questions.q: Volume versus bind mount?
questions.a: A volume is storage created and managed by Docker, independent of the host's directory layout and portable across hosts. A bind mount maps a specific host path into the container, so it depends on the host and is ideal for development. Both outlive the container.

questions.topic: Lesson · Volumes and container networking
questions.q: How do containers find each other?
questions.a: On a user-defined network Docker runs an embedded DNS server that resolves container and service names to their current addresses. Containers on the same network connect by name and container port, with no published ports needed.

questions.topic: Lesson · Volumes and container networking
questions.q: What does EXPOSE do?
questions.a: It documents which port the image listens on and is used by tools as a hint. It does not publish the port; only -p or a Compose ports entry does.

questions.topic: Lesson · Production images: small, secure, reproducible, debuggable
questions.q: What is a multi-stage build and why use it?
questions.a: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where later stages copy selected files from earlier ones. Build tools, source and intermediate files stay in the discarded stages, so the final image holds only what is needed at run time: smaller, faster to pull and with less attack surface.

questions.topic: Lesson · Production images: small, secure, reproducible, debuggable
questions.q: Tag versus digest?
questions.a: A tag is a movable name that can be pointed at a different image later. A digest is the hash of the image content and never changes. Deploying by digest guarantees every node runs identical bytes.

questions.topic: Lesson · Production images: small, secure, reproducible, debuggable
questions.q: How do you debug a container that has no shell?
questions.a: Attach an ephemeral debug container that shares its process and network namespaces (kubectl debug, docker debug), read its logs and exit code, and reproduce locally with the entrypoint overridden on a debug variant of the image.

questions.topic: Lesson · Production images: small, secure, reproducible, debuggable
questions.q: How would you reduce vulnerabilities in your images?
questions.a: Fewer packages first: minimal base and multi-stage. Then pin and regularly rebuild to pick up patches, scan in CI with a policy on fixable criticals, and remove what the scan keeps finding rather than accepting it.

questions.topic: Lesson · Images, containers and the Dockerfile
questions.q: Image versus container?
questions.a: An image is an immutable template made of layers. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of it: the image layers plus a thin writable layer and an isolated process.

questions.topic: Lesson · Images, containers and the Dockerfile
questions.q: How does Docker layer caching work?
questions.a: Each instruction produces a layer keyed by the instruction and its inputs. If nothing changed, the cached layer is reused. Once one layer changes, every later layer is rebuilt, so stable steps such as dependency installation go before frequently changing ones such as copying source.

questions.topic: Lesson · Images, containers and the Dockerfile
questions.q: CMD versus ENTRYPOINT?
questions.a: ENTRYPOINT is the executable that always runs; CMD supplies default arguments that docker run can override. With only CMD, the whole command is replaceable.

questions.topic: Lesson · Docker Compose: a whole stack in one file
questions.q: What does depends_on guarantee?
questions.a: Start order. By default only that the dependency's container has been started. With condition: service_healthy it waits until the dependency's healthcheck passes. It never replaces retry logic in the application, because dependencies can restart later.

questions.topic: Lesson · Docker Compose: a whole stack in one file
questions.q: How do services in a Compose project reach each other?
questions.a: Compose creates a network for the project and attaches every service. Docker's DNS resolves each service name to its container, so the api connects to db:5432 using the container port. Published ports are only for access from the host.

questions.topic: Lesson · Docker Compose: a whole stack in one file
questions.q: Compose versus Kubernetes?
questions.a: Compose runs a set of containers on one machine from one file: ideal for development and tests. Kubernetes schedules across many machines, replaces failed instances, scales, rolls out updates gradually and manages configuration and secrets. The concepts map closely: service to Deployment plus Service, volume to PersistentVolumeClaim, healthcheck to probes.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kubernetes internals: networking, DNS, admission and operators
questions.q: How does a pod reach a Service by name?
questions.a: The pod's resolver asks CoreDNS, using search domains to expand the short name. CoreDNS returns the Service's virtual IP. Rules installed on each node by kube-proxy (or an eBPF data plane) rewrite that address to one of the ready pod IPs from the Service's endpoints, and the network plugin routes the packet there.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kubernetes internals: networking, DNS, admission and operators
questions.q: What does a CNI plugin do?
questions.a: It is called when a pod starts to give it a network interface and an IP address and to set up routes so every pod can reach every other pod without NAT. Many also enforce NetworkPolicy and provide encryption or observability.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kubernetes internals: networking, DNS, admission and operators
questions.q: What are admission controllers?
questions.a: Steps that run after authentication and authorisation and before an object is stored. Mutating ones can change the object, such as adding defaults or sidecars; validating ones can reject it, such as Pod Security or image policy. They can be built in or external webhooks.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kubernetes internals: networking, DNS, admission and operators
questions.q: What is an operator?
questions.a: A controller that manages an application through custom resources. You declare the desired state in an object of a new kind, and the operator creates and maintains the underlying resources, encoding the operational knowledge a person would otherwise apply.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kubernetes internals: networking, DNS, admission and operators
questions.q: What is etcd and what happens if it is lost?
questions.a: The consistent key-value store holding all cluster state. Running pods keep running without it, but nothing can change: no scheduling, scaling or healing. Without a backup, the cluster's definition is gone.

questions.topic: Lesson · Service mesh: what it adds and what it costs
questions.q: What is a service mesh?
questions.a: An infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication. A data plane of proxies, usually one sidecar per pod, carries all traffic; a control plane configures them. It provides mutual TLS, traffic management such as retries, timeouts and weighted routing, and uniform telemetry, without application changes.

questions.topic: Lesson · Service mesh: what it adds and what it costs
questions.q: When would you not use one?
questions.a: With few services, a small team, or needs that NetworkPolicy, an ingress controller and OpenTelemetry already meet. A mesh adds latency, resource cost, upgrade work and a new failure layer.

questions.topic: Lesson · Service mesh: what it adds and what it costs
questions.q: How does mutual TLS work in a mesh?
questions.a: The control plane issues each workload a short-lived certificate tied to its service account. Proxies on both sides present and verify certificates, so traffic is encrypted and each side knows the other's identity. Rotation is automatic.

questions.topic: Lesson · Service mesh: what it adds and what it costs
questions.q: Sidecar versus sidecar-less meshes?
questions.a: Sidecars put a proxy in every pod: strong isolation per workload, but cost per pod and lifecycle problems. Newer designs use a per-node component or eBPF for the basics and shared proxies only where needed, reducing overhead.

questions.topic: Lesson · Service mesh: what it adds and what it costs
questions.q: How does a mesh enable canary releases?
questions.a: Routing rules split traffic by weight or by request attributes between versions, independent of how many pods each has. A controller can raise the weight step by step while watching error rate and latency, and roll back automatically.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running more than one cluster
questions.q: Why would you run several Kubernetes clusters instead of one large one?
questions.a: To limit blast radius, so that a bad upgrade or a control-plane fault affects only part of the system. To separate environments, so that experiments in staging cannot harm production. To be present in more than one region for latency or disaster recovery. For hard isolation between tenants or for compliance. And sometimes because of scale limits. The cost is more upgrades, more spend on control planes and idle capacity, and the constant risk of drift, so each additional cluster should have a stated reason.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running more than one cluster
questions.q: How do you keep many clusters consistent?
questions.a: With GitOps. A single repository describes every application and add-on, with a shared base and small per-cluster overlays. A controller such as Argo CD or Flux, driven by something like an ApplicationSet with a cluster generator, applies it to every registered cluster and reverts manual changes. Cluster creation is itself code, policies are enforced by an admission controller everywhere, and version differences are reported as a matter of routine.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running more than one cluster
questions.q: Compare active-active and active-passive across two regions.
questions.a: In active-passive, one region serves all traffic and the other stands ready; failover means redirecting traffic and promoting the database. It is simpler and data stays consistent, but the standby is unproven until used and failover takes minutes. In active-active both regions serve users, which gives lower latency and no idle capacity, and failover is just removing one region. The difficulty is data: either writes go to one primary across regions, or you adopt a database built for multi-region writes and accept its trade-offs.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running more than one cluster
questions.q: How can a service in one cluster call a service in another?
questions.a: The simplest way is through the other cluster's public or internal ingress, treating it like any external dependency with its own name, TLS and authentication. For closer integration, the Multi-Cluster Services API exports a Service so that it gets a shared name across a set of clusters, and service meshes such as Istio, Linkerd and Cilium can join clusters so that calls are encrypted and load-balanced across them. Each step adds coupling, so it is worth asking first whether the regions can be independent.

questions.topic: Lesson · Pods, Deployments and Services: how checkout stays up
questions.q: What happens when you run kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml?
questions.a: kubectl sends the object to the API server, which authenticates, authorises, runs admission, validates and stores it in etcd. The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pod objects. The scheduler assigns each pod to a node. The kubelet on that node tells the container runtime to pull the image and start the containers, runs probes and reports status back.

questions.topic: Lesson · Pods, Deployments and Services: how checkout stays up
questions.q: Liveness versus readiness probe?
questions.a: Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic; failing it removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it. Liveness decides whether the container is restarted. Pointing liveness at a dependency can cause restart storms.

questions.topic: Lesson · Pods, Deployments and Services: how checkout stays up
questions.q: How does a rolling update avoid downtime?
questions.a: New pods are added gradually (maxSurge) and old ones removed only as new ones become Ready (maxUnavailable). Traffic goes only to Ready pods, and old pods get SIGTERM with a grace period to finish requests.

questions.topic: Lesson · Pods, Deployments and Services: how checkout stays up
questions.q: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through it.
questions.a: describe the pod for events and last state (exit code, reason). logs --previous for the crash output. Check recent changes: image, config, secrets. Reproduce the container command locally if needed. Roll back if it started with a deploy.

questions.topic: Lesson · ConfigMaps and Secrets: configuration outside the image
questions.q: ConfigMap versus Secret?
questions.a: Both hold key-value data consumed as environment variables or files. Secrets are meant for sensitive data: they are base64-encoded, can be encrypted at rest, are kept in memory-backed volumes on nodes and can be access-controlled separately. Neither is encrypted by default in a way that protects against someone with API access.

questions.topic: Lesson · ConfigMaps and Secrets: configuration outside the image
questions.q: You updated a ConfigMap and the application did not change. Why?
questions.a: If it is consumed as environment variables, those are set at container start. Mounted files do update, after a delay, but only help if the application re-reads them. The normal fix is to roll the pods, ideally triggered automatically by a content hash in the name or a pod-template annotation.

questions.topic: Lesson · ConfigMaps and Secrets: configuration outside the image
questions.q: How should secrets be managed with GitOps?
questions.a: Never commit plain or base64 values. Either commit encrypted secrets that only the cluster can decrypt (Sealed Secrets, SOPS) or commit references and let an operator fetch the values from a secrets manager (External Secrets Operator, CSI driver).

questions.topic: Lesson · Health probes and graceful shutdown
questions.q: Explain liveness, readiness and startup probes.
questions.a: Readiness controls membership of Service endpoints: failing means no traffic, no restart. Liveness controls restarts: failing means the kubelet kills and restarts the container. Startup disables both until it succeeds, to protect slow-starting applications from being killed during startup.

questions.topic: Lesson · Health probes and graceful shutdown
questions.q: What goes wrong if liveness checks the database?
questions.a: A database problem makes every pod fail liveness at once. They are all restarted, which cannot fix the database, removes all capacity, and adds a thundering herd of reconnecting pods when it recovers. Dependency state belongs in readiness.

questions.topic: Lesson · Health probes and graceful shutdown
questions.q: How do you achieve zero-downtime shutdown of a pod?
questions.a: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, so for a short time traffic still arrives. Add a preStop delay so routing catches up, then on SIGTERM stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests and exit, all within the termination grace period.

questions.topic: Lesson · Requests, limits and quality of service
questions.q: Requests versus limits?
questions.a: Requests are reserved capacity used for scheduling and as the guaranteed share under contention. Limits are enforced ceilings at run time: CPU above the limit is throttled, memory above the limit gets the container OOM-killed.

questions.topic: Lesson · Requests, limits and quality of service
questions.q: Why do some teams not set CPU limits?
questions.a: CPU is compressible: under contention each container still gets its requested share, so a limit mainly throttles workloads when spare CPU exists, which hurts tail latency. Memory is not compressible, so a memory limit is still needed.

questions.topic: Lesson · Requests, limits and quality of service
questions.q: What are the QoS classes and why do they matter?
questions.a: Guaranteed, Burstable and BestEffort, derived from requests and limits. They set OOM scores and eviction order when a node is under pressure: BestEffort goes first, Guaranteed last.

questions.topic: Lesson · Requests, limits and quality of service
questions.q: A pod is Pending though nodes look idle in monitoring. Why?
questions.a: The scheduler works from requests, not usage. Nodes can be fully reserved by requests while using little. Check Allocated resources on the nodes, and also taints, affinity and volume constraints.

questions.topic: Lesson · Services, DNS, Ingress and NetworkPolicy
questions.q: What are the Service types?
questions.a: ClusterIP: a virtual IP reachable inside the cluster. NodePort: also opens a fixed port on every node. LoadBalancer: also provisions an external load balancer through the cloud provider. ExternalName: a DNS alias to an outside name. Headless (clusterIP: None): no virtual IP, DNS returns pod IPs directly.

questions.topic: Lesson · Services, DNS, Ingress and NetworkPolicy
questions.q: How does a pod find another service?
questions.a: Through cluster DNS. The pod's resolv.conf points at CoreDNS and has search domains for its namespace, so "inventory" resolves to inventory.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local and returns the Service ClusterIP.

questions.topic: Lesson · Services, DNS, Ingress and NetworkPolicy
questions.q: Service versus Ingress?
questions.a: A Service load-balances TCP or UDP to a set of pods at layer 4. An Ingress routes HTTP at layer 7 by host and path to Services, sharing one entry point and one place for TLS.

questions.topic: Lesson · Services, DNS, Ingress and NetworkPolicy
questions.q: What is the default network behaviour between pods, and how do you restrict it?
questions.a: Every pod can reach every other pod in the cluster. NetworkPolicies select pods and list allowed sources or destinations; once a pod is selected by any policy, everything not allowed is denied. A default-deny policy per namespace is the usual baseline.

questions.topic: Lesson · Storage and other workload types: StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob
questions.q: Deployment versus StatefulSet?
questions.a: Deployment pods are interchangeable, get random names and share nothing. StatefulSet pods have stable ordinal names and network identities, a dedicated PersistentVolumeClaim each from volumeClaimTemplates, and are created, updated and deleted in order.

questions.topic: Lesson · Storage and other workload types: StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob
questions.q: Explain PV, PVC and StorageClass.
questions.a: A PVC is a namespaced request for storage. A StorageClass defines how volumes are provisioned. A PV is the provisioned volume, cluster-scoped, bound to exactly one claim. Dynamic provisioning creates the PV when the claim appears.

questions.topic: Lesson · Storage and other workload types: StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob
questions.q: When would you use a DaemonSet?
questions.a: For something that must run on every node, or every node of a kind: log and metrics agents, CNI and CSI components, node security agents.

questions.topic: Lesson · Storage and other workload types: StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob
questions.q: How do you run a database migration in Kubernetes?
questions.a: As a Job (or a pre-upgrade hook that creates one) that runs to completion before the new application version rolls out, written to be idempotent and backward compatible so a rollback of the app still works.

questions.topic: Lesson · ServiceAccounts and RBAC: who may do what
questions.q: Role versus ClusterRole, and RoleBinding versus ClusterRoleBinding?
questions.a: A Role is namespaced; a ClusterRole is cluster-wide and can also cover non-namespaced resources. A RoleBinding grants a Role or a ClusterRole within one namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding grants a ClusterRole in all namespaces. Binding a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding is a common way to reuse one definition per namespace.

questions.topic: Lesson · ServiceAccounts and RBAC: who may do what
questions.q: How does a pod authenticate to the Kubernetes API?
questions.a: With its ServiceAccount token, projected into the pod as a short-lived, automatically rotated file. The API server validates it and RBAC authorises the call against bindings for that ServiceAccount.

questions.topic: Lesson · ServiceAccounts and RBAC: who may do what
questions.q: How would you give a CI pipeline permission to deploy safely?
questions.a: A dedicated ServiceAccount with a namespaced Role limited to get, list, watch, patch and update on the specific workload kinds, no access to Secrets, short-lived credentials obtained through OIDC federation, and separate identities per environment.

questions.topic: Lesson · Autoscaling and scheduling: HPA, cluster autoscaler, affinity, taints, disruption budgets
questions.q: How does the HPA decide how many replicas to run?
questions.a: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetricValue ÷ targetValue), computed from the average across ready pods, clamped to min and max, with a tolerance band and a stabilisation window to avoid flapping. CPU percentage is relative to the pods' CPU requests.

questions.topic: Lesson · Autoscaling and scheduling: HPA, cluster autoscaler, affinity, taints, disruption budgets
questions.q: HPA, VPA and cluster autoscaler: how do they fit together?
questions.a: HPA changes pod count, VPA changes pod requests, the cluster autoscaler changes node count in response to unschedulable pods and underused nodes. HPA plus cluster autoscaler is the common pairing; VPA is used in recommendation mode or for workloads that cannot scale out.

questions.topic: Lesson · Autoscaling and scheduling: HPA, cluster autoscaler, affinity, taints, disruption budgets
questions.q: What is a PodDisruptionBudget and what does it not protect against?
questions.a: It limits voluntary disruptions, such as drains and autoscaler scale-down, to keep a minimum number of pods available. It does nothing for involuntary failures such as a node crashing.

questions.topic: Lesson · Autoscaling and scheduling: HPA, cluster autoscaler, affinity, taints, disruption budgets
questions.q: Taints and tolerations versus node affinity?
questions.a: A taint repels pods from a node unless they tolerate it: the node chooses. Node affinity attracts a pod to nodes with certain labels: the pod chooses. Dedicated node pools usually need both.

questions.topic: Lesson · Troubleshooting Kubernetes: a method for any broken workload
questions.q: A deployment was rolled out and the service returns 503. Walk me through it.
questions.a: Confirm scope and check whether to roll back immediately. Then: does the Ingress route to the right Service, does the Service have endpoints, are the new pods Ready, what does describe say about probes, what do the logs say. Compare with the previous revision: image, config, secrets. Roll back, fix, add a check that would have caught it.

questions.topic: Lesson · Troubleshooting Kubernetes: a method for any broken workload
questions.q: What is the difference between kubectl logs, describe and get events?
questions.a: logs is the application's output. describe is Kubernetes' view of one object, including its recent events and last container state. get events is the namespace-wide stream of what controllers and kubelets did.

questions.topic: Lesson · Troubleshooting Kubernetes: a method for any broken workload
questions.q: How do you debug a container that has no shell?
questions.a: kubectl debug adds an ephemeral container with tools that shares the target's namespaces, or creates a copy of the pod with a different image or command. Combined with logs, exit codes and port-forwarding.

questions.topic: Lesson · Troubleshooting Kubernetes: a method for any broken workload
questions.q: Pods are Pending. List the causes.
questions.a: Insufficient CPU or memory for the requests, taints without tolerations, node selectors or affinity that match no node, unbound or zone-pinned volumes, a namespace quota, or too many pods per node. describe pod states which.

questions.topic: Lesson · Helm: charts, values, releases and rollbacks
questions.q: What is a Helm chart, a release and a revision?
