questions.a: A chart is a versioned package of templates and default values. A release is a named installation of a chart in a namespace. Each install, upgrade or rollback creates a new revision of the release, recorded so it can be inspected or re-applied.

questions.topic: Lesson · Helm: charts, values, releases and rollbacks
questions.q: How do values override each other?
questions.a: The chart's values.yaml is the base. Files given with -f are merged over it in order, later ones winning. --set and --set-string are applied last. Maps merge key by key; lists are replaced whole.

questions.topic: Lesson · Helm: charts, values, releases and rollbacks
questions.q: What does helm rollback do, and what does it not do?
questions.a: It applies the manifests of an earlier revision as a new revision. It does not restore data, undo database migrations or revert anything outside the release's Kubernetes objects.

questions.topic: Lesson · Helm: charts, values, releases and rollbacks
questions.q: Helm or Kustomize?
questions.a: Helm is templating plus packaging and release management: best for distributing software with many options. Kustomize patches plain YAML with no templates: best for varying your own manifests per environment. Many teams use charts for third-party software and Kustomize for their own, or render charts and patch the result.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kustomize: a base and overlays, with no templates
questions.q: How does Kustomize differ from Helm?
questions.a: Kustomize has no templates or packaging: it layers patches and transformations over plain YAML. Helm templates YAML from values and manages versioned releases. Kustomize is simpler to read and review for your own manifests; Helm is better for distributing configurable software.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kustomize: a base and overlays, with no templates
questions.q: What is the hash suffix on generated ConfigMaps for?
questions.a: The name changes whenever the content changes, and Kustomize rewrites references to it. The pod template therefore changes, which triggers a rolling update, and a rollback returns to the previous ConfigMap as well.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kustomize: a base and overlays, with no templates
questions.q: What is a strategic merge patch?
questions.a: A partial resource merged into the target using knowledge of Kubernetes types: maps merge by key and certain lists, such as containers, merge by a key field (name) instead of being replaced. The alternative is a JSON 6902 patch, which lists explicit add, replace and remove operations by path.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitOps with Argo CD: Git as the source of truth
questions.q: What is GitOps?
questions.a: An operating model with four properties: the desired state is declared, stored and versioned in Git, pulled automatically by an agent, and continuously reconciled so the running system converges on it and drift is corrected or reported.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitOps with Argo CD: Git as the source of truth
questions.q: Push-based versus pull-based deployment?
questions.a: Push: a pipeline holding cluster credentials runs apply or helm upgrade. Simple, but the pipeline is highly privileged and the cluster can drift unnoticed. Pull: an in-cluster controller fetches from Git and applies. No external credentials, continuous drift detection, and Git is the record.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitOps with Argo CD: Git as the source of truth
questions.q: Sync status versus health in Argo CD?
questions.a: Sync status compares live resources with what Git renders: Synced or OutOfSync. Health assesses whether the resources work: a Deployment with crashing pods is Degraded. They are independent: an application can be Synced and Degraded.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitOps with Argo CD: Git as the source of truth
questions.q: How do you roll back with GitOps?
questions.a: Revert the commit in Git and let the controller sync. That keeps Git truthful and goes through review. A tool-level rollback changes the cluster only, is refused under automated sync in Argo CD, and leaves the application out of sync.

questions.topic: Lesson · GitOps with Argo CD: Git as the source of truth
questions.q: How does an HPA interact with GitOps?
questions.a: The HPA changes replicas in the cluster, which differs from Git if Git sets replicas, so the controller reports drift or fights the HPA. Omit replicas from the manifest for autoscaled workloads, or tell the controller to ignore that field.

questions.topic: Lesson · Infrastructure as code and the Terraform workflow
questions.q: What is infrastructure as code and why use it?
questions.a: Describing infrastructure in versioned files that a tool applies, instead of creating it by hand. It gives review, history, repeatable environments, fast recovery and a single place that says what should exist.

questions.topic: Lesson · Infrastructure as code and the Terraform workflow
questions.q: What do init, plan and apply do?
questions.a: init downloads providers and modules and connects to the state backend. plan refreshes the state from the real resources, compares it with the configuration and prints the changes without making them. apply performs a plan through the provider APIs and records the results in the state.

questions.topic: Lesson · Infrastructure as code and the Terraform workflow
questions.q: What does declarative mean here?
questions.a: You state the end result, not the steps. Terraform works out which API calls are needed and in what order, and running it again when nothing has changed does nothing.

questions.topic: Lesson · Infrastructure as code and the Terraform workflow
questions.q: How does Terraform decide the order of operations?
questions.a: From references. If one resource uses an attribute of another, it depends on it. Terraform builds a graph, creates along it, destroys in reverse, and runs independent resources in parallel. depends_on is for the rare dependency that no reference expresses.

questions.topic: Lesson · Infrastructure as code and the Terraform workflow
questions.q: Terraform or Ansible?
questions.a: Terraform is for creating and changing infrastructure through APIs, with a state that tracks what it owns. Ansible is for configuring what runs inside machines. Many teams use both, and containers have reduced the need for the second.

questions.topic: Lesson · State, remote backends, locking and drift
questions.q: What is Terraform state and why is it needed?
questions.a: A record mapping each resource block to the real object it created, with that object's attributes. Terraform needs it to know what it owns, to find ids assigned by the cloud, to detect what was removed from the configuration, and to plan quickly.

questions.topic: Lesson · State, remote backends, locking and drift
questions.q: How do teams share state safely?
questions.a: A remote backend that stores one copy, encrypts it, keeps versions and locks during operations. With S3 that means a versioned, encrypted bucket with locking enabled, separate keys per environment, and tight access.

questions.topic: Lesson · State, remote backends, locking and drift
questions.q: What is drift and how do you handle it?
questions.a: A difference between real infrastructure and what Terraform last recorded, caused by a change made outside Terraform. Plan reports it. Either apply to revert it, or change the configuration to adopt it. Prevent it by removing console write access and detect it with scheduled plans.

questions.topic: Lesson · State, remote backends, locking and drift
questions.q: How do you rename a resource without recreating it?
questions.a: Add a moved block from the old address to the new one, or run terraform state mv. Without either, Terraform sees one resource removed and another added and plans a destroy and a create.

questions.topic: Lesson · State, remote backends, locking and drift
questions.q: How do you bring an existing resource under Terraform?
questions.a: Write the resource block, then import the real object into the state with an import block or the import command, and adjust the block until plan shows no changes.

questions.topic: Lesson · Variables, outputs, modules and environments
questions.q: How do you manage several environments with Terraform?
questions.a: Shared modules hold the definitions. Each environment has its own directory that calls them with its own values, its own state and its own credentials. Promotion is applying the same module version to the next environment. Workspaces are an alternative for short-lived copies.

questions.topic: Lesson · Variables, outputs, modules and environments
questions.q: What is a module?
questions.a: A directory of Terraform files used as a unit, with input variables and outputs. The directory you run Terraform in is the root module; it can call child modules from local paths, Git or a registry.

questions.topic: Lesson · Variables, outputs, modules and environments
questions.q: What is the order of precedence for variable values?
questions.a: From lowest to highest: the default, environment variables named TF_VAR_name, terraform.tfvars, *.auto.tfvars files, then -var and -var-file options in the order given.

questions.topic: Lesson · Variables, outputs, modules and environments
questions.q: Variables, locals and outputs: what is the difference?
questions.a: Variables are inputs set from outside. Locals are named expressions computed inside the module to avoid repetition. Outputs are values the module exposes to its caller or to people.

questions.topic: Lesson · Variables, outputs, modules and environments
questions.q: When would you not write a module?
questions.a: When there is only one use and no clear boundary. A premature module adds parameters for cases that never arrive and makes simple changes harder to follow.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reading a plan, replacement, and Terraform in CI
questions.q: What does -/+ mean in a plan and why does it happen?
questions.a: The resource will be destroyed and a new one created, because an argument that cannot be changed on an existing resource was modified. The plan marks that argument with "forces replacement". The new resource has a new id and usually new addresses.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reading a plan, replacement, and Terraform in CI
questions.q: How do you avoid downtime when a resource must be replaced?
questions.a: create_before_destroy so the new one exists before the old one goes, when two can coexist. Otherwise put the resource behind a load balancer or DNS name and replace one of several at a time, or do a blue-green switch.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reading a plan, replacement, and Terraform in CI
questions.q: How would you run Terraform in CI/CD?
questions.a: On pull requests: fmt check, validate, linting, security scan, then plan with a read-only role and publish the plan. After merge: an approval gate, then apply the saved plan with a write role, with a concurrency limit per state. Remote state with locking, short-lived credentials, and no applies from laptops.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reading a plan, replacement, and Terraform in CI
questions.q: What do prevent_destroy and ignore_changes do?
questions.a: prevent_destroy makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail. ignore_changes tells Terraform not to act on differences in named arguments, for fields another system manages, such as a replica count set by an autoscaler.

questions.topic: Lesson · Reading a plan, replacement, and Terraform in CI
questions.q: A colleague removed a resource block and the plan shows a destroy of a production bucket. What do you check?
questions.a: Whether removal was intended, whether the block was renamed or moved into a module (needs a moved block), and whether the right state is in use. If Terraform should stop managing it without deleting it, use a removed block or state rm.

questions.topic: Lesson · AWS accounts and IAM: who may do what
questions.q: What is the difference between an IAM user and a role?
questions.a: A user is a permanent identity with long-lived credentials. A role has no credentials of its own: a trusted identity assumes it and receives temporary credentials. Roles are preferred for people (through federation) and for workloads.

questions.topic: Lesson · AWS accounts and IAM: who may do what
questions.q: How does IAM decide whether a request is allowed?
questions.a: It gathers every policy that applies. A matching explicit Deny ends it. Otherwise the request needs an Allow, and must also pass any organisation policy and permissions boundary. With no matching Allow the result is an implicit deny.

questions.topic: Lesson · AWS accounts and IAM: who may do what
questions.q: How should an application on AWS get credentials?
questions.a: From a role attached to where it runs: an instance profile on EC2, a task role on ECS, Pod Identity or IRSA on EKS. The SDK fetches and renews temporary credentials automatically. No keys in code, images or environment files.

questions.topic: Lesson · AWS accounts and IAM: who may do what
questions.q: How does a CI pipeline deploy to AWS without stored keys?
questions.a: OIDC federation. The CI provider issues a signed token for the job; an IAM role trusts that provider with conditions on repository and branch; the job exchanges the token for temporary credentials.

questions.topic: Lesson · AWS accounts and IAM: who may do what
questions.q: What is least privilege in practice?
questions.a: Start from nothing, grant the specific actions on the specific resources the job needs, measure what is used, and remove the rest. Guard dangerous actions with explicit denies and separate accounts.

questions.topic: Lesson · VPC networking: subnets, routes, gateways and firewalls
questions.q: What makes a subnet public or private?
questions.a: Only its route table. A public subnet has a default route to an internet gateway. A private one does not: it has a default route to a NAT gateway for outbound access, or no default route at all.

questions.topic: Lesson · VPC networking: subnets, routes, gateways and firewalls
questions.q: Security group versus network ACL?
questions.a: A security group is attached to a resource, is stateful (replies are allowed automatically) and has allow rules only. A network ACL is attached to a subnet, is stateless (each direction needs its own rule) and has numbered allow and deny rules.

questions.topic: Lesson · VPC networking: subnets, routes, gateways and firewalls
questions.q: How does an instance in a private subnet reach the internet?
questions.a: Its subnet's default route points to a NAT gateway in a public subnet. The NAT replaces the private source address with its own public one and tracks the connection so replies return. Nothing outside can start a connection to the instance.

questions.topic: Lesson · VPC networking: subnets, routes, gateways and firewalls
questions.q: A service in a private subnet cannot reach its database. How do you debug?
questions.a: Timeout or refused? Timeout: confirm both are in the VPC and the right subnets, check the database security group allows the port from the service's security group, then network ACLs both ways. Refused: the database is not listening on that address or port. Reachability Analyzer and flow logs confirm.

questions.topic: Lesson · VPC networking: subnets, routes, gateways and firewalls
questions.q: How do you design a VPC for high availability?
questions.a: Subnets of each tier in at least two zones, a load balancer spanning them, instances spread by an Auto Scaling group, a database with a standby in another zone, and a NAT gateway per zone so zones do not depend on each other.

questions.topic: Lesson · EC2, Auto Scaling and load balancers
questions.q: What does an Auto Scaling group do?
questions.a: It keeps a desired number of instances running from a launch template across the subnets you give it, replaces unhealthy ones, and changes the desired number between a minimum and maximum according to scaling policies or schedules.

questions.topic: Lesson · EC2, Auto Scaling and load balancers
questions.q: Application Load Balancer versus Network Load Balancer?
questions.a: An ALB works at the HTTP layer: it routes by host and path, terminates TLS and understands requests. An NLB works at the TCP and UDP layer: very high throughput, static addresses, and it passes connections through without reading them.

questions.topic: Lesson · EC2, Auto Scaling and load balancers
questions.q: The load balancer returns 502, 503 or 504. What does each suggest?
questions.a: 503: no healthy targets to send to. 502: a target returned a broken response or closed the connection. 504: a target did not respond before the timeout. Each points to a different place to look.

questions.topic: Lesson · EC2, Auto Scaling and load balancers
questions.q: How do you deploy a new version to instances with no downtime?
questions.a: Build a new image, update the launch template, and run a rolling instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage, relying on health checks and connection draining. Or create a second group and switch the load balancer: blue-green.

questions.topic: Lesson · EC2, Auto Scaling and load balancers
questions.q: How would you reduce EC2 cost?
questions.a: Right-size from utilisation data, scale in when idle, use Savings Plans for the baseline and Spot for interruptible work, move to newer or ARM instance families, and delete unattached volumes and idle load balancers.

questions.topic: Lesson · S3, CloudFront, RDS and ElastiCache
questions.q: Multi-AZ versus read replica in RDS?
questions.a: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another zone for automatic failover; it is for availability and you do not read from it in the classic setup. A read replica is an asynchronous copy you can query; it is for scaling reads and may lag. Many production databases use both.

questions.topic: Lesson · S3, CloudFront, RDS and ElastiCache
questions.q: How do you recover from accidental data deletion in a database?
questions.a: Point-in-time recovery: restore to a new instance at a moment just before the mistake, then either switch the application to it or copy the affected rows back. This works only within the backup retention period.

questions.topic: Lesson · S3, CloudFront, RDS and ElastiCache
questions.q: How do you serve private files from S3 to users?
questions.a: Keep the bucket private. For shared content, CloudFront with origin access control so only the distribution can read the bucket. For per-user files, short-lived presigned URLs generated by the backend after it checks the user.

questions.topic: Lesson · S3, CloudFront, RDS and ElastiCache
questions.q: Is a standby a backup?
questions.a: No. A standby copies every change, including a mistaken delete or corruption, within milliseconds. Backups let you go back in time. You need both.

questions.topic: Lesson · S3, CloudFront, RDS and ElastiCache
questions.q: How do you choose an S3 storage class?
questions.a: By how often and how fast the data is read. Standard for frequent access, infrequent-access classes for data read rarely, Glacier classes for archives. Intelligent-Tiering when the pattern is unknown. Lifecycle rules move objects automatically.

questions.topic: Lesson · EKS: running checkout-api on Kubernetes in AWS
questions.q: What does EKS manage and what do you manage?
questions.a: AWS runs the control plane: API server, etcd, scheduler, their availability and patching. You own nodes (unless using managed options), add-ons, networking, IAM integration, workloads, and deciding when to upgrade.

questions.topic: Lesson · EKS: running checkout-api on Kubernetes in AWS
questions.q: How do pods on EKS get AWS permissions?
questions.a: A Kubernetes service account is linked to an IAM role. With EKS Pod Identity, an association maps cluster, namespace and service account to a role, and an agent on each node hands the pod temporary credentials. IRSA does the same through an OIDC provider and a web identity token. Neither uses stored keys.

questions.topic: Lesson · EKS: running checkout-api on Kubernetes in AWS
questions.q: How does traffic from the internet reach a pod on EKS?
questions.a: DNS to an Application Load Balancer created by the AWS Load Balancer Controller from an Ingress. In IP mode the load balancer sends directly to pod addresses, which are real VPC addresses thanks to the VPC CNI; in instance mode it goes through a node port.

questions.topic: Lesson · EKS: running checkout-api on Kubernetes in AWS
questions.q: How do you upgrade an EKS cluster safely?
questions.a: Read the release notes for removed APIs, upgrade staging first, then the control plane one minor version, then add-ons, then nodes by rolling replacement with PodDisruptionBudgets protecting capacity. Control plane upgrades cannot be rolled back.

questions.topic: Lesson · EKS: running checkout-api on Kubernetes in AWS
questions.q: What is specific about networking on EKS?
questions.a: The VPC CNI gives each pod an address from the VPC subnets, so pods are directly routable and security groups and flow logs apply, but address space can run out. Subnet sizing matters more than on overlay networks.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running code without servers: Lambda, ECS and Fargate
questions.q: What is a Lambda cold start and how do you reduce it?
questions.a: When no warm execution environment is free, AWS creates one: it sets up a small sandbox, loads the code and runs the initialisation outside the handler. That adds from tens of milliseconds to seconds to that request. To reduce it, keep the deployment package small, avoid heavy work at import time, choose a faster-starting runtime, raise memory, and for paths that must always be fast use provisioned concurrency, which keeps environments initialised.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running code without servers: Lambda, ECS and Fargate
questions.q: What is the difference between the ECS task role and the task execution role?
questions.a: The execution role is used by the ECS agent to get the task running: pulling the image from ECR, sending logs to CloudWatch and fetching secrets referenced in the task definition. The task role is assumed by the application inside the container when it calls AWS, for example to read an S3 bucket. Mixing them up gives either a task that cannot start or an application with far more access than it needs.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running code without servers: Lambda, ECS and Fargate
questions.q: When would you choose ECS on Fargate over EKS?
questions.a: When the team wants to run containers without operating Kubernetes. ECS has fewer concepts, no control plane to upgrade and tight integration with IAM and load balancers; Fargate also removes node management. EKS is the better choice when the organisation already has Kubernetes skills and tooling, needs the ecosystem of operators and controllers, or wants portability across clouds.

questions.topic: Lesson · Running code without servers: Lambda, ECS and Fargate
questions.q: A Lambda function reads from an SQS queue and one message keeps failing. What happens and how do you handle it?
questions.a: The message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and is retried, potentially blocking progress and wasting invocations. Configure a redrive policy on the queue so that after a set number of receives the message moves to a dead-letter queue, report partial batch failures so that good messages in the batch are not retried, alarm on the dead-letter queue depth, and make the handler idempotent.

questions.topic: Lesson · DNS in depth with Route 53
questions.q: What is the difference between an alias record and a CNAME?
questions.a: A CNAME is standard DNS: it says this name is another name, cannot exist at the zone apex, and the resolver makes a second lookup. An alias is a Route 53 extension: it is created as an A or AAAA record whose value Route 53 fills in with the current addresses of an AWS resource such as a load balancer or CloudFront distribution. It works at the apex, follows the resource when its addresses change, and queries for it are not charged. From the outside it looks like an ordinary A record.

questions.topic: Lesson · DNS in depth with Route 53
questions.q: Which Route 53 routing policies do you know and when would you use each?
questions.a: Simple returns one answer. Weighted splits traffic by proportion, for gradual migrations or testing a new stack. Latency sends users to the region that responds fastest for them. Failover returns a primary while its health check passes and a secondary otherwise, for active-passive disaster recovery. Geolocation answers by the user's country or continent, for legal or content reasons, and geoproximity shifts traffic by distance with a bias. Multivalue answer returns several healthy records for simple client-side spreading.

questions.topic: Lesson · DNS in depth with Route 53
questions.q: You need to move a service to a new load balancer with no downtime. How do you use DNS?
questions.a: A day or more before, lower the record's TTL so that caches turn over quickly. Bring up the new load balancer and verify it directly. Add it as a weighted record with a small weight, watch error rates, and raise the weight in steps. When it is at 100%, keep the old target running for longer than the old TTL plus a margin, because some clients cache beyond it. Then remove the old record and raise the TTL again.

questions.topic: Lesson · DNS in depth with Route 53
questions.q: Why is DNS failover not instant, and what can you do about it?
questions.a: Three delays add up: the health check must fail several times before Route 53 changes its answer, resolvers keep serving the cached answer until the TTL runs out, and some clients ignore TTLs or hold open connections. With a 30-second check, three failures and a 60-second TTL, expect around two to three minutes. For faster failover, use shorter intervals and TTLs, or move the switch below DNS with a global load balancer or anycast service such as Global Accelerator, which changes routing without waiting for caches.

questions.topic: Lesson · Azure and Google Cloud: the same jobs, different names
questions.q: How would you compare AWS, Azure and Google Cloud?
questions.a: They offer equivalent core services with different names and some structural differences: how accounts are organised, whether networks and subnets are regional or global, and how identity and permissions are modelled. Strengths vary by area and change over time, so I compare for the specific workload rather than in general.

questions.topic: Lesson · Azure and Google Cloud: the same jobs, different names
questions.q: What are the equivalents of EC2, S3 and EKS?
questions.a: Virtual Machines, Blob Storage and AKS on Azure; Compute Engine, Cloud Storage and GKE on Google Cloud.

questions.topic: Lesson · Azure and Google Cloud: the same jobs, different names
questions.q: Should a company go multi-cloud?
questions.a: Only for a concrete reason: regulation, an acquisition, a service that exists on one provider, or negotiating position. The costs are duplicated tooling and skills, harder networking and security, and using the lowest common denominator. Many who say multi-cloud mean different systems on different clouds, which is far easier than one system on two.

questions.topic: Lesson · Azure and Google Cloud: the same jobs, different names
questions.q: What makes a workload portable between clouds?
questions.a: Containers and Kubernetes for running it, infrastructure as code for creating its environment, open protocols for data (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, S3-compatible APIs) and open standards for telemetry. Identity, networking and proprietary managed services are what must be redone.

questions.topic: Lesson · Azure and Google Cloud: the same jobs, different names
questions.q: You know AWS and join a team on Google Cloud. What do you learn first?
questions.a: The resource hierarchy and IAM, then networking (global VPC, regional subnets, firewall rules), then GKE and how workloads get permissions. After that the service names, which are a lookup.

questions.topic: Lesson · Azure for someone who knows AWS
questions.q: Explain the Azure hierarchy from tenant to resource.
questions.a: A tenant is an instance of Microsoft Entra ID: the directory of users, groups and application identities. Under it, management groups organise subscriptions and carry policy. A subscription is the billing and quota boundary and the usual unit for an environment. Inside a subscription, resource groups hold resources that share a lifecycle. Role assignments and policies set at a higher level are inherited by everything below.

questions.topic: Lesson · Azure for someone who knows AWS
questions.q: What is a managed identity and how does it compare with an AWS IAM role?
questions.a: A managed identity is an identity in Entra ID that Azure creates and rotates for a resource such as a virtual machine or an AKS workload. Code on that resource asks a local endpoint for a token and uses it to call other Azure services, so no secret is stored. It plays the same part as an IAM role attached to an EC2 instance or a pod. System-assigned identities live and die with one resource; user-assigned ones are separate objects that several resources can share.

questions.topic: Lesson · Azure for someone who knows AWS
questions.q: How does Azure role-based access control decide whether a request is allowed?
questions.a: Each role assignment joins three things: a principal, a role definition listing allowed actions, and a scope. Azure collects the assignments that apply at the resource's scope and above, and allows the request if any of them includes the action and no deny assignment blocks it. Management actions and data actions are separate, so a role that can configure a storage account does not necessarily read its contents. Azure Policy is evaluated as well and can refuse a compliant-looking request.

questions.topic: Lesson · Azure for someone who knows AWS
questions.q: What differs between an Azure virtual network and an AWS VPC?
questions.a: Both are private address spaces divided into subnets. In Azure a subnet spans all availability zones in the region rather than sitting in one, and outbound internet access has historically been available by default rather than needing a gateway, though explicit outbound through a NAT gateway is the recommended design. Network security groups attach to subnets or network interfaces and have numbered priority rules with both allow and deny, unlike AWS security groups, which only allow.

questions.topic: Lesson · Google Cloud for someone who knows AWS
questions.q: What is a Google Cloud project and why does it matter?
questions.a: A project is the container that owns resources and the boundary for billing, enabled APIs, quotas and access policy. Every resource belongs to exactly one. Because projects are cheap and isolated by default, the normal design is one per environment per team, arranged in folders under the organisation, with shared policy inherited from above. It plays the part that an AWS account plays, but is lighter to create.

questions.topic: Lesson · Google Cloud for someone who knows AWS
questions.q: How does a Google Cloud VPC differ from an AWS VPC?
questions.a: A Google Cloud VPC network is a global resource: one network can have subnets in many regions and they route to each other privately without peering. Subnets are regional and span all zones in the region, whereas an AWS subnet sits in one availability zone and a VPC is confined to one region. Firewall rules belong to the network and select targets by network tag or service account rather than being attached to instances as security groups are.

questions.topic: Lesson · Google Cloud for someone who knows AWS
questions.q: What is a service account, and how does a GKE pod use one safely?
questions.a: A service account is an identity for software rather than a person. It is also a resource, so there are roles about who may use or impersonate it. With Workload Identity, a Kubernetes service account in a namespace is linked to a Google service account; pods running under it receive short-lived Google credentials from the metadata server. No key file is created or mounted, access is specific to that workload, and credentials rotate on their own.

questions.topic: Lesson · Google Cloud for someone who knows AWS
questions.q: How are permissions granted in Google Cloud IAM?
questions.a: Permissions are grouped into roles, and an allow policy on a resource binds roles to members such as users, groups or service accounts. Policies are inherited from organisation to folder to project to resource, and the effective access is the union of all of them, so a broad grant high up cannot be narrowed lower down except by deny policies or conditions. That is why grants should be made at the lowest level that works, using predefined roles instead of the old basic ones.

questions.topic: Lesson · PostgreSQL in production: connections, slow queries and locks
questions.q: An application starts failing with "too many connections". How do you handle it?
questions.a: Confirm with pg_stat_activity: how many, from which application, in what state. If a scale-out or deploy caused it, reduce pool sizes or scale back to restore service. If connections are idle in transaction, find the leak. Longer term add a transaction-mode pooler so application scale is decoupled from database connections.

questions.topic: Lesson · PostgreSQL in production: connections, slow queries and locks
questions.q: Why not simply raise max_connections?
questions.a: Each connection is a server process with memory, and many active connections contend for CPU and locks. Past a point throughput falls. A database serves a few hundred queries at once well; thousands of mostly idle client connections are better multiplexed by a pooler.

questions.topic: Lesson · PostgreSQL in production: connections, slow queries and locks
questions.q: How do you find and fix a slow query?
questions.a: Find it by total time in pg_stat_statements or by duration in pg_stat_activity. EXPLAIN it, with ANALYZE if it is safe to run. Look for sequential scans on large tables, wrong row estimates and sorts on disk. Fix with an index built concurrently, a rewritten query or fresh statistics, and measure again.

questions.topic: Lesson · PostgreSQL in production: connections, slow queries and locks
questions.q: What does "idle in transaction" mean and why is it harmful?
questions.a: A session began a transaction and is not running anything. It holds its locks, occupies a connection and stops vacuum from removing dead rows newer than its snapshot. A few of them can stall a busy database.

questions.topic: Lesson · PostgreSQL in production: connections, slow queries and locks
questions.q: What does a connection pooler change, and what does it break?
questions.a: Many client connections share a few server connections, lent per transaction. Applications can scale without touching the server limit. Anything that depends on one session persisting, such as session-level settings, advisory locks or some prepared statement usage, needs care.

questions.topic: Lesson · Replication, failover, RPO and RTO
questions.q: Define RPO and RTO.
questions.a: Recovery Point Objective: the maximum amount of recent data, measured in time, that may be lost in a failure. Recovery Time Objective: the maximum time the service may be unavailable. They are set by the business and drive the choice between backups, asynchronous replicas and synchronous standbys.

questions.topic: Lesson · Replication, failover, RPO and RTO
questions.q: Synchronous versus asynchronous replication?
questions.a: Synchronous: a commit is acknowledged only after a standby has it, so a failover loses nothing, at the cost of latency on every write and of availability if the standby is unreachable. Asynchronous: the primary does not wait, so writes are fast, but the replica lags and a failover loses whatever had not arrived.

questions.topic: Lesson · Replication, failover, RPO and RTO
questions.q: What is split brain and how is it prevented?
questions.a: Two nodes each believing they are the primary and accepting writes, so the data diverges. It is prevented by requiring a quorum to elect a primary and by fencing: making sure the old primary is stopped or isolated before a new one is promoted.

questions.topic: Lesson · Replication, failover, RPO and RTO
questions.q: A replica is 30 seconds behind. Who is affected?
questions.a: Anything reading from it sees old data: a customer may not see an order just placed. If it is the failover target, a failover now would lose 30 seconds of writes. Reporting usually does not care.

questions.topic: Lesson · Replication, failover, RPO and RTO
questions.q: How do you test your high availability setup?
questions.a: Trigger a real failover on a schedule, in staging and then production, and measure the time until the application is healthy again and whether any acknowledged write is missing. A setup that has never failed over is an assumption.

questions.topic: Lesson · Backups you can restore, and schema changes without downtime
questions.q: How do you know your backups work?
questions.a: By restoring them, regularly and automatically, into a fresh instance, checking it starts and that key tables have plausible contents, and timing the whole process. The measured time is the real RTO.

questions.topic: Lesson · Backups you can restore, and schema changes without downtime
questions.q: What is point-in-time recovery?
questions.a: Restoring a base backup and replaying the archived write-ahead log up to a chosen moment. It lets you go back to just before a mistake, which neither a nightly dump nor a replica can do.

questions.topic: Lesson · Backups you can restore, and schema changes without downtime
questions.q: Is a replica a backup?
questions.a: No. A replica reproduces every change, including destructive ones, almost immediately. It protects against losing a machine, not against losing data through error or attack.

questions.topic: Lesson · Backups you can restore, and schema changes without downtime
questions.q: How do you rename a column with zero downtime?
questions.a: Expand and contract: add the new column; deploy code that writes both; backfill in batches; deploy code that reads the new one; when nothing uses the old column, drop it. At each step the previous release still works, so code rollback is always safe.

questions.topic: Lesson · Backups you can restore, and schema changes without downtime
questions.q: Why can a simple ALTER TABLE take down a busy site?
questions.a: It needs an exclusive lock on the table. If a long transaction holds any lock on it, the ALTER waits, and every later query on that table queues behind the ALTER. A lock timeout turns that pile-up into a quick, retryable failure.

questions.topic: Lesson · Redis: caching, expiry, eviction and what happens when it is gone
questions.q: Explain the cache-aside pattern.
questions.a: The application reads the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL and returns it. On updates it writes the database and deletes the cached key. The cache holds only what was asked for, and the application keeps working, more slowly, if the cache is unavailable.

questions.topic: Lesson · Redis: caching, expiry, eviction and what happens when it is gone
questions.q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: When a hot key expires or the cache is emptied, many requests miss at once and all run the same expensive query, overloading the database. Prevent it with a lock so one request rebuilds, by serving the stale value while refreshing, by spreading TTLs randomly, and by limiting concurrency towards the database.

questions.topic: Lesson · Redis: caching, expiry, eviction and what happens when it is gone
questions.q: Which eviction policy would you choose?
questions.a: For a cache, allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu: when memory is full, drop what is least useful. noeviction refuses writes, which is right when Redis holds data that must not vanish, such as a job queue. Mixing both uses in one instance forces a bad compromise, so separate them.

questions.topic: Lesson · Redis: caching, expiry, eviction and what happens when it is gone
questions.q: Redis is single-threaded. What does that mean in operation?
questions.a: Commands execute one at a time, so each is atomic and there are no locks, but one slow command delays everyone. Avoid KEYS, huge range reads and big blocking deletes; use SCAN, paging and UNLINK; watch SLOWLOG.

questions.topic: Lesson · Redis: caching, expiry, eviction and what happens when it is gone
questions.q: Your Redis cache is lost. What happens and how should the system be designed for it?
questions.a: All reads fall through to the database. If it was sized assuming a 90 percent hit ratio it gets ten times the load and may fail, turning a cache outage into a full outage. Design with database headroom, concurrency limits, cache warming, replicas with failover, and load tests with a cold cache.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kafka: partitions, consumer groups and lag
questions.q: What is consumer lag and how do you reduce it?
questions.a: The difference, per partition, between the latest offset written and the offset the group has committed. Reduce it by adding consumers up to the number of partitions, making each event cheaper to process, fixing slow downstream calls, or adding partitions. If lag is concentrated in one partition the cause is a hot key or a slow consumer and more consumers do not help.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kafka: partitions, consumer groups and lag
questions.q: How do partitions and consumer groups relate?
questions.a: Within a group each partition is read by exactly one consumer, and a consumer may read several partitions. So the partition count is the upper limit on parallelism for a group. Different groups read the same topic independently, each with its own offsets.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kafka: partitions, consumer groups and lag
questions.q: What delivery guarantees does Kafka give?
questions.a: At-least-once by default when you commit after processing: nothing is lost, duplicates are possible. At-most-once if you commit before processing. Exactly-once processing is available within Kafka through idempotent producers and transactions, but effects outside Kafka still need idempotent handling.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kafka: partitions, consumer groups and lag
questions.q: What happens during a rebalance?
questions.a: When consumers join, leave or time out, the group coordinator reassigns partitions. With the classic protocol all consumers stop and resume; with cooperative rebalancing only the partitions that move are paused. Frequent rebalances stall consumption.

questions.topic: Lesson · Kafka: partitions, consumer groups and lag
questions.q: How do you avoid losing events when a broker dies?
questions.a: Replication factor of at least 3, producers with acks=all, and min.insync.replicas of 2, so a write is acknowledged only when it is on at least two brokers. Then losing one broker loses nothing, and losing two stops writes rather than silently losing them.

questions.topic: Lesson · RabbitMQ and choosing between a queue and a log
questions.q: How does RabbitMQ differ from Kafka?
questions.a: RabbitMQ is a queue broker: it routes messages to queues, pushes them to workers, and deletes each one when acknowledged. It offers flexible routing, per-message acknowledgement and retries. Kafka is a partitioned log: events are kept for a retention period, consumers track their own position and can replay, and many groups read the same events. Queues suit tasks; logs suit event streams and high throughput.

questions.topic: Lesson · RabbitMQ and choosing between a queue and a log
questions.q: What are exchanges, queues and bindings?
questions.a: Producers publish to an exchange with a routing key. Bindings connect exchanges to queues with a pattern. The exchange type decides matching: direct matches the key exactly, topic matches patterns, fanout copies to every bound queue. Consumers read from queues.

questions.topic: Lesson · RabbitMQ and choosing between a queue and a log
questions.q: What does prefetch do?
questions.a: It limits how many unacknowledged messages the broker will give one consumer. It spreads work fairly, provides back-pressure, and bounds how much is redelivered if a worker crashes.

questions.topic: Lesson · RabbitMQ and choosing between a queue and a log
questions.q: What is a dead-letter queue for?
questions.a: A place for messages that cannot be processed: rejected without requeue, expired, or delivered too many times. It stops a poison message from blocking the queue forever and keeps it for inspection.

questions.topic: Lesson · RabbitMQ and choosing between a queue and a log
questions.q: A queue has two million messages. What do you do?
questions.a: Find out why consumption fell behind: consumers missing, slow, or crash-looping on a poison message. Restore consumption and scale workers. Decide with the owners whether old messages are still worth processing. Afterwards add length limits, message TTLs and alerts on depth and age.

questions.topic: Lesson · Metrics and Prometheus: rate, errors, duration
questions.q: What are the metric types in Prometheus?
questions.a: Counter: only increases, such as requests served; read it with rate(). Gauge: goes up and down, such as memory in use. Histogram: counts observations into buckets, such as response times, from which quantiles are estimated and which can be aggregated across instances. Summary: quantiles computed in the client, which cannot be aggregated.

questions.topic: Lesson · Metrics and Prometheus: rate, errors, duration
questions.q: Why does Prometheus pull instead of having services push?
questions.a: Prometheus decides what to scrape and how often, so it knows at once when a target is missing ("up" becomes 0), services need no knowledge of the monitoring system, and you can open any target's /metrics page in a browser to debug. Short-lived jobs that cannot be scraped push to a gateway instead.

questions.topic: Lesson · Metrics and Prometheus: rate, errors, duration
questions.q: What are RED and USE?
questions.a: RED is for request-driven services: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE is for resources: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors. RED tells you whether users are affected; USE helps find which resource is the cause.

questions.topic: Lesson · Metrics and Prometheus: rate, errors, duration
questions.q: How is a 95th percentile computed from a histogram?
questions.a: The histogram counts requests under each bucket boundary. Take the rate of each bucket, find the bucket where the cumulative count crosses 95 percent, and interpolate linearly inside it. It is an estimate whose accuracy depends on the bucket boundaries.

questions.topic: Lesson · Metrics and Prometheus: rate, errors, duration
questions.q: What is cardinality and why does it matter?
questions.a: The number of distinct time series, which is the product of the distinct values of every label. Each series costs memory. One unbounded label, such as a user id, can create millions of series and bring Prometheus down.

questions.topic: Lesson · Dashboards and alerts that page for the right reasons
questions.q: What makes a good alert?
questions.a: It is actionable, urgent and about real or imminent user impact. It fires on a symptom, waits long enough to skip blips, says in plain words what is wrong, and links to a runbook. If the response is "ignore it" or "wait", it should not page.

questions.topic: Lesson · Dashboards and alerts that page for the right reasons
questions.q: What does the "for" clause do?
questions.a: The expression must stay true for that long before the alert moves from pending to firing. It filters short spikes at the cost of slower detection, so its value is a deliberate trade between noise and delay.

questions.topic: Lesson · Dashboards and alerts that page for the right reasons
questions.q: What does Alertmanager do that Prometheus does not?
questions.a: Prometheus decides that an alert is firing. Alertmanager decides who hears about it: it deduplicates and groups related alerts, inhibits consequences of a known bigger failure, applies silences, and routes by labels to the right receiver with retries.

questions.topic: Lesson · Dashboards and alerts that page for the right reasons
questions.q: What is burn-rate alerting?
questions.a: Alerting on how fast the error budget of an SLO is being consumed. A burn rate of 1 uses the budget exactly over the SLO period. Page on a high rate over a short window, for example 14 times over an hour, and open a ticket for a low rate over days. It ties alerts directly to user impact and keeps them quiet when impact is small.

questions.topic: Lesson · Dashboards and alerts that page for the right reasons
questions.q: How do you reduce alert fatigue?
questions.a: Delete or downgrade every alert that is not actionable, alert on symptoms, group and inhibit, add "for" durations, review each page in a weekly meeting, and measure pages per shift as a number the team owns.

questions.topic: Lesson · Centralised, structured logging
questions.q: Why structured logging?
questions.a: Each line is machine-readable with named fields, so it can be filtered, aggregated and joined reliably: all errors for one order, counts by status, lines for one trace. Free text needs fragile pattern matching and breaks when wording changes.

questions.topic: Lesson · Centralised, structured logging
questions.q: How do logs get from a pod to a central store in Kubernetes?
questions.a: The container writes to standard output. The container runtime writes that to files on the node. An agent running as a DaemonSet tails those files, enriches lines with pod metadata and ships them to the store. The application is unaware of any of it.

questions.topic: Lesson · Centralised, structured logging
questions.q: Loki versus Elasticsearch or OpenSearch?
questions.a: Loki indexes only labels and stores log content compressed in object storage, so it is cheap to run and you query by selecting streams then filtering. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch index the content of every line, so arbitrary text search is fast, at a much higher storage and operating cost.

questions.topic: Lesson · Centralised, structured logging
questions.q: How do you correlate logs across services for one request?
questions.a: Generate or accept an id at the edge, propagate it on every downstream call (the W3C traceparent header does this), and include it in every log line. Searching for that id returns the request's lines from every service.

questions.topic: Lesson · Centralised, structured logging
questions.q: What should never be in logs?
questions.a: Credentials, tokens, payment card data, and personal data beyond what is needed. Logs are copied widely, kept for a long time and read by many people, so they are a common source of leaks.

questions.topic: Lesson · Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
questions.q: What are a trace and a span?
questions.a: A span is one timed operation with a name, start, duration, status and attributes. A trace is the set of spans for one request, linked by a shared trace id and parent-child relationships, forming a tree that shows the request's path and timing across services.

questions.topic: Lesson · Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
questions.q: How does trace context travel between services?
questions.a: In request metadata. The W3C traceparent header carries the trace id, the calling span's id and a sampled flag. Instrumentation injects it into outgoing calls and extracts it from incoming ones; for messaging it goes in message headers.

questions.topic: Lesson · Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
questions.q: Metrics, logs and traces: when do you use which?
questions.a: Metrics tell you that something is wrong and how widespread it is, cheaply and for everything. Traces tell you where in the request path the time or the failure is. Logs tell you the detail of what happened at that point. They are most useful linked by a shared trace id.

questions.topic: Lesson · Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
questions.q: Head sampling versus tail sampling?
questions.a: Head sampling decides when the trace starts, so it is cheap and simple but blind: it may drop the one trace you needed. Tail sampling decides after the trace is complete, usually in the collector, so it can keep all errors and slow requests, at the cost of buffering whole traces.

questions.topic: Lesson · Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
questions.q: What is OpenTelemetry?
questions.a: A vendor-neutral standard and toolkit for telemetry: APIs and SDKs for traces, metrics and logs in many languages, automatic instrumentation for common libraries, the OTLP wire protocol and a collector. It separates how you instrument from which backend stores the data.

questions.topic: Lesson · Security in the pipeline: scanning, SBOMs and signing
questions.q: What security checks belong in a CI/CD pipeline, and where?
questions.a: On the pull request: secret scanning, static analysis of the code, dependency scanning and infrastructure-code scanning, because fixes are cheapest there. At build: image scanning, an SBOM, and signing the image digest. At deploy: an admission policy that accepts only signed images that meet pod security rules. In operation: periodic rescans of what is running.

questions.topic: Lesson · Security in the pipeline: scanning, SBOMs and signing
questions.q: SAST, SCA and image scanning: what is the difference?
questions.a: SAST analyses your own source code for dangerous patterns such as injection. SCA checks the libraries you depend on against databases of known vulnerabilities. Image scanning does the same for everything inside the built image, including operating system packages from the base image.

questions.topic: Lesson · Security in the pipeline: scanning, SBOMs and signing
questions.q: What is an SBOM and why keep one?
questions.a: A software bill of materials: a machine-readable list of every component and version in an artifact. When a new vulnerability is announced you can tell in minutes which of your services contain the affected component, instead of scanning everything again.

questions.topic: Lesson · Security in the pipeline: scanning, SBOMs and signing
questions.q: Why sign container images?
questions.a: So the cluster can verify that an image was produced by your pipeline from reviewed code and has not been altered. Without it, anyone who can push to the registry, or tamper with it, can run arbitrary code in production.

questions.topic: Lesson · Security in the pipeline: scanning, SBOMs and signing
questions.q: A critical CVE is announced in a library you use. Walk through your response.
questions.a: Find where it is, from SBOMs or a scan. Judge exposure: is the vulnerable function used and reachable? If a fix exists, upgrade, rebuild and redeploy, most exposed services first. If not, mitigate by configuration, filtering or disabling the feature. Track until fixed, and check logs for signs of exploitation.

questions.topic: Lesson · Secrets: storing, delivering, rotating, and what to do when one leaks
questions.q: How do you manage secrets for an application on Kubernetes?
questions.a: Values live in a secret manager with access control, audit and rotation. An operator such as External Secrets, or a CSI driver, brings them into the cluster, so Git holds only references. RBAC limits each secret to its service account, etcd is encrypted at rest, and where possible the application uses a workload identity instead of any stored secret.

questions.topic: Lesson · Secrets: storing, delivering, rotating, and what to do when one leaks
questions.q: A developer committed an API key to a public repository. What do you do?
questions.a: Revoke or rotate the key immediately; that is the only step that removes the risk. Then check the provider's audit log for use by anyone else and handle that as an incident if found. Afterwards clean the history and add scanning with push protection. Deleting the commit first achieves nothing, because the key was copied the moment it was public.

questions.topic: Lesson · Secrets: storing, delivering, rotating, and what to do when one leaks
questions.q: Are Kubernetes Secrets secure?
questions.a: Not by themselves. They are base64-encoded objects in etcd: readable by anyone with get on secrets or the ability to run a pod in the namespace, and stored in plain form unless encryption at rest is configured. They are a delivery mechanism; security comes from RBAC, encryption, and keeping the source of truth elsewhere.

questions.topic: Lesson · Secrets: storing, delivering, rotating, and what to do when one leaks
questions.q: How do you rotate a database password without downtime?
questions.a: Use two valid credentials during the change. Create a new user or password, store it, roll the application to it, confirm nothing uses the old one, then remove the old one. Managed rotation with alternating users does exactly this.

questions.topic: Lesson · Secrets: storing, delivering, rotating, and what to do when one leaks
questions.q: Why are short-lived credentials better than long-lived keys?
questions.a: They expire on their own, so a leak is useful to an attacker for minutes or hours, not years. They are issued to an identity at run time, so nothing needs to be stored, distributed or rotated by hand.

questions.topic: Lesson · Hardening workloads on Kubernetes
questions.q: How would you harden a pod?
questions.a: Run as a non-root numeric user, set allowPrivilegeEscalation false, drop all capabilities, use the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile and a read-only root filesystem with emptyDir for scratch paths. Set resource limits, do not mount the service account token unless needed, and pin the image by digest. Then enforce it for the namespace with the restricted Pod Security level.

questions.topic: Lesson · Hardening workloads on Kubernetes
questions.q: What are the Pod Security Standards?
questions.a: Three policy levels defined by Kubernetes. Privileged is unrestricted. Baseline forbids known privilege escalations such as privileged containers, host namespaces and hostPath volumes. Restricted adds current hardening practice: non-root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped, a seccomp profile and a limited set of volume types. A built-in admission controller applies a level per namespace in enforce, warn or audit mode.

questions.topic: Lesson · Hardening workloads on Kubernetes
questions.q: What does a NetworkPolicy do, and what is the default without one?
questions.a: Without any policy every pod can talk to every pod in every namespace. A NetworkPolicy selects pods and lists the allowed inbound and outbound connections; once a pod is selected by any policy, everything not allowed is denied. It only works if the network plugin enforces it.

questions.topic: Lesson · Hardening workloads on Kubernetes
questions.q: Why is running as root in a container dangerous if containers are isolated?
questions.a: Isolation relies on kernel features, and root inside the container is the same user id as root on the node. A kernel or runtime vulnerability, a mounted host path or an extra capability can turn container root into node root. A non-root user removes most of those paths.

questions.topic: Lesson · Hardening workloads on Kubernetes
questions.q: How do you roll out stricter pod security to a cluster that has none?
questions.a: Measure first: dry-run the label or use warn and audit modes to list violations. Fix workloads team by team, with checks in pull requests to stop new ones. Then enforce baseline everywhere and restricted on application namespaces, with system components in exempt, tightly controlled namespaces.

questions.topic: Lesson · SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
questions.q: Define SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget.
questions.a: SLI: a measured indicator of service quality, such as the proportion of successful requests. SLO: the internal target for it over a period, such as 99.9% over 30 days. SLA: a contract with customers, with consequences if missed, set looser than the SLO. Error budget: one minus the SLO, the amount of failure permitted, here about 43 minutes a month.

questions.topic: Lesson · SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
questions.q: Why not aim for 100%?
questions.a: It is unattainable and each step closer costs far more than the last. Users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% through their own network and devices. And a 100% target leaves no room to change anything, since change is the main cause of failure.

questions.topic: Lesson · SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
questions.q: What happens when the error budget is exhausted?
questions.a: By a policy agreed in advance, the team stops feature releases and works on reliability until the budget recovers, with exceptions for security and for fixes. The value is that the decision is made by a rule, not by whoever argues hardest that day.

questions.topic: Lesson · SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
questions.q: How do you choose a good SLI?
questions.a: Start from what users would call broken: the request failed or was too slow. Express it as good events over valid events, measured at the edge, on the operations that matter such as checkout. Avoid internal causes like CPU.

questions.topic: Lesson · SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
questions.q: What is burn rate?
questions.a: How fast the budget is being consumed relative to the rate that would use it exactly over the SLO period. A burn rate of 1 lasts the whole month; 14.4 uses 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. Alerts on burn rate over paired long and short windows page for real damage and stay quiet for blips.

questions.topic: Lesson · Toil, on-call and capacity
questions.q: What is toil?
questions.a: Work tied to running a service that is manual, repetitive, automatable, reactive, without lasting value, and that grows as the service grows. Restarting a stuck job by hand each morning is toil; writing the fix that stops it sticking is engineering.

questions.topic: Lesson · Toil, on-call and capacity
questions.q: Why cap toil at around 50%?
questions.a: Because toil expands with the system. Without a cap, operations consumes all the time, nothing gets automated, and headcount must grow with load. The cap guarantees time to remove causes, and exceeding it is a signal to hand work back or stop taking on more.

questions.topic: Lesson · Toil, on-call and capacity
questions.q: What makes an on-call rotation sustainable?
questions.a: Enough people that shifts are infrequent, few and meaningful pages, runbooks and clear escalation, a secondary on call, compensation or time off, and a team that reviews every page and fixes what caused it.

questions.topic: Lesson · Toil, on-call and capacity
questions.q: What do you check in a production readiness review?
questions.a: SLOs and alerts tied to them, dashboards, runbooks, ownership and on-call, capacity and load test results, dependency failure behaviour and timeouts, deployment and rollback method, backups and restore tests, security review, and cost.

questions.topic: Lesson · Toil, on-call and capacity
questions.q: How do you plan capacity?
questions.a: Measure current use and its drivers, forecast growth from history and business plans, load test to find the real limits, add headroom for failures and peaks, and remember the limits that are not CPU: database connections, quotas, IP addresses, partitions. Then let autoscaling handle the short-term variation inside those limits.

questions.topic: Lesson · Incident response: the first thirty minutes
questions.q: You are paged for a major outage. What do you do in the first ten minutes?
questions.a: Acknowledge and assess impact. Declare an incident, open a channel and get someone to handle communication. Check what changed recently. If a change lines up, roll it back; otherwise mitigate by failing over, adding capacity or shedding load. Post a first update for users. Make one change at a time and write down what is seen and done.

questions.topic: Lesson · Incident response: the first thirty minutes
questions.q: What does an incident commander do?
questions.a: Owns the response: sets priorities, assigns roles, decides which action to take next, keeps people from colliding, calls for escalation, and ensures communication happens. They do not do the hands-on debugging, because someone must keep the whole picture.

questions.topic: Lesson · Incident response: the first thirty minutes
questions.q: Why mitigate before finding the root cause?
questions.a: Because every minute of diagnosis is a minute of user harm, and most mitigations, such as rollback or failover, do not require knowing the cause. Diagnosis is easier and safer once the pressure is off, using the evidence collected.

questions.topic: Lesson · Incident response: the first thirty minutes
questions.q: How do you define severity levels?
questions.a: By user impact and urgency, in terms anyone can apply: SEV1 is a critical function down or data at risk for many users and needs everyone now; SEV2 is serious degradation or a partial outage; SEV3 is minor impact with a workaround. Each level fixes who is paged and how often updates go out.

questions.topic: Lesson · Incident response: the first thirty minutes
questions.q: How should you communicate during an incident?
questions.a: Early, regularly and plainly. A first acknowledgement within minutes, then updates on a fixed interval saying what users experience, what is being done and when the next update comes. No guesses about cause, no blame, no internal jargon.

questions.topic: Lesson · Postmortems and runbooks: learning from incidents
questions.q: What is a blameless postmortem?
questions.a: A written review of an incident that assumes everyone acted reasonably with what they knew, and looks for the conditions in systems, tools and process that allowed the outcome. It covers impact, timeline, contributing factors and concrete actions, and names roles, not culprits, so people share what really happened.

questions.topic: Lesson · Postmortems and runbooks: learning from incidents
questions.q: Why blameless? Is nobody accountable?
questions.a: People are accountable for taking part honestly and for completing the actions. Punishing mistakes makes people hide them, which removes the information needed to fix the system. Blamelessness is the price of that information, and it produces better outcomes than fear.

questions.topic: Lesson · Postmortems and runbooks: learning from incidents
questions.q: What makes a good action item?
questions.a: It is specific, has one owner and a date, can be verified as done, and changes the system rather than asking people to try harder. "Add a pipeline check that fails when a required setting is missing in production" is good. "Be more careful with configuration" is not.

questions.topic: Lesson · Postmortems and runbooks: learning from incidents
questions.q: What goes in a runbook?
questions.a: What the alert means in terms of user impact, how to confirm it, the first diagnostic steps with exact commands, the known mitigations in order of safety, when and whom to escalate to, and links to dashboards. It is written for someone woken at night who did not build the service.

questions.topic: Lesson · Postmortems and runbooks: learning from incidents
questions.q: Tell me about an incident you learned from.
questions.a: Structure the answer like a postmortem: the impact, how it was detected, what you did to mitigate, the contributing factors, and what was changed afterwards. Interviewers listen for ownership without blame, for mitigation before diagnosis, and for a concrete improvement that outlived the incident.

questions.topic: Lesson · Disaster recovery: surviving the loss of a region
questions.q: What is the difference between high availability and disaster recovery?
questions.a: High availability keeps a service running through expected, small failures such as a server or zone, usually automatically and without data loss. Disaster recovery restores service after a major event such as losing a region or the data itself, with defined recovery time and data-loss targets, often with human decisions involved.

questions.topic: Lesson · Disaster recovery: surviving the loss of a region
questions.q: Describe the common disaster recovery strategies.
questions.a: Backup and restore: only backups elsewhere; hours to days to recover; cheapest. Pilot light: data replicated and minimal core running; servers started on demand. Warm standby: a scaled-down full copy running; scale up and switch. Multi-site active/active: both regions serve traffic; near-zero recovery time at roughly double the cost and with hard data consistency problems.

questions.topic: Lesson · Disaster recovery: surviving the loss of a region
questions.q: How do you choose between them?
questions.a: From the RTO and RPO the business sets for each service, and their cost. Tier the services: revenue-critical ones justify warm standby or active/active; others are fine with pilot light or backups. Then validate the choice by measuring an actual recovery.

questions.topic: Lesson · Disaster recovery: surviving the loss of a region
questions.q: Your database is replicated to another region. Are you protected against data loss?
questions.a: Against losing the region, yes, apart from replication lag. Against deletion, corruption or ransomware, no: those are replicated too. That needs point-in-time recovery and immutable backups in a separate account.

questions.topic: Lesson · Disaster recovery: surviving the loss of a region
questions.q: How do you test a disaster recovery plan?
questions.a: In stages: restore backups regularly; run tabletop walk-throughs; then real failover drills for tier 1 services, first in staging and then in production at a quiet time, measuring time to recover and data lost against the targets. Each drill produces fixes, like an incident.

questions.topic: Lesson · Performance, load testing and finding the bottleneck
questions.q: How do you find the bottleneck in a slow system?
questions.a: Measure where requests spend time. High CPU on the service means the service. Low CPU with slow responses means waiting: look at connection pools, database activity, locks and downstream calls, using traces. Fix the first limit, re-test, and expect a different one to appear next.

questions.topic: Lesson · Performance, load testing and finding the bottleneck
questions.q: Why does latency rise sharply near capacity?
questions.a: Requests arrive unevenly. As utilisation approaches 100%, the chance that all slots are busy rises fast, so requests queue. Waiting time grows without bound as utilisation nears one, which is why systems are run with headroom.

questions.topic: Lesson · Performance, load testing and finding the bottleneck
questions.q: Load, stress, soak and spike tests?
questions.a: Load: expected peak, to confirm targets are met. Stress: beyond peak, to find the limit and how it fails. Soak: hours at normal load, to find leaks. Spike: a sudden jump, to test autoscaling and recovery.

questions.topic: Lesson · Performance, load testing and finding the bottleneck
questions.q: Horizontal versus vertical scaling?
questions.a: Vertical means a bigger machine: simple, limited, and a single point of failure. Horizontal means more machines: needs stateless services and a load balancer, scales further and survives failures. Databases are usually scaled vertically first, then with replicas, caching and partitioning.

questions.topic: Lesson · Performance, load testing and finding the bottleneck
questions.q: What happens when a system is pushed past capacity, and how do you protect it?
questions.a: Queues grow, everything times out, and retries add load, so it can stay down after traffic falls. Protect it by rejecting excess early: rate limits, concurrency limits, short timeouts, retries with back-off and budgets, circuit breakers, and a queue in front for known peaks.

questions.topic: Lesson · FinOps: understanding and reducing the cloud bill
questions.q: How would you reduce a cloud bill?
questions.a: First visibility: tags and cost per team. Then in order: delete unused resources, schedule non-production, right-size from measured use, move interruptible work to spot, and commit to the steady baseline. Then storage classes and data transfer. Keep it going with budgets, alerts and regular reviews.

questions.topic: Lesson · FinOps: understanding and reducing the cloud bill
questions.q: What is right-sizing and what are the risks?
questions.a: Matching provisioned capacity to measured need. The risks are sizing from averages and missing peaks, ignoring memory, and removing the headroom needed to survive a zone failure. Do it gradually while watching the SLO.

questions.topic: Lesson · FinOps: understanding and reducing the cloud bill
questions.q: When would you use spot instances?
questions.a: For work that tolerates interruption: batch jobs, CI runners, stateless services with enough replicas across instance types. Not for databases or anything that cannot lose a node at two minutes' notice.

questions.topic: Lesson · FinOps: understanding and reducing the cloud bill
questions.q: What is unit cost and why does it matter?
questions.a: Cost divided by a business measure, such as per order or per active user. Total cost rising with the business is fine; unit cost rising means the system is getting less efficient.

questions.topic: Lesson · FinOps: understanding and reducing the cloud bill
questions.q: How do you make engineers care about cost?
questions.a: Show them their own spend next to their own services, make the cheap option the default in the platform, set budgets with alerts to the team, and celebrate savings like features. Blame and central policing do not work.

questions.topic: Lesson · Platform engineering: golden paths and self-service
questions.q: What is platform engineering?
questions.a: Building and running an internal product that gives development teams self-service access to everything needed to ship and operate software: templates, pipelines, infrastructure, observability and guardrails. Its goal is to reduce the effort and knowledge each team needs, while keeping standards consistent.

questions.topic: Lesson · Platform engineering: golden paths and self-service
questions.q: What is a golden path?
questions.a: An opinionated, supported route for a common task, such as creating a production-ready service, with security, deployment and monitoring already built in. It is optional, and succeeds by being the easiest way.

questions.topic: Lesson · Platform engineering: golden paths and self-service
questions.q: How is platform engineering different from DevOps and SRE?
questions.a: DevOps is the practice of teams owning both building and running software. SRE applies engineering to reliability with SLOs and error budgets. Platform engineering provides the shared tools that make both practical at scale, so each team does not rebuild them.

questions.topic: Lesson · Platform engineering: golden paths and self-service
questions.q: How do you measure a platform team?
questions.a: Adoption of the golden path, time from idea to first production deploy, deployment frequency and lead time across teams, the volume of tickets, reliability of the platform itself, and what developers say in surveys.

questions.topic: Lesson · Platform engineering: golden paths and self-service
questions.q: What are common ways a platform fails?
questions.a: Building what the platform team finds interesting instead of what users need, mandating use, becoming a ticket queue, hiding so much that teams cannot debug, and never updating templates so every team drifts.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: A server is "slow". What are the first commands you run and why?
questions.a: uptime for load average against core count; top for which processes use CPU and memory and whether time is user, system or iowait; free -h for available memory; df -h for full disks; then the service logs. Each one rules a resource in or out before touching anything.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does high iowait tell you?
Load average is 12 on a 4-core box but CPU is idle. What is happening?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Restarting the service first, which destroys the evidence and usually does not fix the cause.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Describe the USE method: for each resource check Utilisation, Saturation and Errors. Mention checking recent changes (deploys, config, traffic) in parallel with the resource sweep.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: Explain what happens, at the kernel level, when you run "kill -9" versus "kill".
questions.a: kill sends SIGTERM. If the process registered a handler it runs it and can shut down cleanly; otherwise the default action terminates it. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which is never delivered to the process: the kernel tears it down directly. No handlers, no flushing, no cleanup.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why might a process survive SIGTERM?
What exit code does the parent see?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying SIGKILL is "a stronger SIGTERM". It is a different mechanism with no chance for cleanup.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Connect it to deploys: graceful shutdown, terminationGracePeriodSeconds, preStop hooks, and why PID 1 in a container needs explicit signal handling.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: df shows the disk is full, but du on the mount point adds up to far less. Why?
questions.a: A deleted file is still held open by a running process, so its blocks are not freed until the process closes it. lsof +L1 lists such files. Restart or signal the process to release the space. Another cause is data hidden under a mount point.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you reclaim the space without restarting the process?
How do you prevent it?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Deleting more files, which does not help because the space is held by the open handle.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Mention truncating through /proc/PID/fd/N as an emergency measure, and logrotate with copytruncate or a reopen signal as the real fix.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: What is the OOM killer and how does it choose a victim?
questions.a: When the kernel cannot reclaim enough memory it kills a process to survive. It scores processes mainly by memory use, adjusted by oom_score_adj, and kills the highest. With cgroups the same happens per cgroup when memory.max is reached.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you confirm an OOM kill happened?
How does Kubernetes use oom_score_adj?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming OOM means the whole node was out of memory; a container hits its own limit independently.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Explain QoS classes: Guaranteed pods get the lowest score, BestEffort the highest, so requests and limits decide who dies first under node pressure.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: What do the permission bits rwxr-x--- mean and how do you set them numerically?
questions.a: Owner can read, write and execute; group can read and execute; others have nothing. Numerically 750: r=4, w=2, x=1 added per set.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does execute mean on a directory?
What is umask?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using chmod 777 to make an error go away.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
