items: Bring up running services as dedicated users, secrets at 600, and that ACLs or SELinux can deny access even when the mode bits allow it.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: What happens when you type a URL into a browser and press Enter?
questions.a: DNS resolves the name. A TCP connection opens to port 443. TLS negotiates keys and the server proves its identity. The browser sends an HTTP request. It may pass a CDN, load balancer and reverse proxy before reaching the application, which may call databases and other services. The response returns along the same path and the browser renders it.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where can caching happen along this path?
Which steps are skipped on a second request?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Jumping straight to HTTP and skipping DNS, TCP and TLS.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Go deeper where the interviewer probes: connection reuse and HTTP/2, TLS session resumption, anycast, and what each hop adds to latency.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: Explain the difference between HTTP 502, 503 and 504.
questions.a: All three come from a proxy or load balancer. 502: the upstream gave an invalid response or refused the connection. 503: no healthy upstream or the service is deliberately refusing load. 504: the upstream accepted the request but did not respond before the proxy timeout.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: A service returns 504 only under load. Where do you look?
How do retries interact with a 503?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating them all as "the server is down".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Use them diagnostically: 502 right after a deploy suggests pods terminating without connection draining; 504 suggests a slow dependency or pool exhaustion.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: How many hosts fit in a /22 and how would you split it into four equal subnets?
questions.a: 32 - 22 = 10 host bits, so 1024 addresses (1022 usable). Splitting into four adds 2 bits: four /24 networks of 256 addresses each.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why can VPC CIDRs not overlap when peering?
How many IPs does AWS reserve per subnet?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Forgetting network and broadcast addresses, or provider-reserved addresses.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Tie it to planning: Kubernetes pod density, IP exhaustion on EKS with the VPC CNI, and leaving room for growth.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: Clients intermittently fail to connect to a service behind a load balancer. How do you investigate?
questions.a: Find the pattern first: which clients, which backends, what fraction. A steady fraction such as one in three points at one bad backend still in rotation. Check target health, hit each backend directly, compare error timing with deploys and scaling events, and look for connection draining problems or exhausted ports or connection limits.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would a misconfigured health check cause this?
What is connection draining?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Looking only at aggregate metrics, which hide a single bad instance.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Discuss keep-alive mismatches between load balancer and backend idle timeouts, a classic source of sporadic 502s, and conntrack or ephemeral port exhaustion.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP? Give a use for each.
questions.a: TCP sets up a connection and guarantees ordered, reliable delivery with flow and congestion control: web, APIs, databases. UDP sends independent datagrams with no guarantees and lower overhead: DNS queries, voice and video, and QUIC.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does HTTP/3 use UDP?
What is head-of-line blocking?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying UDP is "unreliable so nobody uses it".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Explain that QUIC rebuilds reliability and encryption in user space over UDP to avoid TCP head-of-line blocking and speed up connection setup.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
questions.a: Merge joins two histories with a merge commit and keeps both lines as they happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, producing a linear history with new commit IDs.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When is rebase dangerous?
What does git pull --rebase do?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Rebasing commits that others have already pulled, which rewrites shared history.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Talk about team conventions: rebase locally to tidy, merge or squash to main, and protected branches that forbid force pushes.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: A bad commit reached main and was deployed. How do you undo it?
questions.a: git revert the commit, which adds a new commit that undoes it, and let the pipeline deploy that. History stays intact and everyone else is unaffected. If customers are hurting, roll back the deployment first, then revert.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why not git reset --hard and force push?
How do you revert a merge commit?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Rewriting history on a shared branch.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Separate the two concerns: restoring service (rollback of the artifact) and correcting source (revert). Roll back first, they are different speeds.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: What is the staging area and why does Git have one?
questions.a: It is the draft of the next commit, sitting between your working files and history. You choose exactly which changes go into a commit, so each commit is one coherent change even when your working tree contains several.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you unstage a file without losing the edit?
What does "git add -p" do?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating "git add ." plus commit as one step and committing unrelated changes together.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Small, single-purpose commits make review, revert, cherry-pick and bisect work. That is the operational payoff.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: When does a merge conflict happen, and how do you resolve one?
questions.a: When both branches changed the same lines of a file differently since their common ancestor, or one deleted a file the other modified. Git writes both versions between markers. You edit the file to the correct result, remove the markers, stage the file and commit. Then you run the tests.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is a semantic conflict?
How do you abandon the merge?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Picking one side wholesale without understanding the other change.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Text-level merging says nothing about correctness. CI on the merge result, and a merge queue on busy repositories, is what protects main.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: Your teammate force-pushed main and commits are missing. What now?
questions.a: Stop further pushes. Anyone who still has the old commits locally can restore them: find the previous tip with the reflog or from a CI build record, and push it back or merge it. Then enable branch protection so force pushes to main are rejected.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is the reflog and how long does it keep entries?
How does --force-with-lease differ from --force?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming the commits are gone for good, or pulling and thereby merging the damaged history.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Treat it as an incident: restore, then fix the control that allowed it. Deployed image tags by commit ID also tell you exactly what main used to be.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: Explain trunk-based development and what it requires to work.
questions.a: Everyone integrates small changes into main at least daily, using short-lived branches. It requires fast, reliable CI, feature flags to hide unfinished work, good automated tests and the ability to roll back quickly.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you ship a large feature this way?
Where do release branches still make sense?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Calling it "no branches" or "no code review".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: It moves risk from big merges to small increments. The prerequisite is engineering discipline, not a branching diagram.

questions.topic: Bash
questions.q: What is an exit code, and how do you use it in a script?
questions.a: Every command returns an integer; 0 is success. It is available as $? and is what if, &&, || and set -e act on. A script should finish with exit 0 on success and a documented non-zero code on each kind of failure.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What exit code does a pipeline return?
What do codes above 128 mean?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Printing an error message but exiting 0, so automation treats the failure as success.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: 128 + N means killed by signal N. Distinct codes for usage errors, expected failures and unexpected ones let callers react differently.

questions.topic: Bash
questions.q: What does "set -euo pipefail" do and why is it recommended?
questions.a: -e stops the script when a command fails, -u makes an unset variable an error, and pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails rather than only the last. Together they turn silent partial failures into immediate, visible ones.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where is -e ignored?
How do you allow one command to fail on purpose?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Believing -e catches everything: it is ignored in conditions and before && or ||.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Pair it with explicit checks of the outcome that matters and a trap for cleanup. Strict mode is a seatbelt, not a substitute for verification.

questions.topic: Bash
questions.q: Why must you quote variables in shell scripts?
questions.a: An unquoted variable is split into words on whitespace and then expanded as a file pattern. A path with a space becomes two arguments, and an empty variable disappears entirely, which can turn "rm -rf $dir/" into "rm -rf /".

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When is leaving a variable unquoted correct?
What does "$@" preserve that $* does not?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Quoting only "when there might be spaces".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Quote by default, lint with shellcheck in CI, and guard destructive commands with ${var:?} so an empty value aborts the script.

questions.topic: Python
questions.q: When would you write automation in Python instead of Bash?
questions.a: When it handles structured data such as JSON or YAML, calls APIs, needs real error handling, or is long enough to deserve functions and tests. Bash remains better for short command sequences and minimal environments.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you run a shell command from Python safely?
How do you package a small tool for a team?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Parsing JSON with grep and sed, or using shell=True with interpolated input.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Maintainability is the deciding factor: can the next engineer change it safely, and is there a test that would catch a mistake?

questions.topic: Servers
questions.q: How does SSH key authentication work, and why is it safer than a password?
questions.a: The server stores your public key. At login your client signs a one-time challenge with the private key, and the server checks the signature. The private key is never sent, so nothing reusable crosses the network, and there is nothing to guess the way a password can be guessed.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is known_hosts for?
What is the risk of agent forwarding?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Copying the private key onto servers so you can hop between them.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: At scale, move from static keys to short-lived SSH certificates or a cloud session manager, so access expires on its own and is audited.

questions.topic: Servers
questions.q: You are given a fresh public Ubuntu server. What do you do in the first hour?
questions.a: Create a personal sudo user with a key and confirm the login works, disable root and password logins, enable a default-deny firewall that allows SSH and the service ports, apply updates and turn on automatic security updates, and check from outside what is reachable. Then turn those steps into a script or image.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: In what order do you change SSH settings and the firewall, and why?
How do you recover from a lockout?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Enabling the firewall or disabling passwords before proving the new access path works.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Treat the server as disposable: the real deliverable is the automation that builds an identical one, not the hand-tuned machine.

questions.topic: Nginx
questions.q: How does nginx decide which location block handles a request?
questions.a: An exact (=) match wins immediately. Otherwise nginx finds the longest matching prefix. If that prefix is marked ^~ it is used. If not, regex locations are tried in file order and the first match wins; if none matches, the longest prefix is used.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why can adding a regex location break an unrelated prefix location?
What is the difference between root and alias?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming the first matching location in the file wins.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Order matters only among regexes. That is why large configurations prefer prefix locations and use ^~ to make precedence explicit.

questions.topic: Nginx
questions.q: Explain the trailing-slash behaviour of proxy_pass.
questions.a: If proxy_pass includes a URI part, even just "/", nginx replaces the part of the request path that matched the location with that URI. Without a URI part the original path is forwarded unchanged. So for location /api/, a request for /api/health reaches the backend as /health in the first case and /api/health in the second.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you debug a 404 that only happens through the proxy?
Which headers should a reverse proxy add?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Changing the slash by trial and error without looking at what the backend received.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Log the upstream request line on the backend or use a request echo service while changing proxy rules, and cover the routes with an automated smoke test.

questions.topic: Nginx
questions.q: A site behind nginx intermittently returns 502. How do you investigate?
questions.a: Read the nginx error log: it names the upstream and the reason. "Connection refused" means a backend is down or restarting; "upstream prematurely closed connection" means it crashed or closed an idle keep-alive connection; "no live upstreams" means all are marked failed. Correlate the timing with deploys, restarts and resource limits, and check each backend directly.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why do 502s appear during deploys?
How do keep-alive timeouts cause sporadic 502s?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Restarting nginx, which is the one component that is working.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Backends should drain on SIGTERM and their keep-alive timeout should be longer than the proxy's, otherwise the proxy reuses a connection the backend has just closed.

questions.topic: TLS
questions.q: What is in a TLS certificate and what does the client check?
questions.a: A public key, the hostnames it is valid for, a validity period, and a signature from a certificate authority. The client checks that the signature chain leads to a root it trusts, that the current date is inside the validity period, that the hostname it asked for is listed, and that the server holds the matching private key.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is an intermediate certificate?
Why does a missing intermediate work in some clients and not others?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying the certificate "encrypts the traffic". It authenticates the server; the session keys do the encrypting.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Certificate transparency logs and CAA records are the controls against mis-issuance; short lifetimes are the control against key compromise.

questions.topic: TLS
questions.q: A certificate expired in production. What is your response and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: Renew and reload the server, verify from outside, then find why automatic renewal failed. Prevent it by automating issuance and renewal, renewing at about two thirds of the lifetime, and monitoring days-to-expiry from outside with an alert at around 14 days.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why monitor expiry rather than the renewal job?
What changes as certificate lifetimes drop to 45 days?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Relying on a calendar reminder or on the renewal job reporting its own failure.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Monitor the outcome the customer experiences. Shorter lifetimes make manual renewal impossible in practice and force every certificate onto automation.

questions.topic: DNS
questions.q: How do you move a live site to a new server without downtime?
questions.a: Lower the DNS record's TTL a day ahead and wait out the old TTL. Bring up the new server and test it by IP using the real hostname. Switch the record, keep both servers running until traffic on the old one reaches zero, then raise the TTL and retire the old server. Keep a rollback at each step.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why keep the old server running after the switch?
What state needs migrating besides DNS?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Switching the record with a one-hour TTL and turning the old server off at once.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: DNS is the easy part. Data and sessions are the hard part: decide where writes go during the overlap, or put a load balancer in front and shift traffic there instead of in DNS.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: What is the difference between continuous integration, delivery and deployment?
questions.a: Integration: every change is built and tested automatically on merge. Delivery: every passing change is packaged and can be released with one decision. Deployment: passing changes are released automatically with no manual gate.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which would you choose for a payments service, and why?
What must be true before removing the manual gate?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using the terms interchangeably.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The gate is replaced by confidence: test coverage, progressive rollout, automated verification and fast rollback. Discuss how regulation may still require approval.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: Describe a deployment strategy that limits the impact of a bad release.
questions.a: Canary: send a small share of traffic to the new version, compare its error rate and latency with the old version, and increase gradually or abort. Rolling updates replace instances in batches behind readiness checks. Blue-green keeps the old environment running for instant switch-back.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle database schema changes with these?
What metrics decide whether a canary passes?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Ignoring that old and new versions run together and must be compatible.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Expand-and-contract migrations, feature flags to decouple deploy from release, and automated canary analysis.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: How do you manage secrets in a pipeline?
questions.a: Store them in a secrets manager or the CI credential store, inject at run time into only the steps that need them, mask them in logs, scope them per environment and rotate them. Never in the repository, the image or the pipeline file.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you detect a secret committed by accident?
What do you do after one leaks?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Thinking that deleting the commit removes the secret. It must be rotated.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Prefer short-lived credentials through workload identity (OIDC) over stored long-lived keys.

questions.topic: Jenkins
questions.q: Explain Jenkins controller and agents. Why not build on the controller?
questions.a: The controller schedules jobs, stores configuration and serves the UI. Agents run the build steps. Building on the controller risks its stability and security, since builds run arbitrary code next to credentials and configuration.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you scale agents?
What is the difference between declarative and scripted pipelines?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Running everything on the controller "because it is simpler".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Ephemeral agents (Kubernetes pods) per build give clean environments and elastic capacity.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
questions.a: A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest operating system with its own kernel. A container is an isolated process on the host kernel, using namespaces for isolation and cgroups for limits. Containers start faster and weigh less; VMs isolate more strongly.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When would you still choose a VM?
What are sandboxes such as gVisor or Firecracker for?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Calling a container a "lightweight VM".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Discuss the shared-kernel attack surface and multi-tenant isolation.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: How do you reduce the size and build time of a Docker image?
questions.a: Small base image, multi-stage build so build tools do not ship, order instructions so rarely changing layers come first, combine and clean within one RUN, use .dockerignore, and cache dependency installation separately from source.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does a file deleted in a later layer still take space?
What is BuildKit cache mount?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Putting COPY . . before installing dependencies, which rebuilds them on every code change.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Smaller images also mean a smaller attack surface and faster node scale-up.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: A container exits immediately after starting. How do you debug it?
questions.a: docker ps -a for the exit code, docker logs for output, docker inspect for the command and configuration. Then run it interactively with the entrypoint overridden to look inside.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do exit codes 1, 126, 127, 137 and 143 mean?
Why does a container need a foreground process?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Not knowing that the container lives only as long as PID 1.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: 126 not executable, 127 command not found, 137 SIGKILL (often OOM), 143 SIGTERM.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: Why build an artifact once and promote it, rather than building per environment?
questions.a: Because only then is the thing running in production the thing that was tested. A second build can pick up a newer dependency, a different base image or different build flags. The artifact stays identical; configuration is what differs between environments.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you inject environment-specific configuration?
Tag or digest: which do you deploy by?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Having separate "staging" and "production" builds of the same commit.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Tie it to supply-chain integrity: an immutable, signed artifact with provenance is what lets you answer "exactly what is running, and where did it come from?".

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: How would you roll out a risky change to a high-traffic service?
questions.a: Behind a feature flag where possible, then as a canary: a small share of traffic to the new version, automated comparison of error rate and latency against the stable version, and step-wise widening with automatic abort. Database changes go out first in a backward-compatible form.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What metrics gate each step?
What if the service has too little traffic for a canary to be meaningful?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Relying on health checks alone, which only show that the process answers.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Low-traffic services need synthetic traffic or longer soak times; and the abort path must be tested as often as the happy path.

questions.topic: Jenkins
questions.q: A build has been "pending" for an hour. What do you check?
questions.a: It is queued, not failing. Check the queue reason: usually no online agent has the required label, or all executors are busy. Then check the agent list and logs for the offline node, and whether a stuck build is holding the only executor.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you get alerted to this?
What changes with ephemeral agents?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Reading the build log, which is empty because nothing has run.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Queue time is a first-class metric for a CI platform, and ephemeral agents turn "the Mac is offline" into a provisioning problem with a timeout instead of a silent wait.

questions.topic: Jenkins
questions.q: How do you keep secrets out of build logs?
questions.a: Bind them with withCredentials around only the steps that need them, reference them from single-quoted shell commands so Groovy does not interpolate the value, never echo them or dump the environment, and treat log masking as a safety net rather than the control. If one leaks, rotate it.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why are double quotes dangerous here?
How do you limit which jobs can use a credential?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Trusting masking: it matches exact strings and misses encoded or partial values.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Prefer credentials that are useless outside the build: short-lived tokens issued through OIDC or a secrets broker, scoped to one repository and one environment.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: How do containers on the same host talk to each other?
questions.a: Put them on the same user-defined network. Docker runs a DNS server for that network that resolves container or service names to their current addresses, so one container connects to another by name and container port. Published ports are only for access from outside the network.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does localhost mean inside a container?
What is different on the default bridge network?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Connecting to localhost, or to the published host port, from another container.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: It is the same model Kubernetes Services give you at cluster scale: a stable name in front of replaceable instances.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: Where does a container's data live, and how do you make it survive?
questions.a: Writes go to a thin writable layer that is deleted with the container. Data that must outlive it goes in a named volume, managed by Docker, or a bind mount of a host directory. The volume is attached at the path the application writes to.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Volume or bind mount for a production database?
How do you back up a volume?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Storing database files in the container layer and losing them on the next image update.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: On an orchestrator this becomes persistent volume claims and storage classes, and the real questions are backup, restore time and which node the data can follow.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: What does depends_on in Compose guarantee, and what does it not?
questions.a: It guarantees start order: by default only that the other container has been started. With a healthcheck on the dependency and condition: service_healthy it waits for readiness at startup. It does not help when a dependency restarts later, so applications still need connection retries.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you write a healthcheck for PostgreSQL?
Why is "sleep 10" a poor substitute?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming "started" means "ready to accept connections".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Start-order tricks fix boot; resilience to dependency loss at any time is an application property. Design for the dependency being briefly absent.

questions.topic: GitHub Actions
questions.q: How do you make a GitHub Actions workflow safe to run on pull requests from forks?
questions.a: Use the pull_request trigger, which gives fork runs a read-only token and no secrets. Keep build and test there. Put anything that needs secrets or deploys in a separate workflow that runs after merge. Pin third-party actions to commit SHAs and set minimal permissions.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is risky about pull_request_target?
How do required reviewers on an environment help?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Switching to pull_request_target to "make the secrets work" for fork PRs.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Untrusted code and privileged credentials must never share a job. That single rule explains most CI supply-chain incidents.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: What is a Pod, and why not just schedule containers?
questions.a: A Pod is one or more containers that share a network namespace and volumes and are scheduled together. It lets tightly coupled helpers (sidecars) live next to the main container and gives a single unit with one IP to schedule and replace.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When would you put two containers in one pod?
What is an init container?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Putting unrelated services in one pod.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Sidecar patterns: proxies, log shippers, and native sidecar containers with ordered lifecycle.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk through your investigation.
questions.a: kubectl describe pod for events, last state, exit code and reason. kubectl logs --previous for the crash output. Check what changed: image, config, secrets. Typical causes are missing environment or secrets, failing dependencies at startup, wrong command, OOM kills, or a liveness probe that is too aggressive.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: The logs are empty. What next?
How does the back-off timing work?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Deleting the pod repeatedly.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Empty logs suggest the process never started (exit 126/127) or was killed. Use an ephemeral debug container. Back-off doubles up to five minutes.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: Explain readiness, liveness and startup probes.
questions.a: Readiness controls whether the pod receives Service traffic. Liveness restarts a container that is stuck. Startup holds off the other two until a slow application has started.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What happens if liveness checks a database?
Why can a pod be Running but not Ready?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using the same endpoint and thresholds for all three.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: A liveness probe on a shared dependency turns one outage into a restart storm across every pod.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: How does a Service route traffic to pods?
questions.a: The Service selects pods by label. The EndpointSlice controller lists the IPs of matching Ready pods. kube-proxy or an eBPF dataplane on every node rewrites traffic for the Service virtual IP to one of those pod IPs. CoreDNS resolves the Service name to the virtual IP.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What are ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer?
What is a headless Service?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Believing the Service is a process that proxies traffic.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Explain externalTrafficPolicy, source IP preservation and topology-aware routing.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: What is the difference between requests and limits, and how do they affect scheduling and runtime?
questions.a: Requests are what the scheduler reserves when placing the pod. Limits are enforced at run time: exceeding the memory limit gets the container OOM-killed; exceeding the CPU limit gets it throttled. Together they set the QoS class.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why do some teams avoid CPU limits?
What happens to BestEffort pods under node pressure?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Setting no requests, so the scheduler overpacks nodes.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: CPU throttling under CFS quotas causes tail latency; memory limit equal to request gives predictable behaviour.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: How does a rolling update work and how would you guarantee zero downtime?
questions.a: A new ReplicaSet scales up while the old scales down, bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable. Zero downtime needs readiness probes that reflect real readiness, graceful SIGTERM handling, a preStop delay so endpoints update before the process stops, enough replicas, and a PodDisruptionBudget.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why can a pod still receive traffic after it gets SIGTERM?
How do you roll back?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming the default settings are enough.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, so in-flight routing lags; hence preStop sleep and connection draining.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: You changed a ConfigMap and the application still uses the old value. Why, and how do you fix it properly?
questions.a: Values consumed as environment variables are fixed when the container starts, so running pods keep the old ones. Mounted files do update after a delay, but only help if the application re-reads them. The proper fix is to make a config change alter the pod template, with a content-hashed ConfigMap name or a checksum annotation, so it triggers a normal rolling update.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is a hashed name better than "rollout restart"?
What happens to the old ConfigMaps?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Deleting pods by hand after every config change.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: A hashed name also makes rollback correct: the previous revision points at the previous configuration, which still exists.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: A Service returns nothing although its pods are Running. What do you check, in order?
questions.a: Whether the Service has endpoints. If not: does the selector match the pod labels, is the Service in the same namespace as the pods, and are the pods Ready. If endpoints exist but connections are refused: does targetPort match the port the container listens on, and does the app bind to 0.0.0.0. Then NetworkPolicy, then the Ingress in front.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which of those leaves endpoints listed but still fails?
How do you test from inside the cluster?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Restarting the pods, which changes none of those four things.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Each step maps to one command: get endpointslices, get pods --show-labels, describe pod, and a curl from a debug pod. Fixed order beats intuition.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: Design the RBAC for a CI pipeline that deploys to production.
questions.a: A dedicated ServiceAccount per environment. A namespaced Role allowing get, list, watch, patch and update on the workload kinds it deploys, and read access to what rollout status needs. No access to Secrets, no create or delete of RBAC objects, no wildcard verbs. Credentials are short-lived, obtained through OIDC federation rather than a stored token.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is "list secrets" dangerous?
How would GitOps change this design?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Giving the pipeline cluster-admin because it is simpler.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: With pull-based GitOps the pipeline needs no cluster credentials at all: it writes to Git and the in-cluster controller applies. That removes the most valuable credential from CI.

questions.topic: Helm
questions.q: What happens during "helm upgrade", and how do you make it safe in a pipeline?
questions.a: Helm merges values (chart defaults, then -f files, then --set), renders the templates, validates the result, computes a three-way merge against the previous manifest and the live objects, applies the changes and records a new revision. For safety: review helm template or a diff first, and run with --atomic and a timeout so a release that does not become healthy is rolled back automatically.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does rollback not undo?
What happens if someone edited the object with kubectl?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming a successful upgrade command means the application is healthy; without --wait it only means the API accepted the objects.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Helm rollback restores Kubernetes objects only. Data and schema changes need their own backward-compatible plan.

questions.topic: Helm
questions.q: Helm or Kustomize: how do you choose?
questions.a: Helm templates manifests from values and adds packaging, versioning and release history: the right tool for distributing software with many options, and for third-party components. Kustomize layers patches over plain YAML with no templating: simpler to read and review for varying your own manifests per environment. They combine well: install charts for third-party software, use overlays for your own services.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you promote a change through environments with each?
What is the config hash in Kustomize for?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Wrapping your own three-file service in a heavily templated chart.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Optimise for reviewability of the rendered output. Whatever the tool, the pull request should show what will actually reach the cluster.

questions.topic: GitOps
questions.q: What is GitOps, and what problem does it solve?
questions.a: The desired state of the system is declared and versioned in Git, and an agent in the cluster continuously pulls it and reconciles the cluster to match. It gives every change a review, an author and a history, removes cluster credentials from CI, detects drift, and makes rollback a revert.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Push-based versus pull-based deployment?
Where do secrets go?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Describing it as "kubectl apply from a pipeline that is triggered by Git".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The essential properties are pull and continuous reconciliation. A pipeline that pushes on commit has neither, and the cluster can drift unnoticed.

questions.topic: GitOps
questions.q: In Argo CD an application is Synced but Degraded. Explain, and say what you do.
questions.a: Sync status compares the cluster with what Git renders; health assesses whether the resources work. Synced and Degraded means Argo CD applied exactly what Git asks for and it does not run: a bad image, a failing probe, a missing secret. Revert the commit so Git describes a working state, let it sync, then fix forward.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why not use the Argo CD rollback button?
How would you have caught this before production?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating "Synced" as "deployed successfully".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Under automated sync Argo CD refuses a rollback, and a manual one leaves Git and the cluster disagreeing. Promotion through environments plus health-gated progressive delivery is the prevention.

questions.topic: GitOps
questions.q: An engineer keeps hot-fixing production with kubectl and the changes vanish. What is happening and what is the right process?
questions.a: Self-heal is reverting drift: the cluster is being pulled back to what Git declares. The fix has to be a commit. For a real emergency, automated sync can be paused on that one application, the change made, and the same change committed before sync is re-enabled.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What are prune and self-heal, and are they on by default?
How do HPAs avoid being reverted?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Turning off self-heal permanently so manual changes stick.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Both prune and self-heal are off by default in Argo CD and are enabled deliberately. Fields owned by other controllers, such as replicas under an HPA, are left out of Git or listed in ignoreDifferences.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: The API server is unavailable. What still works and what does not?
questions.a: Existing pods keep running and serving traffic, because the kubelet and dataplane work from their last known state. Nothing can change: no deploys, scaling, rescheduling or replacement of failed pods; endpoints stop updating.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if etcd loses quorum?
How do you design the control plane for high availability?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying the whole cluster goes down.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Three control-plane nodes across zones, etcd quorum maths, and why static stability is a design goal.

questions.topic: Monitoring
questions.q: What would you alert on for a checkout API?
questions.a: Customer-visible symptoms: error ratio and latency against the SLO, plus saturation signals that predict trouble such as queue depth or connection pool use. Page only when a human must act now; everything else is a ticket or a dashboard.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is the difference between RED and USE?
How do you reduce alert fatigue?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Paging on every cause, such as CPU above 80%.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Multi-window burn-rate alerts on the error budget.

questions.topic: SRE
questions.q: Define SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget.
questions.a: SLI: a measured indicator such as the share of successful checkout requests. SLO: the internal target for it, for example 99.9% over 30 days. SLA: a contract with consequences. Error budget: the allowed unreliability, 0.1% here, about 43 minutes in 30 days.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you do when the budget is spent?
Why not aim for 100%?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Confusing the SLO with the SLA.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The budget is a decision tool that balances release speed against reliability work.

questions.topic: Security
questions.q: How would you secure a container image and its deployment?
questions.a: Minimal pinned base image, non-root user, no secrets in layers, vulnerability scanning in CI, signed images, read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, least-privilege ServiceAccount and default-deny network policies.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is an SBOM?
How do you enforce these rules cluster-wide?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Relying on scanning alone.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Admission policy to enforce, and provenance attestation for the supply chain.

questions.topic: Troubleshooting
questions.q: Latency doubled right after a deploy, but error rate is flat. What do you do?
questions.a: Roll back if the SLO is at risk; latency after a deploy is guilty until proven innocent. Then compare versions: new queries or N+1 patterns, changed timeouts or pool sizes, lost caching, resource limits and throttling. Use traces to find the slow span.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: The rollback did not help. Now what?
How do you tell CPU throttling from a slow dependency?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Debugging in production while customers wait.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Correlation with the deploy is strong evidence but check concurrent events: traffic shift, node change, dependency release.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: Walk me through what happens when you run terraform plan.
questions.a: Terraform loads the configuration and variables, takes the state lock, and refreshes: it reads every resource recorded in the state from the provider API. It builds a dependency graph from references, evaluates each resource in order, and compares the result with the refreshed state. The output lists creates, in-place updates, replacements and destroys. Nothing is changed.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why are some values shown as "known after apply"?
What is different about plan -refresh-only?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying plan compares the files with the state only, and forgetting that it reads the real infrastructure first.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Mention saving the plan with -out so that what is applied is exactly what was reviewed, and that a saved plan goes stale if the state changes.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: What is in the Terraform state, and what happens if you lose it?
questions.a: The state maps each resource address to the real object's id and records its attributes and dependencies. If it is lost the infrastructure keeps running, but Terraform no longer knows it owns any of it: a plan would try to create everything again. Recovery is restoring an older version from the versioned backend, or importing every resource.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is the state sensitive?
How do you stop two people applying at once?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating the state as a cache that can be regenerated.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Remote backend with versioning, encryption and locking; one state per environment and component to limit blast radius; access to the state is access to the infrastructure and its secrets.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: A one-line change shows "-/+ must be replaced" on a production database. What do you do?
questions.a: Do not apply. Find the argument marked "forces replacement". Check whether the same goal can be reached in place: a different argument, a provider upgrade that supports modification, or a native migration such as snapshot and restore or a replica promotion. If replacement is unavoidable, plan it as a migration with a backup, a maintenance window and a rollback path.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would prevent_destroy have helped?
When is create_before_destroy the answer, and when is it not?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Trusting the summary line, or assuming Terraform would warn more loudly about data loss.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Guard data stores with prevent_destroy and deletion protection, run policy checks that fail any plan destroying a stateful resource, and keep such resources in their own state.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: Someone changed a security group in the console during an incident. How should the team handle it?
questions.a: That is drift. The next plan reports it and proposes to revert it. Decide deliberately: if the change was a temporary workaround, apply and let Terraform remove it; if it was correct, write it into the configuration through a pull request so the plan shows no changes. Then find out why the console path was needed and whether it should stay available.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you detect drift before someone trips over it?
What does lifecycle ignore_changes do, and when is it appropriate?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Running apply without reading, which silently removes a fix that was keeping production up.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Scheduled drift-detection plans, read-only console access in production with a break-glass role, and a rule that emergency changes are codified the same day.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: A request is denied with AccessDenied. How does IAM decide, and how do you debug it?
questions.a: IAM collects every policy that applies. An explicit Deny in any of them ends it. Otherwise there must be an Allow, and the request must also pass organisation policies and any permissions boundary; with no Allow it is an implicit deny. To debug: confirm the identity with sts get-caller-identity, read the error for the exact action and resource, compare the resource ARN with the policy, then look for a Deny in resource policies, boundaries and organisation policies.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does s3:GetObject on a bucket ARN without /* fail?
What is different for cross-account access?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Adding broader Allow statements when the cause is an explicit Deny, or a mismatched ARN.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: CloudTrail shows the denied call and, for many services, which policy type denied it. The policy simulator answers the question without making the call.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: Design the network for a three-tier web application on AWS.
questions.a: One VPC across at least two Availability Zones. Public subnets hold only the load balancer and NAT gateways. Private application subnets hold the service; private data subnets hold the database. Public subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway, private ones to a NAT gateway in the same zone. Security groups chain: the load balancer accepts 443 from the internet, the service accepts its port only from the load balancer's group, the database accepts its port only from the service's group.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What breaks if the NAT gateway is placed in a private subnet?
When would you add VPC endpoints?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Putting application servers in public subnets, or allowing database access from the whole VPC range.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Address planning for growth and for pods on EKS, a NAT gateway per zone, flow logs, and endpoints for S3 and ECR to keep traffic private and reduce NAT cost.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: Customers get 5xx errors from an Application Load Balancer. How do you narrow it down?
questions.a: Start with which code. 503 means no healthy targets: check target health and why health checks fail. 502 means a target sent a broken response or closed the connection: look at application crashes and keep-alive timeouts shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout. 504 means a target did not answer in time: check latency, a slow dependency, or a security group blocking the load balancer. Split load balancer errors from target errors in the metrics, and correlate with deploys and scaling activity.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Health checks pass but users still see errors. Why might that be?
How does connection draining affect deployments?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Restarting instances before reading the target health reason.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: A health endpoint that is too shallow hides real failures and one that is too deep causes cascading removal of every target when a shared dependency blips. Design it deliberately.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: How does a pod on EKS get permission to call S3 without any stored keys?
questions.a: The pod runs under a Kubernetes service account that is linked to an IAM role. With EKS Pod Identity, an association maps cluster, namespace and service account to the role, the role's trust policy allows the pods.eks.amazonaws.com service, and an agent on each node gives the AWS SDK temporary credentials for that role. IRSA achieves the same with an OIDC provider and a projected token. The role's permission policy then decides what the pod may do.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: A new pod still gets AccessDenied. What are the possible causes, in order?
Why should pods not use the node's role?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Putting access keys in a Kubernetes Secret, or giving the node role broad permissions that every pod inherits.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: One role per workload, block pod access to instance metadata, and manage associations and roles in Terraform next to the service.

questions.topic: Databases
questions.q: After scaling a service from 6 to 12 pods, new pods fail with "too many clients". Explain and fix.
questions.a: Each pod keeps its own connection pool, so connections grow with the pod count: 12 pods with a pool of 10 want 120 against a PostgreSQL limit of 100 minus a few reserved. Restore service by reducing the pool size or scaling back. The lasting fix is a transaction-mode pooler such as PgBouncer or RDS Proxy, so many client connections share a few server connections and application scale no longer touches the database limit.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why not raise max_connections to 1000?
What breaks under transaction-mode pooling?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Raising max_connections first. Each connection is a server process; the database gets slower and runs out of memory.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Do the arithmetic for the worst moment, a rolling deploy with surge on top of peak scale, and alert on connection usage as a share of the limit.

questions.topic: Databases
questions.q: Define RPO and RTO, and design for RPO 0 and RTO under two minutes.
questions.a: RPO is how much recent data may be lost; RTO is how long the service may be down. RPO 0 needs synchronous replication: a commit is acknowledged only when a standby in another zone has it. RTO under two minutes needs automatic failure detection and promotion, a stable endpoint that moves to the new primary, and applications that reconnect and retry. Then rehearse it, because the application side is usually what breaks the target.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does synchronous replication cost?
Why is a read replica not enough?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Quoting the database failover time and forgetting that applications holding dead connections extend the outage.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: RPO and RTO are business decisions with a price. Different data sets deserve different targets, and backups are still required for mistakes that replication faithfully copies.

questions.topic: Databases
questions.q: How do you rename a column on a table that is in constant use, with no downtime?
questions.a: Expand and contract across several releases. Add the new column. Deploy code that writes both and reads the old. Backfill existing rows in small batches. Deploy code that reads the new column. When nothing uses the old one, drop it in a later release. At every step the previous version of the code still works with the schema, so a rollback is always safe.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why can a plain ALTER TABLE freeze a busy application?
How do you add an index to a large live table?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Doing the rename and the code change in one release: during the rolling deploy one of the two code versions is always broken.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Set lock_timeout on schema changes so they fail fast instead of queueing every query behind them, and run migrations from the pipeline, not by hand.

questions.topic: Redis
questions.q: Your Redis cache restarts empty at peak traffic. What happens, and how do you design against it?
questions.a: Every read misses and goes to the database. If the database was sized for the traffic left after a 90 percent hit ratio, it now receives ten times its normal load and can fail, turning a cache restart into an outage. Design for it: database headroom, a limit on concurrent database reads, a lock or stale-while-revalidate around rebuilding hot keys, random spread on expiry times, and replicas or persistence so a restart is not an empty start.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is a cache stampede?
Which eviction policy for a cache, and why?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating the cache as a pure optimisation and never load-testing with it cold.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The cache is optional for correctness but has become mandatory for capacity. Say which of the two your design assumes and prove it with a cold-cache load test.

questions.topic: Kafka
questions.q: Consumer lag on a topic keeps growing. How do you investigate?
questions.a: Describe the consumer group to see lag per partition. If the group has no members or keeps rebalancing, fix the consumers first. If lag is spread evenly, the group is too slow: add consumers up to the partition count or speed up processing. If lag sits in one partition, it is a hot key or one slow consumer, and adding consumers will not help. Then look at what each consumer is waiting on downstream.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why can you not have more working consumers than partitions?
What happens to ordering if you add partitions?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Adding consumers without checking the distribution of lag, or resetting offsets and silently skipping events.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Alert on lag as time behind, per partition, and on its trend. Make consumers idempotent because rebalances and crashes will redeliver.

questions.topic: Monitoring
questions.q: How would you instrument and monitor a new HTTP service?
questions.a: Expose a request counter and a duration histogram labelled by route template and status class. From those, graph and alert on rate, error ratio and latency percentiles: the RED signals. Add saturation signals for what the service depends on, such as connection pool use and queue depth. Structured logs with a trace id, and tracing through OpenTelemetry. One standard dashboard and two or three symptom-based alerts with runbooks.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why histograms rather than averages?
What is label cardinality and why does it matter?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Dozens of cause-based alerts (CPU, memory, restarts) and no measurement of what users experience.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Tie the alerts to an SLO and page on error-budget burn rate, with a fast window for outages and a slow one for gradual degradation.

questions.topic: Monitoring
questions.q: An alert has a "for: 5m" clause. Walk through what happens during a 3-minute error spike and a 20-minute one.
questions.a: When the expression first evaluates true the alert becomes pending. In the 3-minute spike the expression turns false before five minutes pass, so it returns to inactive and nobody is notified. In the 20-minute case it stays true for five minutes, becomes firing, and Alertmanager groups and routes it. Because the expression uses a rate over a window, it also crosses the threshold a little after the fault begins, so detection takes several minutes in total.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you detect a complete outage faster?
What are the costs of removing the "for" clause?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming the alert fires the moment the threshold is crossed, or tuning "for" to zero to be fast and then drowning in pages.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Use two burn-rate windows: a short one that pages quickly for severe failures and a long one for slow leaks, instead of one threshold trying to do both.

questions.topic: Observability
questions.q: A request is slow but every team says their service is healthy. How do you find where the time goes?
questions.a: Take a trace of one slow request. The waterfall shows every span with its duration, so the long step is visible at once: a slow query, many small queries in a loop, or a downstream call waiting for a timeout and retrying. Use each span's own time, not its total, to avoid blaming a parent for its child. Then use the trace id to pull that request's logs from every service for the detail.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if the trace is split into separate traces per service?
How do you make sure slow traces are kept?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Comparing per-service average latencies, which hide both the tail and the time lost between services.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Link the three signals: exemplars on latency histograms point to traces, traces carry ids found in logs. Sample at the tail so errors and slow requests are always retained.

questions.topic: Security
questions.q: What security checks would you add to a CI/CD pipeline, and in what order?
questions.a: On the pull request: secret scanning, static analysis of the code, dependency scanning and scanning of Terraform, manifests and Dockerfiles. These are fast and the fix is cheapest there. At build: scan the image, produce an SBOM and sign the image digest. At deploy: an admission policy that accepts only images signed by the pipeline and pods that meet the security standard. In operation: rescan what is running, because new vulnerabilities are published for old images.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which would you add first to a pipeline that has none?
How do you stop the checks being bypassed?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Adding every scanner at once with no thresholds, so the results are ignored.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Fail only on high and critical findings that have a fix, keep exceptions in the repository with an owner and expiry, and treat a slow or noisy check as a pipeline bug.

questions.topic: Security
questions.q: An engineer tells you they pushed an AWS access key to a public repository ten minutes ago. What now?
questions.a: Deactivate or rotate the key immediately: that is the only step that removes the risk, and automated scanners find public keys within minutes. Then check CloudTrail for anything the key did from unknown addresses and treat any misuse as a security incident: remove created users and resources, review data access. Only afterwards clean the history. Then prevent a repeat with push protection, and replace the long-lived key with short-lived credentials.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is deleting the commit not enough?
How should a pipeline authenticate to the cloud without stored keys?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Starting with a history rewrite, or waiting for evidence of misuse before rotating.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Thank the engineer for reporting quickly. The system failed by allowing a long-lived, over-privileged key to exist and by having no scanning at push.

questions.topic: Security
questions.q: How would you harden workloads on a Kubernetes cluster that currently has no restrictions?
questions.a: Measure first: dry-run the restricted Pod Security level, or use warn and audit modes, to list violations. Fix workloads to run as non-root, forbid privilege escalation, drop all capabilities, set a seccomp profile and use a read-only filesystem. Add a default-deny NetworkPolicy per namespace with explicit allows, including DNS. Give each workload its own service account with no API permissions and no mounted token unless needed. Then enforce: baseline everywhere, restricted for application namespaces, and an admission policy for signed images from your registry.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What breaks when you add a default-deny network policy?
Why is the ability to create pods so powerful?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Switching enforcement on without measuring, which blocks the next deploy of every team.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Put the same rules in pull-request checks so teams hear about violations in review, and keep system components in separate, exempt namespaces with tight access.

questions.topic: SRE
questions.q: What is an error budget and how does it change how a team works?
questions.a: It is the amount of unreliability an SLO permits: for 99.9% over 30 days, 0.1% of requests or about 43 minutes. While budget remains the team releases freely and takes risks; when it is spent, by a policy agreed beforehand, feature releases stop and reliability work comes first. It replaces a recurring argument between speed and stability with a number both sides accepted in advance.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Who has to agree to the policy for it to work?
What if the budget is never touched?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating the SLO as a target to maximise, or having a budget with no consequence when it runs out.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: An untouched budget means the team could move faster or the target is too loose. Budget status belongs in weekly planning, not only in incident reviews.

questions.topic: SRE
questions.q: Explain multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting.
questions.a: Burn rate is how fast the error budget is being used relative to using it exactly over the SLO period. Alerts combine a rate with two windows. Typical values for a 30-day SLO: page at 14.4 times over one hour and five minutes, which is 2% of the budget; page at 6 times over six hours and thirty minutes, which is 5%; open a ticket at 1 times over three days. The long window proves the damage is significant, the short one proves it is still happening so the alert clears quickly afterwards.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does a simple threshold alert perform worse?
How does this behave during a total outage?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: One fixed threshold with a long "for": slow for big outages, blind to slow leaks, noisy for blips.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: It ties paging directly to user-visible damage, and it means a ten-minute spike that costs half a percent of the budget wakes nobody.

questions.topic: Incidents
questions.q: You are paged: error rate on the main API is 40%. Walk me through your response.
questions.a: Acknowledge and confirm the impact. Declare an incident, open a channel, and get someone to own communication so I can work. Ask what changed: deploys, configuration, flags, traffic, dependencies. If a change lines up in time, roll it back before trying to understand it. If not, mitigate another way: fail over, add capacity, shed load. One change at a time, each announced and noted with its effect. Update users on a timer. Once stable, keep the timeline and schedule the review.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: The rollback did not help. What next?
When do you escalate?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Debugging the cause while users are down, or several people changing things at once.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Mitigation rarely needs the root cause. Declaring early and escalating early are cheap; doing either late costs the whole outage.

questions.topic: Incidents
questions.q: What is a blameless postmortem and what makes one useful?
questions.a: A written review that assumes people acted reasonably with what they knew and asks how the system allowed the outcome. It has the impact, a timeline, contributing factors, what went well and badly, and action items. It is useful when the factors describe systems and process, when each action is specific, owned and dated and actually gets done, and when it is shared so others learn from it.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you respond to "the root cause was human error"?
What is a bad action item?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Stopping at a name, or writing actions like "be more careful" and "improve monitoring".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Classify actions as guard, detection or recovery, and review open items monthly. Look for patterns across postmortems: the same contributing factor in three incidents is the real finding.

questions.topic: Disaster Recovery
questions.q: Design disaster recovery for an e-commerce platform. How do you decide what to build?
questions.a: Start from business targets, per service. Checkout and payments might need an RTO of minutes and an RPO near zero: a warm standby in a second region with continuously replicated data, or active/active if the cost is justified. Catalogue and search can use pilot light. Analytics can rebuild from backups. Everything is defined as code so it can be recreated; backups are immutable and in a separate account because replication copies deletion and ransomware; DNS fails over on health checks. Then rehearse real failovers and measure against the targets.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is replication not a backup?
What usually goes wrong in the first failover drill?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Giving every service the most expensive tier, or having a plan that has never been executed.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Present the options to the business as prices for recovery times. The first drill usually fails on quotas, a missing secret or image, or people lacking access in the recovery region.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
questions.a: A process has its own memory and resources. Threads live inside a process and share its memory. Processes are isolated from each other; threads are cheaper to create and switch between but one crashing thread can take down the process.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you see the threads of a process?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying they are the same thing with different names.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: On Linux both are tasks to the scheduler; containers add namespaces and cgroups on top of ordinary processes.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: What do the permission bits rwxr-x--- mean?
questions.a: Owner may read, write and execute; group may read and execute; everyone else has no access. On a directory, execute means permission to enter it and read means permission to list it.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does chmod 640 give?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using 777 to make an error go away.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Mention umask, setuid/setgid, the sticky bit on /tmp, and that ACLs and SELinux can also deny access.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: A disk shows 100% full but du finds little data. Why?
questions.a: A deleted file is still held open by a running process, so its space is not released. Find it with lsof | grep deleted and restart or signal the process. It can also be inodes exhausted (df -i) or data hidden under a mount point.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you free the space without restarting the process?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Deleting more files, which changes nothing.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Truncate through /proc/PID/fd/N, and fix log rotation so it signals the process to reopen its file.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: What do SIGTERM and SIGKILL do, and why does it matter for containers?
questions.a: SIGTERM asks a process to stop and can be handled, so the process can finish requests and close connections. SIGKILL cannot be caught and ends it at once. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits the grace period, then SIGKILL.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What exit code does a SIGKILL produce?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Applications that ignore SIGTERM and lose in-flight requests on every deploy.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Exit code 137. The process must be PID 1 or have signals forwarded, which a shell-form entrypoint does not do.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: How do you find which process is listening on port 8000?
questions.a: ss -ltnp | grep :8000 shows the listening socket with the PID and program name; lsof -i :8000 does the same. Then inspect the process with ps or systemctl status.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does "address already in use" mean?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Killing the process before finding out what it is.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Check whether it listens on 127.0.0.1 or 0.0.0.0: a service bound to loopback is unreachable from outside.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: Explain load average. Is a load of 8 bad?
questions.a: It is the average number of tasks running or waiting to run, plus on Linux those blocked on uninterruptible I/O, over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare it with the number of cores: 8 on 16 cores is fine, on 2 cores it means a queue.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Load is high and CPU is idle. Why?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Reading it without the core count.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: High load with idle CPU points to I/O wait: check iostat and for stuck NFS or disk.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: What are cgroups and namespaces?
questions.a: Namespaces limit what a process can see: its own process list, network, mounts, hostname and users. Cgroups limit what it can use: CPU, memory, I/O, process count. A container is an ordinary process with both applied.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What happens when a cgroup hits its memory limit?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Describing containers as lightweight virtual machines.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The kernel OOM killer kills a process in that cgroup; CPU limits throttle instead of killing.

questions.topic: Linux
questions.q: How does systemd restart a failed service, and how would you debug one that keeps failing?
questions.a: Restart= and RestartSec= in the unit control it, with a start limit that stops endless loops. Debug with systemctl status for the exit code and last lines, then journalctl -u NAME -b for the full log, and run the ExecStart command by hand as the service user.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does "start-limit-hit" mean?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Restarting repeatedly without reading the journal.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Check the environment the unit runs with: user, working directory, environment file and permissions differ from your shell.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
questions.a: The name is resolved by DNS to an address. A TCP connection is opened, then TLS is negotiated and the certificate checked. The browser sends an HTTP request, which passes load balancers and proxies to a server, and the response returns the same way.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where can each step fail?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Skipping DNS and TLS and starting at "the server".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Add caching at each layer, connection reuse, the CDN, and how each failure looks to the user: no resolution, timeout, certificate error, 5xx.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
questions.a: TCP sets up a connection, delivers bytes in order and retransmits losses, at the cost of latency. UDP sends independent packets with no guarantees and little overhead. HTTP/1 and 2 use TCP; DNS, video and HTTP/3 (QUIC) use UDP.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does DNS mostly use UDP?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Calling UDP "unreliable so never used".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: QUIC builds reliability and encryption on UDP to avoid head-of-line blocking.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: What is the difference between "connection refused" and "connection timed out"?
questions.a: Refused: the host answered and nothing is listening on that port, or a firewall actively rejected it. Timed out: no answer at all, so packets are being dropped by a firewall or security group, or there is no route.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which one suggests a security group?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating both as "the network is down".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Refused proves the path works. That one fact halves the search.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: How many usable addresses are in a /24 and a /28?
questions.a: /24 has 256 addresses, 254 usable. /28 has 16, 14 usable. In AWS five are reserved per subnet, leaving 251 and 11.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is 10.0.0.0/16 in a range?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Forgetting cloud providers reserve addresses.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Plan for pod IPs on Kubernetes and for non-overlapping ranges before peering networks.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: What do HTTP status codes 301, 401, 403, 404, 429, 502, 503 and 504 mean?
questions.a: 301 moved permanently. 401 not authenticated. 403 authenticated but not allowed. 404 not found. 429 rate limited. 502 the proxy got a bad response from the upstream. 503 no healthy upstream or overloaded. 504 the upstream did not answer in time.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which of these are the client's fault?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up 401 and 403, or 502 and 504.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: 4xx and 5xx go on different dashboards; a 5xx counts against your SLO.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: What is a reverse proxy and how does it differ from a load balancer and an API gateway?
questions.a: A reverse proxy accepts requests on behalf of servers: TLS termination, caching, routing. A load balancer spreads traffic over several servers and removes unhealthy ones. An API gateway adds authentication, rate limiting and per-route policy. One product often does all three.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Layer 4 versus layer 7 balancing?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating them as three unrelated products.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Layer 4 forwards connections and is fast; layer 7 understands HTTP and can route by path and host.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: How does NAT work and why can it be a bottleneck?
questions.a: It rewrites the source address and port of outgoing packets to a public address and keeps a table to map replies back. Each connection uses a port on the NAT, so many connections to one destination can exhaust ports.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you see NAT port exhaustion?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming NAT has unlimited capacity.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Reuse connections, add NAT addresses, or use private endpoints so traffic to cloud services bypasses NAT.

questions.topic: Networking
questions.q: Intermittent failures reaching one service from another in the same cluster. How do you debug?
questions.a: Decide whether it is name resolution, connection or response: test DNS, then a TCP connect, then an HTTP request from a pod. Check the Service has endpoints, readiness probes, network policy, and whether failures tie to one node or pod.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you tell a DNS problem from a network one?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Restarting pods until it stops happening.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Intermittent often means one bad backend among several, conntrack limits, or DNS under load.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
