questions.a: fetch downloads new commits from the remote and updates remote-tracking branches without touching your work. pull is fetch followed by a merge or rebase into your current branch.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When would you prefer fetch?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Thinking fetch changes your working files.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Fetch, inspect, then integrate deliberately; set pull to rebase or fast-forward only.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: Merge versus rebase?
questions.a: Merge joins two histories with a merge commit and keeps what happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch for a linear history, rewriting them. Rebase private branches; never rebase commits others have based work on.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does a fast-forward merge mean?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Rebasing a shared branch and forcing it to the server.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Teams usually squash or rebase feature branches and keep main linear for easy revert and bisect.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: How do you undo a commit that is already on the shared main branch?
questions.a: git revert creates a new commit that undoes it, keeping history intact for everyone. Reset rewrites history and is only for commits that have not been shared.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you revert a merge commit?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using reset --hard on a shared branch.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: In GitOps a revert is also the rollback, reviewed and recorded like any change.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: How would you find which commit introduced a bug?
questions.a: git bisect: mark a known good and a known bad commit, and Git checks out the midpoint repeatedly while you mark each good or bad. It finds the commit in about log2(n) steps and can be automated with a script.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What makes bisect hard to use?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Reading every diff by hand.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Small commits that each build and pass checks make bisect work; huge mixed commits defeat it.

questions.topic: Git
questions.q: Trunk-based development versus long-lived feature branches?
questions.a: Trunk-based: small changes merged to main at least daily, incomplete work hidden behind flags. It avoids big merges and suits continuous delivery. Long-lived branches delay integration and make conflicts and releases painful.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you ship unfinished work safely?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Equating trunk-based with "no review".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: It needs fast checks, feature flags and the discipline of small pull requests.

questions.topic: Bash
questions.q: What does set -euo pipefail do?
questions.a: -e exits when a command fails, -u treats unset variables as errors, and pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails, not only the last. Together they stop a script continuing after an error.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where does -e not apply?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Scripts that carry on after a failed cd and delete the wrong directory.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Know the gaps: commands in if conditions and with || are exempt. Add a trap for clean-up.

questions.topic: Bash
questions.q: Why should variables be quoted in shell scripts?
questions.a: Unquoted, a value is split on spaces and expanded as a filename pattern. A path with a space becomes two arguments and an empty value disappears. "$var" keeps it as one argument.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does "$@" do?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: rm -rf $DIR/ with DIR unset.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Use shellcheck in CI; it finds these before production does.

questions.topic: Bash
questions.q: How do you make a cron job reliable?
questions.a: Use absolute paths and set the environment explicitly, log output somewhere, prevent overlapping runs with a lock, exit non-zero on failure, and alert when it fails or does not run.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does a script work by hand and not from cron?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Jobs that fail silently for weeks.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Monitor for the absence of success, and consider a Kubernetes CronJob or a scheduler with retries.

questions.topic: Bash
questions.q: When should a script be rewritten in Python or Go?
questions.a: When it needs data structures, error handling beyond exit codes, unit checks, JSON or API work, or grows past a screen or two. Shell is right for gluing commands together.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you parse JSON in a shell script?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A 600-line Bash script nobody dares change.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Use jq for small jobs; choose by who must maintain it.

questions.topic: Servers
questions.q: How does SSH key authentication work?
questions.a: You hold a private key; the server has the matching public key in authorized_keys. The server sends a challenge only the private key can answer, so the key itself never crosses the network.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why disable password login?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Sharing one private key among a team.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: One key per person, a passphrase and agent, short-lived certificates or a session manager at scale.

questions.topic: Servers
questions.q: What are the first things you do to harden a new server?
questions.a: Update packages, create a non-root user with sudo, allow key-only SSH and disable root login, enable a firewall that allows only needed ports, turn on automatic security updates, and send logs elsewhere.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: In what order, so you do not lock yourself out?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Enabling the firewall before allowing SSH.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Better still, build it from an image or code so every server is identical.

questions.topic: Servers
questions.q: Pets versus cattle: what does it mean?
questions.a: A pet server is unique, repaired by hand and missed when it dies. Cattle are identical and replaceable: when one is unhealthy you replace it. Immutable images and autoscaling groups make servers cattle.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What must change in the application?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Logging in to fix production servers by hand.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: No local state, configuration from outside, and patching by replacing instances.

questions.topic: Nginx
questions.q: What is a reverse proxy used for?
questions.a: It receives client requests and forwards them to backend servers. It terminates TLS, serves static files, balances load, caches, and hides the backends.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What header tells the backend the client address?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Exposing application servers directly.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Set X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto and make the application trust only the proxy.

questions.topic: Nginx
questions.q: Nginx returns 502. What do you check?
questions.a: The upstream: is the application running and listening on the address in proxy_pass? Read the nginx error log, which states the reason: connection refused, reset, or an invalid response. Then check the application logs.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does 504 differ?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Editing nginx when the application is down.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Keep-alive timeout mismatches between proxy and application cause intermittent 502s.

questions.topic: Nginx
questions.q: How does Nginx choose a location block?
questions.a: Exact matches (=) win. Otherwise the longest matching prefix is remembered; if it has ^~ it wins. Then regular expressions are tried in file order and the first match wins. If none match, the remembered prefix is used.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does order matter only for regex locations?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming blocks are checked top to bottom.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Validate with nginx -t and reload, never restart, to keep connections.

questions.topic: Nginx
questions.q: How do you reload Nginx configuration with zero downtime?
questions.a: nginx -t to validate, then nginx -s reload. The master starts new workers with the new configuration and lets old workers finish their connections.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if the new configuration is invalid?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Restarting, which drops connections.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: A failed reload keeps the old configuration running, which is why you always validate.

questions.topic: TLS
questions.q: What does a TLS certificate prove?
questions.a: That the holder of the private key controls the domain name, as checked by a certificate authority the client trusts, and that it is within its validity dates. It enables an encrypted connection to the right party.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is a certificate chain?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Believing a padlock means the site is safe to trust with anything.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Automate issuance and renewal, and alert on days to expiry from outside.

questions.topic: TLS
questions.q: A certificate expired in production. How do you make sure it never happens again?
questions.a: Automate renewal with ACME, alert on failed renewals and on fewer than 14 days remaining measured by an external probe, and keep an inventory of every certificate with an owner.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why was nothing visible on service dashboards?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A calendar reminder as the only control.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Shorter certificate lifetimes force automation and make this failure mode rarer.

questions.topic: DNS
questions.q: What are A, CNAME, MX and TXT records?
questions.a: A maps a name to an IPv4 address. CNAME makes a name an alias of another name. MX names the mail servers. TXT holds text, used for domain verification and email policy.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why can a CNAME not sit at the zone apex?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Putting a CNAME next to other records for the same name.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Providers offer alias records to solve the apex case.

questions.topic: DNS
questions.q: What is TTL and how do you use it in a migration?
questions.a: How long resolvers may cache a record. Lower it a day or two before a change so the switch takes effect quickly, change the record, verify, then raise it again.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why do some users still see the old address?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Changing a record with a 24-hour TTL and expecting instant effect.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Keep the old target serving until the old TTL has fully expired.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: Continuous integration, delivery and deployment: what is the difference?
questions.a: Integration: every change is merged, built and checked automatically. Delivery: every change that passes is ready to release, with a manual approval. Deployment: it is released automatically with no human step.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which does a regulated company usually choose?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using the three terms interchangeably.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The practice matters more than the label: small changes, fast feedback, a pipeline that is the only way to production.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: What makes a good pipeline?
questions.a: Fast feedback, with quick checks first. One build artifact promoted through environments. Reproducible and defined as code. Secure handling of secrets. Clear failures. A safe, practised rollback.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How long should it take?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Rebuilding the artifact separately for each environment.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Measure lead time, failure rate and time to restore; treat a slow or flaky pipeline as a production problem.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: Blue-green versus canary versus rolling?
questions.a: Rolling replaces instances gradually. Blue-green runs the new version beside the old and switches all traffic at once, with instant rollback. Canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version and increases it while watching metrics.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which needs double capacity?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Canary without automated analysis of metrics.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: All three need backwards-compatible database changes, since two versions run together.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: How do you handle database migrations in a pipeline?
questions.a: Apply backwards-compatible (expand) changes before deploying code, and destructive (contract) changes in a later release. Run them as a pipeline step or job with a lock timeout, and never couple a schema change with the code that requires it in one step.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if the migration fails half way?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Migrations that only the new code understands.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Make migrations idempotent and reversible, and keep backfills separate and resumable.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: What are feature flags and what are the risks?
questions.a: Switches that turn code paths on or off at run time, separating deployment from release. They allow gradual rollout and instant disabling. The risks are stale flags, untested combinations and a flag system that becomes a critical dependency.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep flags under control?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Flags that live for years.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Give every flag an owner and expiry; default to safe when the flag service is unreachable.

questions.topic: CI/CD
questions.q: What are the DORA metrics?
questions.a: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. Together they measure how fast and how safely a team delivers; high performers are good at all four.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Can you improve speed without hurting stability?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Optimising one metric alone.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: They are outcomes of small batches, automation and fast recovery, not targets to game.

questions.topic: Jenkins
questions.q: What is a Jenkinsfile?
questions.a: A text file in the repository that defines the pipeline as code: agent, stages, steps, environment and post actions. It is versioned and reviewed with the application.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Declarative versus scripted?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Configuring jobs by clicking in the UI.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Declarative for structure, shared libraries for reuse across repositories.

questions.topic: Jenkins
questions.q: Why should builds not run on the Jenkins controller?
questions.a: The controller schedules work and holds credentials and configuration. Builds run untrusted code and consume resources, so they belong on agents, ideally short-lived ones.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is an ephemeral agent?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A single overloaded controller doing everything.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Kubernetes or cloud agents created per build give isolation and clean environments.

questions.topic: Jenkins
questions.q: How do you use secrets in a Jenkins pipeline?
questions.a: Store them in the credentials store and bind them with withCredentials or the credentials helper, scoped to the steps that need them. Jenkins masks them in the log.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How can a secret still leak?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Echoing variables or passing secrets as build parameters.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Prefer short-lived cloud credentials through OIDC over stored keys.

questions.topic: Jenkins
questions.q: A build is flaky: it fails one time in five. What do you do?
questions.a: Find out whether it is the code, the environment or a dependency: compare failing and passing runs, look for shared state, timing, order dependence and external services. Quarantine the flaky check while it is fixed so the pipeline stays trusted.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is "just retry" dangerous?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Teaching the team to ignore red builds.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Track flakiness as a metric; a pipeline people do not trust stops protecting anything.

questions.topic: GitHub Actions
questions.q: What are workflows, jobs and steps?
questions.a: A workflow is a YAML file triggered by events. It contains jobs, which run on runners, in parallel unless one needs another. A job is a list of steps: shell commands or reusable actions.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What triggers a workflow?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: One enormous job with everything in it.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Split into jobs for parallelism and clear failure, and reuse with composite actions or reusable workflows.

questions.topic: GitHub Actions
questions.q: How should a workflow authenticate to a cloud provider?
questions.a: With OIDC: the job requests a signed token, the cloud trusts GitHub as an identity provider for that repository and branch, and returns short-lived credentials. No long-lived secret is stored.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What goes in the trust condition?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Storing an access key as a repository secret.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Restrict by repository, branch and environment, and use separate roles for plan and apply.

questions.topic: GitHub Actions
questions.q: What are the security risks of third-party actions and pull requests from forks?
questions.a: An action runs with your job's permissions and can change if referenced by a movable tag. Fork pull requests can run attacker code. Pin actions to a commit, set minimal permissions, and never expose secrets to untrusted code.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is pull_request_target dangerous?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Default write permissions and actions pinned to @main.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Treat the pipeline as production: review workflow changes and require approval for first-time contributors.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: What is the difference between an image and a container?
questions.a: An image is a read-only package of files and metadata. A container is a running instance of an image: a process with its own writable layer and isolation. Many containers can run from one image.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What happens to a container's files when it is removed?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Storing data inside the container.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Images are immutable and versioned; state belongs in volumes or external services.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
questions.a: ENTRYPOINT is the program that always runs; CMD supplies default arguments, or the command if there is no entrypoint. Arguments to docker run replace CMD.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Shell form versus exec form?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Shell form, so signals never reach the application.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Use exec form so the application is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: How does layer caching work and how do you order a Dockerfile for it?
questions.a: Each instruction creates a layer, reused if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged. Once one layer changes, all later ones rebuild. Copy dependency manifests and install first, then copy the source.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does COPY . . early hurt?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Reinstalling every dependency on each code change.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Add a .dockerignore, and use cache mounts for package managers.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: How do you make an image smaller?
questions.a: A slim or distroless base, multi-stage builds so compilers and build tools stay out of the final image, cleaning caches in the same layer, a .dockerignore, and installing only what runs.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does a smaller image matter?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Deleting files in a later layer and expecting the size to drop.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Smaller means faster pulls and fewer vulnerabilities.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: A container exits immediately. How do you debug it?
questions.a: docker ps -a for the exit code, docker logs for the output, docker inspect for the configuration. Run it interactively with a shell as the entrypoint to look inside.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do exit codes 1, 137 and 127 suggest?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Rebuilding repeatedly without reading the logs.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: 137 is a kill, often out of memory; 127 is command not found; 126 is not executable.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: Two containers on one host cannot reach each other by name. Why, and how do you fix it?
questions.a: On a user-defined bridge network, containers resolve each other by name through Docker's built-in DNS. Published ports are for access from the host or outside, not needed between containers.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is the default bridge different?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using localhost to reach another container.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Inside a container localhost is that container; use the service name.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: Why should containers not run as root?
questions.a: Root in a container is the same user id as root on the host. A kernel or runtime flaw, a mounted host path or an extra capability can turn it into host root. A non-root user removes most of those routes.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you set it?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Relying on isolation alone.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: USER with a numeric id in the image, runAsNonRoot in Kubernetes, drop capabilities, read-only filesystem.

questions.topic: Docker
questions.q: What is the difference between a tag and a digest?
questions.a: A tag is a movable name; a digest is a hash of the exact content. The same tag can point to different images over time; a digest cannot.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is :latest a problem in production?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Deploying :latest and not knowing what is running.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Deploy and sign by digest; use unique tags per build for people.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: What is a Pod, and why not run containers directly?
questions.a: A Pod is one or more containers that share a network address and volumes and are scheduled together. It is the unit Kubernetes schedules, heals and scales, and lets a helper container sit beside the main one.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When do you put two containers in one Pod?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Creating bare Pods instead of Deployments.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Sidecars for proxies or log shippers; anything that scales independently gets its own Pod.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: Deployment, StatefulSet and DaemonSet: when do you use each?
questions.a: Deployment for stateless, interchangeable replicas. StatefulSet when each replica needs a stable name and its own storage, such as a database. DaemonSet to run one Pod on every node, such as a log agent.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does a Job do?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Running a database as a Deployment with one shared volume.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Prefer managed databases; StatefulSets need careful thought about ordering and data.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: What are the Service types?
questions.a: ClusterIP gives an internal virtual address. NodePort opens a port on every node. LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer. ExternalName is a DNS alias. Headless (clusterIP: None) returns Pod addresses directly.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does a Service find its Pods?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Exposing every service with a LoadBalancer.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Use ClusterIP inside and one Ingress or Gateway at the edge.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: Liveness, readiness and startup probes?
questions.a: Readiness decides whether the Pod receives traffic. Liveness decides whether the container is restarted. Startup holds the other two off until a slow application has started.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What should a liveness probe never check?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A liveness probe that checks the database, restarting every Pod when the database blips.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Liveness: is the process stuck. Readiness: can it serve now, including key dependencies.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: Requests versus limits?
questions.a: Requests are what the scheduler reserves and guarantees. Limits are the ceiling: exceeding the memory limit gets the container killed; exceeding the CPU limit throttles it. Together they set the quality-of-service class.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Should you set a CPU limit?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: No requests, so the scheduler overpacks nodes.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Always set requests and a memory limit; CPU limits are debated because of throttling.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: A Pod is Pending. What are the causes?
questions.a: No node has enough unreserved CPU or memory, a node selector, affinity or taint excludes all nodes, a volume cannot be bound, or a quota is exceeded. kubectl describe pod shows the scheduler's reason.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does it differ from ContainerCreating?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Looking at logs, which do not exist yet.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Events first; then node capacity, taints and the autoscaler.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: ConfigMap versus Secret?
questions.a: Both inject configuration as environment variables or files. Secrets are meant for sensitive values: base64-encoded, access-controlled separately, and optionally encrypted at rest. Neither is encrypted by default.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Does a Pod see a changed ConfigMap?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating base64 as encryption.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Mounted files update eventually; environment variables need a restart. Keep real secrets in an external store.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: How does a rolling update work, and what do maxSurge and maxUnavailable do?
questions.a: The Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and scales it up while scaling the old one down. maxSurge is how many extra Pods may exist; maxUnavailable is how many may be missing. Readiness gates each step.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you roll back?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: maxUnavailable at its default with few replicas, dropping capacity during deploys.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: maxUnavailable 0 with a good readiness probe means a bad version never takes traffic.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decide?
questions.a: It compares a metric, usually CPU as a percentage of requests, with a target and sets replicas to current replicas times current over target, within minimum and maximum, with stabilisation to avoid flapping.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why does HPA need resource requests?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Autoscaling a service whose bottleneck is the database.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Scale on what reflects load, such as requests per second or queue length, and check downstream limits.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: What happens when a node fails?
questions.a: The node stops reporting, is marked NotReady, and after a timeout its Pods are evicted and recreated on other nodes by their controllers, if capacity exists. Pods with local data lose it.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How long does that take by default?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming failover is instant.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Spread replicas across nodes and zones, keep spare capacity, and use PodDisruptionBudgets.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: What is a PodDisruptionBudget?
questions.a: A rule that limits how many Pods of an application may be down at once during voluntary disruptions such as node drains and upgrades.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Does it protect against a node crash?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A budget so strict that nodes can never be drained.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: It covers voluntary disruption only; pair it with enough replicas and spread constraints.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: How does Kubernetes RBAC work?
questions.a: Roles list allowed verbs on resources. RoleBindings grant a Role to users, groups or service accounts in a namespace; ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding do the same cluster-wide. Everything is deny by default and there are no deny rules.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you check what an identity can do?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Binding cluster-admin to make an error go away.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: kubectl auth can-i --as; one service account per workload with the least it needs.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: Walk through what happens when you run kubectl apply for a Deployment.
questions.a: kubectl sends it to the API server, which authenticates, authorises, runs admission and stores it in etcd. The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pods. The scheduler assigns nodes. Each kubelet pulls images and starts containers through the runtime, the CNI gives addresses, probes pass and endpoints are updated.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where would a wrong image name show up?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Describing Kubernetes as one program that "runs the container".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Every component watches the API and reconciles; nothing calls anything else directly.

questions.topic: Kubernetes
questions.q: How do you upgrade a cluster safely?
questions.a: Read release notes for removed APIs, upgrade a non-production cluster first, then control plane one minor version, then add-ons, then nodes by replacing them gradually with disruption budgets in place.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Can you skip minor versions?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Upgrading production first, or several versions at once.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Keep version skew within supported limits and scan manifests for deprecated APIs beforehand.

questions.topic: Helm
questions.q: How do you manage different values for different environments?
questions.a: A base values file with defaults and one file per environment passed with -f, with later files overriding earlier ones and --set last. The chart stays identical across environments.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where do secrets go?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A different chart per environment.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Keep environment files small; a large difference between them is a warning sign.

questions.topic: Helm
questions.q: A helm upgrade failed half way. What state are you in and what do you do?
questions.a: The release is marked failed and some resources may be updated. helm history shows it; helm rollback returns to the last good revision. --atomic does that automatically on failure.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does --wait do?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Running upgrade again and again on a failed release.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Use --atomic with a timeout in pipelines, and helm diff to review changes first.

questions.topic: Helm
questions.q: Helm versus Kustomize?
questions.a: Helm templates manifests with values and manages releases with history and rollback; good for packaging and distribution. Kustomize patches plain YAML with overlays and no templating; good for per-environment variation of your own manifests.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Can they be combined?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Arguing one is always better.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Many teams render Helm charts and apply Kustomize patches on top, driven by GitOps.

questions.topic: GitOps
questions.q: What are the benefits of GitOps over a pipeline that runs kubectl apply?
questions.a: Git is the single record of what should run, every change is reviewed and reversible, the cluster pulls so the pipeline needs no cluster credentials, and drift is detected continuously.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is drift?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Manual hotfixes in the cluster that Git knows nothing about.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Rollback is a revert; disaster recovery is pointing a new cluster at the repository.

questions.topic: GitOps
questions.q: How do you promote a release across environments with GitOps?
questions.a: CI builds one image and commits its tag or digest to the staging configuration. After verification, a pull request copies the same reference to production. The image is never rebuilt.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Branches or directories per environment?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Rebuilding per environment, so what was verified is not what ships.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Directories on one branch are easier to compare and automate than long-lived branches.

questions.topic: GitOps
questions.q: How do you handle secrets in a GitOps workflow?
questions.a: Never plain in Git. Commit encrypted secrets (Sealed Secrets, SOPS) or commit references and let an operator fetch values from a secret manager.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which approach rotates more easily?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A private repository treated as a safe place for secrets.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: External references keep one source of truth and rotation outside Git history.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: What is a provider?
questions.a: A plugin that knows how to talk to one API, such as AWS or Kubernetes, and defines its resource types. Terraform core computes the plan; providers make the calls.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why pin provider versions?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Unpinned providers changing behaviour between runs.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Commit the lock file so everyone and CI use identical versions.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: count versus for_each?
questions.a: count creates N copies addressed by index, so removing one from the middle shifts the rest and recreates them. for_each creates one per map or set key with stable addresses.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When is count fine?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A list with count, then deleting the first element.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Use for_each for anything with identity; count for simple on/off.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: What are data sources?
questions.a: Read-only lookups of things Terraform does not manage in this configuration: an existing VPC, the latest image id, the current account. They are read during plan.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Resource versus data source?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Hard-coding ids that differ per account.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Too many lookups couple configurations; prefer outputs and remote state or parameters.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: How do you structure Terraform for a large organisation?
questions.a: Small states split by environment and component to limit blast radius, shared versioned modules, remote state with locking, a pipeline that plans on pull requests and applies after approval, and policy checks.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do components share values?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: One giant state for everything.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Clear ownership per state, and outputs or a parameter store between them.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: How do you handle secrets in Terraform?
questions.a: Do not put them in code or tfvars. Read them from a secret manager or let the cloud generate them, mark variables sensitive, and protect the state, which stores values in plain form.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Does sensitive encrypt the state?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A database password in a committed tfvars file.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Encrypted remote state with tight access; prefer references the workload resolves at run time.

questions.topic: Terraform
questions.q: How do you refactor Terraform without destroying resources?
questions.a: moved blocks to rename or relocate addresses, import blocks to adopt existing resources, removed blocks to stop managing without deleting, and a plan that must show no destroys before applying.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What did people use before moved blocks?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Renaming a resource and applying.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Refactor in separate changes with no functional change, reviewed by the plan.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: What are regions and Availability Zones?
questions.a: A region is a geographic area. Each has several Availability Zones: separate data centres with independent power and networking, close enough for fast links. Spreading across zones survives a data-centre failure.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What survives a region failure?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Everything in one zone.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Multi-zone is the default for production; multi-region is a deliberate, costly choice.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: What is the shared responsibility model?
questions.a: The provider secures the cloud: buildings, hardware, the virtualisation layer. You secure what you put in it: identities, network rules, data, operating systems and applications.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Who patches an RDS database's operating system?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming the provider secures your data and configuration.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The line moves with the service: more managed means less is yours, never none.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: Security group versus IAM policy?
questions.a: A security group controls network connections to a resource. An IAM policy controls who may call which AWS APIs. Reaching a database needs the security group; creating or deleting it needs IAM.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which one applies to reading an S3 object?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Trying to fix a network timeout with IAM.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Timeout suggests network; AccessDenied suggests IAM.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: How do you choose between EC2, ECS, EKS and Lambda?
questions.a: EC2 when you need the machine. ECS for containers with little operational overhead. EKS when you want Kubernetes and its ecosystem. Lambda for event-driven, short, spiky work.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What are Lambda's limits?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Choosing Kubernetes for one small service.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Decide by team skills and operational cost as much as by features.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: How do you make an S3 bucket secure?
questions.a: Block public access, encrypt, grant least-privilege access to named roles, enable versioning, log access, and serve public content through a CDN, not the bucket.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you give temporary access to one object?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Public buckets for convenience.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Presigned URLs or CloudFront with origin access control; object lock for backups.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: How does an Application Load Balancer decide a target is healthy?
questions.a: It calls a path on each target at an interval. Several consecutive successes mark it healthy, several failures unhealthy, and unhealthy targets get no traffic.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What makes a bad health endpoint?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A health check that tests every dependency.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Too shallow hides failures; too deep removes every target when one dependency blips.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: How do you connect two VPCs, or a VPC to an office?
questions.a: VPC peering for two networks, Transit Gateway for many, PrivateLink to expose one service. For an office: site-to-site VPN or a dedicated Direct Connect line.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why must address ranges not overlap?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Overlapping ranges that make connection impossible later.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Plan address space centrally from the start.

questions.topic: AWS
questions.q: How would you organise many AWS accounts?
questions.a: One organisation with accounts per environment and team, grouped in units with guardrail policies, single sign-on, central logging and security accounts, and account creation automated.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why accounts instead of one account with tags?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Production and development in one account.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The account is the strongest isolation boundary for access, blast radius and cost.

questions.topic: Databases
questions.q: What is an index and what does it cost?
questions.a: A sorted structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the table. It speeds reads on the indexed columns and costs storage and slower writes, since every insert and update maintains it.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When is an index not used?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Indexing every column.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Index for the queries you run; check with EXPLAIN and remove unused ones.

questions.topic: Databases
questions.q: What do the letters in ACID mean?
questions.a: Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: rules always hold. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming every database gives all four at full strength by default.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Isolation has levels; read committed allows anomalies that serialisable prevents, at a cost.

questions.topic: Databases
questions.q: SQL versus NoSQL: how do you choose?
questions.a: Relational for structured data with relationships, transactions and flexible queries. Key-value, document or wide-column stores when the access pattern is simple and known, the scale is very large, or the schema varies.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you give up with NoSQL?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Choosing by fashion.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Start relational unless you can state why it will not work.

questions.topic: Databases
questions.q: How do you scale a relational database?
questions.a: First optimise queries and indexes. Then a bigger instance, caching, and read replicas for reads. Then a connection pooler. Finally partitioning or sharding, which adds real complexity.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What breaks with sharding?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Sharding before fixing slow queries.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Cross-shard joins and transactions go away; pick the shard key with great care.

questions.topic: Databases
questions.q: What is a deadlock and how is it handled?
questions.a: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. The database detects it and aborts one, which must be retried.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you reduce them?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Not retrying aborted transactions.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Take locks in a consistent order and keep transactions short.

questions.topic: Redis
questions.q: What can go wrong with Redis used as a cache?
questions.a: A cold or lost cache sends all load to the database, hot keys expire and stampede, memory fills, stale data is served after an update, and one slow command blocks everyone.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you prevent a stampede?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: No TTL and no eviction policy.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: TTL with jitter, single-flight rebuilds, and a database that survives a cold cache.

questions.topic: Redis
questions.q: RDB versus AOF persistence?
questions.a: RDB writes point-in-time snapshots: compact, fast to load, loses changes since the last one. AOF logs every write: more durable, larger, slower to replay. They can be combined.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Does a cache need persistence?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming Redis never loses data.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: For a cache it mainly avoids a cold start; for a store, replication plus AOF.

questions.topic: Redis
questions.q: How would you implement rate limiting with Redis?
questions.a: A counter per client and time window with INCR and an expiry, or a sliding window or token bucket, done atomically in a script.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why must it be atomic?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Read then write in two calls, which races.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Decide what happens when Redis is down: fail open or closed.

questions.topic: Kafka
questions.q: How does Kafka keep messages in order?
questions.a: Order is guaranteed within a partition only. Messages with the same key go to the same partition, so they stay in order relative to each other.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What breaks ordering?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Expecting order across a whole topic.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Retries without idempotence and changing the partition count both disturb it.

questions.topic: Kafka
questions.q: What do acks, replication factor and min.insync.replicas do together?
questions.a: With replication factor 3, acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, a write is acknowledged only when at least two replicas have it, so one broker can fail without losing data.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What happens when two brokers are down?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: acks=1 for data that matters.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Writes are refused, which is correct: unavailable beats silently lost.

questions.topic: Kafka
questions.q: Queue versus log: when would you choose Kafka over RabbitMQ or SQS?
questions.a: Kafka when several consumers need the same events, replay is needed, or throughput is very high. A queue when each message is a job done once, with per-message retry and routing.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is easier with a queue?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Kafka for a simple background job.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Operational cost counts: a managed queue is far less to run.

questions.topic: Kafka
questions.q: What is the outbox pattern?
questions.a: Write the business change and an event row in one database transaction; a separate process publishes the rows to the broker. This avoids updating the database and failing to publish, or the reverse.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What delivery guarantee does it give?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Writing to the database and the broker in sequence and hoping.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: At-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

questions.topic: Monitoring
questions.q: Monitoring versus observability?
questions.a: Monitoring checks known conditions: is it up, is the error rate high. Observability is being able to ask new questions of the system from its telemetry, to explain behaviour you did not predict.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What are the three signals?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Buying a tool and calling it observability.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Metrics, logs and traces, linked by shared identifiers.

questions.topic: Monitoring
questions.q: What are the four golden signals?
questions.a: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation. For a request-driven service they cover what users feel and how close the system is to its limit.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do they relate to RED and USE?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Dashboards full of CPU graphs and no user signal.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: RED is the first three for services; USE is for resources.

questions.topic: Monitoring
questions.q: Black-box versus white-box monitoring?
questions.a: Black-box tests the system from outside like a user: synthetic probes. White-box uses internal metrics and logs. You need both.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which caught the expired certificate?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Only internal metrics.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Outside probes find what internal metrics cannot see: DNS, TLS, the network path.

questions.topic: Monitoring
questions.q: How long should you keep metrics, logs and traces?
questions.a: By usefulness and cost: metrics at full resolution for weeks and downsampled for a year or more, logs for days to weeks with audit logs longer, traces for days with sampling.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is downsampling?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Keeping everything forever at full detail.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Retention is a cost decision reviewed like any other.

questions.topic: Monitoring
questions.q: What is a synthetic check and a dead man's switch?
questions.a: A synthetic check performs a user action on a schedule from outside. A dead man's switch is an alert that fires when an expected signal stops, catching a monitoring system that has itself failed.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where should the switch run?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Monitoring that lives only inside what it monitors.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Outside the monitored system, with its own path to the pager.

questions.topic: Security
questions.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
questions.a: Every identity gets only the permissions it needs for its task, for only as long as it needs them.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you find out what is needed?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Admin access "to save time".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Start from nothing, measure use, remove the rest; time-bound elevation for people.

questions.topic: Security
questions.q: Authentication versus authorisation?
questions.a: Authentication proves who you are. Authorisation decides what you may do. A 401 is a failure of the first, a 403 of the second.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where do tokens fit?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Checking identity and never checking permission.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Check authorisation on every request and every object, not only at login.

questions.topic: Security
questions.q: Encryption in transit and at rest?
questions.a: In transit protects data moving over networks, with TLS. At rest protects stored data on disks and in backups, with keys held in a key management service.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does encryption at rest not protect against?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Believing disk encryption protects against a compromised application.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: An application with access reads decrypted data; access control still decides.

questions.topic: Security
questions.q: What is defence in depth?
questions.a: Several independent layers of control, so one failure does not mean compromise: network segmentation, identity, hardening, scanning, monitoring, backups.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Give an example from Kubernetes.

points.title: Common mistakes
items: One strong perimeter and trust inside.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Assume each layer fails sometimes; a hardened pod, a network policy and no mounted token each stop an attacker.

questions.topic: Security
questions.q: What is zero trust?
questions.a: No request is trusted because of where it comes from. Every call is authenticated, authorised and encrypted, between internal services too.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What replaces the trusted network?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A VPN and a flat internal network.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Workload identity, mutual TLS and per-request policy.

questions.topic: SRE
questions.q: What is the difference between SRE and DevOps?
questions.a: DevOps is a culture of shared ownership between building and running. SRE is one way to do it: software engineers running production with SLOs, error budgets, toil limits and blameless reviews.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Does a small company need an SRE team?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Renaming the operations team.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The practices matter more than the team name.

questions.topic: SRE
questions.q: A service depends on five others, each 99.9% available. What availability can it expect?
questions.a: If all five are hard dependencies in series, about 99.5%: the availabilities multiply. To do better, make dependencies optional with caches, fallbacks and queues.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do timeouts and retries change this?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Promising more than your dependencies deliver.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Classify each dependency as critical or degradable in the design.

questions.topic: SRE
questions.q: What is graceful degradation?
questions.a: When part of the system fails, the rest keeps working with reduced function instead of failing entirely: serve cached data, hide a feature, queue the work.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Give an example for checkout.

points.title: Common mistakes
items: One failing dependency taking down a page.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Decide in advance which features are sacrificed first, and exercise it.

questions.topic: SRE
questions.q: What is chaos engineering?
questions.a: Deliberately injecting failure, in a controlled way, to check that the system and the people respond as designed: kill a pod, drop a zone, slow a dependency.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you start safely?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Random destruction in production with no hypothesis.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: State a hypothesis, limit the blast radius, have a stop button, start in staging.

questions.topic: Incidents
questions.q: How do you decide whether to roll back or fix forward?
questions.a: Roll back when a recent change is the likely cause and it is reversible: it is fast and known. Fix forward when rollback is impossible, such as after a data migration, or the fix is trivial and certain.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What makes rollback impossible?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Writing a fix under pressure while users wait.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Design changes to be reversible so rollback is always an option.

questions.topic: Incidents
questions.q: How do you run a good on-call handover?
questions.a: A written note of open incidents, ongoing risks, recent changes, silenced alerts and anything unusual, with a short conversation.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What goes wrong without one?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Knowledge that lives in one person's head.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Review the previous shift's pages together and assign owners for repeats.

questions.topic: Incidents
questions.q: What is a cascading failure?
questions.a: One component's failure overloads others, which fail in turn: a slow dependency fills thread pools, retries multiply load, health checks remove struggling instances and overload the rest.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you stop one?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Unlimited retries with no back-off.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Timeouts, retry budgets with back-off and jitter, circuit breakers, load shedding and bulkheads.

questions.topic: Performance
questions.q: Latency versus throughput?
questions.a: Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many are completed per unit of time. They trade off near capacity: pushing throughput to the limit sends latency up.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which percentile do you report?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Quoting the average.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Percentiles for latency, and the load at which they were measured.

questions.topic: Performance
questions.q: What is back-pressure?
questions.a: A way for an overloaded component to tell its callers to slow down, instead of accepting work it cannot finish: bounded queues, rejecting with 429 or 503, limited concurrency.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What happens without it?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Unbounded queues that hide overload until memory runs out.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Reject early and cheaply; a fast failure beats a slow timeout.

questions.topic: Performance
questions.q: Why are timeouts and retries dangerous together?
questions.a: A slow service causes timeouts; clients retry; the retries add load to a service that is already struggling, making it slower. This retry storm can keep a system down.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is jitter?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Three immediate retries at every layer, multiplying load 27 times.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Retry once, at one layer, with exponential back-off, jitter and a retry budget.

questions.topic: Performance
questions.q: How would you prepare a system for a 10x traffic event?
questions.a: Forecast, load test at and beyond it, find and raise the first bottlenecks, check autoscaling limits, quotas and database connections, pre-scale, prepare feature flags to shed load, freeze risky changes, and staff an incident room.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you switch off first?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Relying on autoscaling to react in time.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Rehearse it, and put a queue in front of the scarcest resource.

questions.topic: FinOps
questions.q: What are the main drivers of a cloud bill?
questions.a: Compute, storage, data transfer, and managed services such as databases. Idle and oversized resources and non-production running all hours are the usual waste.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which is most often overlooked?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Looking only at instance prices.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Data transfer and NAT, logging volume, and orphaned storage.

questions.topic: FinOps
questions.q: On-demand, reserved or savings plans, and spot?
questions.a: On demand: full price, no commitment. Commitments: a discount for one or three years, for the steady base. Spot: a large discount on spare capacity that can be taken back, for interruptible work.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What share should be committed?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Committing to 100% of today's usage.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Cover the stable baseline after right-sizing, leave the rest flexible.

questions.topic: FinOps
questions.q: How do you allocate cost in a shared Kubernetes cluster?
questions.a: By namespace and labels: each team's share of CPU and memory requests, plus its storage and load balancers, with shared overhead split by a stated rule.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why requests and not usage?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: One undivided cluster bill.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Requests reserve capacity; show both so teams see what they waste.

questions.topic: Platform
questions.q: What is an internal developer platform?
questions.a: A set of self-service tools and templates, run as a product, that lets teams create, deploy and operate services without assembling the infrastructure themselves.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is in a minimum version?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A portal with nothing behind it.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: One paved path for the most common service type, end to end.

questions.topic: Platform
questions.q: How do you decide what to standardise?
questions.a: Standardise what every service needs and nobody wants to differ on: build, deploy, security baseline, observability. Leave product choices to teams.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle exceptions?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Standardising everything, or nothing.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Offer a default with an escape hatch, and the team that leaves the path owns the result.

questions.topic: Platform
questions.q: How do you migrate hundreds of services to a new platform?
questions.a: Prove it with a few willing teams, make migration mostly automatic, publish progress, support both paths for a limited time, and set a date for the old one once most have moved.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What stalls such migrations?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: A big-bang cut-over date.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The long tail: budget for helping the last 20%, which takes most of the effort.

questions.topic: System Design
questions.q: What does it mean for a service to be stateless, and why does it matter?
questions.a: It keeps no data between requests that another instance could not handle; state lives in a database or cache. Any instance can serve any request, so it scales and heals easily.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where do sessions go?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Sessions in local memory, breaking on every deploy.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Push state to the edges of the design and keep the middle disposable.

questions.topic: System Design
questions.q: What is idempotency and where do you need it?
questions.a: An operation that has the same effect whether performed once or many times. Needed wherever retries happen: payments, message consumers, API writes over unreliable networks.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you implement it?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Retrying a non-idempotent charge.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: An idempotency key stored with the result, checked before doing the work.

questions.topic: System Design
questions.q: Explain the CAP theorem in practical terms.
questions.a: When a network partition separates nodes, a system must choose: refuse some requests to stay consistent, or answer with possibly stale data to stay available. Without a partition you can have both.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which does a payment system choose?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Reciting "pick two of three".

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The choice is per operation: browse can be available, checkout must be consistent.

questions.topic: System Design
questions.q: What is a circuit breaker?
questions.a: A wrapper around a remote call that stops calling a failing dependency for a while and fails fast, then lets a few test calls through to see whether it has recovered.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you return while it is open?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Waiting the full timeout on every call to a dead service.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Pair it with a fallback and with metrics on its state.

questions.topic: System Design
questions.q: Design the deployment and operations for a new service that takes payments.
questions.a: Stateless service on Kubernetes across three zones, a managed database with a synchronous standby and point-in-time recovery, idempotent APIs, secrets from a manager, a scanned and signed image deployed by GitOps with canary, SLOs with burn-rate alerts, runbooks, and a tested recovery plan.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What would you cut for a first version?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Listing tools without tying each to a risk.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: State the RTO, RPO and SLO first; every component should trace back to one of them.
